title: Nōgaku hyakuban zenhen morkuroku 能楽百番 前編 目録 (One Hundred Prints of Noh, first volume, table of contents)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927) - attributed to the artist

title: New Army Recruits (清国の困苦民兵 Shinkoku konku minpei)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin, a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
In front of a Chinese officer holding a sword are a line of new recruits - old senile men. In the background another Chinese officer marches with various disabled recruits. While the war was over when this print was published in August 1895, it was still popular to ridicule the Chinese military.

title: Thunder God and Demons
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description: The second of nine prints from the series Comical Record of Japanese History,  a parody of Hyakki Yakō (Night Parade of One Hundred Demons). The nine prints read as a scroll when placed next to each other and commemorate the Japanese military victory over China in April 1895. <br>The titles for the top and bottom sections of this print are given on the first print of the scroll, with the top section titled "Newly Designed Night Parade of a Hundred Demons” (Shin’an hyakki yagyô 新案百鬼夜行) and the bottom section titled "Newly Designed Night Parade of a Hundred Demons” (Shin’an hyakki yagyô 新案百鬼夜行). <br>"Each yōkai [demon or ghost] is designed to represent and ridicule soldiers from the Chinese army conquered in the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895), in Meiji Japan's first important military victory." - Source: Traditional Monster Imagery in Manga, Anime and Japanese Cinema, Zilia Papp, Brill, 2010, p. 90.

title: Night Cherry Blossoms (夜ざくら Yozakura)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
This print, picturing the cherry trees at night in the Gion District of Kyoto, is the original issue (first edition) published by Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936 as part of the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto. Uchida mounted these prints on a display board with Tokuriki’s authentication seal on the reverse. These square format prints on board were part of a premium set of designs originally packaged in a handmade box.
<br>This same print, with modifications and not mounted on board, was later released as part of the series Twelve Months of Kyoto (Kyō-meisho junikagetsu).

title: Gion Festival (きをん會 Gionkai)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
This print, picturing the festivities on the night before the Gion Festival in Kyoto, is the original issue (first edition) published by Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936 as part of the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto. Uchida mounted these prints on a display board with Tokuriki’s authentication seal on the reverse. These square format prints on board were part of a premium set of designs originally packaged in a handmade box.  For an image of the box, please see Index for the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto. 
<br>This same print, with modifications and not mounted on board, was later released as part of the series Twelve Months of Kyoto (Kyō-meisho junikagetsu).

title: Daimonji (大文字)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
This print, picturing the fires lit to celebrate the end of the O-Bon festival in Kyoto, is the original issue (first edition) published by Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936 as part of the series Thirty Subjects [Views] of Kyoto. Uchida mounted these prints on a display board with Tokuriki’s authentication seal on the reverse. These square format prints on board were part of a premium set of designs originally packaged in a handmade box.
<br>Uchida reissued this print after WWII as part of the series Twelve Months of Kyoto (Kyo-meisho junikagetsu).

title: Niwa 80-K (庭 80-K)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa.  Also see Niwa (Sunshine), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (April) and Niwa (Winter Scenery) in this collection.

title: Night at Ginza (夜の銀座 Yoru no Ginza)
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description:
"This witty hot pink and bright blue Ginza (ぎんざ, the word is written vertically along the image's right edge) is clearly the bustling place of the moga (modern girls) and mobo (modern boys). The fashionable young women promenading down the street turn their heads to observe and be observed. Kawakami creates a sense of immediacy - of the viewer being part of the crowd - with strong color and by cropping the figures in foreground and middle ground, as well as with the objects inserted along both sides of the picture surface. He is best known for including curious old foreign objects in his prints; the masked profile face seen through the rear window of the car on the left looks like a character from the Italian commedia dell'arte. The artist's consciously rough, simplified carving and his flamboyant color convey the modish modernity characteristic of the place and its habitués." - Source: Terrific Tokyo A Panorama in Prints: from the 1860s to the 1930s, Elizabeth de Sabato Swinton, Worcester Art Museum. 1998 p. 76.
<br>See IHL.0033 to view a later reissue of the print. 
<br><br>SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
<br>Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. -  Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

title: Illustration of the Hard Fight at Fenghuangcheng  (鳳凰城ニ将士奮闘之図 Hōōjō ni shōshi funtō no zu)
creator: Ogata Gekkō 尾形月耕 (1859-1920)
description:
Perhaps more accurately titled as "Picture of the Not So Hard Fight at Fenghuangcheng," this print depicts a battle that was planned by the Japanese as a present for the emperor on his birthday, but which did not occur due to a retreat by the Chinese. Historical accuracy was not the aim of most war triptychs.
<br>War correspondent and artist Kubota Beisen (1852-1906) reported: “Our troops were to attack Fenghuangcheng on His Majesty’s birthday, November 3. Scouts reported to General Tatsumi Naobumi that the enemy had set the citadel on fire around 5:00 PM, October 29, and fled. The enemy officers had gone to Mukden, whereas the men escaped to the coast. The following day, the Japanese entered the fort without fighting and found two hundred civilian homes burned down. Two mountain cannons, three mortars, and countless rifles and tents were left.” Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, 1894-95, Shumpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983
<br>Other impressions of this print carry the name of another publisher 松野米治郎 (Matsuno Yunejirō) in the left margin rather than this impression's "pot-shaped" publisher seal reading 関口政治郎 (Sekiguchi Masajirō) found in the lower corner of the right sheet.

title: Kichiemon in the role of Yura Hyōgo (吉右衛門 由良兵庫)
creator: Natori Shunsen 名取春仙 (1886-1960)

title: Ennosuke in the role of the Exiled King and Tōzō in the role of the Warrior Priest Kōku (猿之助 流離王 東蔵 好苦梵士)
creator: Ishii Hakutei 石井柏亭 (1882-1958)
description:
The actors Ichikawa Ennosuke II in the role of the exiled king and Nakamura Tōzō II as the warrior priest Kōku in the play Washimo Shiranai わしも知らない staged at tje Gekijō, Tokyo on June 28, 1915. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.<br><br>SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)<br>
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

title: Paper Hat, Mask, Collar, Military Decorations (紙帽子・仮面・襟・勲章)
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description: Like most of Kawakami's prints, this still life of a paper hat, a mask, carnations, a starched color and two military medals is untitled.  Whether this work is just an artistic exercise or poking fun at something or someone is unknown. The print is embossed and hand colored by the artist in the unique style that he started using in the 1930s. Extensive embossing (karazuri 空摺) is used throughout the design and silver metallic highlights are seen on the medals.<br> Another version of this print uses a different color scheme and has the artist's seal in the lower right of the image, which is not present on this print.

title: Atago Kūya 愛宕空也
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Illustration of the Emperor's March from the East Castle (東城御道行之図 Tōjōon (go) michiyuki no zu or Azuma jō go michiyuki no zu)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: It is April 1900 and two carriages with the Imperial Seal are departing the Imperial Palace after crossing Nijubashi, seen in the background. The occupants of the first carriage are unseen, but are assumed to be Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken. They are followed by Crown Prince Yoshito and his bride-to-be Kujō Sadako, daughter of the patriarch of one of the "five regent families" (gosekke). The procession is likely one of the pre-marriage rituals set down in one of a number of laws and regulations relating to the Imperial Household that were to govern the upcoming wedding of the Crown Prince on May 10, 1900.  It may well be that the Emperor and his entourage are heading for the Imperial Palace in Kyoto.

title: Illustration of the April Negotiations (清和談判之図 Seiwa danpan no zu)
creator: Yūsai Toshiaki 幽斎年章 (1864-1921)
description:
The title of the print makes reference to the "April negotiations," meaning the negotiations between Japan and China to conclude the Treaty of Shimonoseki ending the Sino-Japanese War.
<br>"With the defeat of the Chinese fleet, the war was over.  Li Hung-chang, the Viceroy of Tientsin, was forced to negotiate with Japanese Prime Minister Ito Hirobumi and sign the Treaty of Shimonoseki (17 April 1895). This brought Japan not only Taiwan, the Pescadores, and a foothold in South Manchuria, but also a handsome indemnity (two hundred million taels), the recognition of Korea’s independence, and most importantly, the same privileges that the Western powers were enjoying in China.  Korea became a Japanese protectorate in 1905 and was annexed in 1910." - Source: "Images of the Sino-Japanese War – A Book Review," Robert Vergez, Ukiyo-e Art:  A Journal of the Japan Ukiyo-e Society, No. Vol. 79, 1983, p. ii.

title: Kichiemon in the role of Takechi Mitsuhide (吉右衛門 光秀)
creator: Terasawa Kōtarō 寺澤孝太郎 (active c. 1915)

title: Fukusuke in the role of Yohei (福助 與兵衛)
creator: Ogawa Hyōe (Heibei) 小川兵衛 (active c. 1915)

title: Fukusuke in the role of Yohei (福助 與兵衛)
creator: Ogawa Hyōe (Heibei) 小川兵衛 (active c. 1915)

title: Beast (けもの)
creator: Yoshida Hodaka 吉田穂高 (1926-1995)
description: This print was done in the middle of the artist's Primitive Energy phase when he was creating abstractions of Pre-Columbian forms.

title: Ichikawa Sanshō V as a Sweetmeat Peddler in the play Uirō (五世市川三升 外郎売)
creator: Natori Shunsen 名取春仙 (1886-1960)
description:
One of thirty-six prints making up the Watanabe-published series Collection of Creative Print Portraits by Shunsen (1925-1929). This print is the series installment no. 15. The character 壽 kotobuki (long life) is written on the actor's fan and refers to the medicine he is peddling.<br>"Ichikawa Sanshō X* appears full-figure, early in his career, in a pose established long before for the role of the fast-talking peddler.  Bearing on his back a pack full of moxa – Japanese mogusa, a medicine to be burned, like incense, on the skin of the patient – Sanshō faces the audience and holds out a sample as he delivers a long sales pitch filled with puns, jokes, and other remarks."- source: Dramatic Impressions: Japanese Theatre Prints from the Gilbert Luber Collection, Chance, Frank L. & Davis, Julie Nelson, University of Pennsylvania Press, 200, p. 41.
<br>*While the actor pictured is identified as Ichikawa Sanshō X, the Kabuki21 website (see http://www.kabuki21.com/sansho5.php [accessed 8-17-23] the Ichikawa Sanshō lineage ended with Ichikawa Sanshō V, who held the name from November 1917 until his death in February 1956.

title: Ichikawa Danshirō as Sanbasō Dancer (市川段四郎 三番叟 Ichikawa Danshirō san daimei)
creator: Natori Shunsen 名取春仙 (1886-1960)
description: Picturing the actor Ichikawa Danshirō III as a Sanbasō dancer. This print is one of 24 in the series New Portraits of Actors on the Stage, the last series Shunsen designed for the publisher Watanabe and the least critically acclaimed. Kendall Brown writes "The intense emotions and melodramatic poses found in many of these prints reveal the self-parody of Shunsen's late work, the stagnation of postwar kabuki, or perhaps both."

title: Ōeyama 大江山 (Demon of Ōeyama)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Kinuta 砧 (The Fulling Block)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Naruko in Spring (御殿場初冬 Haru no Naruko)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description: Mica highlights and embossing add interest to this undated abstract composition by Hagiwara, likely created very late in his career.

title: Azuma Bridge (あずまばし Azumabashi)
creator: Utagawa Kunitoshi 歌川国利 (1847-1899)
description:
Azumabashi 吾妻橋, built in 1887, was the first metal bridge spanning the Sumida River.  It was officially dedicated and opened to the public on December 9, 1887. It served the bustling pleasure quarter of Asakusa on one side and a beer factory on the other. Kunitoshi and other artists of the period who depicted the bridge drew its vertical posts and diagonal eyebars in Western perspective, populating the walkway with ladies in bustles and the deck with top-hatted gentlemen in carriages. 
<br>For other prints depicting Azumabashi see IHL.0446, IHL.2151 and IHL.2435.

title: Mekari 和布刈 (The Seaweed Gatherer)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: View of Yomiuri Shimbun, Kyobashi Industrial Site (京橋風景読売新聞社・勧業場 Kyobashi fukei Yomiuri shinbunsha, kangyō-jō)
creator: Takeuchi Keishū 武内桂舟 (1861-1942)
description: Scene showing the offices of Tokyo's first newspaper, the Yomiuri shimbun 読売新聞社 on Kyobashi street in the Ginza district. The founder and first president of the Yomiuri shimbun, Takashi Koyasu, was a confident of the members of the literary coterie Kenyūsha (Friends of the Inkstone) which this print's designer Takeuchi Keishū (1861-1942) belonged to.

title: Bear Hunting for Gall in Kaga Province (加州熊并ニ胆ヲ取ル図 Kashū-gama narabi ni kimo o toru zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, the Asian black bear (note the white chest mark) is being hunted for his gall. Kaga Province (加賀国, Kaga no kuni) was an old province in the area that is today the southern part of Ishikawa Prefecture. Ruled by the Maeda clan, the capital of Kaga was Kanazawa. Kaga bordered on Echizen, Etchū, Hida, and Noto Provinces. It was part of Hokurikudō Circuit.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.1496.

<br>The artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" or, as in the case of this print, practiced in the same manner in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

title: Speculators Talking Amiably (山師の笑談 Yamashi no shōdan)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of twelve issued as part of the second set of prints from the series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the enemy. The text on the pints was provided by the writer  Nishimori Takeki (1861-1923), alias Koppi  Dōjin.<br>
Four speculators sit around a map of the Taiwanese archipelago (including the Pescadores) figuring out the riches they'd make developing Japan's newest colony.

title: Hubbub in the Dragon King's Palace (竜宮の騒ぎ Ryūgū no sawagi)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
Kiyochika gives us a scene in the Dragon King’s palace, where a giant anchor has dropped to the seabed floor frightening him and his daughter while fish flee. The anchor is from one of the Chinese battleships sunk by the Japanese navy in the battle of the Yellow Sea.

title: A Bunraku Puppet Head
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
This collection contains two different printings of this depiction of the head of a bunraku puppet, IHL.0275 and IHL.0314. These two versions may both be artist's proofs. This print IHL.0275 carries the artist's signature written in pencil "T. Tokuriki 1962." in the lower left corner within the image. Print IHL.0314 bears the artist's signature in the lower right corner within the image.
<br>This print was released as a numbered edition of 100 prints.

title: Bird on Bamboo Branch
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: This sumi-e by Tokuriki is one of several I've seen with traditional kachō-ga motifs. Sumi-e was introduced into Japan in the 14th century by Zen Buddhist monks visiting from China.  It uses only brush-applied black ink on paper.

title: Untitled Illustration for a novel or magazine
creator: Unidentified (possibly Biho Hirose, act. 1904/1910)
description: A priest, perhaps, bearing the characters 莱庵 on his bald head appears to have fallen asleep at his writing table. In his dream he sees a man carrying another man, perhaps injured, while a lightning storm rages. Likely an illustration (kuchi-e) for a novel or story. An unread signature appears in the bottom left corner of the image along with what is likely the artist's seal which has been obliterated by bleeding of its red ink.

title: Shunzei Tadanori 俊成忠度 (Shunzei and Tadanori)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 169) - Okabe no Rokuyata, who has killed Tadanori in battle, brings Shunzei a poem which he found in Tadanori's quiver. Tadanori's ghost then appears and after complaining that Shunzei has included a poem of his in an anthology as an anonymous one, and talking of poetry in general, he speaks of the torments a warrior suffers after death.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Wait. Again (再び待つ)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: This print is a different state than the print pictured in the artist's catalog raisonné and it may well be a different print entirely, given the differences between the images.

title: Comedy, Fueteiru (喜劇フェーテール Kigeki fueteiru)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)
description: Picturing a "shinpageki" or a New School drama in the comedy style of customs and manners in contemporary (Meiji) Japan. The database of the the National Theatre of Japan identifies the actor on the right swinging the battledore and playing the role of Fukutoku Yumesuke (the wealthy merchant Yumesuke) as Yamaguchi Sadao 山口定雄 (1861-1907), one of the first generation of shinpa actors who was trained as a kabuki onnagata. The actor in the center is identified as Shirakawa Koichi 白川広一 playing the role of nyōbō Ofuku (Ofuku, the wife).  Art historian Lynn Katsumoto comments that there is some wordplay going on here as "Fukutoku" also means fortune, or happiness, making "this duo a particularly felicitous couple. No doubt, the play plays with their happy naming and twists things up humorously."

title: Zensetsū Temple, Sanshū (讃州 善通寺 Sanshū Zensetsū-ji)
creator: Kawase Hasui 川瀬巴水 (1883-1957)
description:
"The largest temple complex on the island of Shikoku, with its five-story pagoda first built in 813, the site attracts pilgrims to worship at the birthplace of Kūkai (弘法大師, 774-835), founder of Shingon esoteric Buddhism. While the towering structure is veiled in rainy mist, it stands as an unchanging icon to the spiritual foundations of Japan - there is no sign of encroaching modernity." -  Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
<br>Like his 19th century predecessor Hiroshige, Hasui was well known for his use of atmospheric effects such as rain and mist.
<br>From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

title: Illustration of His Majesty the Commander-in-Chief Return in Triumph to the Palace  (大元帥陛下　凱旋皇居御入城之図 Daigensui-heika gaisen kōkyo go-nyūjō no zu)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944) - attributed to the artist
description: While the print is titled 大元帥陛下 凱旋皇居御入城之図, which translates to "Illustration of His Majesty the Commander-in-Chief's Triumphal Return to the Palace," the print clearly depicts a visit by Emperor Meiji and the royal family to the reconstructed (the second) Diet Building, likely in 1891. The emperor is seen stepping out of the Phoenix carriage in front of the Diet Building to be greeted by dignitaries, the crown prince (center sheet), and the Empress Shōken (right sheet). While this print does not carry either an artist's signature or seal, or a publisher's seal, the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston listing for this print states "possibly by Nobukazu."  One wonders if the publisher, realizing the title and scene portrayed didn't match, decided not to apply either his seal or the artist's signature to this print.

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō, Nakamura Sōjūrō and Iwai Hanshirō in the play Gempei Nunobiki no Taki (市川団十郎、中村宗十郎、岩井半四郎・ 源平布引滝)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: Gempei Nunobiki no Taki (The Genji and Heike at Nunobiki Waterfall), a five act play, was originally written for the puppet theater in 1749. It was adapted for kabuki in September 1757.<br> In the play, a woman is believed to have given birth to a full-grown human arm, rather than a baby. And later, when this same arm is rejoined to the woman's body from which it came, the dead woman comes back to life for a while. - source: Kabuki 21 website http://www.kabuki21.com/sanemori.php (Summary written by Watanabe Hisao and edited by Jeff Blair) [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Report of the Japanese Conquest of Port Arthur Startles Li Hung-chang (我軍旅順口占領之報ヲ聞テ李鴻章驚嘆之図 Waga gun Ryojunkō senryō no shirase o kiite Ri Kōshō kyōtan no zu)
creator: Bairin 梅林 (active 1894)
description: Within a month after landing at Chinchou, the Japanese Second Army conquered the “unconquerable” Port Arthur. The fortress fell on November 21, 1894, as Japan continued its Liaotung Peninsula operation. This print is an imaginary portrayal of the Chinese leader Li Hung-chang as he hears of the fall of his most important military base in Manchuria.

title: Daimotsu, Amagasaki (尼崎大物 Amagasaki Daimotsu)
creator: Kawase Hasui 川瀬巴水 (1883-1957)
description:
"In this moonlit nocturne, Hasui focuses on the reflected light, the movement of water, the surface of the masonry and the wafting smoke from a flame that softly illuminates a workman’s face. The reality of smokestacks and factories appear here as an obscured background. In the decades to come, Amagasaki’s growth as an industrial port demolished locations like this, turning this harbor view into a relic of a bygone era." -  Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
<br>Narazaki, Hasui's biographer, writes: "This is the Daimotsu bay made famous in the Heike monogatari (The Tale of Heike) of the early Kamakura period (1185-1333). These days there are few opportunities for a traveler to experience this area as it once was since it is now part of the harbor district in the Hanshin industrial belt. For this reason Hasui's depiction is interesting." Amagasaki is situated in Hyogo prefecture.
<br>From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

title: Ritsuko in the role of Okon (律子 お紺)
creator: Natori Shunsen 名取春仙 (1886-1960)
description:
The actress Mori Ritsuko in the role of the beautiful courtesan Okon in the play Ise Ondo Koi no Netaba 伊勢音頭恋寝刃 performed at the Imperial Theatre (帝国劇場, Teikoku Gekijō), Tokyo on July 1, 1915. One of thirty prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.<br><br>SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)<br>
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

title: Beauty Combing Her Hair
creator: Oda Tomiya 小田富弥 (1896-1990)
description: One of two known bijin-ga prints designed by Oda for the publisher Ōsaka Mokuhansha. This print shows the influence of his teacher Kitano Tsunetomi (1880-1947) in composition, with the beauty shown in profile with her head bent forward to expose her sensuous neck. Her skin is pale (although somewhat darkened by the effects of age on the print) suggesting the white powder worn by geisha.

description: A double-bookplate removed from the first volume of Kawanabe Kyōsai's four volume work Kyōsai Gadan. Kyōsai based this drawing on an image of the Greek marble sculpture Laocoon and His Two Sons (second century B.C. to the first century A.D.)  in the Musei Vaticani, Rome, focusing on the anatomical aspects of the sculpture.<br>Beginning with the fourth illustration [of Kyosai gadan], Kyosai offered his readers a series of anatomy drawings showing the alignment of muscles or the underlying skeletal structure of the human body. According to Josiah Conder, Kyosai regarded with profound respect the scientific knowledge of anatomical form, perspective and sciography revealed to him in foreign works.

description: A double-bookplate removed from the first volume of Kawanabe Kyōsai's four volume work Kyōsai Gadan.<br>This drawing from Kyōsai gadan is from the "Learning to Paint" section and displays an example of the work of Tenshō Shūbun 天章周文  (1414-1463) as redrawn by Kyōsai. The inscription along the right edge of the right page reads 相国寺ニ住ス僧周文ノ筆意 (painting of Shūbun, a monk who lives in Shokōkuji Temple)<br>Kyōsai Gadan "reveals how widely Kyōsai studied masterpieces from the past." It includes his copies of works by Song and Yuan dynasty painters, the great Japanese master Sesshu, generations of Kano-school artists such as Motonobu and Tan’yu, Tosa and Maruyama school painters, Ogata Korin and Tani Buncho and ukiyo-e artists such as Suzuki Harunobu, Kitagawa Utamaro and Katsushika Hokusai. - source: Suntory Museum of Art https://www.suntory.com/sma/exhibition/2019_1/display.html [accessed 3-26-2021]

title: Hurrah for the Empire! Illustration of His Majesty, the Commander-in-chief, Welcoming [military officers] to the Imperial Palace with the Emperor’s Gift Cup (帝國萬歳 大元師陛下御歓迎上皇城於御盃賜圖)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: The emperor, empress and crown prince are hosting a year-end celebration for the military after Japan's victory in the Sino-Japanese War which ended in April 1895. A similar, if not the same event, as in Nobukazu's print IHL.0160 depicting the emperor and empress at a military celebration. In both, Empress Haruko is in traditional rather than Western dress. The emperor and next to him the crown prince sport their military uniforms.

title: Sawamura Tosshō as Tomiki Saburō, Nakamura Shikan as Hidetarō and Ōtani Tomoemon as Fyjanu Jirō in the play Sangoku Kumiage Tōrō (冨貴三郎 沢村訥升、英太郎 中村芝翫、深見次郎 大谷友右衛門 ・和漢竺爼上灯篭)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The three actors (R to L) Sawamura Tosshō II, Nakamura Shikan IV, and Ōtani Tomoemon V are shown dancing in lion wigs and peony (botan) hats in the play Sangoku Kumiage Tōrō at the Morita-za. Nakamura Shikan in the white wig is performing the dance with his two cubs in the red wigs. He brandishes a peony branch in what has been described as a "heaven-earth" pose. Each actor's head is adorned with a peony on top of two open fans.

title: After the Bath (入浴 nyūyoku)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
This print is from a series of 40 scenes documenting life inside the women quarters of the shogun's palace in Edo, prior to the Meiji Restoration in 1868. It shows a young beauty after her bath, wearing a blue and white cotton kimono, a towel on a stand next to her. An attendant offers her a cup of tea, while another turns the handle of a fan to cool her. A faint pattern of hollyhock leaves, symbol of the Tokugawa Shogunate, is printed in the background. As with other prints in this series, this print exists in at least two states.

<br><br>THE INNER PRECINCTS OF CHIYODA<br>
 "Chikanobu imagines something he never saw—the inner precincts of Edo Castle, which housed the shogun’s mother, wife, and concubines. The area was off limits to all men other than the shogun himself or his young male heir."[1]
 "The Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku) series of 1895-1896, together with his 1897 series Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the Chiyoda Inner Palace set, Chikanobu documented various annual ceremonies in the women’s quarters, especially those at New Year’s, and seasonal activities, particularly those conducted in the palace gardens. While Chikanobu did not indicate specific events or name certain people that would link these images to a single date or time period, the scenes give an overall impression of what the shogun’s private quarters might have looked like in the mid-19th century. "Most women depicted in Chiyoda Inner Palace are portrayed as elegant dignified ideal feminine figures, showing little emotion or excitement. No one seems happy or sad, ebullient or upset. In fact, these imaginary depictions suggest a realm of tranquil harmony, without conflict or illness. Only two old women are shown, and most of the more than 150 featured figures are youthful looking, appearing to be in their 20’s or early 30’s. A few girls are present, but even they are well behaved; no babies or pregnant women are evident. There is a sense of tension among the women, though, as ritual gestures and prescribed ceremonies are carried out with great seriousness. Although some settings are animated by secondary figures (servants, actors, parade participants, etc.) or pet animals, overall the quiet rhythm of life in the Chiyoda Inner Palace is predominant and well described."[2] 

<br><br> [1] Portland Art Museum http://portlandartmuseum.us/mwebcgi/mweb.exe?request=record;id=46772;type=101 [accessed 8-30-23]
<br>[2] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 169.

title: A List of the House of Representatives, illustration of House of Representatives Meeting (帝國議會衆議院議員名鑑, 衆議院會議之図)
creator: Nagashima Shungyō 永嶌春暁 (active 1882-1905)
description: This print pictures the emperor and empress in bust portraits flanking the interior of the First Temporary Diet Building. The Meiji government published an imperial rescript in 1881 calling for the first session of the Imperial Diet to be convened in 1890. The first House of Representatives election was held on 1 July 1890 (Meiji 23), with 300 seats to be filled. The franchise was limited to males, with only some one percent of the total population eligible to vote.

title: Atagoyama (愛宕山)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description:
This print picturing the NHK Museum of Broadcast in Atagoyama in Tokyo, formerly the Tokyo Broadcasting Station, is one of only two prints by Sekino published by Watanabe Shōzaburō, the seminal publisher of shin hanga. While this print does not bear any Watanabe publishing seals, other impressions bear the publisher's 6mm round seal in the lower left portion of the image.<br>
The museum is known as "the birthplace of Japanese broadcasting" and opened to the public in 1956, just after this print was published.

title: Great Imperial Victory at the Fierce Battle at Pyongyang (平壌激戦 帝国大勝利)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)

title: Illustration of the Japanese Second Army Fierce Battle at Jinzhou Castle (第二軍金州城大激戦之  Dai ni gun Kinshūjōdaigekisen no zu)
creator: Nakamura Shūkō 秋香 (active c. 1894-1904)
description:
On September 26, 1894, the Japanese imperial headquarters had organized the Second Army.  Its objective was to conquer the Chinese dockyard and arsenal of Port Arthur and then to embark on a campaign into the Peking region after winter. On October 24, while the First Army was crossing the Yalu River and entering China, the Second Army landed on on the Liaotung (Chinchou) Peninsula. By November 3, the Second Army advanced toward Chinchou, the major stronghold before Port Arthur.  With a full-scale assault on November 6, the Second Army broke the stiff resistance at Chinchou, taking the fortress before noon.<br>
Private First-Class Kubota Chuzo, a twenty-one-year-old farmer, wrote in his war diary: "Today our company had lunch in the southern section of Chinchou.  Chinese corpses were piled everywhere. . . . Some enemy soldiers were found among the dead feigning death. Our litter corps found them and slashed or stabbed them to death."

title: Reproduction of: Dutch Beauty with Pekinese from the portfolio Nagasaki Old Prints, Volume 1 (複製：阿蘭陀美人と狆・長崎古版画 第一集 Nagasaki kohanga dai 1 shū)
creator: Unknown
description:
One of ten prints included in a portfolio of woodblock reproductions of Nagasaki-e 長崎絵, "woodblock prints, paintings, and illustrated woodblock-printed books made in the port of Nagasaki. Often serving as miyage hanga (souvenir prints: 土産版画), nagasaki-e were inexpensive mementos for merchants or scholars who traveled to Nagasaki on business. Moreover, the market for such images was large and profitable, as the Japanese were themselves endlessly curious about foreign visitors whom they were typically forbidden to meet. Nagasaki-e were sold not only in Nagasaki, but also in Edo and Osaka, and no doubt in the provinces." - Source: website of John Fiorillo's Viewing Japanese Prints https://www.viewingjapaneseprints.net/texts/topics_faq/nagasakie.html [accessed 8-25-23]
<br>The prints in the portfolio were done under the auspices of the Nagasaki Shiritsu Hakubutsukan 長崎市立博物館 (Nagasaki Municipal Museum).

title: Girl with Fan from the magazine Han geijutsu, volume 6 (版芸術　第6号)
creator: Ryōji Chōmei 料治潮鳴 (1899-1982)
description:
This small print of nude girl holding a fan by Ryōji Chōmei (Kumata) (1899-1982) was created for his dōjin (coterie magazine) Han geijutsu (Print Art), Volume 6, published in August 1932 in Tokyo by his publishing company Shiro to Kurosha. 
<br>From four to five hundred copies of each volume of Han geijutsu were printed and each issue was priced at 50 sen. The magazine was published from April 1932 until December 1936. The printing for most of the prints was done by placing woodblocks directly in commercial printing presses, but one or more hand-printed works, such as this print, were included in each issue.
<br>Better known as a print publisher than an artist, Ryōji was born in Okayama prefecture with the given name Kumata 熊太 which he used in association with his publishing activities. In the 1930s he published the small art magazines Shiro to kuro (White and Black), Han geijutsu (Print Art), along with others, including three devoted to folk toys. His own work often appeared in these magazines.

title: Illustration of the the Army and Navy Protecting the Legations and Japanese Residents (海陸兵・公使館及ビ日本居留民保護之図 Kairikuhei kōshikan no Nihon kyoryūmin hogo no zu)
creator: Unknown

title: Four Stories, Including the Story of the Shimabara Brothel, No. 7 appearing in the Nishikie Shinbun [Kyoto]  (錦画新聞 [京都]・第七号・ 島原廓の話 など４件)
creator: Kinoshita Hironobu II 木下広信 (1844-?)
description: This print depicting actors being arrested in a gambling den at the Shimomura brothel, was published in Kyoto long after the news nishikie boom had come and gone in 1874-1876. The cartouche reads "Nishikie shinbun" / "No. 7" / "Meiji 14-4-21" [21 April 1881].

title: Police Confront Man in Black Makeup from the News Illustrated (新聞圖會 Shinbun zue)
creator: Utagawa Yoshitaki 歌川芳滝 (1841-1899)
description: This news nishiki-e relates an amusing case of mistaken identity as explained in the below translation.<br>Translation of text on print: "A patrolman was doing his rounds at midnight in Takatsu-chō 5, 12th small ward, 2nd large ward. He saw a house whose door had been left open, so he stopped to have a look, thinking a thief might have sneaked in. Then he heard a voice, like a tiger or a wolf snoring, so he went inside. Something with a pitch black face and glittering eyes tried to grab him. Its breath was so foul that the patrolman could hardly face it. He cried out, 'Are you a fox or a tanuki? Do you not recognize a policeman?' But the black faced creature itself shouted, 'You’re a thief pretending to be a policeman.' The angry voice was using speech, so the patrolman brought his corporal to investigate. The corporal was just as astonished at the black faced creature, but when he looked closely he saw it was the master of the house. Puzzled, he asked why the man’s face was black. At last the man remembered and apologized for his rudeness. 'Last night I was invited to a drinking party at my neighbor’s house. Under the influence we painted our faces black and began playing rock-paper-scissors. I simply could not beat my opponent, and in the end my face was completely covered with soot. I came home like that, but I remember nothing more. I must have gone to sleep with the door open. All of this happened because I drank so much,' he said. The matter was let go with an apology, according to the Ōsaka News. Oh, how important it is to drink only in moderation! Self control is the key!" - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literature, University of Oregon

title: The Tori-no-machi Festival at Senzoku (千束酉の町大きな唐の芋頭をかつぐ Senzoku torinomachi ōkina tōno imo gashira o katsugu)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: One of forty prints from the series Crazy Pictures of Famous Places in Tōkyō (Tōkyō kaika kyōga meishō) picturing "Tori no machi" (Bird Day) festivities in the Senzuko area of Tokyo, where one gives thanks for a safe year and prays for happiness in the next. The reveler in the back is holding a lucky kumade (bamboo rake) which is believed to rake in good luck.

title: Woman from Ohara (大原女 Oharame)
creator: Kotozuka Eiichi 琴塚英一 (1906-1979) - attributed to the artist
description:
An "Oharame" (a woman from the town of Ohara) is seen resting. Oharame is a kind of hisame (a woman peddler) often pictured carrying firewood, charcoal or baskets of flowers bound for sale in Kyoto. Today, the Oharame is gone. However, the Ohara Tourist Information Center (Ohara Kanko Hoshokai), offers an "Oharame experience" where one can don traditional dress for a small fee. The following mid-20th century description would have been roughly contemporary with this print's publication.<br> "[Oharame] carry heavy loads on their heads and they have a very fine bearing. Their dress also is peculiar, as they wear narrow obi (sashes), and cover their heads with kerchiefs while over their legs and arms they wear white cotton-cloth. Parties of these naive peasant-women may frequently be seen in the streets of Kyoto, selling flowers or carrying heavy merchandise." - Source: Japan The Official Guide, Tourist Industry Bureau Ministry of Transportation (ed.), Japan Travel Bureau, 9th edition, 1962, p. 712.

<br> This print has been attributed to both Kotozuka Eiichi (1906-1979) and his contemporary Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000), as various impressions bear different markings that can be attributed to one or the other artist. This print bears a round seal in the bottom right corner of the image that may be some variation of Kotozuka's self-printed seal "Toku kako za" and also carries the notation  "PRINT T. Tokuriki", which could indicate either that he created the design or that he just did the printing with Kotozuka being responsible for the design. The two artists worked closely together, establishing the joint publishing company Koryokusha, along with the artists Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977) and Takahashi Tasaburō (1904-1977), in 1948.

title: A Bunraku Puppet Head
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
This collection contains two different printings of this depiction of the head of a bunraku puppet, IHL.0275 and IHL.0314. These two versions may both be artist's proofs.  This print, IHL.0314, carries the notation written in pencil "(2.) T. Tokuriki 1962.6.8" in the lower right corner within the image. Print IHL.0275 bears the artist's signature in the lower left corner within the image.
<br>This print was released as a numbered edition of 100 prints.

title: Bunraku Puppet Head
creator: Kamei Tōbei  亀井藤兵衛 (1901-1977)
description: This print of a puppeteer's hand holding a bunraku puppet head (likely a "shako mage" used for knowing, vivacious women of middle age) is from a numbered edition of 200 prints issued by Kōrokusha 紅録社, the publishing house jointly created by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), Tokuriki Tomikichiro (1902-2000) and Kotozuka Eiichi (1906-1979).  At least two other numbered edition of this print exists, attesting to the print's popularity.

title: Ichikawa Gonjūrō, Bandō Shūchō, Ichikawa Kuzō, Kataoka Gadō and Takasagoya Fukusukei in the play A Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani (市川権十郎、坂東秀調、市川九蔵、市川九蔵、熊谷陣屋、高砂屋福助・一谷嫩軍記)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: Picturing the "Kumagai Jin'ya" scene, the last scene in the play Ichinotani Futaba Gunki, a dramatization of the Heike Monogatari tale of the battle of Ichinotani. Pictured are the actors (right to left): Ichikawa Gonjūrō as Yoshitsune, Bandō Shūchō II as Fuji no Kata, Ichikawa Kuzō III as Kumagai Jiro Naozane, Kataoka Gadō as Midaroku and Takasagoya Fukusuke III as Sagami.

title: My Town (わが街)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: "Though the elements in Takahashi's prints seem to float in an untamed cosmos, or are simply reduced to a square or an oblong in perfect equilibrium, they fall unmistakably into place, arranged as precisely as the utensils for a formal tea ceremony. The space is so ideally formulated that no furnishings are necessary; its architecture eliminates everything but that which is aesthetically and structurally indispensable. The space itself is a product of light and shadow displayed in an 'unbalanced' tension. The search for such 'unbalanced' forms has almost become an obsession, but it is nevertheless a positive aesthetic expression. In such traditional Japanese arts as flower arranging or calligraphy, particularly in the informal styles associated with them, the consummate grace and elegance which can be achieved through the asymmetrical organization of forms in space is especially sought after. Takahashi's forms possess a freedom in space, yet are nonobstructive in their simplicity and color.  The austere sublimity of his works in the quintessence of his masterly use of asymmetry." - source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha International Ltd., 1973, p. 148-149.

title: Flying Angel No. 3 (天使昇天 No. 3)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description: Between 1968 and 1972, Hagiwara used a brighter color palette, and the resulting prints have a new lightness. He abandoned two-sided printing which, while providing great depth to his images, kept his colors rather somber. This print, with its vivid orange highlighted with mica and playful floating forms, is a fine example of this change. To produce the etching-like lines, the artist used sharpened nails to mark the woodblock and inking techniques similar to those used in intaglio printmaking, one of many innovative woodblock techniques for which Hagiwara is famous.

title: Japanese Troops Attack the Chinese Cavalry in the Vicinity of Hushan (虎山附近騎兵ヲ攻撃ス Kozan fukin kihei o kōgekisu)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)

title: View of Nihonbashi Bridge in the Eastern Capital (東都日本橋之勝景 Tōto Nihonbashi no shōkei)
creator: Utagawa Sadahide 歌川貞秀 (1807-1873)
description:
One of at least three triptychs designed by Sadahide depicting daimyo processions. The depiction of the cranes in this print may be reference to the procession of Lord Minamoto Yoritomo, the 12th-century military leader, who is said to have courted Buddhist favor by releasing wild cranes. Mt. Fuji rises in the background and whitewashed warehouses line the banks of the Sumida. The procession is crossing Nihonbashi and Edobashi is seen in the background.
<br>"The Tokugawa shoguns, who in effect ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867, introduced a system whereby all daimyo were required to spend alternate years at Edo (modern-day Tokyo) in attendance on the shogun. This was known in Japanese as ‘sankin kotai’. This system maintained control over the regional daimyo, who were the appointed feudal rulers of Japan. In the Edo period they were either members of the Tokugawa family or had pledged direct allegiance to the Tokugawa shogun. The daimyo was required to maintain residential estates in Edo as well as in their regional domains. A daimyo generally travelled to the capital every other year and returned to his province after a year's service. He travelled with a retinue of 150 to 300 or more. The journeys and the upkeep of a daimyo's Edo and country estates consumed about 70 to 80 percent of his income." Source: website of Victoria and Albert Museum https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O92993/the-procession-of-the-lord-woodblock-print-utagawa-sadahide/#:~:text=The%20Tokugawa%20shoguns%2C%20who%20in,Japanese%20as%20'sankin%20kotai'. [accessed 8-27-23]

title: Abstract monochrome design (untitled)
creator: Hacker, Ernst (1917-1987)
description: One of a number of small abstract monochrome woodblocks created by Hacker, possible done while he was stationed with the Occupation forces in Japan.

title: A Lady in Waiting Hands the Noh Mask to an Actor (御能楽屋)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
This print is from a series of 40 scenes, published 1895-1896, documenting life inside the women quarters of the shogun's palace in Edo, prior to the Meiji Restoration in 1868. A lady in waiting hands a noh mask to an actor in the Chiyoda Palace before a performance.[1] Extensive use is made of burnishing (shomen zuri [front printing]) which leaves a reflective-polished finish on the black areas and embossing which is seen in the white areas of the lady's robes.

<br><br>THE INNER PRECINCTS OF CHIYODA<br>
"Chikanobu imagines something he never saw—the inner precincts of Edo Castle, which housed the shogun’s mother, wife, and concubines. The area was off limits to all men other than the shogun himself or his young male heir."[2]

"The Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku) series of 1895-1896, together with his 1897 series Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868.  In the Chiyoda Inner Palace set, Chikanobu documented various annual ceremonies in the women’s quarters, especially those at New Year’s, and seasonal activities, particularly those conducted in the palace gardens.  While Chikanobu did not indicate specific events or name certain people that would link these images to a single date or time period, the scenes give an overall impression of what the shogun’s private quarters might have looked like in the mid-19th century.  

"Most women depicted in Chiyoda Inner Palace are portrayed as elegant dignified ideal feminine figures, showing little emotion or excitement.  No one seems happy or sad, ebullient or upset.  In fact, these imaginary depictions suggest a realm of tranquil harmony, without conflict or illness.  Only two old women are shown, and most of the more than 150 featured figures are youthful looking, appearing to be in their 20’s or early 30’s.  A few girls are present, but even they are well behaved; no babies or pregnant women are evident.  There is a sense of tension among the women, though, as ritual gestures and prescribed ceremonies are carried out with great seriousness.  Although some settings are animated by secondary figures (servants, 
actors, parade participants, etc.) or pet animals, overall the quiet rhythm of life in the Chiyoda Inner Palace is predominant and well described."[3]

<br><br>
[1] The play to be performed has been identified as both Chikubushima (The God of The Island of Chikubu) and Kasuga ryujin (The Kasuma Dragon God). Both plays, I believe, use the red wig and dragon helmet.
<br>[2] Portland Art Museum http://portlandartmuseum.us/mwebcgi/mweb.exe?request=record;id=46772;type=101 [accessed 8-30-23]
<br>[3] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 169.

title: Polishing-sand of Iga Province (伊賀国 磨砂 Iga kuni migakizuna)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, workers are mining a white sand that will be be used in tooth powder, for polishing rice to make uruchi, and other applications using polishing sand. Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi, Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces.<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.1488.

title: Coal Mine in Iga Province (同国 [伊賀国] 石炭山之図 dōkoku sekitan yama no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting coal miners entering a mine with pickaxes (tsuruhashi) in hand and exiting the mine carrying yoked baskets (sena) of coal, this color woodblock print (nishiki-e) was one of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. As the series’ name implies, each print depicted an economic activity in a province or district of Japan. In addition, each activity was described on the print in a scroll-like cartouche.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.1486.
Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi,Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces. The Saruka mountains which bordered Iga were noted for their coal reserves. An 1878-1879 geological survey describes Iga coal as being "black and shining." The print's scroll mentions that the coal produced is like the color of lacquer.

title: Producing Vitriol in Hyūga Province (日向緑礬製之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. The following description is provided in an 1878-1879 geological survey which discusses the author's tour of copper mines throughout Japan.  ".. [B]lister copper  is made with roasting in kilns and smelting in small hearths in the old Japanese style; and blue vitriol (copper sulfate) is manufactured with roasting, leaching, boiling down and crystallizing."

title: Burdock Harvest in Iyo Province (伊予国牛蒡堀之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

title: Burdock Harvest in Iyo Province (伊予国牛蒡堀之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.

<br>Harvesting "Gobou" (burdock root) in Iyo (Ehime prefecture), some of which grow to about 120cm in length. It has a thin, brown root with a distinct, earthy flavor. It is used in medicine in China, but in Japan it is treated as a vegetable, and is generally cut into thin strips or shavings and soaked in vinegar to remove bitterness before cooking. It is an excellent source of dietary fiber and nutrients, and therefore aids digestion and detoxification.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0326.

title: Rose, originally appearing in the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花  ・薔薇  Shikashū・Nihon no hana・bara)
creator: Kawanishi Hide 川西英 (1894-1965)
description:
Issued as an illustration for the poem of the same name, "Rose," by Yoshiaki Sasazawa (1898-1984), in the 1946 poetry and print book "Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," "Rose" was one of three woodblock prints, along with "Thistle" (see IHL.0603) by Kawakami Sumio (1895-1972) and "Plum" (IHL.0396) by Maekawa Senpan (1888-1960), that were tipped into the book. This collection's print is stand-alone, being either removed from the book it was tipped into or separately printed as a stand-alone print.
 <br>"Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," was edited and designed by Onchi Kōshirō, a seminal artist in the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement and pioneering book designer. Contributing twelve prints and one poem, he along with poet Inoue Yasufumi 井上康文 (1897–1973), selected the book's thirty poems by poets such as Satō Haruo (1892-1964), Kitahara Hakushū (1885-1942), Noguchi Yonejirō (1875-1947), Kaoru Maruyama (1899-1974), Tatsuji Miyoshi (1900-1964), Ryuko Kawaji (1888-1959) and Andō Ichirō (1907-1972). 
<br>When this book was published in May 1946 "much of the country, including Tokyo where it was printed, remained in ruins following the previous year’s aerial bombardments. . . . Nihon no hana demonstrated the sophisticated aesthetic sensibility of the Japanese people, while providing a hopeful image for the future rebuilding—or 're-flowering'—of the country and its people." - Source: Commentary by Alicia Volk, https://pulverer.si.edu/node/462/title/1 [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Michimori 通盛
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 107) - A priest visiting Naruto goes out one evening to read sutras for the souls of the Taira warriors who perished there, and meets a woman and an old man who approach the shore by boat. They tell him how Kozaisho no Tsubone, the wife of Michimori, drowned herself there at the news of her husband's death, and then disappear among the waves. The priest prays for them and after a while they reappear, Michimori being this time in his true form. The priest hears the story of the battle, and Michimori and his wife rejoice that they have been able to attain salvation together.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: A Moaning Monologue in the Chinese Kyōgen (清狂言の降状 Shin kyōgen no kōjō)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
In March 1895 when this print was published, negotiations were underway for a cease fire and in a month the Treaty of Shimonoseki ending the war would be signed. The "moaning monologue" being delivered by a "bad actor" relates to the defeat of Li Hongzhang, the Chinese forces Supreme Commander. The Westerner opening the curtain relates to the intervention of the Western countries who wanted an end to the fighting and to promote their own interests on the Liaodong Peninsula.

title: Huai River Moon - Wu Zixu ( 淮水月 伍子胥 Waisui no tsuki - Goshishō)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
Two possible stories are associated with this print, as follows: Story 1 - Late in his life, the Chinese general Wu Zixu avenged his father's death. A fisherman on the Huai River told him the location of the grave of his father's murderer. He found the grave, exhumed the body, and beat it as a punishment. <br>
Story 2 - "The title of the print states that its subject is the somewhat obscure Wu Zixu, but the design itself, a smiling fisherman with a rod, sitting at ease, being discovered by a high-ranking Chinese in military dress by the side of a river, suggests a much more popular story, that of the Daoist sage, Jiang Ziya.  If the figure is Jiang Ziya, it would be satisfying in that it made the fisherman the subject of the print rather than the smaller military figure.  The moon is incidental to both stories."[1]
<br>This print is from the album issued by publisher Akiyama Buemon shortly after Yoshitoshi's death and retains its original album backing.

<br><br>ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
<br>One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
<br>"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[2]

[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, print 48.
<br> [2] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

title: Takakura Moon - Hasebe Nobutsura (高倉月　長谷部信連 Takakura no tsuki - Hasebe Nobutsura)

Prince Mochihito, a son of the Emperor Takakura (1161-1181), and another are escaping from an attack on the palace by disguising themselves as women. Hasebe Nobutsura, Mochihito's retainer who is watching them leave, was captured, but refused to reveal the prince's whereabouts even under torture.[1]<br>

title: Makiginu 巻絹 (Rolls of Silk)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 98) - A Court official announces that he has been charged with the task of collecting a thousand rolls of silk to be sent from the various provinces to the Kumano Shrines, in accordance with a dream the Emperor has had. The man bringing the silk from the capital, however, has stopped on the way to offer up a poem at the shrine of the god Otonashi no Tenjin, and arrives late. The official therefore orders him to be bound and punished, but the god takes possession of a priestess to save the man in gratitude for his offering.  Speaking through the mouth of the priestess, the god then recites some prayers at the request of the official and finally dances.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Yoshino Shizuka 吉野静

creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

This he obtains from a hatmaker in the place who is sympathetic to his cause. In exchange he gives him his sword but the hatmaker insists on returning it to him. He then travels on with his companions to the town of Akasaka where they seek a night's lodging. There they are attacked by a band of robbers led by Kumasaka no Chōhan, but they put them to flight and Chōhan himself is killed by Ushiwaka.
