title: Orochi 大蛇
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 136.) - This is a version of the widespread legend of the princess who is saved from a dragon, and is based on accounts found in Japanese works of the eighth century. When Susano-o descends from Heaven to Izumo in the legendary Age of the Gods, he finds an old couple weeping over their daughter. They tell him that every year a dragon living in the nearby river takes one of their daughters and that this year their last child is due to be given up to him. On being promised the princess if he succeeds in saving her, Susano-o prepares eight boats laden with sake. After the interlude, he and the princess are shown arriving in the upper reaches of the river.  The dragon appears, angry and powerful, but becoming drunk on the wine that has been brought, is killed by Susano-o.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Breathe - Earth B (呼吸・大地 B)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: Lavender and teal make this an unusual color combination for the artist. Deep embossing of curved lines nicely balance the ocher-colored partial ellipse. Several states of this print exist with this print likely being the same state as shown in the artist's catalogue raisonné #234.  While the catalogue raisonné gives the English title as Breathe (Earth), the title written on the print by Takahashi is Breathe (Earth) B.

title: Illustration of a Visit by the Empress to the General Staff Headquarters (参謀本部行啓之図 Sanbō honbu gyōkei no zu)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description: Empress Haruko (Shōken) presents a general with a tray of rolled bandages. "As president of the Lady's Volunteer Nursing Association, the empress was eager to alleviate the sufferings of the wounded and set to work with the palace ladies to make antiseptic bandages: six thousand were sent from the imperial household to the Red Cross Society on October 13, 1894. The imperial figure was a model for the earnest ladies of the upper classes who met almost daily from eight in the morning until half-past five in the afternoon in the rooms of the Tokyo Red Cross Hospital." - Source: The World of the Meiji Print: Impressions of a New Civilization, Julia Meech-Pekarik, Weatherhill, 1986, p. 209-211.

title: Naval Officers Discussing the Battle Strategy for the Invasion of China (海軍将校等征清の戦略議論する図 Kaigun shōkō tō seishin no senryaku giron suru no zu)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)

title: The Arraignment of Ōyama Tsunayoshi (大山綱良糺問之図 Ōyama Tsunayoshi kyūmon no zu)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
Ōyama Tsunayoshi 大山綱良, vice-governor of Kagoshima at the outbreak of the Satsuma Rebellion (a.k.a. West-South or Seinan War) in February 1877 and close friend of the rebel leader Saigō Takamori, faces a tribunal having been accused of treason.
<br>
The leftmost figure on the right panel is National Police Chief Kawaji Toshiyoshi 川路利良 (1834-1879) who was responsible for sending Satsuma natives to their home province with orders to infiltrate the Shigakko (military academies for samurai led by Saigō) and dissuade them from anti-government action.
<br>There are three published accounts of Governor Oyama's fate. The first, an 1879 account by Augustus Henry Mounsey (Great Britain's Japan Legation Secretary, 1876-?) states that Oyama was executed. The second, an 1881 account by John R. Black (newspaper editor), states that Oyama was made a "close prisoner."  The third, from a recently published work by Mark Ravina (The Last Samurai: The Life and Battles of Saigo Takamori, p. 207), states that Oyama was sent to "Osaka for the duration of the war." Black states that the charges against Oyama "were never distinctly defined" while Mounsey provides the text of the charges and the sentence handed out. References to 1877 as the date of Oyama's death support Mounsey's account.

title: Illustration of Azuma Bridge from Famous Places in Tokyo (東京名所 吾妻橋之図 Azumabashi no zu, Tokyo meisho)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description:
The artist depicts Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken in front of the Azuma Bridge, possibly for its public opening in December 1887. Whether the emperor and empress ever visited the bridge is unknown. It was not unusual to picture the royal couple in various imagined public settings.
<br>Azumabashi was the first metal bridge spanning the Sumida River. It was officially dedicated and opened to the public on December 9, 1887. It served the bustling pleasure quarter of Asakusa on one side and a beer factory on the other. Japanese woodblock artists drew its vertical posts and diagonal eyebars in Western perspective and for good measure populated the walkway with ladies in bustles and the deck with top-hatted gentlemen in carriages. (For another print of Azuma bridge see IHL.0269, Azumabashi by Utagawa Kunitoshi.)
<br><br>For other prints depicting Azumabashi see IHL.0269, IHL.2151 and IHL.2435.

title: Report on the Actual Condition at the Battlefield (戰地実況聞奏之図 Senchi jitsukyō bunsō no zu)
creator: Kobayashi Toshimitsu 古林年光 (active 1876–1904)
description:
Military, police and government officials are observing a map depicting the regions of conflict in Satsuma province where the Satsuma Rebellion 西南戦争 [or the Seinan Sensō (Southwestern War)] is raging. In September 1877, when this print was published, disgruntled samurai under the charismatic leadership of ex-Meiji official and samurai Saigō Takamori 西郷 隆盛 had been waging war against the imperial government for almost nine months. However, on September 24, 1877 the war would end with the decimation of Saigō's army at the Battle of Shiroyama and Saigō's death.<br>
Pictured in the print are Sanjō Sanetomi 三条 実美 (1837-1891), Prime Minister (left panel, holding sword); Ōkubo Toshimichi 大久保利通 (1830-1878), Minister of the Interior (center panel under red cartouche); Count Itō Hirobuni 伊藤 博文 (1841– 1909) (center panel, right most figure); and Kawaji Toshiyoshi 川路利良 (1834-1879), Chief of the National Police (right panel under red cartouche).

title: The Wealthy Chiefs Inspecting the Decapitated Heads of Enemies (財魁ノ首級実検之図 Saikai no shakyū jitsuken no zu)
creator: Kobayashi Toshimitsu 古林年光 (active 1876–1904)

title: Record of the War in Kagoshima (鹿児嶋戦記 Kagoshima senki)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
Saigō Takamori 西郷隆盛 is front and center upon horseback in this print depicting one of the engagements associated with the siege of Kumamoto Castle in Kagoshima during the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. A banner with a slogan "A New Government, Rich in Virtue", fabricated by woodblock artists and perpetuated by the press, is carried by an unidentified rebel. Saigō's comrades pictured in the print on horseback are, from left to right, Shinohara Kunimoto 篠原国幹, Murata Shinpachi 村田新八, Kirino Toshiaki 桐野利秋, Saigō Kokei 西郷小平 (Takamori's younger brother) and Murata Sansuke 村田三助.
<br>
By the time this print was issued on March 23, 1877 the war had been raging for one month. The first major engagement was the siege of Kumamoto Castle by the rebels. As both sides sent in reinforcements the rebels entrenched themselves on a strategic hilltop and a fierce battle involving some 20,000 men, evenly divided between the armies, ensued with 4,000 casualties on each side. On March 20 the better supplied government troops seized the hill, forcing the rebels to retreat.
<Chikanobu designed at least 45 triptych prints that "documented" the rebellion in Kagoshima. At least ten of them were titled "Kagoshima senki" ("war chronicle") and they read like breaking news stories. At least eight different publishers contracted with Chikanobu, as each publisher rushed to get the latest news out to an eager public.

title: Illustration of the Rebels Being Suppressed at Kagoshima (鹿児嶋賊徒平定圖 Kagoshima zokuto heijō no zu)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: Saigō Takamori 西郷隆盛 is front and center upon horseback, sword in hand, as bullets fly around him. When this print was issued in October 1877, the Satsuma Rebellion was over, the rebels were defeated and Saigō was dead. As in the print "Kagoshima senkin" (IHL.0449) the rebels imagined slogan "A New Government, Rich in Virtue" is again on display. Twelve red cartouches containing the names of those pictured are displayed including those of Saigō and ten of his comrades including Beppu Shinsuke 別府新介, Murata Shinpachi 村田新八, Nagayama Yachirō 永山矢一郎 (commander of the 2nd battalion), Kirino Toshiaki 桐野利秋, Kawano Shiro 河野四郎 and Higo Sukezaemon.

title: Illustration of the Rebels Being Suppressed at Kagoshima (鹿児嶋賊徒平定圖 Kagoshima zokuto heijō no zu)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description:
Saigō Takamori's 西郷隆盛 body is front and center upon horseback in this print depicting the Battle of Shiroyama, the final battle of the Satsuma Rebellion. His head, however, has left his body, ascending to heaven to join a faint ghost-like apparition visible to the left of his head. Pictured with Saigō and named in the red cartouches are his fellow rebels Beppu Shinsuke (to the left of Saigō), Fuchibe Takaaki and Ikegami Shiro (to the right of Saigō.)
<br><b>Battle of Shiroyama</b>
<br>On September 24, 1877, with their numbers reduced to no more than 400 men "[t]he rebels made their last stand in the hills of Shiroyama behind Kagoshima Castle, overlooking Kagoshima Bay."[1]
<br>Imperial army troops and marines under the command of Yamagata Aritomo (1838‐1922) and Kawamura Sumiyoshi (1863-1904) launched their assault on Tabaru-zaka hill in the early morning and by 7:00am "Saigō and his troops descended the hill to face the Japanese army and die."[2]
<br><b>Saigō's Death and Seppuku</b>
<br>"Halfway down the hill, Saigō was shot in the right hip. The bullet passed through his body and exited at his left femur.  Saigō fell to the ground."[3] At this point reality and myth put forward two different scenarios of Saigō's final moments. The Saigō myth has him calmly asking his lieutenant Beppu Shinsuke to be his second and then committing ritual suicide, seppuku, by disembowelment, followed by Shinsuke lopping off his head. Reality, however, while confirming a clean decapitation of his head, suggests that Saigō was crippled and in shock from the bullet wound to his thigh and "unable to dispatch himself with traditional samurai honor."[4]
<br><b>Saigō's Missing Head</b>
<br>In either event, his head and his body did wind up in two different places, his head being hidden by his manservant. For a fascinating discussion of the importance of Saigō's head to the Meiji government, which had stopped the practice of the presentation of heads of enemies to the victors as part of their reforms, see Mark Ravina's work The Last Samurai, cited below in the footnotes.
<br>Strangely, there is a version of this print, seemingly identical in all respects, except that Saigō's head is intact upon his shoulders.
<br><br>
[1] The Last Samurai: The Life and Battles of Saigo Takamori, Mark Ravina, John Wiley & Sons, Inc., 2004, p. 3.
<br>[2] Ibid, p.4,
<br>[3] Ibid.
<br>[4] Ibid, p. 5.

title: Figures from Ōtsue Folk Paintings Playing Games (大津絵の戯 Ōtsue no tawamure)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: This print titled Ōtsue no tawamure depicts two sumo wrestlers in battle with various observers, including a very red demon.  The word ōtsue is a reference to small woodblock prints and sketches of popular religious subjects that were popular into the 1880s and the word tawamure can be translated as "joke" or "fun."<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Bad News Travel Quickly (悪事千里を走るAkuji senri o hashiru)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: This print illustrates the proverb "bad news travels quickly" or "bad news has wings." (Lit.: bad new runs one thousand "ri" [about 2.44 miles], a traditional measure of distance in Japan.)<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: The Luck of Men is Like Saiō's Horse; The Mouth is the Gate of Misfortune (間万事塞翁が馬 口は禍の門 Kuchi wa wazawai no kado Ningen banji Saiō no uma)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: This print has two inscribed proverbs - Ningen banji Saiō no uma 人間万事塞翁が馬 and Kuchi wa wazawai no kado 口は禍の門. The first translates as "The luck of men is like Saiō's horse" referring to a well-known Chinese folktale, in which bad news turns to good news, good news turns to bad news, and nothing is what it seems. Basically, this saying means there's no way to know how things will turn out.  The second translates as "The mouth is the front-gate of all misfortune" or "The mouth is the root of trouble."  I do not know how the two proverbs play against each other in this print.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Mirror of Our Country’s Revered Deities and Esteemed Emperors (本朝拝神貴皇鏡 Honchō hiji kiōkagami)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
In the 1870s and 1880s, a number of print artists depicted the imperial lineage for informational and propaganda purposes. Usually the composition showed the 122nd emperor of Japan, Mutsuhito (1852-1912, posthumously known as the Meiji Emperor), and his consort Ichijo Haruko (1850-1914, posthumously known as Empress Shoken), in the center sheet of a triptych composition, with deities and past emperors gathered around.<br>
Here Chikanobu presents the primordial deity Kunitokotachi no mikoto above them, flanked by the two deities of Ise, Yojin to his right and Injin to his left. The first emperor Jimmu is at the far right, holding a bow on which an eagle [actually the mythical Yatagarasu, or three-clawed crow, sent by Amaterasu to guide Jimmu through a difficult part of his eastward journey] is alighting. Next to Jimmu are the 117th emperor Go-Sakuramachi (reigned 1763-1770) and Mutsuhito's father the 121st emperor Komei (reigned 1847-1866), below the deities Ninigi no mikoto (also known as Susa-no-o, the Storm God) and his sister Tensho daijin (also known as Amaterasu Omikami) who is holding a mirror, emblem of the sun and one of the sacred treasures of the imperial family. On the other side are the deities Hikohoho demi no mikoto, holding a fishing pole, and his brother Ugayafuki aezu no mikoto with a sword, standing above the 118th emperor Go-Momonozono (r. 1771-1779), the 119th emperor Kokaku (reigned 1780-1817) and the 120th emperor Ninko (reigned 1817-1846). - Source:  Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 73.

title: Nakamura Jusaburō, Onoe Kikugorō V and Iwai Hanshirō VIII in Rainy Season Kimono and Old-Time Silks (中村寿三郎、五代目 尾上菊五郎、髪結新三・ 梅雨小袖昔八丈 Tsuyu kosode mukashi hachijō)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
The actors, from right to left, Nakamura Jusaburō (中村寿三郎) in the role of Bandō Chushichi (番當忠七); Onoe Kikugorō V (尾上菊五郎) in the role of Kamiyui Shinza (髪結新三) and Iwai Hanshirō VIII (岩井半四郎) in the role of Shirakoya Okuma (白子屋お熊) in the play Rainy Season Kimono and Old-Time Silks. The actors are placed against a textile pattern often used as a backdrop for actor prints.
<br> Play Synopsis: "An 1873 Tokyo domestic play (sewamono) by Kawatake Mokuami. Its formal title is Tsuyu Kosode Mukashi Hachijo (Rainy Season Kimono and Old-Time Silks). It is commonly known as Kamiyui shinza (Shinza the Barber). Based on a 1727 incident, it tells of a love affair between shop assistant Chushichi and Okuma, daughter of a lumber dealer, which is disrupted when Okuma’s mother, seeking to get out of debt, arranges a marriage for her to someone else.  A rascally barber, Shinza, learns of the lovers’ planned elopement and kidnaps the girl en route, using the situation to extort money for her release.  Eventually, Shinza’s devious ways lead to his death." - Source: The Man Who Saved Kabuki: Faubion Bowers and Theatre Censorship in Occupied Japan, Shiro Okamoto, University of Hawaii Press, 2001, p. 162.

title: Nakamura Nakazō, Ichikawa Sadanji, Ichikawa Danjūrō, Onoe Kikugorō and Nakamura Sōjūrō each in the role of Yuranosuke in the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (中村仲蔵、市川左団次、市川団十郎、尾上 菊五郎、中村宗十郎・大星 由良之助・ 仮名手本忠臣蔵)
creator: Toyohara Chikayoshi 豊原周義 (active 1870s-1880s)
description: Five actors, from left to right, Nakamura Nakazō III, Ichikawa Sadanji, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, Onoe Kikugorō V and Nakamura Sōjūrō, each in the role of Ōboshi Yuranosuke, the leader of the 47 rōnin, from the play, Kanadehon Chūshingura. While undated, this print corresponds to a particular performance in November 1878 at the Shintomi Theater, with the leading roles being rotated each day among different actors.<br>The "dog-toothed" pattern surrounding the print and the register panel, is taken from the black-and-white cloak design popular in 19th-century representations of the rōnin which "symbolized . . . their unwavering devotion both by day and by night." - Source: Chushingura and the Floating World, David Bell, Japan Library, 2001, p. 30.

title: Granddaughter-in-law, No. 838 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・八百三十八号)
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description: At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞.  This print depicts another sensational story drawn from real life - this one about an old man who fathers a child with a maid, who turns out to be a daughter of his son's wife by another man.<br>The writer for this print is identified as Tentendo Shujin, a pen name for the writer better known as Takabatake Ransen 高畠藍泉 (1838-1885). Takabatake Ransen was a gesaku writer and journalist who joined Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun shortly after its start in 1872 and often worked with the artist Yoshiiku.<br>At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

title: Gossip: Sino-Japanese War (日清戦争余聞 Nisshin sensō yobun)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: Nobukazu pictures troops celebrating after a "great victory" at Asan, Korea with sake served from barrels labeled 日本一 nipponichi ("Japan's best" or "number one in Japan.")  The small red cartouche in the center panel reads 寄贈品 kizōhin ("gift"), indicating a gift from the emperor. The small red cartouche in the lower right hand corner of the right sheet sits above captured Chinese weapons and reads 分捕物 ("loot" or "plunder").

title: Illustration of the Navy Landing at Sukuchi Village (海軍須口村上陸之図 Kaigun Sukuchi-mura jōriku no zu)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: One of many triptych prints by Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892) chronicling various battles of the Satsuma Rebellion.  This print depicts a night time landing of naval forces in the early March battle of Tabaruzaka Hill in northern Kagoshima, one of the most intense campaigns of the war.  Interestingly, this print omits all references (in the form of cartouches containing names) to specific rebel leaders or government military officers involved in the events, an almost universal component of Satsuma Rebellion prints.

title: Mat Making in Bingo Province (備後國 疊表ヲ製圖)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the making of tatami mats 畳表 in Bingo Province (備後国, Bingo no kuni) which is now part of Hiroshima Prefecture.<br>
See IHL.1921 for the crêped (chirimen) version of the print.

title: Sedge Hat Making in Kaga Province (加賀國 菅笠ヲ造ル圖)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts a traditional rain hat [sedge hats (sugegasa 菅笠)] maker in Kanazawa in Kaga Province (加賀国, Kaga no kuni) which is now part of Ichikawa Prefecture.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.1502.

title: Three Battles between Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin (武田信玄と上杉謙信三つの戦い)
creator: Utagawa Yoshitora 歌川芳虎 (active c. 1836-1882)

title: A Water Imp's Fart (河童の屁 Kappa no he)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: This print depicts a legendary kappa (water-imp) farting, sending two fishermen flying. While the literal translation of Kappa no he 河童の屁 is "a water-imp's fart" it carries the meaning "good for nothing."<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. title: Ōtsue Figures Imitating Narihira's Journey to the East (大津絵の東下り Ōtsue no azuma kudari)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: This print is a parody of a scene in the chapter Azuma kudari (Journey to the East) in the Tales of Ise, a 10th century collection of anecdotes recording the amorous adventures of Ariwara no Narihira. The standard iconography associated with this scene, which can be traced back to the early 14c, shows Narihira on horseback with his attendants and companions, as Mt. Fuji towers in the background.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. title: The Great Tengu Does Calligraphy, A Nose-pulling Contest with an Elephant (書の大天狗 象の鼻引 Sho no daitengu, Zō no hanahiki)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: Kyōsai has drawn both winged bird-like and human-form long-nosed tengu (demons), several of whom are in a tug-of-war match with an elephant and others who are engaged in calligraphy<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. title: A Fruit-bearing Tree is Known From Its Flowers, Fighting Like Dogs and Monkeys (実のなる木は 花からしれる 犬とさる Mi no naru ki wa hana kara shireru, Inu to saru)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: There are two proverbs being illustrated in this print. On the top is written Mi no naru ki wa hana kara shireru (A fruit-bearing tree is known by its flowers.)  The book Japanese Proverbs and Sayings states that this "saying teaches that a man who is destined to be a great person shows promise even in his youth."  The bottom inscription reads Inu to saru (Fighting Like Dogs and Monkeys) a proverb that is applied to people who don't get along.  It is unclear how either of these relate to each other.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Sawamura Hyakunosuke, Nakamura Sōjūrō, Iwai Hanshirō VIII and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in A Strange Tale of Castaways: A Western Kabuki) (沢村百之助、中村宗十郎、八代目 岩井半四郎、九代目 市川団十郎・漂流奇談西洋劇 Hyōryō Kidan Seiyō Kabuki)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
Kunichika portrays a scene from the "cropped-hair" play A Strange Tale of Castaways: A Western Kabuki. Written by the renowned playwright Kawatake Shinshichi II (1816-1893), it tells the tale of a "fisherman [Shimizu no Mihozō] who is separated from his father when their boat wrecks. Rescued and brought to San Francisco by a steamship, he embarks on a journey to Washington . . . . While crossing the desert plains, his train is attacked by Indians, and he is kidnapped by the chief. One adventure leads to another -- and to Europe, where Mihozō reunites with his father, Gozaemon, at an opera in Paris. The curtain closes with the two men agreeing that 'Nothing is as deep as the kindness of people in other countries.'"[1]
<br>"The term 'cropped-hair play' came into use to identify plays about contemporary life because, in 1871, a government regulation had advised citizens to cut their hair short in the Western manner, wear uniforms or informal clothing, and abandon wearing swords. The Meiji emperor cut off his topknot in 1873, thereby setting a seal of approval on the new hairstyle."[2]

<br>Morita Kan'ya XII 守田勘弥 (1846-1897), owner of the Shintomi-za theater, staged this play in September 1879, using actors and actresses in a touring English troupe to perform in several scenes along with Japanese actors. Several Italian-style operettas were inserted into the play. Kan'ya's radical staging was not welcomed by the audience and comments such as "What the Westerners were saying did not make sense at all" and "The voice of a British actress sounded just like the barking of a Western dog" were reported.[3] In commenting on the female character Wakaba with her Western dress, played by the onnagata Sawamura Hyakunosuke, an actors' critique stated "When he [Sawamura] sits down in a chair, however, we notice the long torso of his male body and unsightly behind. He later fixes this, thus hiding his behind, which was an improvement."[4] The play's failure resulted in a loss of over 20,000 yen to Kan'ya, which he never recovered from.[5]

<br><br>[1] William Wetherall's website http://www.nishikie.com/articles/Tonichi_Iwakura_Embassy.html [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[2] Kabuki Plays on Stage Restoration and Reform, 1872-1905, vol. 4, ed. James Brandon and Samuel Leiter, University of Hawai'i Press, 2003, p. 18.
<br>[3] National Diet Library website article "Theatrical Performances and Theaters in the Meiji Period (1): Shintomiza - Morita Kanya's Western Influence"
<br>[4] "Customs of the Meiji Period and Kabuki's War Dramas" by Akira Kamiyama as translated by Joseph Ryan, appearing in Comparative Theatre Review, Vol. 11, No. 1 (English Issue), March 2012, p. 11.
<br>[5] A Kabuki Reader: History and Performance, Samuel L. Leiter, ed., M.E. Sharpe, 2002, p. 149.

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Hanakawa Toagemaki no Sukeroku in the play Sukeroku (九世市川団十郎 花川戸揚巻ノ助六・助六)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, playing the role of Hanakawa Toagemaki no Sukeroku in the kabuki play Sukeroku. He wears the purple headband associated with the character Sukeroku.  Above Danjūrō is an unidentified actor playing the role of Ikyū 意休, an older samurai who seeks to steal Agemaki away from Sukeroku.
<br>"The story centers on Sukeroku, a samurai and otokodate, a prominent patron of the Yoshiwara, and especially of Agemaki, the top courtesan of the Miura-ya teahouse. Drawing upon elements of the classic Soga Monogatari, Sukeroku is later revealed to be Soga Gorō in disguise, working to seek out his father's killer and avenge his father's death.
<br>The play is well-known for a number of iconic elements, including Sukeroku's purple headband, bullseye-pattern umbrella, and distinctive kumadori (face makeup) pattern. After the hero of Shibaraku, Sukeroku might be among the most recognizable characters in kabuki."[1]
<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
<br>"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2]
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

<br><br>[1] The Samurai Archives SamuraiWiki website https://samurai-archives.com/wiki/Sukeroku [accessed 8-23-23]
<br>[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

title: Kakigara-machi Rice Trading Exchange and View of Eitai Bridge (蛎売町米市場・永代橋景)
creator: Utagawa Kunitoshi 歌川国利 (1847-1899)
description:
An uncut sheet depicting two famous places in Tokyo. On top we have the Rice Trading Exchange building in the Kakigara-cho neighborhood of Tokyo. The vertical red cartouche near the Exchange's tower reads 商行会社, referencing the Shōkō Company, which established the exchange in 1874. The vertical red cartouche to the left of the Rice Trading Exchange reads Suitengū 水
天宮, the shrine where couples pray for fertility and safe births.  On the bottom is shown busy Etail (Yetai) Bridge 永代橋 spanning the Sumida and connecting its east bank with Tsukuda Island. There has been a bridge is this spot since 1698, when it was opened to serve as a link between the central part of Edo to the east and the then newly developing area to the west.

title: A List of Noted Places at the Second National Industrial Exposition at Ueno Park (東京名所 上野博覧会一覧 Tōkyō meisho Ueno hakurankai ichiran)
creator: Utagawa Kunitoshi 歌川国利 (1847-1899)
description: A "quick and dirty" triptych giving us a bird's eye view of the notable sites at the Second National Industrial Exposition held in 1881 a Ueno Park in Tokyo from March 1 through June 30. The view provided here by Kunitoshi omits the most famous building at the Exposition, the young British architect Josiah Conder's new art museum with its distinctive twin domed towers. (See IHL.0105 and IHL.1222 for depictions of Conder's museum.)  The Western-style brick building in the upper portion of right panel is the art museum from the the First National Industrial Exhibition held in 1877, which was retained "to serve as a permanent extension to the future museum complex," the cornerstone of which was to be Conder's museum. It may be that the new art museum was not yet completed when this print was published at the end of January 1881.

title: Minamoto no Yorimitsu, No. 27  (源頼光)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
"The famous warrior Minamoto no Yorimitsu (948-1021), also known as Raikō, was devoted to the goddess Benzaiten, who appeared to him in a dream and gave him a special bow and arrow to help him in the way of the martial arts. The inset above the main panel depicts Kidōmaru in the snow wearing the skin of a bull waiting to ambush Yorimitsu. Kidōmaru will meet his fate on the receiving end of an arrow shot from the special bow."[1]

<br><br>This series, consisting of 50 prints, drew its subject matter from 12th through 16th century historical epics and war chronicles. It also uses  "a three part format of a large primary scene topped by a title cartouche at right and a secondary panel set into the upper left corner.  This compositional arrangement encouraged a visual and intellectual conversation among the three segments, allowing subtle commentaries and inflections to be created and/or narratives to be explored."[2]

<br><br>
[1] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 126.
<br>[2] Ibid., p. 37.

title: Surrender of Goryōkaku (函館 五稜郭の降伏)
creator: Hayakawa Shōzan 早川松山 (1850-1892)
description: This print is one of a number of "redemption" prints created during and immediately after Saigō Takamori's failed 1877 Satsuma Rebellion against the Meiji government. These prints sought to redeem Saigō by portraying his earlier exploits fighting to overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate and his subsequent defense of the Meiji government against continuing insurrection by rebellious samurai.<br>This print depicts the June 1869 surrender of the Ezo rebels at Goryōkaku, the "star fort" in Hakodate in southern Hokkaidō. The Ezo rebels were loyalists to the defeated shogunate and the last significant military threat to the Meiji imperial forces. In this scene Saigō Takamori (central figure in the center panel) is demanding (or, perhaps, accepting) the surrender of Enomoto Takeaki 榎本武揚 the leader of the short-lived Ezo Republic (seated and leaning forward in the right panel.)<br>Placing Saigō at the scene of the surrender is taking historical license as Saigō did not reach the rebels stronghold until after the surrender was made to Kuroda Kiyotaka 黑田 清隆, who is not shown in the print.<br>In addition to Saigō and Enomoto, other figures represented are Matsudaira Tarō  海軍 松平太郎, vice president of the Ezo Republic (right panel, figure in green robe); Hijikata Toshizō 土方 歳 三, vice minister of the Ezo army, (right panel, seated behind Matsudaira, and partially hidden from view); Kasuga? Zaemon 春日 左衛門, a captain in the Ezo army (right panel, seated far right in blue-gray shirt); Ootori Keisuke 大鳥圭介 Tokugawa retainer and commander-in-chief Ezo Republic (right panel into center panel, seated and leaning towards Enomoto); Beppu Shinsuke 別府 府助, an officer in the Imperial army and a loyal follower of Saigō (center panel, seated to the left of Saigō); and Arai Chokunoshin? 浅井 直之進, a follower of Saigō (left panel kneeling). The names of the remaining Saigō supporters in the left panel are currently unidentified, i.e. their names in the cartouches have not been translated. The red wigs seen in the left panel identify their wearers as imperial soldiers of the Tosa Domain.<br>Pictured in the background are three ships at anchor in Hakodate Bay, including the Kaiyō Maru 海陽丸 one of Japan's first modern warships and part of the flotilla that Enomoto sailed to Hakodate, and the Kasuga Maru  春日丸, both part of the imperial Japanese navy.

title: Retreat of the Insurgents to the Defensive Position at Hyūga (日向険地江暴徒引退図 Hyūga no kenchi e bōto shirizoku zu)
creator: Yamazaki Toshinobu 山崎年信 (1857-1886)
description:
One of approximately thirty prints by the artist portraying the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877. In this print Saigō Takamori, the rebellion's leader, is seen in the center sheet looking out to the Yatsuhiro Sea where government warships are seen. When this print was issued in May, the rebels have already suffered a major defeat at battle of Tabaruzaka Hill in northern Kagoshima and are in retreat. While the government had offered the rebellious samurai several opportunities to "repent their opposition to the Imperial authority and submit themselves to the same" and be pardoned, they fought on until their final defeat on September 24 at the Battle of Shiroyama.<br>
As in many of the prints portraying the Rebellion the white banner carrying the slogan "Shinsei kotoku" (New Government rich in virtue) is prominently featured. The historian Mark Ravina points out that this slogan never appeared on Saigō's battle pennants, being wholly created by journalists and artists "covering" the rebellion.

title: Ginza Brick Building (銀座煉瓦造 Ginza renga tsukuri)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III (1842–1894) designed at least nine different series depicting early Meiji Era Tokyo landmarks. This scene shows the headquarters of one of the many newspaper offices (possibly that of Nipposha, the publishers of the Tokyo Nichinichi Shinbun) located along the Ginza "Brick Street."  If it is the Nipposha office, it dates this print between the time Nipposha first moved its offices to Ginza in May 1874 to their move to new offices at the end of 1876 at Oharicho 1-chome 1-banchi in Kyobashi-ku.

title: View from Asakusa Bridge to Yanagi Bridge (浅草橋より柳橋の景 Asakusabashi yori Yanagibashi no kei)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III (1842–1894) designed at least nine different series of prints depicting Tokyo landmarks. This scene shows Asakusa Bridge in the foreground with a double-decker horse drawn omnibus on the bridge and Yanagi Bridge in the background along the Kanda River.<br> 
The numbers 一五七 (157) are shown in the left margin. It is not known what these numbers reference. Other prints in this series do not show any numbers in the left margin.

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō as Minamoto no Yoritomo and and Nakamura Fukusuke as Minamoto no Yoshitsune in Kaikei genji yuki no shirahata (会稽源氏雪白旗・市川 団十郎、源兵衛佐頼朝・中村 福助、源九郎義経)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actor Nakamura Fukusuke (IV) in the role of Minamoto no Yoshitsune (left panel) and Ichikawa Danjūrō (IX) in the role of Minamoto no Yoritomo (right panel) in the play Kaikei genji yuki no shirahata 会稽源氏雪白旗 written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893).

title: Wedding Protest, No. 12 appearing in the Ōsaka Nishikiga Shinbun (大阪錦画新聞・第十二号)
creator: Utagawa Yoshitaki 歌川芳滝 (1841-1899)
description:
The wedding of a 15 year old bride is protested by her ex-husband in this print appearing in the "Osaka nishikiga shinbun" (Osaka Illustrated News), which featured woodblock illustrations of stories from various newspapers. The print's text was written by 正情堂九化 (name unread).
<br> At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 and 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability. Following their introduction in Tokyo, nishiki-e shinbun made their appearance in Osaka. The Osaka issued prints differed from their Tokyo counterparts in being half-size (chūban rather than ōban size).

title: Old Man Receives Award appearing in the [Osaka] Nichinichi Shinbun, No. 9 (日々新聞・第九号)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description:
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.<br> This print features an old farmer who has received some type of reward from the government. It is print number 9 out of a known 32 prints appearing in the Osaka-based Nichinichi Shinbun (Daily News) which illustrated stories published in other papers. The red cartouche in the upper left hand corner provides the name of the paper 日々新聞 (Daily News) and the print number 第九号 (9).<br>
Following their introduction in Tokyo, nishiki-e shinbun made their appearance in Osaka. The Osaka issued prints differed from their Tokyo counterparts in being half-size (chūban rather than ōban size).

title: Mt. Fuji Time 25
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: Takahashi has given us at least five views of Mt. Fuji in this print and, possibly, 25 if we take the print's title literally. Wonderful embossing throughout and a barely visible reflection of Fuji in the upper right of the bottom margin.

title: Geometric shapes and half-eye (untitled)
creator: Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955)
description: A posthumous printing of this small monochrome work, printed by Yoneda Minoru, likely under the auspices of the artist's family. It is likely that the original block, carved by Onchi, was used for this print. The print is undated and the artist's catalogue raisonné does not provide a title or date.

Uzaemon in the role of Shirai Gonpachi

creator: Natori Shunsen 名取春仙 (1886-1960)

title: Building (untitled)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Tokuriki gives us an unidentified, likely Shōwa era, building absent any human presence.

title: Castle (城)
creator: Takagi Shirō  高木志朗 (1934-1998)
description:
A castle rises above the trees and hills but this scene is stolen by the intense blue sky. The artist has reused the blocks from his earlier 1967 work titled Evening Over the Castle.<br>
Hirosaki Castle, built in 1611, is the likely model for this print.

title: Pulling Pine Shoots in a Garden, with a Suspension Bridge (小松曳園生之釣橋 Komatsubiki sonō no tsuribashi)
creator:
Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
<br>Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description:
"This triptych was a product of two major Meiji artists, Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889), who designed the scenic imagery, and Toyohara Kunichika, who focused on the characters. The women dressed in red hakama, a style of formal, pleated trousers, seen both in the left and center sheets, are engaged in the once traditional New Year’s custom of pulling young pines. Their garments and hairstyles evoke the imperial court of a millennium earlier when the lady-in-waiting known as Murasaki Shikibu wrote Tale of Genji. The elaborately attired gentleman (right) possibly portrays the novel’s central character, Prince Genji. But there is a twist: his unusual hairstyle appeared first in illustrations for the 1830s serialized parody, Rustic Genji, Fake Murasaki (偐紫田舎源氏) designed by Utagawa Kunisada, Kunichika’s teacher. To add further humorous time warps to the depiction, the British-designed Yamazato suspension bridge of 1870 spans the background."[1]

<br>The artists have signed the print in the areas of their contribution. Kunichika’s signature in the right panel is proceeded with the two characters 人物  (“jinbutsu”) meaning “human figure by.”

<br>Kunichika and Kyōsai were two of the most popular woodblock print artists of the 1870s. Contemporaries, they were “well-acquainted, but at times adversarial, companions.”[2] It was not unusual for publishers to have multiple artists work on different portions of a single print, each being assigned their design strength. Kyōsai and Kunichika first collaborated in 1875 on four single sheet prints in the series Collection of Famous Views of Modern Tokyo, published by the same publisher as this triptych. See this collection's print IHL.0688 for another collaborative print by these two artist.

<br><br>[1] Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)
<br>[2] "Kawanabe Kyosai and Toyohara Kunichika," by Shigeru Oikawa appearing in Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), by Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999, p. 40, 42.

title: View of Yorohibashi from Edobashi (江戸ばしよりよろひ橋の景)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III (1842–1894) designed at least nine different series of prints showing similar depictions of Tokyo landmarks. This scene shows Edobashi Bridge (江戸橋) in the foreground with the First National Bank (daiichi kokuritsu ginko 一国立銀行), constructed in 1872 by Shimizu Kisuke II, in the background (partially covered by the title cartouche.)  As in all "famous view" prints of bridges from this era there is a great deal of hustle and bustle both on and below the bridge.

title: Utō 善知鳥 (Birds of Sorrow)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Minamoto no Yoshiie (源義家)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)

title: Illustration of Debate Over Invading Korea (征韓議論図 Seikangiran zu)
creator: Suzuki Toshimoto 鈴木年基 (active c. 1877-1890s)
description:
This 1877 print depicts the 1873 seikanron debates in the Meiji government's Court Council over whether to invade Korea for ignoring the diplomatic overtures of the Meiji government and "insulting" the Japanese nation. This print is one of many issued in 1877 depicting seikanron, whose outcome led to Saigō Takamori's resignation from the government.  (Saigō would go on to lead the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion against the Meiji government.)<br>
The leaders of opposing factions, Iwakura and Saigō, are prominently shown in the center panel with their partisans shown in the side panels. The debates were fueled by political infighting and the artist Suzuki Toshimoto (active c. 1877-1890s) captures the intensity of emotions.

title: Reeves's Pheasant from Bairei's Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Earth (江南雉,ヲナガキジ・楳嶺百鳥画譜 續編 地 Onagakiji・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, chi)
creator: Kōno Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895)
description: A pheasant is fixated on, and appears ready to attack, a snake in this 2-page print, the 17th double plate in the second volume of Bairei Hyakuchō Gafu, Zokuhen (Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing).

title: Red Capped Black Crane from Bairei's Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Earth (玄鶴, クロヅル 丹鳥 タソテウ・楳嶺百鳥画譜 續編 地 Kurozuru . . . ・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, chi)
creator: Kōno Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895)
description: Red-capped black cranes and their chicks roosting under a full moon are depicted in this two-page print, the 16th double-plate in the second volume of Bairei Hyakuchō Gafu, Zokuhen (Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing).

title: Monkeys Living a Quiet Life in Seclusion
creator: Imao Keinen 今尾景年 (1845-1923) - attributed to the artist
description: A double bookplate, removed from an unknown picture book (gafu 画譜) attributed to the artist Imao Keinen, best known for his kachō-ga, picturing monkeys romping about in a tree. The unread title of the print (partial and unconfirmed 幽棲美術應〓) is written in seal script in the right margin.

title: Leader of the Kinpeibai Quarters (金瓶梅廓魁)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
A male customer coyly holds a fan while a bevy of courtesans vie for his attention.  His gift indicating his choice is being presented to the courtesan on the far right by the young child.<br>
"How to account for the popularity of woodblock prints in Japan ever since their commercialization in the late 1600s? Besides the colorful graphics, the fashions and glimpses of vicarious pleasures, the pictures often held multiple layers of meaning for people to ponder and relish. Scenes that looked like one thing might be cleverly hiding historic intrigues, inside jokes, parodies and more, offering a welter of ways to construe a scene. Here, the reference is to Jinpingmei (Kinpeibai in Japanese), one of China’s Six Classic Novels. To literati, the 16th-century epic marked a new development in narrative art, but to the general reader, it was salacious erotica. In the early 19th century, a serialized version of the novel with illustrations by Kunichika’s teacher, Utagawa Kunisada, had made it widely accessible, beginning a stream of take-offs and re-imaginings, like in this triptych." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

title: Drunken Husband Striking His Wife from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club)
creator: Yamamoto Eishun 山本英春 (1879-?)
description:
A frontispiece woodblock illustration appearing in an unknown issue of the literary magazine Bungei kurabu 文芸倶楽部 (Literary Club), depicting a man about to strike a woman, possibly a husband about to strike his wife in a drunken rage. 
<br><br>THE LITERARY MAGAZINE BUNGEI KURABU
<br>Bungei Kurabu 文芸倶楽部 was a very popular literary magazine published from 1895-1933 by Hakubunkan. It was one of the most dominant venues for Meiji literature, publishing noted authors such as Izumi Kyōka, Kunikida Doppo, Higuchi Ichyō, and Kawakami Bizan.  In the magazine's later years, post 1907, it became a less elevated popular entertainment magazine.

title: Kesa Gozen (袈裟御前)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)

title: Phoenixes from Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Sky (鳳凰, ホウワウ ・楳嶺百鳥畫譜, 續編 天 Hōō・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, ten)
creator: Kōno Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895)
description: Two mythical phoenixes in flight with Mt. Fuji in background. The first plate in the first volume of Bairei Hyakuchō Gafu, Zokuhen (Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing).

title: Common Cormorants from Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing, Sky (鸕鷀, ウ・楳嶺百鳥畫譜, 續編 天 U・Bairei hyakuchō gafu, zokuhen, ten)
creator: Kōno Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895)
description: Three cormorants, one grooming and two fishing, are depicted in this double-page print, the 3rd double plate in the first volume of Bairei Hyakuchō Gafu, Zokuhen (Bairei's Picture Album of One Hundred Birds, Continuing). The title appearing on the print reads 鸕鷀 ウ, combining the Chinese characters 鸕鷀 for cormorant and the Japanese katakana ウ for cormorant.

title: Priest on a Virtuous Path and Priest on a Debauched Path (善道へ導く僧  佛道を破る僧)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
One of twenty prints from the series Moral Lessons through Pictures of Good and Evil picturing a virtuous priest who guides people along the proper path and a debauched priest who destroys the Buddhist path by seducing a woman. 
<br><b>About The Series Moral Lessons through Pictures of Good and Evil</b>
<br>These lessons in morality were originally issued as twenty single oban-size sheets containing two paired chūban-size prints contrasting "good" behavior with "bad" behavior.  Over time many of the full-size oban sheets have been cut into separate chūban size prints.
<br>Little figures portraying good souls (zendama) and evil souls (akudama) populate each print. The faces of the zendama and akudama show variations of the characters 善 (good) and 悪 (evil).  These figures originated with the author and printmaker Santō Kyōden in his 1790 book Shingaku hayasomegusa (“Learning of the Mind [or Heart] in Fast Dyes”) and they started commonly appearing in woodblock prints shortly thereafter. 
<br>Each print in the series carries the signature "ryōdōjin Yoshitoshi giga." Ryōdōjin, a person who knows both ways, suggests that the artist, perhaps like ourselves, knows both the good and evil in himself.

title: Apprentices who Obey their Master and Apprentices who Disobey their Master (主人の教へを守る丁稚  主人の教へを守らざる丁稚)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
One of twenty prints from the series Moral Lessons through Pictures of Good and Evil picturing diligent apprentices working by lamplight who follow their master's advice and apprentices at a street stall being lead astray, not regarding their master's care.
<br><b>About The Series Moral Lessons through Pictures of Good and Evil</b>
<br>These lessons in morality were originally issued as twenty single oban-size sheets containing two paired chūban-size prints contrasting "good" behavior with "bad" behavior.  Over time many of the full-size oban sheets have been cut into separate chūban size prints.
<br>Little figures portraying good souls (zendama) and evil souls (akudama) populate each print. The faces of the zendama and akudama show variations of the characters 善 (good) and 悪 (evil).  These figures originated with the author and printmaker Santō Kyōden in his 1790 book Shingaku hayasomegusa (“Learning of the Mind [or Heart] in Fast Dyes”) and they started commonly appearing in woodblock prints shortly thereafter. 
<br>Each print in the series carries the signature "ryōdōjin Yoshitoshi giga". Ryōdōjin, a person who knows both ways, suggests that the artist, perhaps like ourselves, knows both the good and evil in himself.

title: Famous Soldiers of Japan (日本 武名 伝図 Nihon bumei den)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
In commenting on this print Roger Keyes states “Most of the aka-e, or red prints, were revolting, but the same colors could produce great beauty when the subject touched the artist’s nobler feelings. The aniline red that Yoshitoshi used for this picture of General Saigo and the other heroes of the Satsuma Rebellion is as striking and effective as the background of the Red Room of Matisse. The portraits seem quite individual and were probably recognizable likenesses. Perhaps this was one of three or four prints that the government commissioned Yoshitoshi to design for display in foreign exhibitions. The artist took these commissions very seriously and spent considerable time on their execution. Yoshitoshi’s drawing had often been tentative and broad; like Daumier, he enjoyed exaggeration and expressive distortions more than literal likeness and detailed renderings. But there was also pleasure in drawing with a finer brush and greater delicacy. The faces of the officers are quite distinct and individual, and Yoshitoshi may have drawn them from life, or from photographs."
<br>A Few Personal Comments on Keyes' Commentary - To my eye Yoshitoshi's renderings of these 15 men are a bit stiff.  In many of the portraits the heads seem stuck on to the bodies. Perhaps several carvers were involved causing this strange effect. As to the likenesses of the portraits, I've located photographs or period renderings of all the subjects and there are definite likenesses between some of the photos and Yoshitoshi's drawings. 
<br>Left sheet: Prince Arisugawa Taruhito 有栖川宮熾仁親王 (1835–1895) (center top), Kabayama Sukenori 樺山資紀 (1837-1922) (upper left), Tani Tateki 谷干城 (1837-1911) (upper right), Kawamura Sumiyoshi 川村 純義 (1836-1904) (lower left), Nozu Shizuo 野津鎮雄 (1835-1880) (lower right)

<br>Center sheet: Saigō Takamori 西郷隆盛 (1827-1877) (seated center), Kawaji Toshiyoshi 川路 利良 (1834-1879) (upper left), Torio Koyata 鳥尾 (1847-1905) (upper right), Prince Yamagata Aritomo 山縣 有朋 (1838–1922) (lower left), Miyoshi Shigeomi 三好 重臣 (1840-1900) (lower right)

<br>Right sheet: Prince Higashifushimi Yoshiaki  少将 東伏見宮 (1846-1903) (center), Kazukatsu? Fukuhara 福原 和勝 (1846-1877) (upper left), Yamakawa Hiroshi 山川 浩 (1845-1898) (upper right),  Saigō Tsugumichi 西郷 従道 (1843–1902) (lower left), Kuroda Kiyotaka 黑田 清隆  (1840-1900) (lower right)

title: The Rising Moon (月の出 Tsuki no de)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)

title: The Living Corpse (生ける屍 Ikerushikabane)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
This print is one of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫  (1929-?).
<br> This print's title "The Living Corpse" references Tolstoy's play of the same name written in 1900 which tells the story of a worthless husband's failure and final sacrifice. The print is a woodblock reproduction of Yumeji's 1917-1918 painting of the same title.
<br>In commenting on Yumeji's women, Lawrence Smith perceives "a subtle transference of European facial expression" even when the women are placed in traditional settings as in this work.
<br>As in this case, the majority of Yumeji's woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934 and were based upon his paintings or previous designs for song sheets and postcards. They were often rescaled to accommodate standardized sizes of paper used for woodblock prints. Major publishers involved with producing these posthumous prints were Kyōto Hanga-in under the direction of Shinagawa Kiyoomi 品川清臣 (1907-?) and Katō Junji 加藤潤二 (1885-1961) and his Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjo.)

title: Neighbor's Dream
creator: Yoshida Tōshi 吉田遠志 (1911-1995)
description: A vibrant and sparkling waterfall of turquoise striations fractured by black and violet organic shapes. "Between 1954 and 1973, Toshi made nearly three hundred nonobjective prints . . . that signal his desire to use color, shape, line, and texture expressively to capture the nature of human experience or the human experience of nature." - Source: A Japanese Legacy: Four Generations of Yoshida Family Artists, Laura W. Allen, Kendall H. Brown, Eugene M. Skibbe, et. al., The Minneapolis Institute of Arts, 2002, p. 76.

title: Illustration of Royal Visit to Ueno Park Exhibition (上野公園博覧会行幸之図 Ueno kōen hakurankai gyōkō no zu)
creator: Kobayashi Ikuhide 小林幾英 (active c. 1880-1898)
description: The emperor, empress and young crown prince are shown arriving at the Third National Industrial Exhibition in Ueno Park, which despite attracting over 1 million visitors was considered somewhat of a failure, held against a backdrop of recession and an influenza epidemic.  <br>Five industrial expositions were held in Japan during the Meiji era, the first three in Ueno Park, Tokyo (1877, 1881, 1890), and the last two respectively in Kyoto (1895) and Osaka (1903). Printmakers were quick to create images of the domestic expositions to be sold as souvenirs. For another print showing the royal family arriving at the exhibition see Illustration of the Emperor and Empress Arriving at the Third National Industrial Exhibition (IHL.0079).

title: Picture of Pyongyang Chinese Generals Capture and Surrender (平壤陷落清將生捕の圖)
creator: Nagashima Shungyō 永嶌春暁 (active 1882-1905)
description: This print portrays the fierce fighting to capture Pyongyang (Pingyang), Korea from the Chinese during the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) and the resulting surrender and capture of five of the Chinese commanders defending the city.  Interestingly, the Chinese Commander Tso Pao-kwei (Zuo Baogui) shown in the orange robe did not surrender and was killed in the fighting, suggesting that, as in many war prints, facts were manipulated for propaganda purposes.

title: Illustration of the Occupation of the Taku Forts and the Hard Fight of Navy Lt. Colonel Hattori (服部海軍 中佐奮戦 太沽砲台 占領之図 Hattori kaigun chūsa funsen Taiko hōdai senryō no zu)
creator: Unknown
description: This 1900 Boxer Rebellion print gives us a bird's-eye view, through the smoke of the artillery shelling, of the attack on the Chinese Taku (Dagu) Forts on June 17, 1900. Lt. Colonel Hattori of the Japanese Navy, in black uniform with raised sword, is pictured directing the attack by Japanese troops on the North-West Fort. Hattori's rank is variously given in historical documents as commander, captain and lieutenant colonel. He was to die in the assault. Stick-like figures scattered throughout the print show soldiers of the Eight Nation Alliance battling Chinese army and Boxer irregular forces. <br>A correspondent from the British newspaper Telegraph recounted, "The first fort was taken by the Japanese, and the second by the British, and then the Germans and Russians secured the south fort . . . . After the forts were captured they were visited by the foreign officers. They presented a ghastly sight. The forts were one mass of ruins, and rivers of blood, mutilated bodies lying everywhere. The Chinese troops fled to Tientsin."

title: The Dance Michiyuki tabiji no, hanamuko, an interact in the play Kanadehon Chūshingura with the characters Koshimoto Okaru, Fukuroku and Daikoku (道行旅路の花聟・仮名手本忠臣蔵・こし元おかる、福ろく、大こく)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description:
This print is the left sheet of a triptych depicting the three main characters Okaru, Kampei and Bannai in the interact hengemono (multi-role dance) Michiyuki tabiji no hanamuko. This dance was staged after Act IV, scene 2, Uramon (“The Rear Gate of the Mansion”) of the kabuki play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers.) The actors and characters pictured in this left sheet are Nakamura Fukusuke (中村 福助) as Koshimoto Okaru (こし元おかる) and, in the insets, Nakamura Fukusuke, again, as Fukuroku (福ろく), one of the Seven Lucky Gods, and Bandō Mitsugorō VI (坂東 三津五郎) as Ōkoku (大こく), another of the Seven Lucky Gods.
<br>This michiyuki or “travel-dance” was added to the play in 1833 and is very often performed separately. The dance depicts the lovers Okaru and Kanpei journeying to the home of Okaru’s parents in the country after Hangan’s death. Kanpei was the retainer who accompanied Hangan to the shogun’s mansion and he is now guilt ridden at his failure to protect his lord. He would take his own life to atone for his sin, but Okaru persuades him to wait. The couple are waylaid by the comical Sagisaki Bannai and his foolish men. They are working for Lord Moronō but Kanpei easily defeats them and they continue on their way.
<br>The performance date for this piece was the 13th day of the 10th month, Ansei 4 (1857) and it was staged at the Morita-za.

title: The True Story of Arashi from Osaka (浪花之嵐實録噺 Naniwa no Arashi jitsuroku hanashi）
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

title: Tsukuba Mountain Seen from Sakura River at Hitachi (常陸桜川より筑波山を臨む Hitachi Sakuragawa yori Tsukubasan o nozomu)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
Number 20 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meishō xue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897. <br>
Kiyochika gives us a view of the double peaks of Tsukuba-san on a windswept day. The figures are leaning into the wind as they attend to their tasks and the tree attests to the force of the wind.

title: Kyōto, Imperial Palace, End (京都・大尾・内裏 Kyōto・Daibi・Dairi)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description: The last print in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Dairi, the Imperial Palace in Kyōto. The characters 大尾 (daibi), "end", appear in the right-most yellow rectangular cartouche in the bottom left of the print telling us that we've arrived, after a long journey, in Kyoto, the Imperial Capital, at the Imperial Palace.<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.<br> Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

title: Odawara, Sakogawa, No. 10 (小田原・酒匂川・十)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Print number 10 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting porters carrying a trunk and a traveler crossing the Sakagawa leading into Odawara the ninth station along the Tōkaidō. Another traveler is mounting a porter on the far shore and four porters bear a traveler in a litter. Odawara was the first post station in the castle town that travelers came to when they exited Edo (modern-day Tokyo).
<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.<br> Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

title: Sakanoshita, Fudesute, No. 49 (坂ノ下・筆捨やま・四十九)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Print number 49 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Fudesute peak in Sakanoshita the forty-eighth station along the Tōkaidō. Sakanoshita is located in the present-day city of Kameyama, in Mie Prefecture, Japan.<br>
The artist provides us a view of Fudesute peak as it might be seen by travelers on the Tōkaidō but, interestingly, no travelers are seen in this print. Fudesute, means literally "to throw away the brush," as its extreme beauty and strangeness is beyond our ability to paint.<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.<br> Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

title: Shōno, Ichirizuka, No. 46 (庄野・一り塚・四十六)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Print number 46 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Shōno the forty-fifth station along the Tōkaidō, located in the present-day city of Suzuka, Mie Prefecture, Japan.  Shōno was the smallest station on the Tōkaidō.
<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. title: Goyu, No. 36 (御油・夕景・三十六)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Print number 36 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting travelers in sedge hats entering Goyu at dusk. It appears as though the travelers are hurrying away from courtesans who are seen grasping at them.<br>Goyu was the thirty-fifth station along the Tōkaidō. Goyu-shuku was established in 1601, at the behest of Tokugawa Ieyasu. At its most prosperous, there were four honjin (inns) in the post town, though there were never less than two at any point.<br>
<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.<br> Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

title: Seki, Honjin, No. 48 (関・本陣・四十八)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Print number 48 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Seki the forty-seventh station along the Tōkaidō. The area around Seki-juku was always a major intersection for travel. During the Edo period, it was a lively post town, because both the Isebetsu Kaidō 伊勢別街道 and the Yamato Kaidō 大和街道 intersected with the Tōkaidō here.<br>
In this print, an arriving daimyō (seated on the litter) and his retinue are being greeted by the owner and staff of the honjin where they will spend the night. The draperies are decorated with the family crest of the arriving daimyō.<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.<br> Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

title: Chiryū, Umaichi, No. 40 (地鯉鮒・馬市・四十)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Print number 40 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting, Chiryū the thirty-ninth station along the Tōkaidō. During the Edo period, Chiryū was the westernmost post town in Mikawa Province. Three hundred and thirty kilometers from Nihonbashi, the start of the Tōkaidō, it took approximately 10 days to get there.<br>
Chiryū-juku was well known as a horse trading town and the artist has pictured horses with their minders in a grassy field.<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.<br> Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description: Print number 45 in this series of 58 prints titled Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road issued in October 1865, depicting Ishiyakushi the forty-fourth station along the Tōkaidō. Ishiyakushi received its name from the nearby Buddhist temple, Ishiyakushi-ji which can be seen in the background of this print.<br>In 1865, four years before his death, Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) produced his third and last Tōkaidō series. This vertical chūban-size series was issued in at least three different editions, plus a crêped edition, attesting to its popularity.<br> Starting with Nihonbashi (the starting point located in Edo for measuring all distances) and ending with Kyoto's Imperial Palace, the series portrayed all 53 stations along the Tōkaidō and contained a total of 58 prints.

title: Greedy Merchant, No. 7
creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)
description: The prints in this series were issued in pairs and show comparisons between good (appropriate) behavior and bad (inappropriate) behavior. In this print which would have been the top print, if it had not been separated from its counterpart, we see a greedy merchant, abacus in hand, being encouraged by six bad souls (akudama) identified by the character 悪 (badness, vice) in the rounds of their faces. In its counterpart, the bottom print, (see IHL.0527) five good souls (zendama) identified by the character ‘zen’ 善 (goodness, virtue) are assisting the merchant in his shop.

title: Solicitous Merchant, No. 7
creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)
description: The prints in this series were issued in pairs and show comparisons between good (appropriate) behavior and bad (inappropriate) behavior. In this print which would have been the bottom print, if it had not been separated from its counterpart, we see five good souls  (zendama) identified by the character ‘zen’ 善 (goodness, virtue) assisting a good merchant in his shop. In its counterpart of good behavior (see IHL.0526) we see a merchant displaying bad 悪 behavior.

title: Illustration of the Attack on the Battery at Weihaiwei (威海衛鹿角嘴砲台攻撃之図)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description: Chinese soldiers' bodies fly as Japanese warships pound the Chinese forts defending Weihaiwei (Ikaiei in Japanese) as Japanese forces storm the battery. The naval port of Weihaiwe fell to the Japanese on February 17, 1895. The Germans had helped the Chinese Qing government build the naval base at Weihaiwei and they designed and equipped the batteries.

title: Illustration of the Viewing of the Captured Chinese Warship Chinen at Yokosuka Naval Port (横須賀軍港鎮遠号観覧之図 Yokosuka gankō Chinengō kanran no zu)
creator: Ogata Gekkō 尾形月耕 (1859-1920)
description:
The Chinese battleship Chinen 鎮遠 (Chinese: Zhenyuan 鎮遠; also romanized as Chenyuen) in its new home port at the Yokosuka navy yard in Kanagawa Prefecture after her capture following the Weihaiwei siege on February 17, 1895. The Chinen was a German-built Chinese Beiyang Fleet turret ship built with 14-inch (360 mm) thick armor and modern Krupp guns, superior to any in the Imperial Japanese Navy at the time. She would see service in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) and be scrapped in 1914.
<br>"After the surrender at Weihaiwei, the Chenyuen [Chinen] was taken to Yokosuka, where the public was invited to see the 7,300-ton ironclad. One war reporter, Nagamatsu of the Jiji Shimpo wrote, 'Since the beginning of the war, all over Japan, men and women, young and old, have spoken of the Chinese ironclads Chenyuen and Tingyuen.  Now that the Chenyuen has been captured and brought to Japan, it is understandable that everyone should want to see it. Before the public opening, Japanese naval officers constantly had to entertain visitors aboard. On August 5, the ship was opened to the public. Throngs from Tokyo and Yokohama, and even some who must travel overnight, are suddenly crowding Yokosuka. Already on the fourth, there was not a vacant room in town. Earlier, in Nagasaki, so many people visited the Chenyuen that the waterline sank one foot. Perhaps it will be worse in Yokosuka; the train between Shinbashi in downtown Tokyo and Yokosuka has been packed.'" - Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Shunpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p. 44.

title: Captain Matsuzaki Crossing the Anjō River and Advancing into the Enemy's Territory  (松嵜大尉 挺オ安城川ヲ渡リ敵中ニ進厶圖)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)
