title: Memoirs of Fallen Flowers, frontispiece from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 7, No.5. (落花録・文藝倶楽部 第七巻, 第五号)
creator: Takeuchi Keishū 武内桂舟 (1861-1942)
description:
This woodblock illustration (kuchi-e) portrays a young woman in her summer robe (yukata) drying herself after bathing. This print was the frontispiece for volume 7, no. 5 of the literary magazine Bungei Kurabu (Literary Arts Club), published in Meiji 34th year (1901) which carried, either in its entirety or a portion thereof, the novel Rakkaroku 落花録 (Memoirs of Fallen Flowers) by the writer Suiin Emi (1869-1934).

<br><br>THE LITERARY MAGAZINE BUNGEI KURABU
<br>Bungei Kurabu 文芸倶楽部 was a very popular literary magazine published from 1895-1933 by Hakubunkan. It was one of the most dominant venues for Meiji literature, publishing noted authors such as Izumi Kyōka, Kunikida Doppo, Higuchi Ichyō, and Kawakami Bizan.  In the magazine's later years, post 1907, it became a less elevated popular entertainment magazine.

title: The Story of Wankyū, Vol. 2, frontispiece from the magazine Bungei kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 6, No.1. (椀久物語・文藝倶楽部 第六巻, 第一号 Wankyū Monogatari dai-nibu・Bungei kurabu dai rokukan, dai ichigō)
creator: Takeuchi Keishū 武内桂舟 (1861-1942)
description:
This print was the frontispiece for volume 6, no. 1 of the literary magazine Bungei Kurabu (Literary Arts Club), published January 1, 1900, which featured the story "Wankyū monogatari, The Story of the Dish-Potter Kyūbei," by Kōda Rohan 幸田露伴 (1867-1947). In this illustration for the story, a potter inspects a full Noborigama kiln. An inset shows an elegant bijin in the style of the Muromachi period. 

<br><br>"Wankyū monogatari, The Story of the Dish-Potter Kyūbei," is based on the true 17th century story of a potter and a courtesan, their love affair and involvement in trade espionage.  "A Kyoto potter Kyūbei begins to seek the favors of a courtesan Matsuyama, after he learns that her father is a debt collector from the Kyushu potters' guild, whose secret of gold-painted porcelain is jealously guarded. Through the help of Matsuyama, he finally induces her unsuspecting father to confide the secret. Kyūbei succeeds in producing a new porcelain even superior to the Kyushu products, but loses his mind after Matsuyama's father is executed for revealing the trade secret inadvertently. He recovers later, eventually to settle down to a happy married life with Matsuyama." - Source: Kōda Rohan, Chieko Irie Mulhern, Twayne Publishers, 1977, p. 127.

title: Making Chinese Soldiers Shiver (清兵の冷かされ Shinpei no hiyakasare)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
In this print Chinese soldiers are shivering before a snowman with the head of a Japanese general. The inscription explains that the generals of the Japanese army, Aritomo Yamagata 山縣有朋 and Ōyama Iwao 大山巌 both have the character "mountain" (山 yama) in their names and are therefore so immovable, impressive and insanely strong that the weak soldiers of the Qing dynasty tremble with fear. There is some wordplay going in the inscription having to do with the same Japanese characters making up the expressions "making someone cold" and "mocking someone."

title: Russo-Japanese War Pictorial part 6: Fierce Fight in the Vicinity of Pyongyang (日露戦争画報其六:平壌附近激戦 Nichiro sensōgahō roku: heijō fukin gekisen)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
From the print's title, it is safe to assume that it is one of a series by the artist Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) depicting battles in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905).<br>
It is unknown what battle is depicted, but the title does tells us that this fierce battle happened in the vicinity of Pyongyang (Pingyang), possibly referring to the following incident, cited in the 1906 account of the war by Great Britain's War Office. <br>"As a preliminary step, however, Pingyang, the most important town in North Korea, lying one hundred and fifty miles, or twelve days’ march, north of Seoul, had been already garrisoned. On the 21st February a party of twenty Japanese infantry with a commissariat officer arrived there, and drove off a small body of Cossacks who attempted to enter the town… [A]nother company of infantry, with a commissariat officer was sent north from the capital , on the 15th, to prepare four line-of-communication posts. By means of this arrangement the cavalry of the 12th Division reached Pingyang from Seoul on the 23rd and assured the safety of the little garrison." - Source: The Russo-Japanese War, Part I, compiled by The General Staff, War Office (Great Britain), London, 1906, p. 45.

title: Iwami Province: Mount Takazuno, Salt Beach (石見国・高津山汐浜  Iwami no kuni・Takazunoyama Shiohama)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
Print number 47 四十七 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints. The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.
<br>This print pictures the harvesting of salt on the beach below Mount Takazuno. Hiroshige III has been inspired by (or just copied) the scene from his master Utagawa Hiroshige I's 1853 print Iwama Province, Salt Beaches at Takatsu from the series Famous Views in the Sixty Odd Provinces.<br>Iwami (石見国; -no kuni) was an old province of Japan in the area that is today the western part of Shimane Prefecture. Iwami bordered Aki, Bingo, Izumo, Nagato, and Suō provinces.<br>The price of the print in rin (rin = 0.001 yen), 定價壹弐五厘 (fixed price of 125 rin) is given beneath the date in the rectangular cartouche in the left margin.

title: Harvesting Lacquer in Mikawa Province (同国 [三河] 漆取之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the tapping of lacquer 漆 trees in Mikawa Province. Mikawa Province (三河国, Mikawa no kuni) is an old province in the area that today forms the eastern half of Aichi Prefecture.

title: Mandarin Orange Plantation in Kii Province (紀伊国蜜柑山畑之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts workers harvesting mandarin oranges in a terraced grove in Kii province. Kii Province (紀伊国, Kii no Kuni), or Kishū (紀州), was a province of Japan in the part of Honshū that is today Wakayama Prefecture, as well as the southern part of Mie Prefecture. Kishū has been a major orange growing area for centuries. Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan describes a scene much as depicted in this print. "We are now in the district of Arida [in Kishū province], notable as the greatest orange-producing centre in Japan; and as we proceed, we find all the lower slopes of the wide sheltered valleys covered with orange-groves.<br>
See IHL.1919 for the crêped version of the print.

title: White Sugar Production in Sanuki Province (讃岐国白糖製造之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts workers refining white sugar in Sanuki province. Sanuki (讃岐国,) was an old province of Japan on the island of Shikoku, with the same boundaries as modern Kagawa Prefecture. It faced the Inland Sea and bordered on Awa and Iyo Provinces. Across Naruto strait it bordered Awaji Province too. Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan, notes that "The chief production of this province of Sanuki are popularly known as ‘the three white things’ (sam-paku), viz, salt, sugar, and cotton. The sugar industry is modern, having been introduced from Satsuma only half a century ago." But he also describes scenes more like the one pictured above. "The cultivation of the rich plain includes indigo and sugar; and those curious in such matters will find establishments here and there where sugar-refining is carried on with very primitive machinery."

title: Camphor Manufacture in Hyūga Province (日向国樟脳製之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts workers preparing camphor 樟脳 in Hyūga province, an old province of Japan on the east coast of Kyūshū, corresponding to the modern Miyazaki Prefecture. Hyūga bordered on Bungo, Higo, Ōsumi, and Satsuma Provinces. Camphor was widely produced throughout Kyūshū Island.

title: The Battle at Tianzhuangdai: The Gathering of Eleven Generals (田庄台之役・将校十一名 Denshōdai no yaku・shōkō jūichimei dōsho ni kai su)
creator: Ogata Gekkō 尾形月耕 (1859-1920)
description:
Nathan Chaikin comments, "one of Gekkō's masterpieces. The range of colours, totally his, the beautiful conception of the 'end of the day,' the raging fire and the tormented pine trees soon to burst into flames, the whiteness of the snow, and a certain sense of futility pervading the morning, the feeling of wastefulness of it all.  Yes, a very great artist, a master . . . .
<br>"The entire staff, an imposing one, stands still as the city is burning. Their names as they appear on the script: Yamaji, Chūjō (Lieutenant-General); Oshima Hisanao, Shōsō (Major-General); Nozu, Taishō (Marshal); Katsura, Chūjō; Nogi, Shōsō; Nishi, Shōsō; Oshima Yoshimasa, Shōsō; Oseko, Shōsō; Kuroda, Shōsō; Oku (perhaps Okuyama?), Chūjō; Ogawa, Shōsō.
<br>"This is the end of the road for the Japanese. The Chinese retreated to North Chinchou (or Chinchow), and the country was now clear of them on both sides of the Liao river for a distance of 30 to 40 miles northeast of Yingkow (or Yingtzu), whilst on the Liaoyang road their most advanced post was north-east of Anchanchan." Source: The Sino-Japanese War, Nathan Chaikin, self-published, 1983, p. 97.

title: Sino-Japanese War: Japanese Military Might Captures Pyongyang (日清戰爭・日勢平壌勝捕圖 Nisshin sensō・Nissei Heijō shōhō zu)
creator: Ogata Gekkō 尾形月耕 (1859-1920)
description:
In late July 1894, Japan began military operations in Korea against China, which had established itself as Korea's suzerain in 1860. Within a month Pyongyang was China's last position held in Korea and by September 16 they had lost this city to a Japanese assault.
<br>"Ogata Gekko, a leading print designer and illustrator, here describes a scene in which Japanese soldiers have captured several Chinese soldiers in the foreground. One has just been pushed over the edge of the wall on the roof of a building they were defending. In the distance, a fierce battle rages, giving rise to billowing smoke and the orange streaks of gunfire." - Source: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, print label.

title: Illustration of the Surrender of Port Arthur (旅順口陷落之圖 Ryojunkō kanraku no zu)
creator: Ogata Gekkō 尾形月耕 (1859-1920)
description:
While seventeen Chinese forts defended Port Arthur, all "heavily armed with powerful Krupp and Armstrong guns,” it took the Japanese forces under five hours to capture them.
<br>The attack was scheduled for November 21, at 6:50 a.m., with all siege guns roaring at the same time, awakening the Chinese garrisons in the Itzu-shan Fort. At 8 a.m. the fort was in Japanese hands (2nd Infantry Sakura Brigade), unopposed; at 8:10, all three forts were taken. At 11:10, the Pine Tree Hill for fell; at 11:25 a.m. the Two Dragon Hill fort was captured; all the other forts were abandoned by their garrisons. 
<br>"With the fall of Port Arthur, the Japanese were in possession of the finest dockyards in the Far East and a splendid naval base of operation at the enemy's back doors. Japanese losses: 18 killed, 258 wounded and 8 missing. The Chinese lost over 1,000 men." - Source: The Sino-Japanese War, Nathan Chaikin, self-published, 1983, p. 82-83

title: Things Suspended in the Sky (そらにかかるもの)
creator: Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955)
description: This print is the frontispiece in the catalogue raisonné of Onchi's prints (and some of his drawings) titled "Prints of Onchi Kōshirō," Keishosha Ltd., 1975 (a limited edition of 670 copies.) The catalogue raisonné titles the print correctly in Japanese そらにかかるもの (Things Suspended from the Sky) but then mistitles the print's English title as Shadow Falling From the Sky, a different print by Onchi.<br>Reprinted by Yoneda Minoru for the catalogue raisonné, likely under the auspices of the artist's family, the print originally appeared in issue III of the small print and poetry magazine "Tsukuhae" (Moonglow), a collaborative effort of Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), Shizuo Fujimori (1891-1943) and Tanaka Kyokichi (1892-1915). This image was again reprinted in 1989 by Onchi's son, Onchi Kunio 恩地邦郎 (1920-2001).

title: Another Garland of Swashbuckling Heroes of the Shrimp Barbershop (又注連餝俠客之海老床 Mata shime kazari isami no ebi doko)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: Three actors stand in front of a barbershop’s shoji decorated with a painting of a giant shrimp (ebi). No specific play is referenced in the print, perhaps making it an advertisement for the Shrimp Barbershop. This is not as strange as it seems, as kabuki stars spent hours in the barbershop having their sakayaki (the shaved part of the forehead) looked after. Perhaps the Shrimp Barbershop business card read “Hairstylists to the Stars."<br>Two translations of the print's title cartouche "Mata shime kazari isami no ebi doko" (又注連餝俠客之海老床) have been suggested, "Another Story of Chivalrous Guys (otokodate) at Ebidoko Barber Shop in the New Year Season" and "Another Garland of Swashbuckling Heroes of the Shrimp Barbershop."<br>The actors pictured, while not named in cartouches on the print, would have been recognizable to the public by the patterns and the partial letters of their stage names visible on their garments. From left to right: Ichimura Uzaemon XIII (possibly Uzaemon XIV), according to the pattern of his clothes; Kawarazaki Gonjūrō by the half-hidden stage name on his collar and Bando Shinsui by the two kanji characters 薪水 (Shinsui) on his robe.

title: Iga Province: Ueno Nagata River (伊賀国・上野 長田川 Iga no kuni・Ueno Nagatagawa)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: Print number 6 六 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints. The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.<br>This print pictures the village of Ueno 上野 and a bridge over the Nagata River 長田川. The village was located near Iga Ueno Castle, built around 1570 and known for having the highest stone wall in Japan. Hiroshige III has been inspired by (or just copied) his master Utagawa Hiroshige I's 1853 print Iga Province: Ueno  from the series Famous Places in the Sixty Odd Provinces.

title: Mustache Shaving, Opposite Mirrors, Laughing Child, Crying Child (髭すりhigesori, 合せ鏡 awasekagami , 笑ってゐる児 warateiru ko, 泣て居る児 naiteiru ko)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
One of twenty-five prints created by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915), each showing four faces in caricature. The first eight prints were issued in 1882  and published by Hara Taneaki under the series title Thirty-Two Faces, New Edition. The series was so popular that it led to a second series in early 1883 titled One Hundred Faces: Supplement to Thirty-Two Faces (Sanjūni sō tsuika hyakumensō), some of which were published by Hara, the remainder by Morimoto Junzaburō.<br>
"[T]he theme of "one hundred faces" (hyakumensō) came originally from a vaudeville act of the late Edo period in which a performer imitated emotional states and social types by rapidly changing facial expression with various props." Kiyochika's prints were so popular that they "led to a staging of the series by the kabuki actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX at the Shintomiza Theater on April 23, 1883 . . . ." - Source: Kiyochika: Artist of Meiji Japan, Henry D. Smith II, Santa Barbara Museum of Art, 1988, p. 60-61.

title: Illustration of Imperial Visit of Mikado Ingyō to Princess Sotoshi (允恭帝衣通姫之許ニ御幸之図 Ingyōtei Soto'ori hime no tokoro ni gyokō no zu)
creator: Kobayashi Eitaku 小林永濯 (1843-1890)
description:
This print depicts a night-time visit by the fifth-century Emperor Ingyō (c. 411-453) to his lover Princess Sotoshi no iratsume (aka Sotori), the younger sister of Empress Oshisaka no Ōnakatsuhime. In order not to offend the Empress, the Emperor provided a residence for Princess Sotoshi far away from the Empress, first in Fujiwara near Asuka and then in Chinu in Kawachi on the Inland Sea, and made secret visits to her. (Of course the Empress knew about the visits.)
<br>In the eighth year, spring, the second month, he (the Emperor) went to Fujiwara and secretly observed the demeanor of Lady Sotori. That evening Lady Sotori was alone, yearning for the Emperor. Unaware that the Emperor had come, she composed a song, saying:<br>

<br>Tonight is the night
<br>My young love will come to me:
<br>Little bamboo crab
<br>Spider’s antics make it clear.
<br>Oh, very clear tonight!
<br>
<br>This poem made Princess Sotori famous, and she later became a deity of poetry. -  Source: A Waka Anthology: The Gem-Glistening Cup, Edwin A. Cranston, 1993, Stanford University Press, p. 85.

title: Album-Leaf (斷片)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
This song sheet for the composition "Album-Leaf" (Senow song sheet No. 623) by the Russian composer Alexander Scriabin スクリアビン (1872-1915), with cover design (a color lithograph) by Takehisa Yumeji (1884-1934), a leading figure in the Taishō Romanticism movement, was issued in 1925 by the music publisher Senow Ongaku Shuppansha. <br><br>
In 1910 the music publisher Senoo (Senow) Ongaku Shuppansha, headed by Senoo Kōjirō 妹尾幸次郎 (1891-1961), also known as Senoo Kōyō 妹尾幸陽, began issuing musical scores, the majority of them by Western composers. Over 1000 scores for classical and popular music, including children’s music, were issued, many under the titles “Senoo Gakufu” (セノオ楽譜) and “Senoo Shin-kouta" (セノオ新小唄). From 1916 until 1929, Yumeji designed over 280 covers for Senoo’s published scores and contributed the lyrics for 24 songs of his own, the most famous of which is “Evening Primrose” (Yoimachigusa), published in 1918. The scores became very popular although few people could read or play the scores. They were bought because of their cover art.

This song sheet for the composition "Oki-no-kamone ni" (Senow song sheet No. 1038) by the composer and conductor Yamada Kōsaku 山田耕筰 (1886-1965), with cover design (a color lithograph) by Takehisa Yumeji (1884-1934), a leading figure in the Taishō Romanticism movement, was originally issued in 1915  by the music publisher Senow Ongaku Shuppansha. This collection's song sheet is a third edition as noted in the colophon. <br><br>
In 1910 the music publisher Senoo (Senow) Ongaku Shuppansha, headed by Senoo Kōjirō 妹尾幸次郎 (1891-1961), also known as Senoo Kōyō 妹尾幸陽, began issuing musical scores, the majority of them by Western composers. Over 1000 scores for classical and popular music, including children’s music, were issued, many under the titles “Senoo Gakufu” (セノオ楽譜) and “Senoo Shin-kouta" (セノオ新小唄). From 1916 until 1929, Yumeji designed over 280 covers for Senoo’s published scores and contributed the lyrics for 24 songs of his own, the most famous of which is “Evening Primrose” (Yoimachigusa), published in 1918. The scores became very popular although few people could read or play the scores. They were bought because of their cover art.

creator: Yukawa Hiromitsu 湯川広光 (active c. 1894)
description:
A depiction of the wounded Chinese Commander Tso Pao-kwei and other Chinese soldiers being led into a Japanese field hospital for treatment after the fall of Pyongyang in Korea to the Japanese forces on September 16, 1894.  While some accounts of the battle reported that Tso Pao-kwei had surrendered, in fact he fought bravely and died in action.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.2427.
<br>This set of prints by is unusal in its being  published in Ōsaka rather than in Tokyo where almost all S-J War prints were published. Its publisher Ōbuchi Wataru of the publishing house Hatsubai Shinshindō was primarily a book publisher and this print was part of a twelve print gafu (picture book), a portfolio titled Sino-Japanese War Picture Book.

title: From Kyobashi to Ginza (京橋より銀座の図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
This 1872 scene presents us with a view from the Kyobashi bridge looking into Ginza Street. A horse drawn carriage crosses Kyobashi bridge within its delimited zone, while pedestrians cross in their designated areas along the sides.  A jinrikisha (rickshaw) awaits its turn on the far side of the bridge and a rider on horseback follows the carriage. Kyobashi bridge sat at the east end of Ginza Street and Shinbashi bridge on the west end.<br> After the Tsukiji area burnt to the ground in 1872, the Meiji government designated the Ginza area as model of modernization. The government planned the construction of fireproof brick buildings, and larger, better streets connecting the Shimbashi Station and the foreign concession in Tsukiji, as well as to important government buildings. Designs for the area were provided by the Irish-born architect Thomas Waters; the Bureau of Construction of the Ministry of Finance was in charge of construction. In the following year, a Western-style shopping promenade on the street from the Shinbashi bridge to the Kyōbashi bridge in the southwestern part of Chūō with two- and three-story Georgian brick buildings was completed.<br>
"Bricktown" buildings were initially offered for sale, later they were leased, but the high rent meant that many remained unoccupied. Nevertheless, the area flourished as a symbol of "civilization and enlightenment" (bunmei kaika), thanks to the presence of newspapers and magazine companies, who led the trends of the day. The area was also known for its window displays, an example of modern marketing techniques. - Source: Wikipedia http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginza

The actor Ichimura Uzaemon (likely Uzaemon XIV) is pictured in this 19th (十九) print in the series Kabuki Thirty-Six Poems. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University identifies the role being portrayed by Uzaemon as  妻笠曽代次郎 which can be read Tsumagasa Soyojirō.<br>
Some prints in this series carry numbers below the cartouche containing the series name and others do not. The actors' names in this series appear in the bottom right of the open book containing, what must be, a poem.

title: The Hiramatsu Restaurant in Nihonzutsumi, with the Geisha Okame of Nihonbashi (日本はし おかめ - 日本堤 平松)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
Picturing the geisha Okame wearing a okoso zukin, a cold weather hood, against a red brocade background, this print is from the series Thirty-Six Tokyo Restaurants which pairs famous geisha with famous Tokyo eateries. In this series, the square panel at top left shows either speciality dishes or views from the eatery. The large yellow cartouche  on the right shows the series' title, name of the geisha and the restaurant's address.
<br>In 1878 Kunichika designed another series Thirty-Six Modern Restaurants (see IHL.2186) which also paired restaurants with beautiful women.  Whether the publisher or the artist received compensation for the advertising given to the restaurants portrayed is unknown, but likely.

creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
Print number 13 十三 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints.  The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.
<br>This print pictures the Monkey Bridge (Saruhashi) over the Kakegawa Gorge in modern-day Yamanashi Prefecture. 
<br>Kai Province (甲斐国, Kai no kuni), also known as Kōshū (甲州), is an old province in Japan in the area of Yamanashi Prefecture. It lies in central Honshū, west of Tokyo, in a landlocked mountainous region that includes Mount Fuji along its border with Shizuoka Prefecture.

title: The Letter from New York (手紙・ニューヨークより)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: One of nineteen prints in Takahashi's series of prints featuring the artist's "letters" from places around the world. This series began in 1984 with the print titled The Letter and concluded in 1994 with the print The Letter (From Season). In this series, Takahashi pays homage to various cities, countries and places including Geneva, Paris, London, New York, Switzerland, Kyoto, Southern Italy, Mexico and Jerusalem.<br>Central Park?, skyscrapers? New York harbor? What is the almost cat-like pink figure in the middle of this print? As with many of his other prints, Takahashi employs deep embossing to bring three dimensionality to this work and "N.Y." is prominently displayed in the white oval. As with the print The Letter from Southern Italy, IHL.0587, Takahashi's abstract script flows across this print.

title: The Letter from Southern Italy (手紙・南イタリアから)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description:
One of nineteen prints in Takahashi's series of prints featuring the artist's "letters" from places around the world. This series began in 1984 with the print titled The Letter and concluded in 1994 with the print The Letter (From Season). In this series, Takahashi pays homage to various cities, countries and places including Geneva, Paris, London, New York, Switzerland, Kyoto, Southern Italy, Mexico and Jerusalem.<br>
Takahashi's use of bright colors and abstracted shapes captures the sun, sky and sea of southern Italy and he writes his letter to us in an abstract script that dances across the print.  As with many of his other prints, Takahashi employs deep embossing to bring three dimensionality to this work. I can't help but seeing Hokusai's great wave at the top of this print.

creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)
description: A night view of Ginza street in the 1880s with brightly illuminated windows and gas lights. People line the street and a horse drawn trolley and several carriages are pictured. It is unknown whether this collection's print is an early or later edition., though it is likely not a first edition. This eidtion uses a different color scheme than other extant editions.

title: Slate Pencil Making in Bizen Okayama (備前岡山石筆製図 Bizen Okayama sekihitsu sei zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the unloading, cutting and hand carving of the limestone used to make slate pencils (kyosha). A merchant in a western-style hat is seen purchasing the pencils. After the beginning of the Meiji Era, the demand for slate pencils for use in primary schools increased.<br> 
Bizen Province (備前国, Bizen-no kuni) was a province of Japan on the Inland Sea side of Honshū, in what is today the southeastern part of Okayama Prefecture.  Bizen borders Mimasaka, Harima, and Bitchū Provinces. Bizen's original center was in the modern city of Okayama. From an early time Bizen was one of Japan's main centers for sword smithing.

title: The Ghost Story of Kasamori under the Moonlight (怪談月笠森 Kaidan Tsuki no Kasamori)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: A triptych depicting a scene from the short play Kaidan Tsuki no Kasamori by the playwright Kawatake Mokuami 河竹黙阿弥 (1816-1893). This play was performed on June 01, 1897 as part of the Kabuki program Yumiharizuki Genke no Kaburaya, which also included the plays Kagekiyo and Gion Sairei Shinkōki. The artist, Kunimasa IV (Baidō Hōsai), was well familiar with ghosts, as Newland, in her article in Andon 89, tells us that the artist spoke of seeing apparitions. She goes on to say, "ghosts and monsters were an integral part Edo popular culture and indeed known for centuries in Japan. They were not an uncommon subject in popular oral history and literature, the theatre, in woodblock prints, and later in newspaper reports."

title: Vegetable Market at Kanda, View 16 (神田青物市場・十六景)
creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description:
The Kanda Market was completed in 1931 as part of the reconstruction of Tokyo's wholesale food markets after the 1923 earthquake. Koizumi comments “Vegetables for all of Tokyo were distributed from this place.”<br><br>
Print number sixteen in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort  . . . .”  - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

title: Tōei 藤榮
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 157-158) - The old mother of Saitō Tsuginobu, one of Yoshitsune's retainers who sacrificed himself for his master at the battle of Yashima, hears that Yoshitsune and his men are escaping dressed as yamabushi priests.  She therefore puts up a notice offering hospitality to priests in the hope that they will call on her. They do so and after the old woman has obviously realised who they are and Tsuginobu's child has been to Yoshitsune to ask him to return his father, they admit their identity. They then describe the bravery and devotion shown in the battle by Tsuginobu and his younger brother Tadanobu. Hospitality is then provided during which the child serves them with wine just as if his father were there looking on.  When Yoshtsune and his men make ready to leave, the boy pleads to be allowed to go with them, but as this is impossible, in tears he and the old lady watch the party leave.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Kosode Soga 小袖曾我

creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: Kunichika depicts the famous scene Yoshinogawa from the third act of the drama Imoseyama Onna Teikin, performed at the Shitomi-za in October 1883. In this scene the young samurai Koganosuke and the beautiful Hinadori decide that they would rather commit suicide than be separated. They exchange glances from their separate verandas on opposite sides of the Yoshino River as Hinadori's widowed mother Dazai Kōshitsu Sadaka and Koganosuke's father Daihanji Kyozumi hold sprigs of cherry blossoms, symbols of their intentions.<br>Kunichika's depiction of the Yoshino River replicates how the river appears in the kabuki theater through the stage device called takiguruma (waterfall wheels) in which the river painted in bright blue and white appears to be flowing out from the back of the stage toward the audience

creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)
description: One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the young Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟) and their mother. Five year old Juro points to five wild geese flying by to remind his younger brother Goro of their duty to avenge their murdered natural father while their mother peers fondly at them. <br>The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.

title: Dainagon Yukinari (大納言行成)
creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)
description: One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing Fujiwara no Sanekata (藤原実方), in the black robe, glaring at the seated Dainagon Yukinari (大納言行成) whose kanmuri (冠 lacquered hat) he has just knocked off. Yukinari, seated on the floor, wears a surprised look as his hand searches for his hat which now lies on the floor. While the print is titled Dainagon Yukinari, whose hat was knocked off, the incident is more associated with Fujiwara no Sanekata who was banished by the emperor to a northern province for knocking off Yukinari's hat. For the original issue of this print see IHL.1402. <br>The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890.

title: Dainin Kamitsukeno Katana (大仁上毛野形名)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
One of forty prints in the 1902 partial re-issue of the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the shogun Kamitsukeno Katana eating while his wife serves him wine and lectures him not to disgrace his name and to defeat the rebels. One of the ladies of the court sits in the background, her hand grasping an arrow, which is a reference to Kamitsukeno's wife stringing ten bows and ordering other women to pluck the bow strings simulating a large army.
<br>The reissued series of prints eliminated the brocade borders of the original series issued between October 1885 and November 1890. For the original edition of this print see IHL.0949.

title: Thistle, originally appearing in the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花  ・薊  Shikashū・Nihon no hana・azami)
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description:
Issued as an illustration for the poem of the same name, "Thistle," by Kurahara Shinjirō (1899-1965), in the 1946 poetry and print book "Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," "Thistle" was one of three woodblock prints, along with "Rose" (see IHL.0327) by Kawanishi Hide (1894-1965) and "Plum" by Maekawa Senpan (1888-1960), that were tipped into the book. This collection's print is stand-alone, being either removed from the book it was tipped into or separately printed as a stand-alone print.
<br>"Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," was edited and designed by Onchi Kōshirō, a seminal artist in the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement and pioneering book designer. Contributing twelve prints and one poem, he along with poet Inoue Yasufumi 井上康文 (1897–1973), selected the book's thirty poems by poets such as Satō Haruo (1892-1964), Kitahara Hakushū (1885-1942), Noguchi Yonejirō (1875-1947), Kaoru Maruyama (1899-1974), Tatsuji Miyoshi (1900-1964), Ryuko Kawaji (1888-1959) and Andō Ichirō (1907-1972). 

<br>When this book was published in May 1946 "much of the country, including Tokyo where it was printed, remained in ruins following the previous year’s aerial bombardments. . . . Nihon no hana demonstrated the sophisticated aesthetic sensibility of the Japanese people, while providing a hopeful image for the future rebuilding—or 're-flowering'—of the country and its people." - Source: Commentary by Alicia Volk, https://pulverer.si.edu/node/462/title/1 [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Niwa - Movement B2 (庭・動 B2)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: Warm, harmonious colors invite quiet reflection in this print, one of the artist’s best-known works. Takahashi’s careful preparation of his water-based inks allow the subtle hues to cleanly overlay one another through multiple printings of extremely thin layers of ink. While over one hundred of Takahashi’s prints bear the title Niwa, or garden, each is a new exploration in composition, color, and form.

title: Akasaka Kinokuni Slope (赤坂紀ノ国坂 Akasaka Kinokuni-zaka)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
This print and its companion print IHL.1289 constitute a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present, which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. This print provides a past  (古 old) view in Akasaka, depicting a busy street on the Kinokuni slope where the Edo residences of the Kishū Tokugawa family were located. It is matched with a present, c. 1894, (今 now) view (IHL.1289), depicting the Akasaka Temporary Palace (Akasaka karikōkyo), which served as the chief imperial residence during the construction of the Tokyo Imperial Palace from 1873 to 1889.
<br>These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart. They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, that make up the series.

title: Demons and Dumplings, No. 1045 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・千四拾五號)
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞.  This print tells the story of relatives who try to steal money from a widow by disguising themselves as demons and get their "just desserts" by eating poisoned beet jam dumplings that were given to the widow by still other relatives.
<br>The writer for this print is identified as Tentendo Shujin, a pen name for the writer better known as Takabatake Ransen 高畠藍泉 (1838-1885). Takabatake Ransen was a gesaku writer and journalist who joined Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun shortly after its start in 1872 and often worked with the artist Yoshiiku.
<br>At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

title: Garden in Kyoto (京の庭)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: The artist's recurring theme of Kyoto and its gardens in one of Takahashi's lovely small prints.

title: Sumida River scene from The Great Thief of the Miyakodori Brothel (都鳥廓白波｜新嶋原新狂言隅田川の場)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)

title: Ueno Park, Illustration of the Japanese Red Cross Society General Meeting (上野公園日本赤十字社總會之図)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: While the Japanese Red Cross Society's general meetings attracted tens of thousands of participants and would have provided an excellent opportunity to sell large numbers of prints, I have come to the conclusion that this collection's print was never released for sale, at least in this print's state which lacks a date of printing in the publisher's seal and has a strange overprinting in purple of the royal couple's likenesses. In looking at the historical records, I can find no record that the Emperor ever personally attended any meetings or celebrations of the Japanese Red Cross held in Ueno Park, although the Empress is recorded as having attended the Society's general meetings numerous times in 1889 (at the Third General Meeting), 1890 (at the Fourth General Meeting), 1892 (at the Sixth General Meeting), 1896 (at the Eighth General Meeting), 1898 (at the Ninth General Meeting) and 1901 (at the Tenth General Meeting).

title: Meguro Arsenal (目くろいゑんひう蔵 Meguro Ienhyūzō)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description: A lone figure stands on a hillock overlooking the Meguro Gunpowder Factory. Mt. Fuji is seen through the smoke generated by the factory. Meguro Arsenal is one of thirty-four prints that make up the never completed series One Hundred Views of Musashi. (Musashi being the name of the province that included Edo (later named Tokyo). The series was inspired by Utagawa Hiroshige's (1797–1858) series One Hundred Views of Edo, published between 1856 and 1859.

title: Hōjō Yasutoki (北條泰時)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
Print number 25 (廿五), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the armor-clad Hōjō Yasutoki 北条 泰時 (1183–1242), the third shikken (regent) of the Kamakura shogunate, being criticized by the seated Taira no Moritsuna 平の盛綱 for wasting valuable time and risking his life in coming to the aid of his younger brother Hōjō Tomotoki 北条 朝時 (1193-1245) who had come under attack. Responding Yasutoki says, “How shall it be called a small affair when my brother is in danger? If I had lost my brother, what consolation would my rank have furnished?"<br>
Devotion to family over personal glory is only one of the reasons Yasutoki is judged by history as a paragon of warrior leadership.<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.1325.<br><br>This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization.  Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

title: Wheels on a Slope; Too Many Sailors Climb a Mountain (坂ニ車　船頭多くして山へ登るSaka ni kuruma, sendō ōkute yama e noboru)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: Soldiers and sailors are seen trying to move a cannon up a waterfall. There is a Japanese saying "Sendō ōkute fune yama ni noboru," literally "too many boatmen will take the ship onto a mountain," or in its English proverb equivalent "too many cooks spoil the broth." Something similar applies to this scene.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Spleen (鬱念 Utsunen)
creator: Yuki Rei 由木礼 (1928-2003)
description: As with many of Rei's prints, the artist has presented us with a landscape "set in ambiguous space", to use Helen Merritt's words. Dark indigo vertical lines which may portray a heavy rain are interspersed with subtle light indigo and yellow-green broken lines to provide depth to the image.  Along with the celestial shapes, Rei gives us a Mt. Fuji-like image on the right and, perhaps, a cityscape along the left part of the dark indigo vertical bar that scoops under Fuji on the right. This print is an artist proof. See IHL.1267 for an editioned copy of this print.

title: Momo Chidori Naruto no Shiranami (もゝちどり鳴門白浪)
creator: Utagawa Yoshitaki 歌川芳滝 (1841-1899)

title: Aoto Fujitsuna (青砥藤綱)
creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)

title: Soga Brothers New Year's Farce
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: It is unknown what play, plays, or scenes are being depicted in this untitled triptych issued in January 1878. The center panel presents us with Ichikawa Danjurō IX as Kudō Suketsune and Ichikawa Sadanji as (Soga no) Gorō Tokimune, characters in the Soga Brothers Revenge, a variation of which is traditionally staged in the beginning of the New Year. The left panel depicts Danjurō, again, playing a priest or monk with the  partial name Mitsume 三つ目 (literally, "third-eye") and Iwai Hanshirō VIII playing a princess, possibly named Otohime おとひめ. In the right panel we see the god of wealth, Daikokuten 大黒天, played by Onoe Kikugorō V, carrying a giant daikon 大根, played by a Bandō family actor. "Daikon yakusha" was an expression for a ham actor.

title: Pilferer (小盗みする者 Konusumisuru mono)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)
description: From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) which show examples of children's good and bad behavior.  In this print a child steals a small item from a napping vendor; an example of bad behavior that will not go unpunished by the looming figure behind the screen above and to the right of the little thief. <br>In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

title: Hearth (いろり)
creator: Hatsuyama Shigeru 初山滋 (1897-1973)
description: A magazine and book illustrator and printmaker, the artist Hatsuyama Shigeru created a number of prints featuring children at play, including this charming image of five children gathered around a hearth. The artist uses blue ai pigment (a deep indigo color) as the background and gives us several perspectives at once. As with all of Hatsuyama's children prints the rendering of the children captures the mischievous, innocent and serious aspects of their nature.

title: Night View of Shinjuku (新宿夜景 Shinjuku yakei)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description:
"Maekawa Senpan depicts his contemporary man, arms on hips, surveying this modern quarter. To the artist’s 1931 viewers [the original publication date for this image] the words 'Night at Shinjuku' meant a night on the town, with drinking and easy women. It still carried the same message in 1945 [when this collection's print was published].[1]
<br>"As in Factory Street at Fukagawa [see IHL.0174], Maekawa re-used a design done in 1931 for the series 'One Hundred Views of New Tokyo' with new blocks, probably cut by himself. The rich dark-blue of the night sky in the original version has been replaced by grey, investing the scene with an appropriately post-war bleakness. At the time of the first series, however, Shinjuku had become known as the most go-ahead and 'modern' of Tokyo districts, and had begun its rise to rival the older centre of the city around Ginza and Marunouchi. Maekawa's cartoonist's eye seems even then to have noticed something ironically lonely about the atmosphere of a place with thousands of bars."[2][3]
<br><br>SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
<br>Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Koshiro (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan.[4]

<br><br>
[1] Terrific Tokyo – A Panorama in Prints from the 1860s to the 1930s, Elizabeth de Sabato Swinton, Worcester Art Museum, 1998, p. 48.
<br>[2] Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945-1952, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 2002, p. 61.
<br>[3] For an account of the post-earthquake rise of Shinjuku see Seidensticker, Edward, 'Tokyo Rising: The City Since the Great Earthquake', New York, 1990, pp. 50-53.
<br>[4] Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

title: Sumida River (Sumidagawa 隅田川)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
A WWII era view of an industrial area along the Sumida River, softened with the presence of the kimono-clad woman with parasol on the left and the sailboats on the river. In the first half of 1942, around the time this print was produced, Japan reached the height of her power, but also suffered the first air raids on Tokyo and her first major defeats, e.g. Battle of Midway, in the latter half of the year.<br>
This print, whose provenance is attributed to the Uchida family archives, is likely a proof print using a different color scheme as compared with the final released version of the print. This proof also omits the print's title and Tokuriki's signature that are seen on the final released version. Note that the grey border around the image is misregistered.

title: Kyoto Town Hall in Snow
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: A partially obscured yellow street sign provides both the speed limit and a splash of color in this atmospheric winter scene. Judging from its shape, the building in the far distance, beyond the tiny figures and cars, is Kyoto city hall. Built in 1927, this imposing building takes up one block on the corner of Kawaramachi-dōri and Oike-dōri.<br>This print was originally issued as part of a series titled Twelve Views of Kyoto 京都十二景.

title: Soga Brothers (曾我兄弟)
creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)

title: Ushi nusubito 牛盗人 (The Cow Thief)
creator: Tsukioka Gyokusei 月岡玉瀞 (1908-1994)
description:
One of thirty-four prints designed by Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994) in the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyōgen Plays) started by her father Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927). She created 34 prints and the table of contents for this series, using the artist name Kōbun 江文. Tsukioka Kōgyo designed sixteen prints for the series before his death.<br>
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p.285-286.) - The Cow Keeper for the Emperor discovers that one of the Emperor's cows has been stolen. He puts up a sign declaring whoever will give information as to the identity or the whereabouts of the Thief will be forgiven any crime, or given anything he asks for.

<br>Before long a Child appears, saying that he wishes to report the name and the whereabouts of the thief. He says the thief is Hyōgo Saburō who lives in the next village.

<br>The Cow Keeper sends Tarō Kaja and Jirō Kaja to go arrest the culprit. They soon drag him in, and before long he confesses his crime.  He also reveals to them the fact that the Child is his son.  He curses and disowns his Child for being a traitor.

<br>They ask him why he stole the cow, and he says it was to pay for a memorial service for his father, and goes on to recite a passage from Buddhist scripture which would seem to sanction such an action.  The Cow Keeper says that no matter, the crime is still the same according to law, and Hyōgo Saburō must be put to death.

<br>At this point the Child speaks up demanding his reward.  They ask him what he wants, and he answers, 'The life of Hyōgo Saburō spared.'  He goes on to explain that when he saw the sign, he decided that this was the only ways to save his Father's life.  Father and Son burst into tears.  The Father pleads for forgiveness from his son for his harsh words of a few minutes before.  The Cow Keeper and his servants are moved by this display of the Child's love for his Father.  They grant him full pardon, and Father and Son set out for home singing for joy.

title: Iori no ume 庵の梅 (The Plum Blossom Hut)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Drawbridge of Amsterdam
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: One of the artist's sōsaku hanga prints depicting the drawbridge on Staalstraat, over Kloveniersburgwal, in the Centrum district of Amsterdam. This print exists in at least two states, one of which is a numbered edition pictured in Tokuriki's book "Wood-block Printing" and the other this collection's print, either an artist's proof or from an unnumbered edition.

title: Around Ochanomizu (お茶の水附近 Ochanomizu fukin)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Picturing the Kanda River running through the Tokyo neighborhood of Ochanomizu, Kitaoka titled this print お茶の水附近 (Ochanomizu fukin), translated as "Around Ochanomizu," and dated it 1949.<br>The gallery label accompanying this print identifies the print as coming from the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Post-war Life and Customs."  The Museum of Modern Art Tokyo titles this print in English "The Kanda River from The Face of Tokyo No. 1" and in Japanese "版画集「東京の顔 No.1」より 2.神田川" and dates it to 1950.<br>This collection's print and images of the 1950 dated print appear to be identical and it is possible that a second printing was done by Kitaoka to create the five-part Face of Tokyo portfolio.  Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the 1950 print.<br>This beautifully designed and, unfortunately, overlooked series, portrays Postwar Tokyo in the social-realist style that Kitaoka embraced after the war and later rejected, telling Statler "I rebelled against their [Japan's proletarian artists] subjugation of art to politics. . . ."

title: Red Memory (赤い記憶)
creator: Kusaka Kenji 日下賢二 (1936-2020)
description:
A full moon over rolling hills, bound by pink and black cables? (One interpretation of this work. )“Kusaka’s work is never improvised, but is the patiently elaborated expression of a simple man. His technique is totally absorbed by the discipline necessary to produce prints of great ingenuity and directness.”[1] In his smooth technique and confident abstraction he resembles others of the first post-war generation of woodblock artists such as [Akira] Kurosaki, Amano Kazumi and Amano Kunihiro.[2]
<br><br>
[1] Contemporary Japanese Prints, Kawakita Michiaki, Kodansha International Ltd., 1967, p. 181.
<br>[2] Modern Japanese Prints: 1912-1989, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 1994, p. 29.

title: Red Shadow 82-5  (赤い影 82-5 Akai Kage 82-5)
creator: Kusaka Kenji 日下賢二 (1936-2020)
description: One of the artist's many prints where color and motion are the statements. Reminiscences of the akai-e of the Meiji period, when red (akai) embodied modernity and the fast pace of change.

title: Amakawaya Gihei (天川屋 儀平)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞 (1823-1880)
description:
This print pictures the virtuous merchant Amakawaya Gihei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers, a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin), based on the real-life Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their lord. The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston identifies the actor in the role of Gihei as Kawarazaki Gonjūrō I, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.<br>
The multi-colored cartouche gives the name of the series as Legends of the Loyal Retainers and the name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of this cartouche, in this case Amakawaya Gihei  天川屋 儀平. The background script may provide an account of Amakawaya Gihei's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.<br>The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.

title: Ōboshi Yuranosuke (大星由良之亮)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞 (1823-1880)
description:
This print pictures the character Ōboshi Yuranosuke from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers, a.k.a. The Forty Seven Ronin), based on the Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their master. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University identifies the actor playing the role of  Ōboshi Yuranosuke as Bandō Hikosaburō V [5]坂東彦三郎, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.<br>
The multi-colored cartouche gives the name of the series as Legends of the Loyal Retainers  and the name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of this cartouche, in this case Ōboshi Yuranosuke 大星由良之亮. The background script may provide an account of Yuranosuke's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.<br>The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.<br>Ōboshi Yuranosuke is the fictitious name in the play for the real-life Ōishi Kuranosuke, Lord Asano's head retainer and the head of the revenge plot to assassinate the senior bakufu protocol official, Kira Yoshinaka. It is Ōishi who took Kira's head and placed it before his master's grave at Sengakuji Temple.

title: Hayano Kanpei (早野勘平)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞 (1823-1880)
description: This print pictures the character Hayano Kanpei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers; a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin). The play is based on the real-life Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their lord. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum Digital Archives Collection identifies the actor playing Hayano Kanpei as Ichimura Kakitsu IV  [4]市村家橘, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.<br>The multi-color cartouche in the upper right corner gives the name of the series, Legends of the Loyal Retainers. The name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of the cartouche, in this case Hayano Kanpei 早野勘平. The background script may provide an account of Hayano Kanpei's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.<br>The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.<br>For another edition of this print see IHL.0927.

title: Waterwheel (水車 suisha)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description: One of five known prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of growing rice and its uses issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print demonstrates use of a foot-powered waterwheel to irrigate rice paddies and various rice food dishes. (For another print in this series see IHL.0633.) <br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

title: Rice Storage (米蔵 komegura)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist.
description: One of five known prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of growing rice and its uses issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print depicts a rice storage house with farmers going about their business and chickens nibbling the stray rice kernels. The top portion of the print presents various rice storage related items. (For another print in this series see IHL.0632.) <br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

title: Small Red Wall A
creator: Tajima Hiroyuki 田嶋宏行 (1911-1984)
description: Layers upon layers of ink give this print a great depth as does the injection of the light turquoise on which the darker colors float.

title: Act XI: The Storming of Moronao’s Mansion (十一段目 Jūichidanme)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description: This print pictures two maids tickling a third maid in a parody of the third scene in act XI of the play Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers).  The circular inset shows the actual scene from act XI in which the ronin, after having staged a night attack on Moronao's mansion, drag Moronao from his hiding place.

title: Summer in Aizu - The Seasons: Summer (会津の夏)
creator: Saitō Kiyoshi 斎藤清 (1907-1997)
description: This untitled print depicts four people quietly going about their business in a rural village, possibly the artist's early boyhood home of Aizu, on a summer's day. When it was released as part of an offering of six Saitō prints by the Book-of-the-Month Club, it was titled "The Seasons: Summer." See IHL.0984 for another print included in the Book-of-the-Month Club set of six prints.

title: Face, Male (顔、男)
creator: Kinoshita Tomio 木下富雄 (1923-c.2011)
description: A prototypical image from the artist. This "male" face, using Kinoshita's early color scheme of orange and sumi ink, takes up almost the entire image area. While dated 1981, the blocks were likely carved earlier, possibly in the mid-1950s. Kinoshita would initially make only several prints for his "artistic satisfaction" and then make additional prints as needed. While, as in this print's case, the total edition might be shown as fifty prints, in many cases the full edition would never be completed.

title: Sumida Park in Kototoi, Mukōjima, View 25 (墨田公園 向島言問・二十五景)
creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description:
The artist depicts Sumida Park in the foreground with a silhouette of Kototoi Bridge, built in 1928, on the left in the background. Koizumi comments “The Takeya ferry once crossed the Sumida River from here. Now the only reminder of the former look of the old river bank is the stone lantern. Now there is a modern park along the river.”<br><br>
Print number twenty-five in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort  . . . .”  - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

title: People of the Snow Country (雪国の人 yuki guni no hito )
creator: Takagi Shirō  高木志朗 (1934-1998)
description: Takagi's colors perfectly fit this winter scene of three figures along a pathway leading to a torii and a small shrine.  A lone bird completes the silence of this scene.

title: Playing Bingo (ビンゴゲーム)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Titled, Playing Bingo ビンゴゲーム,  Kitaoka gives us a view of a crowded bingo hall in postwar Tokyo.<br>This print, dated 1949, was issued as part of the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Postwar Life and Customs" and subsequently included in the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio, each portfolio containing five prints, titled Print Collection, The Face of Tokyo kyo 版画集 東京の顔.<br>Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the print included in the later portfolio.

title: Outside Shinjuku Station, the West Exit (新宿西口)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Kitaoka shows us a possibly mid-day scene outside the west entrance of Tokyo's busiest railway station.<br>This print, dated 1949, was issued as part of the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Postwar Life and Customs," and subsequently included in the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio (each portfolio containing five prints), titled Print Collection, The Face of Tokyo kyo 版画集 東京の顔.<br> Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the print included in the later portfolio.

title: Behind the Stage (舞台裏)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Stagehands building a set for an unknown play.<br>This print, dated 1949, was issued as part of the series 戦後風俗 (Sengo fūzoku), translated as "Postwar Life and Customs" and subsequently included in the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio (each portfolio containing five prints,) titled, Print Collection, The Face of Tokyo 版画集東京の顔 . Kitaoka used a mica impregnated paper for this 1949 print and the print included in the later portfolio.

title: A Comparison of Actors' Wages, Tokyo (俳優 見立給金競 東京)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: A depiction of eight different actors in nine roles, along with a listing of their salaries along with the names and salaries of 56 additional Tokyo-based actors. The actors' identifying crests (mon) are shown above their names. The sloppy production, stray ink marks and poor registration, along with the lack of a date of issue for this print indicate it may have been some type of proof copy. (However, the print does carry a price of six sen below the publisher's seal.) <br>Rankings like this were issued periodically as fans clamored to know who was on top.

title: Mt. Yoshino (吉野山 Yoshinoyama)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Tokuriki cuts off the top part of the head of one of the Nio statues guarding the Kimpusen-ji temple on Mt. Yoshino in Nara prefecture, perhaps to draw our attention to the surrounding countryside and its cherry trees in bloom. The bottom part of the sign board on the pillar reads 金峯山寺 Kinpusen-ji Shrine. Note the votive slips pasted to the supporting timbers.

title: Ichikawa Ichizō III as Nadare no Wakamatsu (なだれの若松　市川市蔵)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description: Actor Ichikawa Ichizō III as Nadare no Wakamatsu in a kabuki enactment of the novel A Present-Day Suikoden.  He wears a kimono adorned with a large shrimp and a rooster head. The series consists of 36 prints designed by Kunisada between 1861 and 1863. Suikoden (Tales of the Water Margin) is the Japanese adaptation of the 14th-century Chinese vernacular novel Shuihu zhuan, which recounts the exploits of a group of 108 robbers (or, depending upon your view, brave and righteous rebels.)

title: No. 9 Good Example (善・九)
creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)

title: Toy Horse
creator: Hiratsuka Un'ichi 平塚運一 (1895-1997)
description: Penelope Moore, granddaughter of Hiratsuka Un'ichi, commenting on this print wrote, "This was a carousel horse outside a party goods store on Wisconsin Ave and Van Ness St." Further elaborating, Penelope remembered being with her grandfather when he sketched this print in their Washington, D.C. neighborhood. "Occasionally, when he was in a patient mood, he took my sister or me, and brought a collapsible 3-legged stool, easel, and either canvasses or sketchpads. . . . Sidwell Friends, Sullivan Toys, the Zebra Room, G.C. Murphy, Giant Foods, the Savings and Loan Bank which was recently a Starbucks, the Johnson Flower Shop . . . all of these were part of our weekly hauntings. My mother used to buy flowers at Johnson's for classes or for my grandfather to draw. There was a small old farmhouse next to the Flower Center, right across from the deep dish Chicago Pizzaria, a small shop that sold party goods, and given the absence of a sign or any palpable activity, I don't think they did much business. An old carousel horse on the porch had caught Ojichan's eye, and over a period of several hours he sketched it with gusto and it became one of my favorite woodblocks."

title: Ichimura Kakitsu IV, Sawamura Tanosuke III, Nakamura Shikan IV in The Popular Children's Word Game of Continuous Phrases (流行しりとり子どももんく Ryūkō shiritori kodomo monku)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: From right to left, the actors Ichimura Kakitsu IV 市村家橘, Sawamura Tanosuke III 沢村(澤村)田之助 and Nakamura Shikan IV 中村芝翫 engage in a contest of shiritori monku ("word game") in the play The Popular Children's Word Game of Continuous Phrases.  Shiritori monku, literally “end-taking phrase”, is a game in which the last word or syllable of a phrase is repeated as the first word or syllable of the next phrase. Even for non-readers of Japanese, you can see the repetition of the last character or characters of the previous word in the following word in the text that surrounds the actors.

title: Sawamura Tosshō II as Tora Ōmaru - Tiger (虎王丸 沢村訥升 - 寅)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.

The actor Sawamura Tosshō II (1838-1886) as Tora Ōmaru, the King of the Tigers. He holds a magical scroll from which a tiger has leaped.  A faint image of the tiger remains on the scroll.

title: Bandō Hikosaburō V as Inugami Hyōbu - Dragon (犬上兵部 坂東彦三郎 - 辰)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.  

The actor Bandō Hikosabu V (1832-1877) as Inugami Hyōbu conjuring a pack of dogs that arise out of the mist. The printer has skillfully used the technique of bokashi (gradation of shade) to render the dogs and mist. The dogs are a reference to the tale of the Eight Dog Heroes in which a princess is forced to sleep with her father’s dog and gives birth to eight magical balls of light. Each of these becomes a man and they are the subject of stories of great heroism and courage, gathered together as a collection popularly called the Hakkenden.

title: Bandō Hikosaburō V as Unryū Kūrō - Monkey (雲龍九郎 坂東彦三郎 - 申)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.<br>
The actor Bandō Hikosabu V (1832-1877) as Unryū Kūrō shown reading a scroll from which he has conjured a dragon. The character is taken from the book Unryū Kurō chūtōden by Shikitei Sanba (1776-1822).

title: Ichikawa Sadanji as Raigō Ajari - Rat (頼豪阿闍利 市川左団次 - 子)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.

<br>In this print the actor Ichikawa Sadanji (1842-1904) is shown as the monk Raigō Ajari (1002-1084) grasping a sutra from which a string of rats emerge. Raigō's prayers have given Emperor Shirakawa (r. 1072-1086) an heir. He asks in return for a raised platform, like the one in the temple of the yamabushi (warrior priests) who terrorized Kyoto, but it is denied. Raigō starves himself to death and his vengeful spirit (onryō, 怨霊) changes into a thousand rats which destroy the Emperor’s sacred library. This is followed by the death of the emperor's son.

title: Nagao Pass (長尾峠)
creator: Tsuchiya Kōitsu 土屋光逸 (1870-1949) - attributed to the artist.
description:
This small print showing Nagao Pass 長尾峠, a 3,000 foot high mountain pass between Hakone and Gotemba City, Shizuoka Prefecture with views of Mt. Fuji and Lake Ashi, was originally published c. 1936 by the Kyoto publisher Baba Nobuhiko. This collection's print is likely a later post-WWII issue.  

<br><b>Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints</b><br>
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in. 
<br>Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
<br>The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
<br>The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints).

description:

The print's title is printed in the upper left corner of the print.

creator: Shien 紫園 (active 1930-1950s)
