creator: Hamada Josen 浜田如洗 (1875-1928)

title: Two Scenes from The Tale of Shiraishi  (白石 噺明神森場  吉原 大黒屋 之 場  碁太平記白石噺 Shiraishi banashi, myōjin mori ba Yoshiwara daikokuya no ba)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
Two scenes from the play The Tale of Shirashi. The multicolored cartouche on the left sheet of the triptych identifies the scene being portrayed as Yoshiwara daikokuya no ba 吉原大黒屋之場. The multicolored cartouche on the right sheet of the triptych identifies the scene being portrayed as myōjin mori ba 明神森場.
<br>"In a powerful composition that slashes the triptych into two scenes, the artist evokes the suspense of a history play about an attempted coup d'etat, with numerous subplots and colorful characters. The massive hairpins of the courtesan, left, were no longer in fashion when this play was staged, but immediately brought to mind the styles and customs of an older era." - Asian Art historian Lynn Katsumoto

title: Sawamura Hyakunosuki, Ichikawa Gonjūrō, Iwai Shijaku and Kataoka Gadō in the play Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety ( 沢村百之助、市川権十郎、岩井紫若、片岡 我童・本朝廿四孝 Honchō nijūshikō)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: Picturing from right to left the actors Sawamura Hyakunosuke 沢村百之助 as Yaegaki hime 八重垣姫  (Princess Yaegaki, Nagao Kenshin's beautiful daughter); Ichikawa Gonjūrō 市川権十郎 as Takeda Katsuyori 武田勝頼 (in love with Yaegaki); Iwai Shijaku IV 岩井紫若 as Nureginu ぬれぎ (Yaegaki’s maid) and Kataoka Gadō 片岡 我童 as Shirasuga Rokurō 白須 賀 六郎 (a retainer of Yaekagi’s father sent to kill Katsuyori) in the Jusshukō scene in the play Honchō Nijūshikō 本朝廿四孝 (Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety.)<br>"The widow of a murdered shogun has threatened two noble families to either find the villain, or sacrifice their sons. Plot turns and mistaken identity add chilling effect, as in this scene that foreshadows the doomed marriage of the beautiful princess, Yaegaki, far right, to the man, center, she knows only by his portrait. Yaegaki's maid appears, left, beneath the specter of a warrior sent by Yaegaki's father to kill the betrothed." - Asian Art historian Lynn Katsumoto

title: New Play at the Kabuki-za (歌舞伎坐新狂言 Kabuki-za Shin Kyōgen)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: A triptych depicting the actors Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 playing the roles of Oogosho Ieyasu 大御所家康公 (right panel) and Kasuga (Lady) Tsubone 春日局 (center panel) and Nakamura Shikan V 中村芝翫 playing the role of Kaji no Tsubone 梶の局 in the play Kasuga no Tsubone, written in 1890 by the one-time journalist and politician Fukuchi Genichirō (1841-1906).<br>The play was performed for the first time in 1891. Given the date of this print, May 1903, it would be one of Danjūrō IX's last stage performances before his death on September 13, 1903.

title: Low Tide: Women of the Bunka Era (汐干・文化頃婦人 Shiohi・Bunka koro fujin)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)
description:
One of thirty-six prints in the series Sanjūroku kasen (also transcribed as Sanjūroku kurabe) depicting a fisherwoman and a stylish geisha gathering seafood at low tide.  he geisha seems to be demurely giggling at the woman struggling with the fish. Embossing is used in both the white cartouche and the fisherwoman's skirt and lacquer has been applied on the geisha's collar and obi of the fisherwoman.  One of the most striking compositions in this series.
<br>The series presents women of different classes from thirty-five different historical eras.

title: Study of Gaslight and Silhouetted Figures
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: This Kyōsai ink and pencil on paper study of silhouetted figures and gas lamps may be a preparatory drawing for a fuller drawing, titled Customs House at Yokohama  in the collection of the Rijksmuseum voor Volkenkunde (Inventory Number : RV-3513-1347), according to Professor Matthi Forrer, curator at the National Museum of Ethnology (Museum Volkenkunde) in Leiden.

title: Selling Toothpicks at Itsukushima and Hiroshima Oyster Farm (安芸国 厳島楊枝ヲ鬻図 ・安芸 広島牡蛎蓄養之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
Two of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. The top print depicts the selling of souvenir toothpicks at Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima island and the bottom depicts oyster farming in Aki Province.  <br>The top is a view from one of the "floating" buildings (Haraiden purification hall of the Marōdo auxiliary shrine) at Itsukushima Shrine. According to the Miyajima Tourist Association "the shrine was a popular landmark in Miyajima where many people came to relax and cool themselves and to buy popular souvenirs such as toothpicks, and a variety of legends and traditions have been created here." - Source: Miyajima Tourist Association http://www.miyajima.or.jp/english/spot/spot_other.html [accessed 8-26-23]
<br>Oyster farming in Aki Province, as seen in the bottom view, began at the end of the Muromachi period around 1532-1555. Initially aquaculture methods such as stone aquaculture (Ishimaki or arranging pebbles on tidal flats, attaching oysters, and waiting for the cultivation period before harvesting it) and double cracks were used. Over the years more advanced methods became common and evolved into the hanging-type aquaculture method shown in this print. - Source: Food In Japan https://www.foodinjapan.org/chugoku/hiroshima-kaki/ [accessed 8-26-23]
<br>Aki Province (安芸国 Aki no kuni) or Geishū (芸州) was a province in the Chūgoku Region of western Honshū, comprising the western part of what is today Hiroshima Prefecture.<br>
This print is reduced in size by the chirimen (crêpe) process to 9 1/8 x 6 5/8 in. (23.5 x 16.8 cm) from the originally issued double-chuban size (two uncut chuban prints) of approximately 14 1/4 x 9 3/4 in. (36.2 x 23.5 cm).

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Mongaku Shōnin in the play The Austerities of Mongaku ( 市川団十郎・ 文覚上人・ 橋供養梵字文覚)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as the priest Mongaku in the play Hashi kuyō bonji no Mongaku (The Austerities of Mongaku). As in keeping with the rest of the series, extensive embossing is employed in the background along with an application of mica.<br><br>One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits.  A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

title: Do Not Give Money to the Indolent, No. 12
creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)

title: Full Moon on the Tatami Mats, Shadows of the Pine Branches - Kikaku (名月や畳の上に松の影其角 Meigetsu ya tatami no ue ni matsu no kage - Kikaku)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
This picture illustrates a verse by Takarai Kikaku (1661-1707), a celebrated haiku master, that reads, "Full moon on the tatami mats; shadows of the pine branches."<br>
"A lady looks at the shadow of pine branches thrown by a bright moon onto the straw mats of her room. That the setting is a teahouse is indicated by the furo, three-legged brazier to the left of the design, and by the rough wood pillar of the tokonoma, ceremonial alcove, to the right. But it is an unusually opulent teahouse. The screen to the left, painted in the brightly colored Rimpa style, is rather gaudy for a teahouse, and the area is large, with tatami mats extending into the foreground. It is a teahouse of the pleasure quarters, either a house where assignations are arranged, or a teahouse in a large and luxurious brothel."[1]

<br>This print is missing the lavender color found on other impressions in the courtesan's robe and the rectangular cartouche in the upper right of the print bearing the series title has only a partial application of the light pink color normally seen in the cartouche.

<br><br>ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
<br>One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
<br>"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[2]

<br><br>
[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, print 5.
<br>[2] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, published by Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

title: Koko ga Edo ko-ude no tatehiki (慈江戸小腕達引)
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description: The actors, from right to left, Ichikawa Kodanji IV (市川小団次), in the role of Ude no Kisaburo (腕ノ喜三郎 "one-arm Kisaburō"), Kataoka Jūzō (片岡十蔵) in the role of Ōtori Ippei (大鳥逸平), Ichimura Kakitsu IV (市村家橘) playing Akebono Genta (曙源太) and Ichikawa Kuzō III (市川九蔵) in the role of Maboroshi Tanizo (幻長蔵) in the kabuki play Koko ga Edo Koude no Tatehiki by Kawatake Mokuami, staged in August 1863 at the Ichimura-za (市村).<br>This scene is set on the Kamakura Hanamizu bridge (鎌倉花水橋, as marked on the bridge post) and we can be sure Ude no Kisaburo, the one-armed swordsman who cut his arm off at the elbow with a saw in order to earn his fencing teacher's forgiveness, is the hero.

title: Auspicious Plays (ワキ狂言 Waki kyōgen)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description: This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts an annual waki kyogen performance starting at dawn, announced by the banging of the large drum, consisting of auspicious dances such as the Dance of the Seven Lucky Gods and the Sanboso dance.  Reference is made in the scroll to both the Ichimura-za and Nakamura-za theaters in Edo. For a later edition of this print see IHL.0612.

title: Aridōshi 蟻通
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 134.) - In the play, the poet Ki no Tsurayuki (waki) annoys the groundskeeper (shite) by riding his horse within the precincts of the Aridōshi Shrine. Tsurayuki soothes the feelings of the shrine deity by reciting a poem he has composed, after which, at the poet’s request, the god recites some Shinto prayers.<br><br>
<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Actors Bandō Takesaburō I, Bandō Shūka I, Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII, Iwai Kumesaburō III and Nakamura Fukusuke I (初代坂東竹三郎、初代坂東しうか、八代目市川団十郎、三代目岩井粂三郎、初代中村福助)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description:
The actors, right to left, Bandō Takesaburō I (初代 坂東竹三郎), Bandō Shūka I (初代 坂東しうか), Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII (八代目 市川団十郎), Iwai Kumesaburō III (三代目 岩井粂三郎) and Nakamura Fukusuke I (初代 中村福助) pictured against a background of wisteria. The subtle transitions of shade and color in the robes is quite impressive.
<br>A version of this print picturing the same actors (using the same woodblocks) but with a checked fabric background can be found in the collection of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston Accession Number 11.44150a-c.

title: Shizuka Gozen (静御前)
creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)

title: Wisteria Maiden (Fuji musume)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Tokuriki's modern interpretation of traditional folk Ōtsu-e (paintings and prints), named after the town of Ōtsu where they originated in the mid-17th century. It is said that Wisteria maiden (fuji musume) adds to your amiability and helps you get a good romantic partner.

title: Standard Bearer (Yarimoichi yakko)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Tokuriki's modern interpretation of traditional folk Ōtsu-e (paintings and prints), named after the town of Ōtsu where they originated in the mid-17th century. A Standard bearer (Yarimoichi yakko) provides safety during travel.  These figures led the traveling daimyo processions, ordering all bystanders to bow down as noblemen passed with their long retinues.

title: Benkei Carrying Bell (Tsurigane Benkei)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Tokuriki's modern interpretation of traditional folk Ōtsu-e (paintings and prints), named after the town of Ōtsu where they originated in the mid-17th century. This print depicts Benkei and the Bell (Tsurigane Benkei). The story is told of how the monk-warrior Benkei took the famous bell of Mii-dera and dragged it up to the summit of mount Hiei. He struck the bell and then got angry when he heard it ringing “eeno eeno”, which means “I want to go back” in the Kansai dialect. In his anger, Benkei threw the bell down to the bottom of the valley.

title: Court Noble from Bairei Drawings, 4 (公卿・楳嶺画鑑 四 (Kuge・Bairei gakan, yon)
creator: Kōno Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895)
description: Bairei depicts a Heian period (794-1185) court noble in this print, which was included in the fourth of his seven volume book of drawings titled Bairei gakan, published 18 years after the artist's death. Originally published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1903, Unsōdō republished it in 1913, 1942 and again in 1982. This collection's print was likely removed from the 1913 edition. Works from the 1913 and 1942 releases, such as this collection's print, can be identified by their vertical centerfold, which is lacking in the 1982 release. Each volume contained 15 prints.

title: Bell-ring Cricket, Mt. Fuji and a Parody of Kusazuri (鈴虫, 富士, 見立草摺)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description:
Kyōsai gives us three images in this harimaze print - Mt. Fuji, a bell-ring cricket (suzumushi - known for its unique song) on a gourd vine with a crescent moon and a comic take on the kabuki play Kusazuri.  Kusazuri is a play "in which Goro and Juro try to get their revenge on Kudo Suketsune for killing their father.  Goro tries to join his brother Juro on stage but Asahina tries to hold him back.  Goro brakes wind, and Asahina loosens his grip." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 220.

<br>This series, consisting of a least ten prints, using "legitimate Kano school subjects as their themes" depicted in comic situations, made Kyōsai quite popular as an ukiyo-e artist. "At the time, these harimaze prints were cut into individual scenes and the small pieces were used to repair the holes in paper sliding doors and screens. Kyosai’s humorous scenes were thus enjoyed in the everyday lives of the Japanese people." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 32-33, 220-225.

title: The scene Kumagai's Battle Camp from the play A Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani ( 熊谷陣屋  一谷嫩軍記 Kumagai jin'ya Ichinotani futaba gunki)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The Kumagai Jin'ya scene, the last scene in the play Ichinotani Futaba Gunki, a dramatization of the Heike Monogatari tale of the battle of Ichinotani. The actors (right to left): Ichikawa Kodanji 市川小團次 in the role of Yoshitsune, Iwai Komurasaki III 岩井小紫 in the role of Fuji no Kata, Nakamura Shikan IV 中村芝翫 in the role of Kumagai Jiro Naozane, Ichikawa Kuzō III 市川九蔵 in the role of Midaroku, and Bandō Shūchō II 坂東秀調 in the role of Sagami. Also see IHL.0316 picturing the same scene but showing different actors.

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Higuchi Jirō Kanemitsu in the play The Secret Art of Rowing Backwards (市川団十郎・ 樋口治郎兼光・ ひらかな盛衰記)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as Higuchi Jirō Kanemitsu, a personal retainer of General Yoshinaka who disguises himself as the boatman Matsuemon who has mastered the naval art of sakaro (rowing backwards) in the play The Secret Art of Rowing Backwards (Hiragana Seisuiki). Extensive shomen zuri (front printing) has been used in the black areas of Kanemitsu's clothing.<br><br>One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits.  A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

title: Presentation of the Emperor's Gift Cup for the Second Time to Commanders Involved in Pacifying Western Japan (西国鎮撫諸将 再度 賜天盃之図)
creator: Utagawa Yoshitsuya II 二代 歌川芳艶  (active 1870s)
description: Military commanders are being entertained at the behest of Emperor Meiji, as a reward for their service in putting down rebellions in Western Japan. While the release of this print corresponds with the suppression of the Satsuma Rebellion, its title seems to also encompass the earlier disturbances in the Saigoku (western area) of Japan in October and November of 1876. Fourteen named senior officers in the Imperial Army are shown in the print, receiving the Emperor's Gift Cup of sake for their contributions. Note the contrast between the officer's stern expressions and those of the geisha serving them.<br>After the last of the rebel forces were decimated by the Imperial Army in late September 1877, the Emperor made sure to visit and congratulate both officers and soldiers.

title: Evening Cool (夕涼み Yūsuzumi)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
One of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫  (1929-?).             
<br>As in this case, the majority of Yumeji's woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934 and were based upon his paintings or previous designs for song sheets and postcards. They were often rescaled to accommodate standardized sizes of paper used for woodblock prints. Major publishers involved with producing these posthumous prints were Kyōto Hanga-in under the direction of Shinagawa Kiyoomi 品川清臣 (1907-?) and Katō Junji 加藤潤二 (1885-1961) and his Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjo.)

title: Signs of Spring Mt. Togakushi (浅春戸隠 Asai haru Togakushi)
creator: Maeda Masao 前田政雄 (1904-1974)
description: Maeda created numerous prints of Japanese mountains. In this print he has used mica highlights throughout the slopes of the mountains. In the artist's words, "A true mountaineer has to get to the top, but the finest panoramas are down in the middle heights. That's where I stop."<br>Togakushi along with Madarao, Myōkō, Kurohime, and Iizuna are collectively known as the Five Peaks of Northern Shinano (Hokushingogaku). They make up the border of Nagano and Niigata Prefectures.<br>Neither signed or sealed by the artist, this print is likely a proof.

title: April Hall (奈良 四月堂 Nara Shigatsu-dō)
creator: Maeda Masao 前田政雄 (1904-1974)
description: Printed during the artist's lifetime by Takahashi Studio which printed a number of Maeda's designs in the 1960s and 1970s.<br>April Hall (Shigatsu-dō), an Important Cultural Property, is located in the Todai Temple grounds and was built in the Edo period. It is called April Hall for the special prayer ceremony, Hokke Sanmai, held there every April.

title: The Seventh Month: Suketaya Takasuke IV  in the role of Hotoke Gozen (七月 助高屋　高助 仏御前)
creator:
Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
<br>Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: One of twelve prints in a collaborative series by Toyohara Kunichika (1835–1900) and Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889). Kunichika depicts the actor Suketakaya Takasuke IV (Sawamura Tossho II) in the role of Hotoke Gozen.  In the fan-shaped inset, Kyōsai depicts two nuns at a solitary mountain cottage, a reference to Hotoke Gozen, whose name means ‘nun’.

title: Battles of Coxinga, Act 1 (国性爺 卷一)
creator: Utagawa Kunikazu 歌川国員 (active 1848-1868)
description:
Act 1 of the play the Battles of Coxinga written by Japan's great Edo-period playwright Chikamatsu Monzaemon 近松 門左衛門 (1653-1724).<br>The image depicts a performance given at the Kado Theater in Osaka January 1859. To the left is Jitsukawa Ensaburō 実川延三郎 as Watōnai; in the center is Arashi Kichisaburō III 嵐吉三郎 as Kanki; to the right is Bandō Hikosaburō V 坂東彦三郎 as Kinshōjō.<br>Synopsis of the play:
"The Battles of Coxinga (Kokusenya kassen) is based on the true adventures of Coxinga/ Watonai, a warrior of Chinese and Japanese parentage, who fought for the restoration of the Ming Chinese government after its defeat in the 17th c. by Manchu invaders. In the kabuki play Watonai joined forces with Kinshojo, his Chinese step-sister, and Kanki, her husband." - Source: The Claremont Colleges Digital Library https://ccdl.claremont.edu/digital/collection/cyw/id/232 [accessed 8-27-2023]

title: Captain Matsuzaki Fights Bravely in the Battle of Songhwan (成観之激戦松崎大尉奮勇ノ図 Seikan no gekisen Matsuzaki taii funyū no zu)
creator: Migita Toshihide 右田年英 (1863-1925)
description:
Before reaching Songhwan, the Japanese troops had to cross the deep Anson river. Forty-year-old Captain Matsuzaki Naoomi from Kumamoto on Kyushu led his men on July 29, 1894, in attacking the enemy on the other side of the river. In this print the fearless captain battles cowering Chinese soldiers. But he was ambushed from one hundred feet and was shot through the leg. Undaunted, he continued to fight gallantly with his sword. When he was struck by another bullet in the head, he is reported to have shouted, “I’ve been hit!” and to have died bravely. Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Shunpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p. 20.<br>
Other prints from this collection featuring the valor of Captain Matsuzaki are The Great Battle of the Ansong Ford: The Valor of Captain Matsuzaki Crossing Anjō (IHL.0168) and Captain Matsuzaki Crossing the Anjō-sen (IHL. 0530), both by Mizuno Toshikata.

title: Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo (鎮西八郎源為朝)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
Pictured is Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo [Minamoto No Tametomo (1139-1177)] slaying a powerful konoha-tengu (Tumbling-leaf tengu), with its characteristic bright red human face, long bulbous nose, wild hair, and bulging eyes. Tametomo has cut off the tengu's head, also severing the cliff edge. Part of the tengu's severed body can be seen beneath the scroll on the right. <br>Tametomo was the hero of many legends, one of which has him being stopped from committing ritual suicide while at sea by a tengu sent by Emperor Sutoku.
<br> The prints in this series were originally issued as a pair of chūban size prints on an ōban size sheet.
<br>Yoshitoshi modeled this design after his teacher's, Utagawa Kuniyoshi (1798-1861), almost identical print created about 30 years earlier for the series Ten Famous Excellences of Tametomo (Tametomo homare no jikketsu), published by Aritaya Seiemon, c. 1848.

title: Numazu: Latticework Tile Wall (沼津 なまこ壁)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description: Sekino's rendition of station number 13, Numazu, along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. This print is the 17th, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekinō created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō, originally made famous by Andō Hiroshige (1794-1858).  Sekino's love of geometry is on show in this print with the diamond latticework, vertical slats, and the kawara (clay roofing tiles) patterns. <br>"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . In 1975, after the completion of the modern Tōkaidō series, the Ministry of Education Award was granted to Sekinō because of his outstanding achievement 'in using every possible technique in woodblock printing, Japanese traditional art, and the recreation of the old fifty-three stations on the Tōkaidō highway in a present-day light.'" - Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p.241-242 and Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 259-260.

title: Strokes 93-7
creator: Hara Takeshi 原健 (b. 1942)
description:
Hara has been working with the theme of 'strokes' since the 1970s. The strokes have been described as paths of light, each one a range of intensities captured by Hara's magnificent technique of colour gradation. His prints, exhibiting "flat coolness and perfect evenness" at first appear to be silkscreens, but they are achieved through lithography often involving multiple printings using the artist's "special technique with a method of applying the ink with huge rollers to give his work an element of unbelievable smoothness, lushness, and control." - Sources: Contemporary Japanese Prints: Symbols of a Society in Transition, Lawrence Smith, Harper & Row Publishers, 1985, p. 28; Collecting Modern Japanese Prints, Then and Now, Mary and Norman Tolman, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1994, p. 126.<br>
There is an indebtedness to traditional Japanese calligraphy, in its movement, by Hara while substituting a rainbow of saturated colors for the traditional black sumi ink.<br>

title: Mountain and Lake (山と湖 Yama to mizuumi)
creator: Miyashita Tokio 宮下登喜雄 (1930–2011)
description:
One of Miyashita's post-1980s prints displaying a move back towards realism from the abstraction of his works created in the 1970s. Miyashita used a similar water and hilly shoreline motif on at least several other prints likely created around the time this collection's print was made.
<br>The intense blues and greens are printed using water-based inks on a carved woodblock with the elevated black outlines and impressed surfaces of the buildings on the shoreline being achieved through soldering wire and bits and pieces to a zinc plate and building up the outlined areas with layers of oil-based intaglio ink.

title: Autumn Moon at Tōin (洞院の秋月 Tōin no aki no tsuki)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
This print pictures Fujiwara no Yasumasa, an aristocrat of distinction, playing his flute, being stalked by the outlaw Hakamadare Yasusuke who wants to steal Yasumasa's clothing. 
<br>"Fujiwara no Yasumasa (958-1036) was a renowned musician and poet in the Heian court. One autumn night Yasumasa made his way home through the isolated Ichiharano moor. He played his flute as he sauntered along. While he believed that he was alone amidst the tall grass, a bandit lay in wait. The highwayman, Hakamadare Yasusuke (also known as Kidomaru) planned to attack the lonely traveler and steal his elegant winter robes. Yet, as the music reached Yasusuke’s ears, he found himself unable to attack. He became enchanted by the beauty of the music and followed Yasumasa all the way home. Upon reaching the courtier’s home, the flutist noticed his unintended audience and offered Yasusuke a fine gift of clothing so that he would not leave empty-handed." - Source: website of Ronin Gallery
<br>Originally issued in April 1868, this print was posthumously reissued (a "second state") using a different color scheme and partially new blocks in April 1894. Three different versions of this reprint exist, with this collection's print being considered the second version distinguished by the orange coat worn by Yasumasa, as opposed to a blue coat in the first version. A final version, perhaps from around 1900, is without a publisher’s seal or Yoshitoshi’s signature.

title: Sakaki, No. 10 (榊 第十号)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
One of an assumed 54 prints in the series The Fifty-Four Chapters in Modern Times by Toyohara Kunichika (1835–1900).  Here we see Genji courting one of his lovers in front of an evergreen tree on which Genji has tied love notes in a scene from chapter 10.
<br>"‘Genji Mania’ may have long peaked before Kunichika’s Fifty-Four Modern Feelings [a.k.a. title: Fujidaiko 富士太鼓 (Fuji's Drum)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis  (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 32) - Hearing that a drum player named Asama had been called in to play at a seven-day concert before the Emperor Hanazono, another famous player named Fuji came up to the capital too. Asama, resenting this, kills Fuji. When the official has announced this, Fuji’s wife arrives with her daughter, having been much disturbed by a dream she has had. Learning what has happened, she puts on her husband’s robes and, overcome with grief, strikes the drum which to her was the cause of her husband’s death.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Disquisition on the Political Affair of the Kyōwa Era (日月星享和政談 Jitsugetsusei kyōwa seidan)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description:
While the play's title is not shown in the print, the actors (right to left), Ichikawa Sadanji, Onoe Kikugorō [V], Iwai Hanshirō [VIII] and Nakamura Nakazō [III] are portraying characters in the play Jitsugetsusei kyōwa Seidan written in 1876 by Kawatake Mokuami (Kawatake Shinshichi II, 1816–1893).<br>
The play is based on the Kyōwa era (1801-1804) incident known as the Enmeiin Affair, in which Nichido an actor-turned-priest used a secret chamber at the Nichiren temple Enmeiin to seduce a number of leading ladies from the shogun’s house. "Nichido was first an actor but became the superior of Enmeiin, a temple of the Nichiren sect in Yanaka, and, with the aid of the priestling Ryuzen, enticed women thither, making the place a den of immorality, visited even by ladies-in-waiting at the Court.  That priests should break their vows of chastity was so common that no one gave it a second thought, but when we have a man who turned priest from actor and alluring women to his temple for immoral purposes, it throws a glaring light on the moral degradation of the age." - Source: The Economic Aspects of the History of the Civilization of Japan – Volume 3, Yosaburō Takekoshi, originally 1930 and republished 2004, Routledge, p. 173.

title: Nest (巣)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description:
This is the only lithograph by Takahashi that I have seen, all of his other print work employs woodblock. He created it in 1965 at the legendary studios of Ken Tyler, owner of Gemini Ltd.
<br>"Tyler established the print workshop Gemini Ltd. in 1965 and set out to work with the very best artists of his day, promising them: ‘Here is a workshop, there are no rules, no restrictions, do what you want to do.’" - Source National Gallery of Australia website http://nga.gov.au/InternationalPrints/Tyler/Default.cfm?MnuID=10 [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>
"Takahashi’s collaboration with Kenneth Tyler followed a strong tradition of artistic exchange between America and Japan in the post-war period. Titled Nest, the print in the NGA collection was produced at the Gemini workshop in 1965. It is representative of Takahashi’s typical mode of abstraction, with depth created by tonal layers and the image vaguely reminiscent of the natural forms Takahashi found so inspiring." - Source: Gwen Horsfield, 2008, National Gallery of Australia website, 
https://nga.gov.au/art-artists/the-kenneth-e-tyler-collection/artists/rikio-takahashi/#:~:text=Takahashi's%20collaboration%20with%20Kenneth%20Tyler,the%20Gemini%20workshop%20in%201965    [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Kazusa Akushichibei in the play Kagekiyo (九世市川団十郎 上総悪七兵衛・景清)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper right panel, playing the role of Kazusa Akushichibei 上総悪七兵衛 in the kabuki play Kagekiyo 景清. He wears "the exaggerated kumadori [stage makeup associated with the aragoto style], bushy hair and gold brocade of the 'loyal warrior'. . . ."[1] Below Danjūrō is an unidentified actor playing the role of Shigetada 重忠. 
<br>"The role of the famous Heike warrior Akushichibyoe [Akushichibei] Kagekiyo is a signature one for the Ichikawa family, and the play is part of the Kabuki Eighteen. The role was first played by Danjūrō IV, whose thin frame and long face made him unsuitable for the pure Ichikawa aragoto roles. Instead he developed his art in other directions, playing the logical and loyal heroes known as jitsugotoshi, as well as villain (katakiyaku) roles. He enjoyed huge success with the part of Kagekiyo. The part adds a new psychological dimension to aragoto, in that Kagekiyo is imprisoned by his enemies, and endures a tearful reunion with his wife and children before smashing his way out of the prison in which he is being held. The makeup he developed for the role used black lines, suggesting his evil nature. Later generations of Danjūrō continued to play the role, and it had a special significance for Danjūrō VII, who acted it to celebrate his return to Edo after seven years banishment. Perhaps we can sense a hint of pride in the way he used Kagekiyo's escape from prison to mirror his own banishment and return."[2]
<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
<br>"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[3] 
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

<br><br>[1] The Kabuki Handbook, Aubrey S. & Giovanna M. Halford, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 12th printing 1981, p. 122.
<br>[2] Naritaya website http://www.naritaya.jp/english/compendium/dictionary_04.html
<br>[3] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

Learning of the extent of Nakamitsu's devotion, Manjū pardons his son and then asks his retainer to perform a dance for them. creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis  (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 86-87) - While the Emperor Gen-sō (Hsuan Tsung) of T'ang is keeping an anxious vigil over the sick-bed of his favourite, Yō-kihi (Yang Kuei-fei), an old man comes to the palace and tells the Emperor that he is the ghost of Shō-ki (Chung K'uei), a former retainer who committed suicide when he failed in an examination. The Emperor, however, graciously appointed him posthumously to Court rank and gave him a fine burial; in return he has now come to drive the sickness away from Yō-hiki. He asks that a certain sacred mirror be placed at the head of her bed, and then disappears. When this is done, the devil who is afflicting Yō-hiki is seen in the mirror, but when the Emperor draws his sword to strike it down, it vanishes. The spirit of Shō-ki returns and succeeds in vanquishing the devil. Having this repaid his debt, Shō-ki promises the Emperor that he will become a protective deity and then disappears again like a figure in a dream.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Ema 絵馬 (The Votive Tablets)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:

O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 26-28) - An Imperial emissary on his way to the Great Shrines of Ise stops overnight at Saikū nearby as it happens to be the last day of winter and he hopes to see something of the votive tablets which are said to be hung up there during that particular night to foretell the fortunes of the coming year, a white one indicating sunny weather and a black one rain. He meets an old couple with such tablets who, after some discussion, agree to put up one of each kind to signify good fortune for everyone. They then disappear into the darkness after telling him that they are in fact two of the gods of Ise. In the second part Amaterasu, the Sun-goddess, appears with the goddess Uzume and the god Tajikarao and performs a dance. The three of them then depict the ancient story of Amaterasu’s withdrawal into a cave: as the world is plunged into darkness by her disappearance, the other gods dance and make merry and eventually succeed in enticing her out again by arousing her curiosity.

creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:

creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:

title: Kabuki Playbill for Kabuki-za featuring the play Motomezuka migawari Nitta and the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: The cover of this kabuki playbill (banzuke) from March 1892 features Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role oa Kusunoki, Masashige’s wife, in the play Onna Kusunoki (top inset) and the role of the pirate Kezori Kyuemon in the play Kezori Kyuemon (bottom inset.) The red cartouches using kanteiryū (the scripted kanji used for kabuki signs and advertising) provide the name of the theater, the Kabuki-za, and its location. The smaller light-colored cartouche contains the signature of the artist Utagawa Kunimasa IV, using his then current artist name Kōchōrō. The price of the playbill is marked as 8 sen.

title: White Sake for Otafuku, No Medicine for Foolishness (おたふくに白酒  ばかにつける薬はない Otafuku ni shirozake, Baka ni tsukeru kusuri mo nai)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: The second part of the print's title, "baka ni tsukeru kusuri wa nai" is a proverb meaning "there is no cure for a fool." Certainly the gentleman in the lower right is acting like a drunken fool, performing some disgusting act that provokes both consternation and hilarity. At the top of the print an otafuku (a homely woman, but also the goddess of mirth) dances and to the right of her bottles of shirozake (sweet white sake) are evident.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Aya no Tsuzumi 綾鼓 (Brocade Drum)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis  (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 11) - An old gardener, who has fallen in love with a lady of the Court, is told that if he can make the sound of a drum in the grounds reach her, she will let him see her again. He gladly strikes the drum but no sound comes, for it is covered only with damask. Overcome with anger and despair, he drowns himself in the lake in the palace grounds.  His angry ghost then appears and gives vent to its feelings of anger against the lady.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Fruitful Year at Fuji (豊年の富士 Hōnen no Fuji)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
This 13th print in the 36 print series depicts farmers harvesting a bountiful autumn crop while Mount Fuji stands guard in all its grandeur. This print is the original issue (first edition between 1939-1940) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company as part of the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. Later editions eliminated the small telephone pole on the right side of the hill and also changed the title from 豊年の富士 to 實りの秋.  To view a later edition of this image please see IHL. 0412, Fall Harvest from the series Eight Views of Fuji.
<br><br>THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF 2600
<br>Published by Uchida Bijutsu Shoshi between 1939 and 1940, this 36-print set (plus an introductory sheet and a table of contents sheet) by Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000) is a more modern take on Hokusai's (1760–1849) famous series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1826-1833). Its publication was timed to coincide with nationalist celebrations in November 1940 marking Kigen 2600, the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. 
<br>
Tokuriki's series was extremely popular with domestic and foreign buyers who purchased one thousand copies within a short time after issuance. Various prints from this series were re-printed in subsequent years and subsets of the thirty-six prints were later repackaged into newly named series, such as Eight Views of Mount Fuji and Four Season of Mount Fuji, released in the 1950s. Later printings omit the information in the margin, modify Tokuriki's signature and change the seals below his signature appearing in the image area of the print.

title: To と
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
One of eighteen prints issued as part of the comic series "ABCs of Educational Lectures" issued between February 1897 and March 1898. This series was a collaboration between Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915) and the writer Nishimori Takeki 西森武城 (1861-1913), also known as Koppi Dōjin, one of the chief comic writers for the newspaper Marumaru chinbun (Blue Pencil News of the Weird). "The conceit of this series is a spoof on the Imperial Rescript on Education (Kyōiku chokugo) issued in 1890 to boost morality by reminding people of Confucian and Shinto values." - Source: Akiko Walley, Maud I. Kerns Associate Professor of Japanese Art, History of Art and Architecture, University of Oregon.
<br>This print represents the syllable “to” (と) with the saying, 'Tori naki sato ni kōmori,' which is roughly equivalent to 'In the Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man is King,' but more literally, 'Bats in the Land with No Birds.' It satirizes the no-good son of a wealthy provincial family returning from his 'Grand Tour' of Tokyo. The 'busker' in the original is more specifically, deroren saimon, or 'trumpet shell prayer.' The mention of 'deroren saimon' is a pun on the phrase 'hora o fuku' (to toot on one’s trumpet shell), meaning to 'boast' or 'tell tall tales.' Deroren was a type of street performance popular during the late Edo (1615-1868) and Meiji (1868-1912) periods. A performer told vendetta' stories in a distinct rhythmic phrasing, blowing the trumpet shell intermittently uttering the nonsensical word 'deroren' to retain audience’s attention." - Source: Akiko Walley, Maud I. Kerns Associate Professor of Japanese Art, History of Art and Architecture, University of Oregon.

(For other prints in this series see IHL.0766 and IHL.0767.) <br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

title: Lever (梃子 teko)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description: One of eight diptych prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of mechanics issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print discusses and demonstrates the principles and practical uses of the lever with the print on the right explaining that in raising the ladder, the closer you are to the ladder's center of gravity, the less force you will need. On the left, the diagrams explain about the lever and fulcrum and its applications. (For other prints in this series see IHL.0765 and IHL.0767.) <br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

title: Wedge (楔 kusabi)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description: One of eight diptych prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of mechanics issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print discusses and demonstrates the wedge, its principles and practical applications. The right side of the diptych relates that "a wedge is a combination of two sloping edges necessary to break wood or rock. The thinner the wedge, the less strength is needed. The thicker, the more power is required" and the left side tells us "When two large sake cups are stacked on top of each other and pressure is applied to the top, it is possible to break only the outer cup, which is also the same as the principle of a wedge." (For other prints in this series see IHL.0765 and IHL.0766.) <br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: Saigō Takamori, the leader of the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion (and identified in the red cartouche on his immediate left as "Saigō Takamori the head rebel" 賊魁西郷隆盛, is flanked by his lieutenants Kirino Toshiaki 桐野利秋 to his right, and Shinohara Kunimoto 篠原国幹 to his left. Saigō, who had been dead several weeks when this print was published in October 1877, is standing on a hybrid tiger/wolf/badger demon, representing the swift-killing disease cholera. Saigō is also pictured with a third arm, the meaning of which remains unclear. The imagery uses Saigō's status as an almost demigod after his death, to publicize a warning about a cholera epidemic that broke out the previous month. However, this is not one of the prints that sought to deify the rebel leader after his death, rather it uses double meanings to suggest that Saigō, and the chaos that resulted from his Rebellion, was responsible for the cholera outbreak.<br>The print carries a price of 1 sen 5 rin 定價一銭五厘.

description:
This print, one of ninety-two full-color supplemental prints to the earlier issued six volume textbook titled Brocade Pictures of Moral Education, illustrates story number 15 in volume 5.<br>
In October 1883 a set of ninety-two full-color oban-size prints designed by students of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi were published by Tsuji Keiji and his publishing house Fukyūsha as supplements, or accompaniments, to the six volume set of textbooks titled "Nishiki-e shūshindan" 錦絵修身談 (Brocade Prints for Moral Education), published earlier by Tsuji and illustrated by Yoshitoshi. creator: Chiura Obata 小圃千浦 (1885-1975) - attributed to
description: Woodblock print of a bass jumping from the water, bounded on top and bottom by a brocade border to appear mounted as if it were a hanging scroll. title: Arashiyama, Spring Scenery (嵐山春景)
creator: Itō Nisaburō 伊藤仁三郎 (1905-2001)
description:
One of four prints in an untitled series with famous sites of Kyoto - Kinkakuji, Kiyomizu, Yasaka Pagoda and this print, Arashiyama. This print presents us with a view of the Togetsukyō bridge stretching across the Ōi River, with Mount Arashi in the background.  Also see IHL.0787, Yasaka Pagoda, Moonlit Night.<br>Arashiyama (嵐山) is a pleasant, touristy district in the western outskirts of Kyoto. The area has been a popular destination since the Heian Period (794-1185), when nobles would enjoy its natural setting. Arashiyama is particularly popular during the cherry blossom and fall color seasons.
<br>The Togetsukyō Bridge is Arashiyama's well known, central landmark.

description: One of four prints in an untitled series with famous sites of Kyoto - Kinkakuji, Kiyomizu, Yasaka Pagoda and this print, Arashiyama. This print presents us with a view of Yasaka Pagoda on a moonlit night in Kyoto. Also see IHL.0786, Arashiyama, Spring Scenery.<br>Yasaka Pagoda is a five-story pagoda located to the west of Ninen-zaka and San'nen-zaka streets within the Hokanji temple precinct. The pagoda is 49 meters high, and is the third highest wooden building in Kyoto after Toji and Kofukuji. The temple has existed from before the transfer of the national capital to Kyoto in 794. It has been destroyed by fire and rebuilt several times with the current pagoda rebuilt in 1440 by Yoshinori Ashikaga, the 6th Shogun of Muromachi government. It is designated as an important cultural property.

title: Ugetsu 雨月 (Rain and Moon)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis  (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 202-203) - Arriving at Sumiyoshi on a pilgrimage to the shrine there, the priest Saigyō seeks shelter in the house of an old couple. They gladly give him lodging when he succeeds in providing a beginning to the second part of a poem which the old man composed about a dispute between him and his wife:
<br>she, liking to watch the moon,
<br>wants the eaves of the house left unthatched
<br> but he enjoys hearing the sound of the rain on the thatching there.
<br>In the second part of the play, Sumiyoshi Miyōjin, the patron god of poetry, takes possession of an old keeper of the shrine to speak of poetry and dance.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

Of three treasures sent from China to be deposited in the Kōfukuji temple two were safely delivered but the third, [a jewel] was seized and taken down to the Dragon Palace in the waters of the bay. The lord whose sister had become the consort of a T'ang emperor and sent the treasures to Japan, formed an alliance with a fisher-girl at Shido-no-ura and when a son was born promised to make him his heir if she would retrieve the jewel. This she did at the cost of her life. The son, the fisher-girl tells him, is the present Minister Fusazaki and she herself is the spirit of his mother. She then disappears but reappears later as a dragon-woman from the depths of the bay where she met her death, and dances as she rejoices that through the power of the Lotus Sutra she has been able to attain Buddhahood.

title: Haiyū mitate asahi shō gun'ei chū no zu (旭将軍營中図)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
The three actors (R to L) Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Tomoe gozen, Onoe Kikugorō V as Yoshinaka (named the "Asahi general" by Emperor Go-daigo), and Nakamura Fukusuke IV as Yamabuki gozen in the play Haiyū mitate Asahi shō gun'ei chū no zu.<br>
These characters are drawn from the The Tale of the Heike (平家物語 Heike Monogatari) which includes the story of Minamoto no Yoshinaka and Tomoe gozen, the famous woman warrior of the Genpei Wars between the Taira and Minamoto clans.

title: Nakamura Jyakuemon, Arashi Rikan and Arashi Kitsusaburō in A True Tale of Butterflies and Plovers (中村雀右衛門、嵐璃寛 、嵐橘三郎・蝶千鳥曽我実録  Nakamura Jyakuemon、Arashi Rikan、Arashi Kitsusaburō・Chō chidori Soga no jitsuroku)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description: The three middle panels of a pentatych depicting the actors Nakamura Jyakuemon II as Wada Yoshimori, Arashi Rikan IV as Ōiso no Tora and Arashi Kitsusaburō IV as Ōji in the play Chō chidori Soga no jitsuroku (A True Tale of Butterflies and Plovers), a tale based on the revenge of the Soga brothers, a Sogomono 曽我物.

title: Chion-In Temple Black Gate Spring Scene (— 智恩院黒門 春景)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), using the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.<br>This print presents a view of Chion-In Temple's Black Gate (Kuromon). A fenced enclosure is seen in the lower left of the print protecting the "squash stone" (uryseki). The stone, which has a very low profile to the ground, was there before the temple was built and is connected to two legends. One is that gourds sprang from this stone, even though no one planted any seeds, and the other is that the god of Yasaka Shrine paid two visits to this stone and on the night after the second visit many gourds sprang from the stone.

title: Gion Shinbashi Neighborhood (祇園新橋附近)
creator: Kamei Tōbei  亀井藤兵衛 (1901-1977)
description:
One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), using the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.<br>
This print provides us with a view of a small bridge over the Shirakawa river in Gion Shinbashi.  A kimono clad woman on the right enters the frame with umbrella in hand on this rainy day.  For another impression of this print see IHL.2193.

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Fuwa Banzaemon in the play Fuwa (九世市川団十郎 不破伴左衛門・不破)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper right panel, in the role of Fuwa Banzaemon in the kabuki play Fuwa. Pictured on the bottom wearing a sedge hat is the character Nagoya 名古屋 (Nagoya Sanza), Fuwa's rival. 
<br>"This story was first played in 1680 at the Ichimura-za in Edo with Ichikawa Danjūrō I. During the cherry blossoms season, two warriors with their faces concealed in fantastic straw hats meet in Yoshiwara, the famous red-light district in Edo. They are Fuwa Banzaemon and Nagoya Sanza. Initially, Fuwa is a nice man but in due course he forgets his wife and his friend, Nagoya and seduces his courtesan lover.
<br>In the true style of the Kabuki Eighteen Fuwa later appeara as Shōki (a powerful man who drives away the God of Plague) and fights off the goblins who try to kill him."[1]
<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
<br>"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2] 
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

<br><br>[1] Kabuki Eighteen Traditional Dramas, Kawatake Toshio, Chronicle Books, 1885, p. 54.
<br>[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description:
"Mr. Funasaka enjoys reducing images to their most basic components: lines, circles, dots and rectangles. The magic of Mr. Funasaka's prints lies in his ability to extract deep meaning from the simplest of images. . . ." 
<br>The colored shapes bordering the open diamond shape are likely produced with woodblock; the blue patterned areas are likely a silkscreen pattern.

title: Work.At21-1969
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: An early work by Funasaka (sometimes called "The Hole Man,") featuring his punched holes through a speckled paper. In this work we see the beginnings of another signature form of the artist, a semi-organic slender vertical form with at least one straight side.

title: Butterfly (蝶)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description: The fourth of ten prints in the first of five sets of prints comprising the series Outdoor Sketches created by the artist between 1928 and 1935.  In this print a man on a jaunty stroll tips his hat to a butterfly. Maekawa created this series of five sets (ten prints each set) of black and white linoleum cuts as, in the artist's words, prints of affection (shin'ai ban).  Each small print, its image area measuring approximately 5 x 5 in. (12.7 x 12.7 cm), depicts a figure engaged in outdoor work or recreation.

title: Reproduction of: Actors Arashi Ryuzo as Ukiyo Matabei and Otani Hiroji III as Tosa no Matahei (複製：嵐竜蔵の浮世又平 三世大谷広次の土佐の又平 Fukusei：Ryūzō Arashi's Ukiyo Matahira Koji Otani III's Tosa no Matahira)
creator: Tōshūsai Sharaku 東洲斎写楽 (active 1794–1795)
description:
158 works and sketches survive of the Japanese artist known only by the art name Tōshūsai Sharaku. Almost all were made over a ten-month period in 1794–1795. This modern reproduction from an unknown publisher is printed on a white mica ground, as was the original.
<br>This print depicts the actors Ōtani Hiroji III as Tosa no Matahei and Arashi Ryūzō as and Tosa's manservant Ukiyo Matahei. Four original copies of this work are known, with one residing in the collection of the Tokyo National Museum.

title: Shuto Expressway (首都高速道路)
creator: Ōhno Takashi 大野隆司 (b. 1951)
description:
Four artists, Ino Eiji 井野英二 (b. 1949), Kamiya Kiyotaka 紙谷清貴 (b. 1951). Sugisawa Osamu 杉沢修 (b. ?) and Ōhno Takashi 大野隆司 (b. 1951) contributed to this portfolio of prints titled One Hundred Scenes in Tokyo at the End of the Century issued between 1988 and 1989. This portfolio follows in the tradition of others that have provided artist interpretations of Edo/Tokyo at various milestones, such as "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo" by Hiroshige issued between 1856 and 1858 which provided, in Henry Smith's words, "the visualization of the new national space";  "100 Views of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa Era" by Koizumi Kishio issued between 1928 and 1940 chronicling the rebuilding of Tokyo after the devastating 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake; "One Hundred Views of New Tokyo" by various artists issued between 1928 and 1932 also chronicling the rise of Tokyo after the 1923 earthquake and "Scenes of Lost Tokyo" by various artists issued in 1945, a visual argument for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan after WWII. 
<br> In this print Ohno depicts a section of the multi-level Shuto Expressway (Metropolitan Expressway) built between 1962 and 1967 to "increase traffic flow efficiency in the Tokyo Metropolitan Area." The expressway covers Nihonbashi, the iconic center of Edo and then Tokyo, but a rerouting of part of the expressway underground will allow Nihonbashi to see daylight sometime around 2040.

title: Kokkai-gijidō Station on the Chiyoda Line (国会議事堂駅)
creator: Ino Eiji  井野英二 (b. 1949)
description:
Four artists, Ino Eiji 井野英二 (b. 1949), Kamiya Kiyotaka 紙谷清貴 (b. 1951). Sugisawa Osamu 杉沢修 (b. ?) and Ōhno Takashi 大野隆司 (b. 1951) contributed to this portfolio of prints titled One Hundred Scenes in Tokyo at the End of the Century issued between 1988 and 1989. This portfolio follows in the tradition of others that have provided artist interpretations of Edo/Tokyo at various milestones, such as "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo" by Hiroshige issued between 1856 and 1858 which provided, in Henry Smith's words, "the visualization of the new national space";  "100 Views of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa Era" by Koizumi Kishio issued between 1928 and 1940 chronicling the rebuilding of Tokyo after the devastating 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake (see IHL. xxxxxx); "One Hundred Views of New Tokyo" by various artists issued between 1928 and 1932 also chronicling the rise of Tokyo after the 1923 earthquake and "Scenes of Lost Tokyo" by various artists issued in 1945 a visual argument for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan after WWII. 
<br> In this print Ino depicts platform 4 at the Kokkai-gijidō Station on the Chiyoda Line, the stop that services the National Diet Building.

title: Illustration of the Imperial Palace Buildings (大日本帝国造営御所之図  Dai nippon teikoku zōei gosho no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: An 1888 bird's eye view of the just completed Imperial Palace complex in Tokyo. The scroll on the left contains details on the complex including the intended uses of the various buildings, which are identified in the small red cartouches.<br>The old Edo Castle had been destroyed by fire in 1873 and for fifteen years the royal family lived in a temporary residence in the Akasaka Detached Palace. The new palace, completed in October 1888, would stand until destroyed by the air raids of WWII.

title: Beautiful Riverside Village (水郷 suigō)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
This print of a cow grazing outside a bucolic village is one of three prints in the fourth of ten envelopes containing the prints comprising set one of Seihō's Masterpieces.

<br><br>SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
<br>Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century." <br>Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.<br>While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

title: Sumo Wrestling
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: "The two outsize bodies are squeezed into the space, giving it energy and drama. By reducing virtually all detail to outline, the artist is able to focus our attention on the tensed toes and leg muscles, the wrestlers' arms grasping and attempting to push each other over, and the fringe and giant bow of their belts. This image is based on a woodblock print by Utagawa Kunisada (1786-1864), and as a tribute his signature is included in the bottom right-hand corner." - Source: Japanese Art in Detail, John Reeve, Harvard University Press, p. 92.

title: Rainbow Night 8
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description:
Ay-O has made a number of variously titled prints, paintings and sculptures showing anatomically correct male and female figures. In this artist's proof, a vibration of color links the two figures.  It is one of ten prints in the series Rainbow Night.<br>
In discussing this series, Ay-o states, "In this series . . . I wanted to express a certain order . . . in the same way that time slowly elapses. I used cut-out dolls when I was drawing the ten prints of Rainbow night . . . . Rainbow night 8 is an angle taken from above of a man and a woman facing upward. Moreover, the form of the man and woman in Rainbow night 8 is a completely identical silhouette.  Hair, breasts, and male genitals deceive the eye."

title: Moon Reflection (月映)
creator: Hasegawa Yuichi 長谷川雄一 (b. 1945)
description:
Hasegawa uses the reductive woodblock technique for his work in which a single woodblock is used, rather than individual carved woodblocks, to print all the colors in a design.  This usually involves 10 to 20 processes of completing the carving for one color, printing that color and then repeating this process for each color. The moon is a recurring subject for Hasegawa's work and in this work the moon's reflected light is scene in the foreground grasses.<br>
In the words of the artist, "“From a long time past, I have been influenced by the deep spirituality of Zen. Up until now, the immense time and space of the Universe, arranged like a Buddhist Mandala, has been my theme. Going beyond that concept, my most recent images have been born from various forms of creation which can be observed in nature. Being resigned to the fact of the long history of mankind in general, I am fumbling to find the personal contribution which I can offer, in the present, and I am striving to create works with a meaningful inner spirit as well.”

title: Heart Sutra (般若心経)
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: Ay-O has immersed the Heart Sutra among seven colors of squares. At the bottom of the print the mantra 掲諦掲諦波羅掲諦羅僧掲諦菩提莎婆呵 (gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha!) is written.<br>“Form is emptiness, emptiness is form,” insists the Heart Sutra, the most popular Buddhist scripture and emptiness. "Nothingness," was a major theme for the Daoist and Zen-influenced Fluxus artists [of whom Ay-O was one], permeating their work. - Source: NYU Grey Art Gallery, 2011 exhibition Fluxus and the Essential Questions of Life

creator: Kubota Beisen 久保田米僊 (1852-1906)
description: An undated sketch album by Kubota Beisen (1852-1906) using sumi and watercolors and consisting of fourteen drawings. Twelve of the drawings are landscapes (sansui ga), one is a drawing of a bird on a plum branch (kachō-ga) and one a scene from the Japanese folktale Kachi-kachi Yama (Crackling Mountain), in which a hare smashes the boat of his rival, a tanuki (a mythical raccoon dog/badger.)<br>In describing Beisen's work, Henry P. Bowie, lawyer, artist, author and student of Beisen's states "Kubota was so skillful in sketching that while traveling rapidly through a country he could faithfully reproduce the salient features of an extended landscape, conformable to the general rule in sketching, that what first attracts the eye is to be painted first, all else becoming subordinate to it in the scheme."

title: Tokyo Dockside (untitled)
creator: Miyashita Tokio 宮下登喜雄 (1930–2011)
description:
While primarily known for his brightly colored prints which combine woodblock and metal plate printmaking techniques, Miyashita also created a number of monochrome etchings, such as this view of old warehouses and purse seiners on an unidentified river. The print is untitled, but was auctioned under the title Tokyo Dockside. While the middle ground warehouses and fishing boats look old, the city buildings seen in the background, including one skyscraper in the distance, are modern. The work, like most of Miyashita's work is undated.<br>
In February 12, 2014 a very similar print with minor changes to the composition and executed in color titled "テームズは  London" (Thames, London) came up for auction.

title: Night Under the Midnight Sun (白夜 Byakuya)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
One of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978-1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫  (1929-?).
<br>The original 1922 painting which this print is made after is in the collection of the Yumeji Art Museum in Okayama. 
<br>As in the case of this  print, the majority of Yumeji's woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934 and were based upon his paintings or previous designs for song sheets and postcards. They were often rescaled to accommodate standardized sizes of paper used for woodblock prints. Major publishers involved with producing these posthumous prints were Kyōto Hanga-in under the direction of Shinagawa Kiyoomi 品川清臣 (1907-?) and Katō Junji 加藤潤二 (1885-1961) and his Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjo.)

title: Man Ousts His Wife and Her Lover, No. 940 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・九百四十号)
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞.  The graphic, created by Utagawa Yoshiiku (1833-1904), and the text, written by Sansantei Arindo (1832-1902), both principles in the newspaper, tells of a man who, tired of his wife's infidelities, presents his wife and her lover with gifts and sends them away.<br>The writer for this print is identified as Sansantei Arindo 山々亭有人, a pen name of the writer Jono Saigiku 条野採菊 (born Jono Denpei 條野伝平). Born in Edo in 1832, by his late teens he had decided to become a writer of gesaku (collective term for prose fiction during the middle to late-Edo period) stories. He published his first story in 1860, and during the 1860s first Yoshiiku, then Yoshitoshi, created illustrations for some of his books. He went on to found the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun, the Keisatsu Shinbun and the Yamato Shinbun and continued to write fiction until his death in 1902.
<br>At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.
