title: Kurozuka 黒塚
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 92) -  Two traveling priests are given shelter for the night in the house of a poor woman at Kurozuka in Adachigahara. When she leaves them to collect firewood, she warns them not to look into her room, but the priest's servant is unable to restrain his curiosity. The horrifying things he sees there convince the priests that they are in the house of a devil. The woman then appears as an angry demon, but is finally overcome by the power of the priests.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: River Breeze (江南風色)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
A river breeze dries someone's laundry as a boatman guides his boat along a crowded river in this print, one of three in the third of nine envelopes containing the prints comprising set two of Seihō's Masterpieces.
<br><br>SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
<br>Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century." <br>Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.<br>While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

While talking with an old man whom he meets there, a tablet with gold writing on it falls from the sky. Taking it up, the envoy read that the god to whom it belongs promises constant protection to the land. The old man then takes the tablet and disappears, revealing as he does so that he is the god, Amatsu Futodama. He then appears in his true form, carrying a bow and arrow with which to subdue demons and ensure the peace of the land.

Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. title: Illustration of the First Soldier on Top of Pyongyang Gate in Pyongyang (平壌玄武門兵士先登之圖 Heijō Genbumon heishi sentō no zu)
creator: Taguchi Beisaku 田口米作 (1864-1903)
description: Private Harada Jukichi is pictured on top of the Genbu Gate in the city walls of Pyongyang. Hailed as a hero for letting his comrades into the city, his true story is less heroic. "Pingyang (Pyongyang) was well protected by walls that had to be surmounted in order to conquer the city. Repeated frontal attacks by the Japanese failed to penetrate, even after exhausting all their ammunition. One volunteer in the Eighteenth Regiment, twenty-seven year-old Harada Jukichi of Aichi prefecture, a mild man with a wife and a daughter, saw his regiment fail three times to penetrate the fortification and fearlessly scaled the wall of Gembu Gate. Harada lowered himself into the midst of the enemy and opened the gate from within. His comrades them flooded into the enemy fort. Harada's action was considered so meritorious that he was immediately promoted to the rank of superior private. Harada received the Order of the Golden Kite for his feat, but his honor proved overwhelming. He began a life of drunken dissipation and later was employed in the theater district reenacting his deed of heroism at Gembu Gate. The military authorities are said to have rebuked him for soiling the honor of the imperial army. It is also said that the soldier who actually climbed the gate first was Matsumura Aktaro, not Harada. Since Harada had already been decorated, this embarrassing fact was silenced. Matsumura was intimidated by the authorities and did not disclose the incident but secluded himself in his father's antique shop seeking truth among the collection of antiques." - Source: Impressions of the Front: Woodcuts of the Sino-Japanese War, Shunpei Okamoto, Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1983, p. 24.

title: March Play at the Kabuki-za (歌舞伎座・三月狂言 Kabuki-za sangatsu kyōgen)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: The actors from right to left, Ichikawa Shinjūrō III 市川新十郎 (1866-1929), Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上菊五郎 (1844-1903) and Kataoka Ichizō III 片岡市蔵 (1851-1906) in the play Zokusetsu bidan Kōmonki, staged at the Kabuki-za on March 15, 1901. While the play is not identified on the print, the title simply saying March Play at the Kabuki-za 歌舞伎座三月狂言, the Tokyo Metropolitan Library database entry for this print provides the play's name, Zokusetsu-bidan Kōmonki (The Popular and Moving Story of Kōmonki). The play tells of the adventures of the historical figure Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628-1700), a daimyo of Mito, responsible for assembling the Mitogaku scholars to compile Dai Nihon shi, a history of Japan, which is credited with the rise of nationalism in Japan.

title: Soga Brothers Confrontation: A New Play at the Meiji-za (明治座新狂言・曽我対面 Meiji-za Shin Kyōgen・Soga Taimen)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: Five actors, from right to left, Ichikawa Enjō 市川莚女 as Keshōzaka Shōshō 化粧坂少将 (a.k.a. Oiso no Tora), Ichikawa Enshō II 市川莚舛升 as Kobayashi Asahina 小林朝比奈 (waring "monkey face" makeup), Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 as Kudō Suketsune 工藤祐経, Sawamura Tosshō III 沢村訥升 as Soga Jūrō 曾我十郎 and Ichikawa Yonezō III 市川米蔵 as Soga Gorō 曾我五郎.<br>"A perennial favorite, the vendetta of the Soga brothers on their father's murderer is a familiar epic, but during kabuki's heyday, playwrights added new twists each season. Recognizable by costume and makeup are the beautiful courtesan, Oiso no Tora, in flamboyant gown and hairpins; the friend, Asahina, in comic 'monkey face' makeup; the murderer Suketsune, a high-ranking official, center; and the two brothers, left. Jūrō, the eldest, restrains the younger Gorō from attacking their foe, since the moment is not yet ripe." - Lynn Katsumoto (wall card from the exhibition Kabuki: A Revolution in Color and Design.)

A young woman sits in a chair in an art gallery.  Likely created as an illustration for a popular novel.
<br>The designer of this print, Okano Sakae (1880-1942), was primarily known as an illustrator and manga artist. Okano graduated from the Western-style painting department of the Tokyo School of Fine Arts in 1902. From 1925 to 1927 he was in Europe on a research mission for the Imperial Household Agency, spending time in France and Italy.

title: Shōchō in the role of Omatsu (松蔦 お松)
creator: Ogawa Hyōe (Heibei) 小川兵衛 (active c. 1915)
description:
The actor Ichikawa Shōchō II (1886-1940) in the role of Omatsu in an unknown play. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.
<br><br>SHIN NIGAO (NEW ACTOR PORTRAITS)<br>
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Actor Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

title: Nakiama 泣き尼 (The Crying Nun)
creator: Tsukioka Gyokusei 月岡玉瀞 (1908-1994)
description:
One of thirty-four prints designed by Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994) in the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyōgen Plays) started by her father Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927). She created 34 prints and the table of contents for this series, using the artist name Kōbun 江文. Tsukioka Kōgyo designed sixteen prints for the series before his death.<br>
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p.185-186.) - A Man comes in from the country in search of a Priest to bless the memorial he has built for his dead father. He stops at the first temple he comes to and presents his case. The Priest makes excuses and refuses until he finds that the Man plans to give a very large donation in return for the services.

<br>The Priest is very poor at preaching and performing ceremonies, so he invites a Nun who is well known for bursting into tears upon the slightest provocation. He finally convinces her to come along by offering her a ten percent commission.

<br>The Priest and the Nun go to the country with the Man.  When the Priest begins his sermon, the Nun, instead of crying, immediately goes to sleep. The Priest tries in vain to wake her by coughing loudly and using the words tear (namida) and cry (naku) over and over in his sermon.  The Nun finally wakes up with a start when the Priest strikes the gong indicating the end of his sermon.

<br>On the way home, the Nun praises the Priest for his sermon and cries. Then she asks for her commission. The Priest says, "No tears, no commission." The Nun grabs hold of him, and tries to throw him down. The Priest knocks the Nun down and leaves. The Nun chases after the Priest complaining in a loud voice, very much awake at last.

title: Seihō's Painting of Vegetables (栖鳳筆野菜圖 Seihō hitsu yasai zu)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
An ink on paper scroll mounted on silk brocade with a bone roller (jikuji), picturing two small eggplants and a recently picked cucumber. On the inside of the box containing the scroll is the inscription 桂華題 (keikadai). The Japanese art historian Lynn Katsumoto explains that the word keikadai denotes, "a genre or subject matter (dai) involving plants and flowers (kei being katsura or cinnamon tree, also carries the sense of something in nature that is beautiful) and (ka being hana or flower, with the connotation of something gorgeous)."
<br>For another hanging scroll by the artist see IHL.1025.

title: Sea of Fire (火の海 Hi no umi)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description:
This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, pictures the ancient fortifications along Hakata Bay erected after the first attempted Mongol invasion in 1274. The wall held back the Mongols second attack in 1281 and the invaders were ultimately defeated by a devastating typhoon which set fire to their ships. Sea of Fire refers to the raging fires in the bay. The print is from the original set of five prints issued in 1918 by Nakajima Jūtarō titled Tsukishi District which was the sixth set of prints in the ten set series Japan Scenery Prints issued between January 1917 and April 1920. <br> "Tsukushi is the ancient name of the area north-west of Kyushu [in the area of Chikuzen and Chikugo provinces] where Sakamoto was born. Sakamoto was rarely involved with sheet-prints, but like his colleagues on this series he had worked as a cartoonist and illustrator and had been a collaborator on the magazine Hōsun hence he was well used to graphic techniques. Indeed, his set [Tsukushi district] is the most strikingly designed in the series, combining impressionist, abstract and Expressionistic elements into a characteristically forceful blend." - Source: Modern Japanese Prints 1912-1989, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 1994, p. 42.
<br><br>"The series Nihon fūkei hanga (Japan Scenery Prints) consisted of ten sets of prints, with each set composed of five small landscapes and a cover print giving the name of the series, the name and number of the set, and the name of the artist. In addition, each set was accompanied by a table of contents and colophon sheet. Specific publication dates ranging from January 1917 through April 1920 indicate that each set was issued separately.  As Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958) designed the majority of prints in the series, it seems likely that Hakutei was the spearhead for the project. The artists asked Igami Bonkutsu to carve the blocks and Nakajima Jūtarō to publish the series." - Source: Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 274-276.
<br>In addition to Sakamoto Hanjirō (1882-1969), the other artists who contributed to the series were Ishii Hakutei (1182-1958), see IHL.1182 and IHL.1183, Hirafuku Hyakusui (1877-1933), Morita Tsunetomo (1881-1933), Kosugi Misei (1881-1964) and Ishii Tsuruzō (1887-1973), elder brother of Hakutei.

title: Fuku no kami jōruri at the Meiji-za (明治座 上るり [浄瑠璃] 福の神)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: A New Year's dance performance titled Fuku no kami staged in January 1897 at the Meiji-za. Fuku no kami is better known as a Noh play in which the God of Happiness, Fuku no kami, appears to worshipers at a shrine and asks them if they know how to find happiness. When they reply, "With money," he tells them it is not money, but the way of life upon which happiness depends. He asks for wine and then dances and sings a song which tells them that the way to find happiness is to make a happy home with one's wife, get up early, and welcome guests with good wine.

title: Illustration of the Great Training Maneuvers by Various Army Corps (諸隊大調錬ﾉ図 Shotai dai chōren no zu)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: This print depicts one of the recurring military training exercises to prepare the recently enlarged army. In 1882, the year previous to the release of this print, the emperor had issued the Imperial Rescript for Military Men, a code of conduct, and his Chief of the General Staff, Yamagata Aritomo informed Army Minister Oyama that the military was not meeting its conscription quotas and that the 40,000 soldiers were insufficient.

title: Record and Transcript of the Korea Incident (朝鮮変報録)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: This print depicts the attack on the Japanese legation in Seoul, Korea on July 23, 1882 by disaffected Korean soldiers.  The right panel pictures the former regent of Korea and the father of the Korean king, the Daewongun (大院君), on horseback, leading the mutineers. The legation is shown burning in the background, while the Japanese ambassador, Hanabusa Yoshitada (identified as 英公使, "Minister Hanabusa," in the center panel) and other legation officers fight them off.  As with many battle scenes depicted in Japanese prints of the Meiji era, Chikanobu constructs this image from his imagination and news reports, and his depiction of the Daewongun actually leading the mutineers in battle is fictitious.

title: Boar (亥)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
This print, picturing a sleeping boar, the twelfth sign of the zodiac, is a later printing, likely c. 1930s-1940s, of the print contained in the earlier, 1900-1915, bound folding album Seiho's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals, published by Unsōdō Publishing.<br>
<br>Each of the prints in Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals is essentially a woodblock facsimile of what must have been an original watercolor created by Seihō, a nihonga, Maruyama-Shijō school painter. In describing an earlier book of prints by the artist, also published by Unsōdō Publishing, Jack Hillier notes that the Meiji printmakers responded to the challenge of reproducing Seihō's watercolors, with "marvelous interpretive skills" and goes on to say “There is, in truth, a complete abnegation of the medium qua woodcut; its own virtues of bold line and flat wash are sacrificed in the cause of a facsimile rendering of a water-colour: this was a fundamental change in technique which led to incredible feats of reproduction…”

title: By The Lake (湖畔)
creator: Uchima Ansei 内間安瑆 (1921-2000)
description:
This print appeared in the 2005 exhibition ""Prints With/Out pressure : American relief prints from the 1940s through the 1960s" organized by the New York Public Library. 
<br><br>"The work of Ansei Uchima reflects a complex fusion of Western and Eastern artistic traditions. Born in California, Uchima returned to Japan at age nineteen, and after World War II studied painting and traditional Japanese printmaking. Through his job as translator for Oliver Statler, an American print collector, who was interviewing artists for a book on contemporary Japanese prints, he was introduced to the sōsaku-hanga (creative print) movement, which incorporated a Western modernist aesthetic. Like other artists in the sōsaku-hanga school, Uchima carved, inked, and printed his own wood blocks, enjoying the accidents and unexpected opportunities that arose spontaneously from interaction with the wood block. His first prints, beginning in 1957, drew from nature and the world around him. After he returned to the United States in 1959, his floating, calligraphic compositions, characteristic of sōsaku-hanga, suggested the growing influence of Abstract Expressionism. Uchima used Japanese paper made especially for him by a Japanese master papermaker and National Treasure, Ichibei Iwano." - Source: New York Public Library http://web-static.nypl.org/exhibitions/pressure/artists3.html [accessed 8-25-23]

title: Shibaraku (暫)
creator: Ōuchi Makoto 大内マコト (1926-1989)
description:
The artist's rendering of multiple scenes from the Kabuki play Shibaraku are presented to us like a 3-dimensional pop-up book. The Ōuchi cube appears as it does in so many of his prints. The hero Kamakura no Gongoro Kagemasa appears on the left page with the right page being composed of the female characters Katsura-no-mae and Taruha along with a Hiroshige-like mountain.  Ōuchi's name in the red cartouche along with an embossed double arch complete the picture.
<br>Ōuchi often paid homage to the great ukiyo-e print masters and here he does so again by appropriating a mountain from Utagawa Hiroshige's print The Lake at Hakone from the series Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō Road.
<br><br>While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

title: Reflection of the New Diet Building, View 45 (新議事堂の影・四十二景)
creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view of the New Diet Building and its reflection prior to its completion in 1936. Koizumi comments on this print, “Late on a winter’s day the new diet building shimmers like a mirage in a golden haze.”<br><br>
Print number forty-five in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort  . . . .”  - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

title: Some Sketches of the Japan-China War, Volume 1 (従征画稿  第1集)
creator: Asai Chū 浅井忠 (1856-1907)
description:
Volume 1 of four bound volumes by the artist Asai Chū (1856-1907) forming a pictorial account of the battles of Japan's Second Army on China's Liaodong Peninsula during the first Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895). Asai's sketches, created at the battle front, were done with pencil and pen and then highlighted with watercolors. They were then reproduced using full-color lithography by the publisher Shinyōdō, who included five or six color plates in each volume accompanied by a table of contents and a preface written by Asai. 
<br>Clicking on the image will allow you to view the color lithographs in the volume.

title: Wind and Clear Water (水風清)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
A small bird perches on a rock in a swift flowing stream in this collotype, one of four prints in the second of ten envelopes containing the prints comprising set one of Seihō's Masterpieces. See IHL.0875 for the print showing a detail of this work. 
<br><br>SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
<br>Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century." <br>Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.<br>While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

title: Cape Kannon (観音埼 Kannonzaki)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
Number 18 of 28 prints from the series Views of the Famous Sights of Japan (Nihon meisho zue) designed by Kiyochika and issued by the publisher Matsuki Heikichi in 1896 and 1897.<br>
Kiyochika pictures a lone boat being plied off the rocky coast of Cape Kannon on the eastern edge of the Miura Peninsula along the southwest portion of Tokyo Bay.  In 1812 the Tokugawa Shogunate set up a lookout here to protect Edo from Western ships. In 1868 a lighthouse was built on the cape under the direction of of the Frenchmen F. L. Verny following the requests of foreign powers under the provisions of the Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Amity and Commerce of 1858. It was the first modern lighthouse to be built in Japan, being first lit on February 11, 1869, immediately after the Meiji restoration, and during the last months of the Boshin War.  It was destroyed by an earthquake in 1922. A second lighthouse was soon destroyed by the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923. The one we can see today is the third one, constructed in 1925.

title: Captain Asakawa and Trooper Private Kimura (浅川大尉 二等騎兵木村源松氏 Asakawa Taii Nitō Kihei Kimura Genmatsu-shi)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty issued as part of the series Mirror of Army and Navy Heroes designed by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915) and published 1895-1896 by Inoue Kichijirō. The series depicts war heroes of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) as models of behavior and self-sacrifice. "Kiyochika’s 'heroes' range from an admiral reading a newspaper to sailors helping a blinded comrade touch a cannon that has helped bring victory, and from an infantryman showing compassion to a Chinese youngster to officers and enlisted men cleaving heads and bayonetting the foe." - source: website of MIT Visualizing Cultures https://visualizingcultures.mit.edu/throwing_off_asia_02/visnav_ii_f.html [accessed 8-17-23]<br>
In this print the loyal trooper Private Kimura Gemmatsu, himself wounded, leans over his wounded commander, Captain Asakawa Toshiyasu, who grieves over his fallen horse.

creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view looking out from Sensō-ji's Niōmon Gate (Hōzōmon Gate) in Asakusa towards bustling Nakamise Shopping Street. Koizumi comments on this print, “The statue of the Kannon Bodhisattva survived the earthquake, but only a few of the shops on Nakamise remained.”<br><br>
Print number ten in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort  . . . .”  - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

title: Gōtokuji Temple in Setagaya Ward, View 42 (世田ケ谷区・豪徳寺・四十二景)
creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view of the gardens surrounding Buddha Hall on the temple grounds of Gōtokuji, the Ii Clan's family temple, where, as is noted by Koizumi, the assassinated Ii Naosuke, Tairō to the Tokugawa Shogun Tokugawa Iesada, is buried. Koizumi comments on this print, “This is the burial place of Lord Ii who was killed at Sakuradamon. It is also famous for a literal mountain of cat statues.”<br><br>
Print number forty-two in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . title: Fan - か (ka)
creator: Ōuchi Makoto 大内マコト (1926-1989)
description:
From a series of at least seven prints incorporating a fan motif and a hiragana character, in this case the character "ka" か which appears right reading on the fan and in its mirror image to the left of the fan. Ōuchi has borrowed the image of the beautiful courtesan entertaining herself with calligraphy from a c. 1794 woodblock titled Portrait of Kasen of Ogiya, a Celebrated Yoshiwara Beauty by the artist Chōbunsai Eishi (1756–1829).
<br>Other prints in this series use the characters "re" れ, "ke" け, "ri" り, "fu" ふ, "e" え and "ni" に.
<br><br>While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

title: Hibachi (ひばち)
creator: Takeda Hideo 武田秀雄 (b. 1948)
description:
In this silkscreen print, one of eleven in the artist's Mon Mon* portfolio, a tattooed Edo-era man, naked except for his fundoshi, sits on a hibachi with iron tongs in hand. The charcoal brazier is covered with an intricate design that includes a guardian lion dog and the legendary Phoenix. 
<br>*Mon Mon is an Osaka word for "representational or figurative tattooing." This word is also associated with the tattoos of yakuza.
<br><b>"Mon Mon," The Series</b>
<br>"Mon Mon is Takeda's first collection of prints. In it, he used tattoos as a theme in order to push the need for color in cartoons to new limits. It was the first collection published by this artist who tried to extract art from cartoons." - statement from the artist's website
<br>The Mon Mon series was issued both in book/portfolio form (Mon-Mon: Takeda Hideo hangashū 紋紋 武田秀雄版画集 [Tattoo: Collection of Prints by Takeda Hideo)] in a limited edition of 500 copies, in 1978 by Internal Co., Ltd. and in a limited edition of 150 stand-alone prints.
<br>In 1976, Takeda won the Bungeishunjū Manga Award (文藝春秋漫画賞 Bungeishunjū Manga Shō) for this print series.

title: Two Turtles and a Rock (untitled)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description: One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) around the turn of the 20th century. In this print a turtle suns itself on an overhanging rock, while another paddles nearby in the stream. The turtle, or tortoise (kame), living as it does to a venerable old age, has become a symbol of longevity in East Asia. It is not only highly esteemed, but even held sacred.

title: Cézanne (セザンヌ)
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: One of Ay-O's hommages to past artists, this one to Cézanne and his 1893-1894 still life Sugarbowl, Pears and Tablecloth. This artist proof was editioned under the title of Rainbow Cézanne 虹のセザンヌ. Ay-O comments, "There was a period in my youth when I, too, was 'infected by Cezanne'. Some people may not believe me, but everything that came within my vision in Japan, the scenery, people and still life, appeared to me to be exactly the same as those of Cezanne's France. Recollections of the waving trees of the forest, the apple looking as if it were made of porcelain, and the nude with a blue shadow - these are at once the heart pains of my youth. To that memory, I dedicate this piece."

title: Mt. Fuji, No. 480
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: Sixteen suns float on and behind Mt. Fuji, bathing it in shimmering (a light dusting of mica in the deep orange) sunlight. Funasaka's unique multi-color vertical forms, which appear in so many of his prints, are printed using reusable woodblock cutouts. The technique used to create the rest of the print is likely silkscreen.

title: Where It All Began
creator: Miyashita Tokio 宮下登喜雄 (1930–2011)

title: Denizen of the Lake Depths
creator: Shinagawa Takumi 品川工 (1908-2009)
description: A beautiful overlay of colors make up this underwater view of a black sea creature swimming through a maze of colorful formations.<br>While Shinagawa worked in many medias, including metal (creating numerous mobiles) and photography, he is best known for his prints. As with many creative print (sōsaku hanga) artists of the period, he studied printmaking with Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955) and his mid-career abstract woodblock prints show the influence of his teacher in their use of simplified forms. His later works were mainly silkscreens rather than woodblock prints.

title: Nostalgy (ノスタルジー)
creator: Yuki Rei 由木礼 (1928-2003)
description:
One of Rei's semi-abstract landscapes created from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. In commenting on the Rei's work, Francis Blakemore notes, "The texture of the woodblock itself creates dappled tones and fragile shades.  The works are light, yet the source of the light is hidden behind fences and arches. It is a light defined by shadows, creating a mood of timeless suspension.
<br>"Leafless branches cast foreground shadows, mysteriously real and abstract, stark and delicate.  The texture of the block, structural unity of the geometric ground figures, subdued coloration and shading, and magical, waving forms together create a locus, a place that is both definite and infinite, haunting and unassuming, vague and too vivid to be mere fantasy." - Source: "Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Frances Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 247.)

title: Winter Composition No. 2 (冬の構成 Fuyu no kōsei 2)
creator: Iwami Reika 岩見禮花 (1927-2020)
description: One of ten modern prints by ten different artists chosen for James Michener’s 1962 seminal work and portfolio of prints "The Modern Japanese Print: An Appreciation," a work that brought the artists to international attention. This print has been removed from the book. See IHL.1336g for another impression of this print still mounted in the Michener book and for Michener's and the artist's comments on the print.

title: Lizard and Cucumber Vines
creator: Kotozuka Eiichi 琴塚英一 (1906-1979)
description:
One of twenty prints contributed by Kotozuka Eiichi (1906-1979) to the series Fifty Kinds of Flowers issued in 1935. This print, published by Unsōdō, but with woodblocks carved by the artist, show a gekko-like lizard emerging from spreading cucumber vines.
<br> It is reported that two editions of this series were released. The first was made available by subscription and the second was released after the subscription was sold out. Also contributing to the series were Tobei Kamei and Tokuriki Tomikichirō.

title: Ueno Park, Congratulatory Celebration for the Thirty-Year Festival of the Capital City (上野公園奠都三十年祭祝賀會)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: On April 10, 1898 a series of celebrations, private and public, were held in Tokyo to commemorate and celebrate the thirtieth anniversary of the transfer of the capital from Japan to Tokyo. The Association for the 30th Anniversary, headed by Viscount Okabe the then Governor of Tokyo, tasked with the job of organizing and promoting the celebrations wrote, "our Tokyo now competes in its grandeur with London and Paris, the great cities of the world." The emperor and empress attended both private events in their palace and the public celebration held in Ueno Park pictured in this print.

title: One Hundred Warrior Poets complete (武家百人一首 全 Buke hyakunin isshu zen)
creator: Utagawa Sadahide 歌川貞秀 (1807-1873)
description: An 1858 version of "Buke hyakunin isshu" by the artist Utagawa Sadahide (1807-1873) and the writer Shōgetsudō Shujin (fl. 1856-1864). This 1858 version of "Buke hyakunin isshu" is prefaced with eight battle scenes (titled, Eight Scenes of Great Battles of Japan 本 朝戦場八景) each occupying a double page, all of which have taken the titles associated with the Chinese literary and artistic theme of "Eight Views."<br>"Buke hyakunin isshu" was originally issued in illustrated form in 1672 by the publisher Tsuruya Kiemon, with illustrations by the artist Hishikawa Moronobu (1618-1694). By signing his name to the 1672 "Buke hyakunin isshu", Moronobu became the first ukiyo-e artist to affix his name to a printed work. "Buke hyakunin isshu" is not a version of the very popular "Hyakunin isshu" (One Hundred Poets), issued six years later in illustrated form and also bearing Moronobu's name, "but an independent work bringing together one hundred poems by one hundred famous samurai," targeted at Edo's samurai class. - Source: Pictures of the Heart : The Hyakunin-isshu in Word and Image, Joshua S Mostow, University of Hawai'i Press, 1996, p. 44, 107.

title: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 1 (日本歴史画報  第一號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai ichigō)
creator: Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki) 高橋松亭 (弘明) (1871-1945), et. al.
description: The first of thirteen volumes published between December 1891 and June 1893 which served as a secondary school pictorial history textbook. Artists who contributed to the books included the chief editor Matsumoto Fūko 松本楓湖 (1840-1923), Takahashi Shōtei 高橋松亭 (1871-1945), the nephew of Matsumoto Fūko, Watanabe Seitei 渡邊省亭 (1851-1918), Mishima Shōsō 三島蕉窓 (1856-1928), Nagamine Shūko 永峯秀湖 (1859-1895), Ōtsuka Sōko 大塚蒼湖 (?-?), Kono Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895) and Muraoka Ōtō 村岡櫻塘 (1773-1947).

title: Tokyo Imperial Hotel (東京帝国ホテル)
creator: Kotozuka Eiichi 琴塚英一 (1906-1979)
description: Torn down in 1968, Frank Lloyd Wright's Imperial Hotel, completed in 1923 and located near the Imperial Palace, is shown on a rainy, but calm, day. Careful viewing of the print reveals that silver mica ink was used to create the very fine vertical striations of rain distributed throughout the image.<br>Wright had long been intrigued by Japanese culture (he was an avid collector of Japanese prints), so when the opportunity came to build the Imperial Hotel in Tokyo, he lobbied for the project.<br>Commissioned in 1916, the hotel was to represent the emergence of Japan as a modern nation and symbolize Japan’s relation to the West. To that end, Wright designed the building as a hybrid of Japanese and Western architecture.

title: Girl in New Year Clothes (正月娘姿)
creator: Yasui Sōtarō 安井曾太郎 (1888–1955)
description:
This print, "published by Kyūryūdō, is faithful to the artist’s figurative style with no hint of the carver’s personal interpretation. The color, deep muted pink with gray and blue, is thick and opaque, with little of the subtle quality that we associate with moku-hanga, and suggests by its appearance that it may have been applied by stencil."[1]

<br>Yasui designed at least sixteen woodblock prints that he then had carved and printed, under his supervision, by others. He viewed prints as "instrumental in expressing things by lines and colors."[2]

title: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 9 (日清戦闘畫報  第 九編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daikyū hen)
creator:
Kubota Beisen 久保田米僊 (1852-1906)
<br>Kubota Beisai 久保田 米齊 (1874-1937)
<br>Kubota Kinsen 久保田 金仙 (1875-1954)
description: Volume 9 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895. Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (Fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century." <br>Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.<br>While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

title: Ram (未)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
This print, picturing a woman walking through a group of sheep, is from the folding album (orihon) Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals, published by Unsōdō Publishing, containing twelve prints each picturing an animal in the zodiac.  This image represents the eighth animal in the set sequence of animals symbolizing the houses of the zodiac in Chinese lore, namely the rat, ox, tiger, hare, dragon, snake, horse, sheep, monkey, cock, dog and pig. Multiple editions of this print were issued by the publisher from c. 1901 into the early 1940s.<br>
<br>Each of the prints in Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals is essentially a woodblock facsimile of what must have been an original watercolor created by Seihō, a nihonga, Maruyama-Shijō school painter. In describing an earlier book of prints by the artist, also published by Unsōdō Publishing, Jack Hillier notes that the Meiji printmakers responded to the challenge of reproducing Seihō's watercolors, with "marvelous interpretive skills" and goes on to say “There is, in truth, a complete abnegation of the medium qua woodcut; its own virtues of bold line and flat wash are sacrificed in the cause of a facsimile rendering of a water-colour: this was a fundamental change in technique which led to incredible feats of reproduction…”

title: Ikina (伊企儺)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)

title: The Teachings of the Mother of Mencius (孟母の教)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: In this print, originally created for volume one of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishiki-e shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi portrays Mencius (c. 371-289 BCE), one of the greatest Confucian philosophers of early China, and his mother at a weaving loom. A lesson about studying diligently will be forthcoming.

title: The Loyalty of Pierre (ピエールの信)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: In this print, originally created for volume one of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishikie shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi portrays the Frenchman Pierre returning the money he had been trusted with by his friend. As told in print's cartouche, it seems Pierre's soldier friend had been gone many years, but although Pierre lived in poverty and could have used his friend's money for business opportunities he did not.

title: Wang Lan Harmony Between Siblings (王覧の悌)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: In this print, created for volume two of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishikie shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi depicts a young Wang Lan (206-278) protecting his older half-brother Wang Xiang (185-269) from the wrath of his mother, who favored her own son. Both brothers were to grow up and become important statesmen during the Chinese Three Kingdoms period (220-280).

title: The Chastity of Shihino Shinasa (四比信紗の貞)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: In this print, created for volume three of the six volume elementary school morals textbook Nishikie shūshindan ("Brocade Pictures for Moral Education"), Yoshitoshi portrays the widow Shihino Shinasa caring for her own children along with the children of her husband's concubine without favor. After her husband's death, she vowed to remain chaste thereby fulfilling the "li" of a woman.

title: Saigō Takamori (西郷隆盛)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: Print number 171 (第十七) in the series Personalities of Recent Times pictures the samurai Saigō Takamori (1827-1877) who fought against the shogunate to restore the emperor to power ushering in the Meiji Era (1868-1912); served as a Meiji government statesman and then resigned in 1873; lead the brief, bloody and unsuccessful 1877 Satsuma Rebellion against the Meiji government, finally committing suicide nine months after the Rebellion began, walking his dog Tsun. The scene is set in a quiet moment before the Rebellion and Saigō bears a walking stick and his hound's leash, as well as his sword.  He wears a western shirt and collar under a traditional kimono.

title: Hayano Kanpei (早野勘平)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞 (1823-1880)
description: This print pictures the character Hayano Kanpei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers; a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin). The play is based on the real-life Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions caused the death of their lord. The Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum Digital Archives Collection identifies the actor playing Hayano Kanpei as Ichimura Kakitsu IV  [4]市村家橘, although the actor's name does not appear on the print.<br>The dark yellow cartouche in the upper right corner gives the name of the series, Legends of the Loyal Retainers. The name of the character portrayed is given to the immediate left of the cartouche, in this case Hayano Kanpei 早野勘平. The background script may provide an account of Yuranosuke's role in the play or actual lines spoken by the character.<br>The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.<br>For another edition of this print see IHL.0631.

title: Sakurajima in Summer (夏の桜島 九州鹿児島)
creator: Akagi Yasunobu 赤城泰舒 (1889-1955)
description: A peaceful Sakurajima, an active volcano, on a summer's day as seen from one of the villages that were gradually incorporated into Kagoshima city. Kagoshima is a city of over 600,000 today.

title: Donjon of the Matsuyama Castle (天守閣 四国松山城)
creator: Akagi Yasunobu 赤城泰舒 (1889-1955)
description: The artist's rendering of the Matsuyama Castle keep. Matsuyama Castle, in Matsuyama in Ehime prefecture, western Shikoku, was first built by Kato Yoshiaki between 1602 and 1627. (It is not to be confused with Bitchu Matsuyama Castle in Okayama prefecture.) The castle is one of Japan's twelve originally surviving castles, although it burnt down twice, once in 1642 and again in 1784, after being struck by lightning. The present structures date from 1854. The impressive, three-story central tower (or, donjon, daitenshu) is listed as an Important Cultural Property.

title: Evening Glow
creator: Ōshiro Sadao 大城貞夫 (1908-1981)
description: A stark view in early evening of Mount Fuji with bare trees in the foreground. While this collection's print appears to be hand signed by the artist, "S. Ohshiro", and is part of a numbered edition (20/100), the Los Angeles County Museum of Art version of the print, carries a stamped signature "S. Ōshiro," and is not editioned.  The LACMA print uses a brighter palette that better reflects the print's title "Evening Glow" than this collection's print.

title: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 4 (日清戦闘畫報 第四編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daishi hen)
creator:
Kubota Beisen 久保田米僊 (1852-1906)
<br>Kubota Beisai 久保田 米齊 (1874-1937)
<br>Kubota Kinsen 久保田 金仙 (1875-1954)
description: Volume 4 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895. Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

title: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 10 (日本歴史画報  第十號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai jūgō)
creator: Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki) 高橋松亭 (弘明) (1871-1945), et. al.
description: The tenth of thirteen volumes published between December 1891 and June 1893 which served as a secondary school pictorial history textbook. Artists who contributed to the books included the chief editor Matsumoto Fūko 松本楓湖 (1840-1923), Takahashi Shōtei 高橋松亭 (1871-1945), the nephew of Matsumoto Fūko, Watanabe Seitei 渡邊省亭 (1851-1918), Mishima Shōsō 三島蕉窓 (1856-1928), Nagamine Shūko 永峯秀湖 (1859-1895), Ōtsuka Sōko 大塚蒼湖 (?-?), Kono Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895) and Muraoka Ōtō 村岡櫻塘 (1773-1947).

title: The Illustrated Journal of Japanese History, number 6 (日本歴史画報  第六號 Nihon rekishi gahō, dai rokugō)
creator: Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki) 高橋松亭 (弘明) (1871-1945), et. al.
description: The sixth of thirteen volumes published between December 1891 and June 1893 which served as a secondary school pictorial history textbook. Artists who contributed to the books included the chief editor Matsumoto Fūko  松本楓湖 (1840-1923), Takahashi Shōtei 高橋松亭 (1871-1945), the nephew of Matsumoto Fūko, Watanabe Seitei 渡邊省亭 (1851-1918), Mishima Shōsō 三島蕉窓 (1856-1928), Nagamine Shūko 永峯秀湖 (1859-1895), Ōtsuka Sōko 大塚蒼湖 (?-?), Kono Bairei 幸野楳嶺 (1844-1895) and Muraoka Ōtō 村岡櫻塘 (1773-1947).

title: Ise Futami Bay (伊勢二見浦)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
The fourth of eight prints in the series the Eight Views of Japan (Nihon hakkei) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company sometime in the 1950s. This print, depicting the "Marriage Rocks" near the town of Futami during summer at daybreak, along with the Futami Okitama Shrine, was originally published in 1941 as part of the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places. 
<br>This series reused eight previously issued images from the 1941 series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) and reissued them in a portfolio of prints titled Eight Views of Japan. The table of contents accompanying the entire series notes that the prints are "Selections from Prints of Places of Historic and Scenic Interest" (a.k.a. Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places) and that it contains "2 each of four seasons."
<br>Meoto Iwa (夫婦岩), or the "Loved one-and-loved one Rocks" (a.k.a "Marriage Rocks"), are a couple of small rocky stacks in the sea off Futami, Mie, Japan. They are joined by a shimenawa (a heavy rope of rice straw) and are considered sacred by worshippers at the neighboring Futami Okitama Shrine (Futami Okitama Jinja 二見興玉神社). According to Shinto, the rocks represent the union of the creator of kami Izanagi (male divine being) and kami Izanami (female devine being). The rocks, therefore, celebrate the union in marriage of man and woman. The rope, which weighs over a ton, must be replaced several times a year in a special ceremony. The larger rock, said to be male, has a small torii at its peak.
<br>Futami Okitama Shrine is dedicated to the food goddess Miketsu. The shrine and the Marriage Rocks are near the Grand Shrine of Ise, the most important shrine in Shinto.

title: Kiyomizu Temple in Kyoto (京都 清水寺)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
The last of eight prints in the series The Eight Views of Japan (Nihon hakkei) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company sometime in the 1950s. This print, depicting Kiyomizu Temple and several of its associated buildings in winter snow, was originally published in 1941 as part of the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places. 
<br>This series reused eight previously issued images from the 1941 series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) and reissued them in a portfolio of prints titled Eight Views of Japan. The table of contents accompanying the entire series notes that the prints are "Selections from Prints of Places of Historic and Scenic Interest" (a.k.a. Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places) and that it contains "2 each of four seasons." This print was also reissued as part of the series Twelve Months of Scenic Views of Japan (日本勝景十二月).
<br>Kiyomizu-dera (清水寺), known more fully as Otowa-san Kiyomizu-dera (音羽山清水寺) is an independent Buddhist temple in eastern Kyoto. The temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities) UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Cherry Blossoms of Mount Shigi (大和信貴山)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)

title: My Space and My Dimension, No. 533
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: Sixteen light tan circles generate a subtle glow as Funasaka's trademark multi-color vertical forms hover within their intense lacquer-black borders. Funasaka creates these vertical forms with reusable woodblock cutouts.

title: Child and Dog (子供と犬)
creator: Azechi Umetarō 畦地梅太郎 (1902-1999)
description: One of Azechi's many small-format prints, most designed as greeting cards. Likely printed in the 1970s by the Yokohama publisher Chikuhōdō, which still offers this design for sale, it is tipped to a 14 1/4" x 9 7/8" sheet folded into quarters with stamped information on the verso giving the name of the artist and publisher.

title: Illustrations of Noh, Index, volume 3 (能楽図絵 後編上 目録 Mokuroku, kōhen jō)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
The third of five Table of Contents prints (mokuroku)  from the series Nōgakuzue (Illustrations of Noh). In the bottom right of the print is the inscription これは武蔵の国の住人 坂巻の耕漁と申者にて候 "This is by Sakamaki Kōgyō, who dwells in the Musashi Abumi region."

<br><br>Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

title: Autumn play at the Kabukiza - Lord Tokihira and the Seven Laughs, Ichikawa Danjūrō (歌舞伎座秋狂言 菅原  時平公七わらひ  市川團十郎 Kabukiza Aki kyōgen Sugawara - Tokihira-kō Nanawarai, Ichikawa Danjūrō)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: Kunichika portrays the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Lord Tokihira in the play "Tokihira-kō Nanawarai" (Lord Tokihira and the Seven Laughs.) The play is a rewrite of an earlier play, revised by Fukuchi Ōchi, the pseudonym of journalist, playwright and politician Fukuchi Gen'ichirō 福地 源一郎 (1841-1906), as an historical drama starring Ichikawa Danjūrō IX. The print's depicted setting fits well with the evil plan Lord Tokihira devised – to bid farewell to Sugawara Michizane who was exiled to Dazaifu. Tokihira, the one who remains behind, will break up laughing in this scene. As revised by Fukuchi, Tokihira does not hatch his evil plan to edge out the obstructing Michizane and the rewritten play failed to draw crowds.

title: Collection of Ten Plays New and Old - Modoribashi (新古演劇十種之内 ・ 戻り橋 Shin koengeki jisshu no uchi・Modoribashi)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: Kunichika portrays Onoe Kikugorō V in the role of the demon of Mount Atago (disguised as Sayuri) in the play Modoribashi (The Bridge of Return) staged at the Ichimura-za. First staged in 1890, it is the prologue to the play Ibaraga [Ibaraki]. It describes how Watanabe no Tsuna, ordered to search for a fiend which is terrorizing the capital, meets a beautiful woman travelling alone at night. He offers to see her on her way. Reaching the Modori bridge, he looks down into the moonlit water, only to see a reflection of a horrible fiend instead of the fair face of his companion. Later he confronts her with his discovery and she assumes her true shape. A fierce fight ensues in which Watanabe cuts off the fiend’s arm, thus leading up to the events which take place in the play Ibaraga.

title: Fireworks (花火)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description: This undated and untitled print, likely issued post-WWII, is after a small woodblock print which originally appeared in Takehisa Yumeji's 1915 book of poetry titled Samisen-kusa (Shamisen Leaves), published by the Tokyo publisher Shinchōsha. The original print appeared as the last of six small woodblock prints bound into the book.

Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play, a list of the roles and, for the noh plays only, a brief synopsis of the story.
