title: Actors Iwai Shijaku, Ichikawa Komazō V and Matsumoto Kōshirō V in the play Date kurabe okuni kabuki (伊達競阿國劇場・ 岩井紫若, 五代目 市川高麗蔵, 五代目 松本幸四郎)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description:
Three sheets that may form part of a five-sheet print of actors in the play Date kurabe okuni kabuki (The Date Rivalry and Okuni kabuki) by Sakurada Jisuke I (1734-1806). The left sheet in the triptych is not contiguous with the sheet to its right, although similar in design. 
<br>From right to left we see the actors Iwai Shijaku (岩井紫若) as Masaoka no Tsubone ( 政岡の局), Ichikawa Komazō V (市川高麗蔵) as Arajishi Otokonosuke (獅子男之助), and Matsumoto Kōshirō V (松本幸四郎) as Nikki Danjō (仁木弾正) in the play Date kurabe okuni kabuki 伊達競阿國劇場.
<br> The left sheet contains an inscription to the left of the actor reading 一世一代 當々 (isse ichidai, ōatari ōatari) meaning "Once in a lifetime performance, big hit, big hit!"
<br>The play Date kurabe okuni kabuki is a derivative of the play Meiboku sendai hagi (The Precious Incense and Autumn Flowers of Sendai.) Precious Incense dramatizes historical events – an attempted coup, in 1660, by retainers of the Date household and the gallant efforts of loyal retainers to thwart the coup. The scandal caused a sensation in its day. - Source: Kabuki Plays On-Stage: Villainy and Vengeance, 1773-1799, ed. James R. Brandon, Samuel L. Leiter, University of Hawaii Press, 2003, p. 50.

title: Actors Bandō Hikosaburō V, Ichimura Kakitsu IV and Ichikawa Danzō VI in a performance from the New Year drama Tsuru no chitose Soga no kadomatsu (鶴千歳曽我門松・五代目 坂東彦三郎, 四代目 市村家橘, 六代目 市川団蔵)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞 (1823-1880)

title: Viewing Fireflies in the Cool of the Evening (蛍見之夕涼 Hotarubi no Yūsuzumi)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description: Five actors portrayed before a rimpa-stye stream enjoying the evening's delights. The names of the actors are not shown on the print, possibly due to censor rules still being enforced in 1859, but the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston which has the right panel of this triptych in its collection, identifies the two actors in the right panel as Nakamura Fukusuke I 初代中村福助 and Iwai Kumesaburō III 三代目岩井粂三郎.  It is unknown what play is depicted in this print.

title: Breeze No. 2 (六月の風 Rokugatsu no kaze)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description: A turquoise sky, shimmering with applied mica, provides the backdrop for Hagiwara's colorful cloth-like objects flapping in the breeze.

title: Midday at the Beach (真晝の浜 Mahiru no hama)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Kitaoka has captured a moment, during the heat of midday, of three villagers gathering seaweed and plants on the beach. This print has a similar feel to the languid Fishing Village in the Afternoon (IHL.0194) one of the artist's best known works created in 1967 four years after this work.

title: Summer Vacation (夏休み)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: The sky is filled with a pale sunlight in this print titled Summer Vacation. The artist's catalogue raisonné indicates that this print appeared in a show titled "Contemporary Japanese Prints" held by The Print Club of Albany, an organization still in existence today, located in Albany, New York. It states there were two editions of this print, one in 1967 of 22 prints and one in 1966 of 50 prints (this collection's print). They note that there are color differences between the two editions.

title: Lamps, jars, clock, geisha
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description: A collector of old foreign language books, Kawakami loved depicting the objects he found in them. This print uses a number of the artist's favorite objects -  lamps, jars, a clock, and geisha. The Yokohama Museum of Art has a hand-colored version of this print.

title: Kanpei's Wife, Okaru (勘平女房 おかる)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞 (1823-1880)
description:
This print pictures the character Okaru, the wife of Hayano Kanpei from the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers, a.k.a. The Forty-Seven Ronin), based on the Akō Incident (1701-1703) in which forty-seven retainers of Lord Asano (the character Enya Hangan in the play) take revenge against the shogun's court official Kira Yoshinaka (the character Ko no Moronao in the play), whose actions in the shogun's palace led to the death of their lord.
<br>The text on the print was written by Yashima Gakutei 八島岳亭 (1786 – 1868), best-known for his surimono (privately commissioned) prints, signing as Gakutei Sadaoka 岳亭定岡文記 with a gourd-shaped seal bearing the character 島 (shima) following his signature.
<br>The theatrical adaptation of the Akō Incident, Kanadehon Chūshingura or simply Chūshingura, combined historical characters from the Akō Incident, assigning them thinly disguised fictitious names, along with unrelated historical characters and fictional characters, mostly added to spice up the play with erotica.
<br>
"Okaru's name immediately associates her with the mistress, also named Okaru, that Kuranosuke took up residence with while living in Yamashina. However, aside from her presence at the teahouse Ichirikiya and Yuranosuke's brief feint at courting her, there are few, if any, comparisons, thematic or otherwise, to draw between the two. It is safe to say that, while the name may have been chosen for the historical resonance it brought to the text and the character, the two Okarus represent two distinctly different personas.
<br> If Hayano Kanpei is someone who is inadvertently tempted by passion to commit a transgression against his lord, then it is Okaru who performs the role of the temptress. She is the central female character in a play that, more often than not, portrays women as nothing better than mere obstacles to samurai duty and virtue. And while it might be anachronistic and heavy-handed to judge Chūshingura as misogynistic, Okaru, through her actions and influence, without a doubt achieves much the same textual status that Eve does in the Old Testament version of Genesis." Source: Columbia University website http://www.columbia.edu/~hds2/chushinguranew/kanadehon/okaru.html [accessed 8-27-23]

title: Oda Nobunaga  and Mito Rekko (Tokugawa Nariaki) of the Tokugawa Sanke (織田信長公 水戸烈公 徳川三家)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description:
From a little seen series of prints pairing heroic figures from recent and past history in imaginary contests. This print pairs Oda Nobunaga 織田信長 (1534-1582), on the right, Japanese military commander in the Azuchi-Momoyama period (c. 1573 to c. 1603) and one of Japan's "Three Great Unifiers," with Mito Rekko 水戸烈公 (1800-1860; also known as Tokugawa Nariaki), on the left, father of the last Tokugawa shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu (1837-1913), and a foremost proponent of the anti-Western sonno-jōi movement.
<br>As the sono-jōi movement weakened the Tokugawa shogunate leading to the Meiji Restoration and the end of the shogunate, I imagine the artist is depicting an angry Nobunaga castigating Nariaki for his role in this movement.

<br>Nariaki, in an effort to strengthen Japan against the Western military threat, instituted extensive reforms in his home province of Mito, including rationalization of the taxation system, the hiring of experts in Western learning to advise him on coastal defense and battleship construction, the training of troops in Western military tactics, establishment of a state school system, combining Confucian and Shintō religious institutions, and taxation of Buddhist temples and rich samurai to fund increased military spending.[1]

<br><br>[1] Japan at War: An Encyclopedia, edited by Louis G. Perez, ABC-CLIO, LLC, 2013, p. 439-440.

title: Semimaru 蝉丸
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: Play synopsis A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p.154-155) -  On the order of the Emperor Daigo, a Court official takes Prince Semimaru, who has been blind since he was a child, to Ōsaka-yama and leaves him there with only his lute to comfort him. The Prince accepts his lot with resignation, feeling that his blindness is the result of some failure of his in a previous existence, and that the present apparent cruelty of his father is only due to a desire to help him gain a happier fate in a future life. Meanwhile, his sister Princess Sakagami has gone out of her mind and is now a wild-haired figure, wandering aimlessly from place to place. She comes one day to Ōsaka-yama and, attracted by the sound of Semimaru's lute, finds her brother again. For a while they forget their loneliness as they talk together and comfort each other, but then the Princess leaves him and continues her sad wanderings.<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Hotoke Gozen (佛御前)
creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)

title: Mōri Shōjumaru (毛利松寿丸)
creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)
description:
Print number 27 (廿七), one of 13 contributed by Kiyochika's student Inoue Yasuji to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the powerful daimyō Mōri Motonari (1497-1571) as a young boy visiting Itsukushima (Miyajima) Shrine with his maidservant, just prior to his coming of age ceremony (genpuku) in 1511. Legend has it that Shōjumaru, Motonari's childhood name, asked a young retainer accompanying him what he had wished for at the shrine. The young retainer replied that he wished for Shōjumaru to become the lord of Aki province. Shōjumaru reprimands the boy, asking why he did not wish for him to become lord of all Japan, as that is a higher goal to meet.<br><br>INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
<br>This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

title: Kusunoki Masashige (楠正成)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)

title: Mexico City, Mexico (メキシコメキシコ市)
creator: Asano Takeji 浅野竹二 (1900-1999)
description: A view of the old Basilica de Santa Maria de Guadalupe in Mexico City from an adjoining plaza. The artist traveled to Mexico in October 1965 as part of a world tour that also would take him to the United States, Spain, Italy, Greece, and Turkey. Upon his return to Japan he began work on a series of ten prints showing views from his travels titled "Here and There in the West."  All of these prints were carved and, most likely, printed and published by the artist.

title: The Farrier (蹄鐵工  其九 teitetsukō sono kyū)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
A horse is prepared for shoeing in this ninth print in the series. According to The Japan Farrier Association, "Modern horseshoeing technique was introduced into Japan in 1873. The government invited a horseshoeing instructor from France to help disseminate the technique."<br>

A translation of the commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "Today all professions pursue efficiency in their method and organisation with extreme care. Although this is frequently caused by an all-consuming supply and demand relationship of contemporary life, in this profession we can still see the continuation of a more relaxed pace. The history of horseshoes is quite old, and it goes without saying that in the future, horses will likely still be running around. Until horses are no longer used to transport goods, manual crafts like these will continue to exist." -  Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 24.
<br>Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The vast majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2] <br><br>
[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Newspaper Photographers, Number 8  (写真班 其八 shashinhan sono hachi)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Picturing two newspaper cameramen photographing two military officials, this print titled Newspaper Photographers was originally issued between 1939 and 1941 by Nishinomiya Shoin as the eighth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.<br>
A translation of the commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "Media reports and news are the eyes and ears of modern life, and the photographer plays a major role as the creator of the depicted records. All his efforts are devoted to the mission of capturing a given incident without missing the next one. It has been said that the best-selling photographers are brave and alert, adventurous and perseverant, and in addition they display a freshness and artistic desire in their work. By night and day, during heat and cold, by heaven and earth, be it leisure or luxury, through their pictures their world truly seems to be extraordinary."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 23.
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Horses in Pasture (馬三代 Uma sandai)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)

title: By now you must be near Komakata, a cuckoo calls - Takao (たか雄 君は今駒かたあたりほとゝきす Kimi wa ima/ Komakata Atari/ hototogisu - Takao)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
Often assumed to be the first print in the series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, it pictures one of the eleven famous courtesans of the Yoshiwara in the 17th and 18th centuries named Takao.  It is believed Yoshitoshi's print pictures the sixth Takao, known for her poetry.<br>
<br>"It is early morning, and Takao's lover has recently left the pleasure quarters to return to the city. Takao hears a hototogisu, a sort of cuckoo, whose call is associated with dawn and with loneliness. Its staccato sound reminds her of the name Komakata, an area on the Sumida river a short distance south of the Yoshiwara, and she imagines her lover arriving at the boat landing in Komakata on his way home. She composes a poem, which eventually became famous. Hiroshige (1797-1858) alludes to it in a design of Komakata in his 'One Hundred Famous Views of Edo.'"[1]

<br><br>ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
<br>One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
<br>"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[2]

<br><br>
[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, published by Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, print 1.
<br>[2] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, Hotei Publishing, , 2001, p. 53.

title: A Jōruri Performance of Chūshingura, 2nd act Three Servants from the play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase (浄瑠璃忠臣蔵 二段め 三人奴・忠臣蔵形容画合 Jōruri Chūshingura Nidan me Sannin Yakko・Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞 (1823-1880)
description:
This print depicts the actors (from right to left) Ichimura Kakitsu IV (四代目 市村家橘) as Momonoi's servant Kitsuhei (桃ノ井下部橘平), Bandō Hikosaburō V (五代目 坂東彦三郎) as Momonoi's servant Tsurubei (桃ノ井下部鶴平), and Sawamura Tosshō II (二代目 沢村訥升) as Momonoi's servant Kinohei (桃ノ井下部紀之平) in a performance from the 2nd act of the play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase which played at the Ichimura-za on May 7, 1865.
<br>At the beginning of the 2nd act in Chūshingura, Momonoi Wakanosuke's servants stand outside his mansion in the garden gossiping about Moronao's humiliation of their master, essentially recounting events from the first act.  
<br>The play Chūshingura Sugata no Eawase by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), is based on the classic Kanadehon Chūshingura and had is debut in 1865 as a dance program at the Ichimura theater in Tokyo.

title: Ryukyu Market (琉球の市場 Ryukyu no ichiba)
creator: Ishikawa Toraji 石川寅治 (1875-1964)
description: Primarily known as a Western-style (yōga) landscape painter, Ishikawa self-published a number of woodblock prints (possibly using the publishing name Ryokū-so Gashitsu 緑雨荘画室版), working with excellent carvers and printers to transfer his designs into prints. In addition to his best-known print series Ten Types of Female Nudes, Ishikawa published a number of landscape prints. This print shows three farmers selling their produce at an unknown location in Japan's Ryukyu Islands, the best known of which is Okinawa. Ishikawa had a fascination with native peoples which can be traced back to visits he made to Taiwan in the early 1900s.

title: Sake Distillers (酒杜氏 saketoji)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Five workers stir the mash during the sake fermentation process in this nineteenth print in the second series of Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 2 published by Nishinomiya Shoin between 1939 and 1941. While there is no sense of trouble brewing in this print, the Second Sino-Japanese War leading into World War II was a tough time for sake production, as the government began to tightly control distribution of rice for war efforts which led to the addition of pure alcohol and glucose to the rice mash before pressing to improve the yield. A translation of the artist's commentary accompanying this print reads, "I have been wondering for a long time about the strangeness of the fact we call the person making the sake a 'brewer'. When I looked it up in the dictionary it was described in roughly the following manner. One explanation is that 'brewer', 'master brewer', and 'sake brewer' all originate from older terms such as 'god of the sake jar'. According to other theories the person, by the name of Du Kang, preparing the sake at the court of The Yellow Emperor long ago was called a brewer. And others seem to think it was a kind of nickname. Some think that the original brewers came from Tanba, and that from this region they moved with the season to other regions. That it is a name that referred to a group of artisans who worked away from home every year to take on the whole brewing process, from washing barrels and rice to the eventual brewing of the end product."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3] 
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Translation taken from Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 59.
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Landscape at Nerima Town in Itabashi Ward, View 73 (板橋区・練馬風景・七十三 景)
creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description:
In this print, Koizumi pictures a farming couple at work pickling daikon, giant radishes. The artist comments, "Daikon of Nerima have been renowned from the time they were presented as gifts to the shogun. The priest Takuan introduced a recipe for pickling these radishes. So they became even more famous.”<br><br>
Print number seventy-three in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort  . . . .”  - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

title: Shower at Nezu Gongen Shrine, View 81 (根津権現の驟雨・八十一四景)
creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description:
In this print, Koizumi presents us with a truncated view of the two-story Rōmon Gate (楼門)  at Nezu Gongen with the Haiden worship hall in the background.  A group of children and adults seek shelter from the rain under the gate.  Koizumi comments, “The patina on this National Treasure shrine is lovely but the temple surroundings seem lonely and poorly kept.”<br><br>
Print number eighty-one in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort  . . . .”  - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

title: Inuhariko, Kimono, Kuma and Flying Carp
creator: Shinagawa Takumi 品川工 (1908-2009)
description:
Four tiny prints by the artist, printed on a gummed paper with perforations between each print, and tipped into a portfolio strangely titled Loving Service Hanga Seal, published by The Central Community Chest of Japan, Inc., to familiarize foreigners with the revival of Japanese woodblock printing.  Descriptions for each print are printed underneath the gummed sheet.  I imagine the small prints were designed as envelope seals, given they were printed on gummed paper.
<br><br>Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955) created the front and back covers of this portfolio, see IHL.1298. which contains ten perforated gummed prints by the artists Kitaoka Fumio (1918-2007), see IHL.0977, and Shinagawa Takumi (1908-2009), published by The Central Community Chest of Japan, Inc. to familiarize foreigners with the revival of Japanese woodblock printing. In addition to the two sets of gummed prints the portfolio contains an introduction to the Japanese Woodcut Print by Onchi and a historical overview of the Japanese Woodcut Print.

title: Asakusa Stalls, The Palace Plaza, The Palace Moat, Kan-eiji Pagoda, The Kabuki Theater, Shinjuku Garden
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Six tiny prints by the artist, printed on a gummed paper with perforations between each print, and tipped into a portfolio strangely titled Loving Service Hanga Seal. Descriptions for each print are printed underneath the gummed sheet.<br><br>Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955) created the front and back covers of this portfolio [see IHL.1298] which contains ten perforated gummed prints by the artists Kitaoka Fumio (1918-2007) and Shinagawa Takumi (1908-2009), see IHL.0976, published by The Central Community Chest of Japan, Inc. to familiarize foreigners with the revival of Japanese woodblock printing. In addition to the two sets of gummed prints the portfolio contains an introduction to the Japanese Woodcut Print by Onchi and a historical overview of the Japanese Woodcut Print.

title: Zōjōji Temple in Snow (増上寺の雪 Zōjōji no yuki)
creator: Tsuchiya Kōitsu 土屋光逸 (1870-1949)
description:
The artist gives us Zōjōji on a calm evening with gently falling snow. The temple's website provides us with the following history of Zōjōji: 
<br>"Zōjōji was founded in 1393 as an orthodox and fundamental nembutsu [literally, "buddha in mind"] seminary for Jōdō shu ["The Pure Land School"] in the Kanto (east Japan) region.
<br>"Zōjōji was relocated to the present site in 1598 after Ieyasu Tokugawa, founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, entered Edo (present-day Tokyo) in 1590 to establish his provincial government. After the start of the Edo Period when the Tokugawa shogunate ruled Japan, Zōjōji became the family temple of the Tokugawa family and an unparalleled grand cathedral was built. Zōjōji also served as an administrative center to govern the religious studies and activities of Jodo shu. In those days, its precincts covered an area of 826,000 square meters which also contained 48 smaller attached temples and about 150 grammar schools. Moreover, as many as 3,000 priests and novices always resided here as students.
<br>"Nevertheless, as the Tokugawa shogunate came to an end and the Meiji Era started, an anti-Buddhist movement got under way. The cathedral, temples and the mausoleum of the Tokugawa family were burned down by air raids during World War II. Thus, Zōjōji was profoundly affected by political and social circumstances. Today, however, its cathedral and other structures have been rebuilt, and Zōjōji continues to serve as the main temple of Jōdō shu and the central nembutsu seminary for priests and novices. Furthermore, it has endeared itself to the general public as both a grand Buddhist temple typical of the metropolis Tokyo and a hub of religious and cultural activities."

<br>This collection's print is a posthumous printing of Kōitsu's original 1933 design published by Doi Hangaten as part of the series Tokyo Views.

title: Hakone: Mt. Fuji Over the Lake (箱根 湖水富士)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description: Sekino's rendition of station number 11, Hakone, along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. This print is the 53rd, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekino created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō, originally made famous by Andō Hiroshige (1794-1858).<br>There are two distinct states for this print. One, as in this collection's print, displays broad blue-gray rays from an unseen sun cutting diagonally across the upper left quarter of the print. These rays are absent in the other state of the print.<br>"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . In 1975, after the completion of the modern Tōkaidō series, the Ministry of Education Award was granted to Sekinō because of his outstanding achievement 'in using every possible technique in woodblock printing, Japanese traditional art, and the recreation of the old fifty-three stations on the Tōkaidō highway in a present-day light.'" - Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p.241-242 and Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 259-260.

title: Riverside (川岸 Kawagishi)
creator: Miyashita Tokio 宮下登喜雄 (1930–2011)
description: One of Miyashita's etchings, done early on in his career, depicting the Tokyo waterfront region where he was born. His later prints, which he is best known for, used combined processes including metal plates, photoengraving and woodblock.

title: Nagoya Castle (名古屋城)
creator: Tsuchiya Kōitsu 土屋光逸 (1870-1949)
description:
Kōitsu's colorful rendering of the walls and inner moat at Nagoya Castle during the height of the spring cherry blossom season.<br>Nagoya Castle was constructed on the orders of Ieyasu Tokugawa to secure an important position on the Tokaido road and to ward off attacks from the direction of Osaka. Construction was completed in 1612, and the castle is typical of those built on flatlands. Until the Meiji Restoration, Nagoya Castle flourished as the castle in which the Owari lineage of the Tokugawa family, the foremost of the family’s three lineages, resided.<br>In May 1945, during the air raids on Nagoya in the Second World War, most of the buildings including the main and small dungeons, and the Hommaru Palace, were burned down. Fortunately, three corner
towers, three gates, and most of the paintings on the sliding doors and walls in the Hommaru Palace survived the fire, and have been handed down as Important Cultural Assets. - Source: Nagoya Castle Official Website http://www.nagoyajo.city.nagoya.jp/13_english/index.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Playground 1 (遊戯場 Yūgijō 1)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description: "Hagiwara creates richly textured and joyfully colourful images. To do this he uses new techniques such as scratching the woodblock like an etching, and printing on the back of the paper. He has won an international reputation for his abstract prints since 1958. Choosing a theme, he then develops a series of studies: this is the first of the ‘playground’ series." -  Source: British Museum from the 2007 exhibition Japan from Prehistory to the Present

title: Picture Card Show (紙芝居 kamishibai)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Picturing two newspaper cameramen photographing two military officials, this print titled Newspaper Photographers was originally issued between 1939 and 1941 by Nishinomiya Shoin as the eighth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.<br>
A translation of the commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "Media reports and news are the eyes and ears of modern life, and the photographer plays a major role as the creator of the depicted records. All his efforts are devoted to the mission of capturing a given incident without missing the next one. It has been said that the best-selling photographers are brave and alert, adventurous and perseverant, and in addition they display a freshness and artistic desire in their work. By night and day, during heat and cold, by heaven and earth, be it leisure or luxury, through their pictures their world truly seems to be extraordinary."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 23.
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Plowing the Rice Field in Spring (春の田んぼを耕す)
creator: Saitō Kiyoshi 斎藤清 (1907-1997)
description: An untitled scene of a lone figure plowing a field with an ox and a primitive looking plow. Various descriptive titles have been assigned to this print, e.g. "Ploughing the Rice Field" and "Ploughing with Ox." When it was released as part of an offering of six Saitō prints by the Book-of-the-Month Club, it was titled "The Seasons: Spring." See IHL.0636 for another print included in the Book-of-the-Month Club set of six prints.

title: Ginkaku-ji, Kyoto
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description:
Funasaka has silkscreened a monotone photograph as the background of this print to simulate a moonlight view of the Mt. Fuji-shaped Kogetsudai ("Moon-viewing platform") at Kyoto's Ginkaku-ji (Temple of the Silver Pavilion.) Superimposed on this photograph are seven of his unique brightly colored vertical forms, along with splotches of black ink. Perhaps his vibrant forms are just visitors to the temple? While the temple dates to the late 1400s, the Zen-inspired moon-viewing platform, made from sand, was added in the 1600s. On moonlit nights the Kogetsudai illuminates the Silver Pavilion.<br>
The artist also created a diptych of this same view of Kogetsudai.  Please see IHL.0987 and IHL.1049 for details on this diptych.

title: M-35
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description:
"The appeal of his work lies not only in its crafted simplicity but also in its formal purity.  He manages to balance the shapes to carve out his own private space and to create tension with these elements." - Collecting Modern Japanese Prints, Then and Now, Mary and Norman Tolman, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1994, p. 83.<br>
The prefix "M" used in the titles of many of Funasaka's works stands for 1,000, an indication that he has produced over one thousand works.

title: 842 (Ginkaku-ji, Kogetsudai)
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: The left print of two prints forming a diptych. Each of the prints use a combination of silkscreen (from a deconstructed photograph image) for the background and woodblock for the artist's signature brightly colored vertical forms. The background image is of the Kogetsudai in the Ginkaku Temple grounds and is the same image as is used in this collection's print Ginkaku-ji Kyoto, IHL.0985.

title: Charcoal Seller (炭屋 sumiya)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
By the time this print, showing a charcoal seller cutting charcoal logs into pieces, was issued during the Pacific War, Japanese homes and small industry were demanding more and more charcoal, adding to the degradation of Japan's large forests. A translation of the artist's commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition (originally print number 14 in the second series) reads "What would be the reason for the mysterious phenomenon nowadays of the upper-class voices on the street supporting the government, while the lower-class are concentrating all their energy on rice and charcoal? And everywhere you go you hear the polite phrase 'The world has become a strange place, don't you think.' As autumn turns to winter, people's eyes are drawn more acutely to rice and charcoal with each passing day. And people go crazy over charcoal to the extent that a lump that before would have seemed completely insignificant to them, now looks like a black diamond. Some people even pine is prison because of it. Because of the current situation, almost every day new substitutes are invented and them substitutes for substitutes. . . . I wonder what on earth will happen to Japan's forests and mountains."[1]
<br> For another impression of this print see IHL.1317.
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]

title: Kawashima Textile Mills, Hand-Woven Tapestry (綴綿手織 tsuzuri-ori teori)
creator: Kotozuka Eiichi 琴塚英一 (1906-1979)
description: This small print depicts weavers at Kawashima Textiles with one of their beautiful large tapestries in the background. One of twelve prints in a portfolio commissioned by the Osaka Railway Division, Japanese National Railways. The table of contents for the portfolio states "Figured Hand-Woven Brocade. Traditional Nishijin, fabric of Kyoto is gorgeous brocade hand-woven with finger-tips."

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Sōma Masakado in the kabuki play Kamahige (九世市川団十郎 相馬将門・鎌髯)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, playing the role of the monk Sōma Masakado in the kabuki play Kamahige (Sickle Beard). Above him is an unidentified actor in the role of the servant Towara Tōda 俵藤太.
<br>Kamahige "was first performed in 1774 at the Nakamura-za in Edo with Ichikawa Danjūrō IV.  This drama is closely associated withh the Ennosuke and Danshirō names of the Ichikawa family.
<br>The Shogun disguised as a traveling monk [Sōma Masakado] and a warrior dressed like a servant [Towara Tōda] appear on stage. The servant holds a sickle with which he is going to shave the monk who holds a water container. The monk tells him that he is immortal when the servant tries cut off his head. When they find out their true identities, they decide to settle their differences on the battlefield."[1] 

<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.

<br>"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selections is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2]
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

<br><br>
[1] Kabuki Eighteen Traditional Dramas, Kawatake Toshio, Chronicle Books, 1985, p. 60.
<br>[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-2023]

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Narukami Shōnin in the play Narukami (九世市川団十郎 鳴神上人・鳴神)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper right panel, playing the role of Narukami Shōnin 鳴神上人 in the kabuki play Narukami 鳴神. Beneath him is an unidentified actor in the role of princess Kumo no Tamahime. 
<br>While not visible in the scanned image of this print, this print, as with others in the series, employs deluxe printing techniques, including embossing covering most of the prints background, the use of mica highlights on Taemahime's collar and a subtle pattern on Narukami's robe visible only when held up to the light at a certain angle.
<br>The story of the play Narukami "originally came to Japan from India and after a Nō play 'Ikkaku Sennin' it was taken up for Kabuki. It is a delightful drama. The holy priest Narukami, angry that his petition to the Imperial Court has been refused, captures the dragon god of rain (ryūjin) and confines him in a rock pool beneath the waterfall which he seals off with a straw rope to indicate the sacred boundary. The country is without rain and so it is decided at the Imperial Court to send the beautiful and clever princess [Kumo no Taemahime] to Narukami. Narukami faints when the princess demonstrates how she had to lift up her skirt to get across a stream to reach her lover. When she revives him with water from her mouth, he for a moment realizes the danger. To prevent any action by him, the princess tells him that she wants to become a nun and when they are left alone she starts to complain of a violent pain. Their embrace only leads to a desire to become husband and wife which has to be celebrated with a drink of sake. Drunk, Narukami tells the princess how to release the god of rain and falls asleep. The princess hastily cuts the straw rope and her mission accomplished, departs. Narukami, in a different, spectacular wig, makeup and costume wakes up and wonders why it is raining and then gets into an uncontrollable rage and runs off after her."[1]

<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
<br>"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2] 
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

<br><br>[1] Kabuki Eighteen Traditional Dramas, Kawatake Toshio, Chronicle Books, 1985, p. 24.
<br>[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Suhō Sōzu in the play Jayanagi (九世市川団十郎 須賔僧都・蛇柳)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, in the role of the Buddhist priest Suhō in the kabuki play Jayanagi (Snake Willow). Above his likeness is an unidentified actor in the role of the priest Kūkai 空海, who is known by his posthumous name Kōbō Daishi.
<br>This rarely performed play was written by Kanai Sanshō and was first performed in 1763 at the Nakamura-za in Edo as the third act of the drama called 'Momochidori Ōisogayoi' with Ichikawa Danjūrō IV.
<br>The text for this play was lost so there is little information about the plot and what information there is is not consistent. It seems that the plot revolves around Tanba no Suketarō, a village idiot, who is possessed by the angry spirit of a willow tree (possibly being the angry spirit of Kiyohime who was spurned by her lover, the Buddhist priest Suhō) on Mt. Kōya and displays vehement jealousy.  The Snake Willow (Jayanagi) refers to a tree at the foot of Mount Koya that was blessed by the Buddhist saint Kūkai and said to represent a thousand year bond between men and women. 
<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.

Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[1]
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

title: Irokezuku sakeguse (色情氣付く酒癖)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description: This print is one of twelve prints issued as part of the comic series known as Twelve States of Mind Resulting from Drinking (Sake kigen jūnisō no uchi) by Kobayashi Kiyochika (1847-1915). "Here we see a woman (the bar’s older sister', apparently) [who] has let her clothing fall away from her body in a drunkenly suggestive manner. Her male companion, who has a sake bottle perched in front of him, looks plainly dismayed, his face conveying complete disinterest." - website of Egenolf Gallery<br>The text in the scroll was written by Honrai Kūjin 奔雷空人, likely a pseudonym.

title: Famous Places of Tokyo, First National Bank (東京名所 第一 国立銀行 Tokyo meisho Dai-ichi Kokuritsu Ginkō)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: The artist designed at least nine prints commemorating the Japan First National Bank built in 1872 (Meiji 5), one of the first pseudo-Western style buildings erected in Japan. This print is from one of THE many different print series created by the artist titled Tokyo meisho (Famous Places of Tokyo.) This particular Tokyo meisho series is distinguished by its Western-style red and yellow frame, an artistic device for highlighting the modernity of the subject.

title: New Year Charm in the Shape of a Love Letter: Woman of the Genroku Era (懸想文・元禄頃婦人 Kesōbumi・Genroku koro fujin)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)
description:
One of thirty-six prints in the series Sanjūroku kasen (also transcribed as Sanjūroku kurabe) depicting delivery of a love poem to a beautiful woman dressed in a Genroku Era (1688-1704) kimono with her hair in the loose style of the period. The bearer of the poem may be the woman's lover, thinly disguised with a scarf about his face, or a messenger sent by her lover.
<br>The series presents women of different classes from thirty-five different historical eras.

title: The Megumi Fire Brigade Fight (神明恵和合取組 Kami-no Megumi Wago-no Torikumi)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: In March 1890, the Shintomiza in Tokyo was the stage for the hit play Kami-no Megumi Wagō-no Torikumi (also called Megumi no Kenka め組の喧嘩 The Firebrigade Fight) which re-enacted the 1805 brawl between a group of drunken firefighters of the Me brigade and a group of sumo wrestlers participating in a show of strength. The fight left one firefighter dead and nearly one hundred men injured. The play, written by Takeshiba Kisuei and Kawatake Shinshichi, pupils of the great playwright Mokuami, consists of four acts. The play was written for Onoe Kigugorō V who is seen in the left panel of this collection's print playing Tatsugorō, the leader of the firefighters.

title: The Teachings of Women (妹背山婦女庭訓 Imoseyama Onna Teikin)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
This print depicts three characters in Act IV, a domestic subplot, of The Teachings of Women. From right to left, we see Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Soga no Iruka, Ichikawa Sadanji as Fukashichi, the fisherman, and, again, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Omiwa, the daughter of a sake seller. Note the fantastic dragon motif on the robe worn by Sadanji in the center panel as he strikes a mie pose.<br>
In Act IV, Omiwa, the daughter of a sake seller, falls in love with the son of Kamatari, one of the leaders of the anti-Soga party. When he refuses to reveal his identity, she attaches a spool of thread to his cloak and follows him, winding the reel. Her lover is following an unidentified princess with the same device, and all finally find themselves at Iruka's palace. Omiwa is noticed by one of Kamatari's subjects, Kanawa Gorō, who is loitering nearby disguised as Fukashichi, the fisherman. He stabs her. As she dies, he reveals that her lover was a courtier and that she will now be helping him to overthrow Iruka. Fukashichi then mixes her blood with the blood of a black-toed deer and smears it on his magic flute, making it possible to recover a certain Sacred Sword from Iruka at last, and sap his power. - Source: The Theatrical World of Osaka Prints, Roger S. Keyes and Keiko Mizushima, David R. Godine in association with Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1973, p. 74.

title: Sanjō Bridge (三条大橋 Sanjō Ōhashi)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Likely a self-printed and published work by Tokuriki, presenting a view from almost underneath the Sanjō Bridge, which crosses Kyoto's Kamo River, out towards the Shijō Ohashi bridge.<br>As with many of Tokuriki's self-printed works, this print exists in at least one other state using slightly different color shades. A a similar view of the bridge presented in a horizontal ōban format also exists. In discussing the ōban version of this print, curator George Kuwayama, notes "Tradition is strong in Tokuriki's work, and compositional analogies to Hiroshige are evident in the Sanjō Bridge. But despite his traditionalism, he is a modern print master. His palette is Fauvist and the strong, expressive lines are gouged with a knife to produce jagged contours."

title: Yoshiwara Park: Army Foot Soldier Private Second Class Mr. Nakamura Fukusaburō (吉原公園 / 陸軍歩　二等卒中村福三郎君 Yoshiwara kōen / Rikugunpo nitōsotsu Nakamura Fukusaburō kun)
creator: Fukunaga Seihan 福永晴帆 (1884-1961)
description: The bravery of Private Nakamura Fukusaburō is depicted, rushing to help people trapped near Yoshiwara Pond as the firestorm that engulfed Tokyo after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake rages.

title: Temporary Omnibus, in the Street of Kyobashi [sic]) (運送馬車 京橋通 Unsō basha Kyōbashi)
creator: Isoda Chōshū 磯田長秋 (1880-1947)

title: House of Yase Women (八瀬女の家 Yase-me no Ie)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Picturing two traditionally dressed women in front of a home in the town of Yase near Kyoto. Women dressed as shown in the print are often referred to Oharame, Ohara being a picturesque and better known town near Yase where many women continued to wear traditional dress, even after WWII. See this collection's prints Oharame (IHL.0313) and Flower Vendors from the series Occupations of Showa Japan in Pictures, Series 1 (IHL.1003) for other depictions of Oharame.<br>
The series Life of Kyoto consists of six chuban-sized prints depicting activities and places in and around Kyoto. The series was published by an unknown publisher identified as 宮脇美風扇版 in the rectangular cartouche in the lower right margin of each print.

title: Kabuki Backstage - Ennosuke II  (歌舞伎 楽屋 - 二代猿之助)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description: The actor Ichikawa Ennosuke II 市川猿之助 (1888-1963) applying makeup in his dressing room.

title: Tōbōsaku 東方朔
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 7 (日清戦闘畫 第七編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daishichi hen)
creator:
Kubota Beisen 久保田米僊 (1852-1906)
<br>Kubota Beisai 久保田 米齊 (1874-1937)
<br>Kubota Kinsen 久保田 金仙 (1875-1954)
description: Volume 7 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895.  Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

title: Park in Canton (廣東公園 Kōtō koen)
creator: Yoshida Hiroshi 吉田博 (1876-1950)
description: This print was based on a sketch done by Yoshida during the last of his "three trips to China between 1939 and 1940, as a war painter for the Japanese Army. Whatever the official purpose, his personal motivation of any of his overseas trips was to sketch the places he visited." - Source: The Complete Woodblock Prints of Yoshida Hiroshi, Tadao Ogura, Abe Corporation, 1996, p. 26, 165.

title: Snow at Kinkaku Temple (Kinkakuji no yuki 金閣寺の雪)
creator: Miki Suizan 三木翠山 (1887-1957)
description: One of the artist's 14 prints created during his lifetime, picturing visitors on the balconies of Kinkaku temple in Kyoto during winter.<br>Officially named Rokuonji Temple, Kinkaku-ji (Temple of the Golden Pavilion) was originally built as a villa by Ashikaga Yoshimitsu (1358-1408). It was converted into a temple after Yoshimitsu's death. The complex, whose gardens and architecture focus around the central Golden Pavilion, is said to evoke paradise on earth and is famous both in Japan and abroad as a symbol of Kitayama culture, which was central in importing various aspects of Ming-dynasty Chinese culture into Japanese society. The temple was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.

title: Hozu River in Early Summer (Shoka no Hozugawa 初夏の保津川)
creator: Miki Suizan 三木翠山 (1887-1957)
description: One of the artist's 14 prints created during his lifetime, picturing an excursion boat being steered down the Hozu River rapids by three boatmen. The Hozugawa is a part of Katsura River in Kyoto Prefecture, Japan. The river begins in the mountains near Kameoka, a town northwest of Kyoto City. It snakes into the Arashiyama  section of western Kyoto before changing its name to Katsura River. Today, excursion boats continue to offer rides through the rapids.

title: Gion Festival (祇園祭 Gion Matsuri)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description:
One of twelve prints from the series Picture Notes on Native Customs of Japan depicting folk rituals from different parts of Japan. It is suggested by Lawrence Smith that the prints paid homage to the Folk Art (mingei) movement that Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), who played an unspecified role in issuing this series, was sympathetic to. 
<br>In the artist's words, "The Gion Festival is held on July 17th and 24th in Kyoto. The musicians on the large float play elegant 'Gion-bayashi' tunes during the procession. The festival officials show their precious antiques and pictures to the spectators which is a unique custom of this festival." - Maekawa Senpan
<br>The artists for this series were Azechi Umetarō, Kawanishi Hide, Kuroki Sadao, Maeda Masao, Maekawa Senpan, Mori Dōshun, Saitō Kiyoshi, Sekino Jun'ichirō, Wakayama Yasoji, and Yamaguchi Gen. This series followed on the heels of the series Scenes of Lost Tokyo (Tokyo kaiko zue), printed in December 1945 and issued by the same publisher, Uemura Masuo of Fugaku Shuppansha. 
<br>The Editor's Statement: "Japan is now on the start-line to the new development. Getting free from militarism Japan is expected to be developed to a nation of civilization. At this time of change, it may be interesting to look back [on] the native customs and festivals as to realize the future images of Japan. These humble customs and festivals will also become the mother's milk for Japanese people to bring up the peaceful heart filled with love and piousness.
<br>"With this purpose the present album has been compiled. The artists are the members of the Japan Artist Engraving Society and are the experts of the Contemporary Original-Engraving in Japan. Japan has been revived to the lovable Japan. We have great pleasure to send you this album at the present delightful time."
<br>For other prints in this series see IHL.0773 and IHL.0774.

title: Portable Shrine Festival (お祭りお神輿)
creator: Mori Yoshitoshi 森義利 (1898-1992)
description:
A dozen revelers carry a movable shrine, an omikoshi, tipping it from side to side, during a shrine festival. Omikoshi お神輿 is a portable Shinto shrine for the gods and spirits carried by the parishioners of a shrine during festivals.  It is paraded around local areas and signifies the warding off of misfortune and wishing for the happiness of its people. Rocking the omikoshi invigorates the deity and enlivens the land.<br>
While almost all of Yoshitoshi Mori's prints are stencil prints, this print appears to be at least partially created using woodblock given the baren rubbing marks on the print's verso.

title: Ducks with Flowering Plum (untitled)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description: One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) around the turn of 20th century.  In this print two mandarin ducks (oshidori), which mate for life, symbolize affection, mutual consideration, and fidelity are paired with plum blossoms symbolizing prosperity and perseverance.

title: Ikarikazuki 碇潜 (The Anchor Draping)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Flag Merchants (旗屋 hataya)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Picturing an artisan painting a banner, Flag Merchants was originally issued in May 1940 by Nishinomiya Shoin as the nineteenth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. This print was not one of the prints from the series reissued after the war by Kyōto Hangain, the successor to the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin. This is not surprising, given that the depiction of nationalist sentiment, e.g. Japanese flags, was not politically acceptable after the war.
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2] <br><br>
[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description:
Bright, primary color is rarely seen in Takahashi’s pre-1965 work, his palette being limited to the soft grays and browns associated with his chosen muse, the ancient city of Kyoto. But this print comes alive with a brilliant burst of yellow sunlight. Takahashi varied the title of this print, with some impressions titled “Summer” and others titled “Seaside”.<br>
All of Takahashi's prints bring to mind the season, whether or not they are titled as such.

title: Dried Persimmons (じろ柿 shiro kaki)

description: An ink on paper scroll mounted on silk brocade with a bone roller (jikuji), picturing two dried persimmons. For a print with the same subject see Dried Persimmons from the series Seihō's Masterpieces (IHL.0908).

creator: Kawase Hasui 川瀬巴水 (1883-1957)
description: An unfinished state, perhaps two impressions, of Matoba Beach at Takehara (Hiroshima ken), 1948. No publisher seal, artist signature or artist seal appear on the print. <br>The artist's second catalog raisonne "Kawase Hasui: The Complete Woodblock Prints," p. 123 notes "Takehara, in southern Hiroshima prefecture, was an important centre for salt production during the Tokugawa period (1600-1868).

description: Print 5 in the Hagiwara's Circus series of prints created in 1968. He followed this series with the series Clowns in 1969 and the circus has been a recurring theme in the artist's work. Here the form of the clown is easily identifiable with his billowing costume.

title: Ejiri Harbor Ship Marina (江尻港船着場 Ejiri-ko funatsukiba)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
This 14th print in the 36 print series depicts the swimming area next to the Ejiri harbor in Shizuoka prefecture and the view out to a snowless Mount Fuji on a quiet summer day. The sign in the lower right reads 三保海水浴場行 (Miho sea bathing area).  This print is the original issue (first edition between 1939-1940) published by Uchida Woodblock Printing Company as part of the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. 

<br><br>THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF 2600
<br>Published by Uchida Bijutsu Shoshi between 1939 and 1940, this 36-print set (plus an introductory sheet and a table of contents sheet) by Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000) is a more modern take on Hokusai's (1760–1849) famous series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1826-1833). Its publication was timed to coincide with nationalist celebrations in November 1940 marking Kigen 2600, the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. 
<br>
Tokuriki's series was extremely popular with domestic and foreign buyers who purchased one thousand copies within a short time after issuance. Various prints from this series were re-printed in subsequent years and subsets of the thirty-six prints were later repackaged into newly named series, such as Eight Views of Mount Fuji and Four Season of Mount Fuji, released in the 1950s. Later printings omit the information in the margin, modify Tokuriki's signature and change the seals below his signature appearing in the image area of the print.

title: Picture of the October Kyōgen at the Meiji-za, Akashi's Patronage (明治座十月狂言・明石引立ノ図)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: A triptych issued in October 1900 depicting thirty-four actors who will be performing during the October lineup of plays at the Meiji-za 明治座 (Meiji Theater) in Tokyo. The actors, mostly part of the Ichikawa lineage, are participating in a kōjō 口上, a ceremony in which the actors present themselves to the audience. The ceremony may also include special announcements, such as an actor assuming a new stage name, or a first appearance on the stage, or memorial services.

title: Miyajima in the Mist, sample print  (霧の宮島・見本 Kiri no Miyajima・mihon)
creator: Kawase Hasui 川瀬巴水 (1883-1957)
description:
This print has the characters 見本 (sample print) written in ink within the image, clearly indicating it was not to be sold. The print pictures Miyajima Shinto shrine on Itsukushima island, located in Hiroshima bay. The shrine and its torii gate are unique for being built over water, seemingly floating in the sea during high tide.
<br>From 1918 until the end of his life, Hasui produced over 600 designs for prints, traveling the country in search of places that retained the character and appearance of the Japan he knew as a child. He sketched outdoors, mostly with pencil, later adding colors and effects when back in his lodgings.

title: Sagami the Wife of Kumagai Naozane (熊谷直実の妻相模)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actor Ōtani Tomoemon V in the role of Sagami, the wife of  Kumagai Naozane, likely in the play Chronicle of the Battle of Ichinotani. This print is from the 1867 series "Parody of Thirty-Six Selected Beauties."

title: China Souvenir (支那土産 Shina miyage)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
In this print we see a Chinese ship, a spoil of war, a souvenir (omiyage). On the side of the ship are written word plays for the various spoils.

The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk. This first print starts with an invitation, perhaps, to the EVENT and it is from this first print that the series takes its name.

creator: Kusaka Kenji 日下賢二 (1936-2020)
description: There's a wonderful mix of perspectives in this print achieved with single point perspective and embossing. The target set in the middle of the horizon leaps forward at us while we travel down a road toward the distant hills with blue sky beyond.

title: Love and Hate
creator: Yoshida Hodaka 吉田穂高 (1926-1995)
description:
Hodaka's semi abstract depiction of a head split by the emotions of love and hate. "Love and Hate shows the energy in emotion. The style is semi abstract, with simplicity of form and elegance in color."[1]  "His idea is that, although love and hatred are two distinct concepts, sometimes they can be double faces of one entity."[2]
