description: Another one of Funasaka's silkscreened images used as a backdrop for his signature brightly colored vertical forms.  This time it's the British Parliament building that he has hand pixelated as part of the print process.

title: Roadside Fortune Teller (大道占師 daidō uranaishi)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
A fortune teller advises a couple in an evening divining session in this tenth print from series two of Occupations of the Shōwa Era in Pictures. This is a first edition print published by Nishinomiya Shoin.
<br>A translation of the artist's commentary originally accompanying this first edition print reads, "The Mainstreet Fortune Teller -for a fee of fifty sen fortunes are told in such diverse areas as marriage, occupation, lost items, missing persons, illness, and the rise and fall of the stock market, by means of reading, physiognomy, fortune telling, and onomancy. At a loss and in dire need they run to this place asking anything that is on their minds. But what are the conditions for trusting this spokesman? First, half of his hair needs to be grey, and he needs to be very old. He definitely shouldn't wear Western clothes. And even if the color is faded, a kimono with one's family crest and a hakama are considered as absolutely necessary parts of the outfit. However, wearing Chinese or Korean clothing seems to be a way to excite people's curiosity even more. What is even more interesting is that the buyer, that is, the person who seeks fortune-telling, forgets that they paid fifty sen and put themselves completely at the mercy of the fortune teller."[1]
<br>For the post-war second edition commentary see IHL.1075.
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 50. 
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Extermination of the Suffering Russian Bear (苦露熊退治 Kurokuma Taiji)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of eight-six prints from the third part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs which presented comic parodies of the Russian enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
In this print we see Japanese soldiers chipping away at the ice surrounding the Russian Bear who has retreated north to the Arctic Ocean in order to "finish him off."

title: Niwa - April (庭・4月)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa.  Also see Niwa (Sunshine), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (Winter Scenery) and Niwa (80-K) in this collection.

title: Good by[e] Winter (冬への別れ)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: The last bit of snow can be seen in the center of a green field with, possibly, a dark rock being heated by the sun. Deep embossing highlights this print.

title: Scene at a Zen Temple (禅寺風景 Zenji fūkei)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Picturing a group of monks, including two visiting monks carrying backpacks, in the courtyard of a Zen temple.<br>
The series Life of Kyoto consists of six chuban-sized prints depicting activities and places in and around Kyoto. The series was published by an unknown publisher identified as 宮脇美風扇版 in the rectangular cartouche in the lower right margin of each print.

title: Stone Lantern in Snow (雪見燈籠 yukimidōrō)
creator: Kawanishi Hide 川西英 (1894-1965)
description: An untitled small print of a stone lantern covered in snow.  Unmistakably Kawanishi Hide in the lack of outlines, use of color and the soft edges of his forms, achieved with the use of a chisel, rather than carving knife, on the woodblock.

title: Rice Planting (田植えTaue)
creator: Kamei Tōbei  亀井藤兵衛 (1901-1977)
description: Two women planting rice in a light rain during early summer.

title: The Plunder Bird (分鳥 Bundori)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
In this print we see the "plunder bird" snatching a Chinese ship as a spoil of war.

title: Sadamisaki (佐田岬)
creator: Asano Takeji 浅野竹二 (1900-1999)
description: A view of the tip of the narrow Sadamisaki Peninsula on Japan's Inland Sea which while 32 km long is never more than a few km wide. Its lighthouse, built in 1918, is one of Japan's "Fifty Famous Lighthouses" and commands one of the most spectacular views of all Japanese lighthouses. This print is one of ten from the series Here and There in Shikoku.

title: Mihonoseki (美保関)
creator: Asano Takeji 浅野竹二 (1900-1999)
description: A view of Mihonoseki harbor which opens up into Miho Bay and the Sea of Japan. This print is one of ten to twelve prints that Asano created from 1964 to 1965 of various scenic views in the San'in Region, encompassing the modern-day prefectures of Shimane, Tottori and the northern area of Yamaguchi. The northern areas of Hyōgo and Kyōto prefectures are sometimes included in the region as well.<br>Mihonoseki is located in the area at the eastern edge of the Shimane-hanto Peninsula in northeastern Shimane. While a charming fishing village today, Mihonoseki was an important trading point during the Edo period when iron, cotton and rice were shipped between Japan and the Korean peninsula.

title: Tottorisakyū (鳥取砂丘)
creator: Asano Takeji 浅野竹二 (1900-1999)
description:
A view of the sand dunes at Tattori on the Sea of Japan. This print is one of ten to twelve prints that Asano created from 1964 to 1965 of various scenic views in the San'in Region, encompassing the modern-day prefectures of Shimane, Tottori and the northern area of Yamaguchi.  The northern areas of Hyōgo and Kyōto prefectures are sometimes included in the region as well.
<br>The Tottori Sand Dunes (鳥取砂丘 Tottori sakyū) are unique sand dunes located near Tottori City in Tottori Prefecture, Honshū, Japan. They are the only large dune system (over 30 km²) in Japan. The dunes were created by sediment deposits carried from the Chūgoku Mountains by the Sendai River into the Sea of Japan. Sea currents and wind help bring the sand from the bottom up onto the shore, where the wind constantly rearranges their shape. The dunes have existed for over 100,000 years, but the area of the dunes has been steadily decreasing due to a government reforestation program following World War II. Additionally, concrete barriers erected to protect the coast (the part of Sanin Kaigan National Park) from tsunamis have disrupted the currents responsible for bringing the sand to shore. In recent years authorities have adopted measures to stop the shrinkage of the dunes, partly because they attract a significant amount of tourism to the area.

title: Tokugawa Yoshinobu (i徳川慶喜)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)

title: Fujiwara no Arihira (藤原在衡)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
Print number 9 (九), and one of 4 contributed by Yoshitoshi to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing Minister of the State Fujiwara no Arihira (891-970) and his assistant, in service to Emperor Murakami 村上天皇 (926-967), making their way through a terrible rainstorm to the palace. Fujiwara was famous for never missing a day of work.<br><br>
This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

creator: Hishikawa Harunobu 菱川春宣 (active 1875-1891)

title: A Gathering of Three Young Magicians (竒術揃三人童子 Kijutsu soroi sannin dōji)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The three most famous actors of their time (from right to left), Ichikawa Danjūrō IX , Onoe Kikugorō V and Ichikawa Sadanji play the roles of the three young magicians Unryūkurō 雲龍九郎 (Cloud Dragon - note Danjūrō's cloud patterned garb); Tora Ōmaru 虎王丸 (Tiger Ōmaru) and Ryūō Tarō 竜王太郎 (Dragon King). It is unclear whether these actors ever appeared together in these roles as the print suggests or whether this is simply a compilation requested by the publishers.

title: Record of What Was Seen and Heard on a Star-filled Moonlit Night (星月夜見聞実記 Hoshizukiyo Kenmon Jikki)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: While only the actor's names and roles are shown on this print, the Tokyo Metropolitan Library identifies the play as Hoshizukiyo Kenmon Jikki (Record of What Was Seen and Heard on a Star-filled Moonlit Night), popularly known as Egara Mondō written by  Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893). The particular performance of the play featured in this print occurred on June 15, 1880 at the Shintomi-za (新富) and was the second play on the program (二番目) which included Mokuami's 5-act play Shimoyo no Kane Jūji no Tsujiura 霜夜鐘十字辻筮 (Crossroads at Ten Bells on a Frosty Night.) Hoshizukiyo Kenmon Jikki is included in Ichikawa Danjūrō IX's Shin Kabuki Jūhachiban (New 18 Kabuki Plays), a list of actually 32 plays favored by the actor.

title: Arashiyama in Spring (untitled)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: One of Tokuriki's half-dozen or so renderings of Togetsukyo Bridge (lit. "Moon Crossing Bridge") with Mt. Arashi (Arashiyama) in the background. This print's scene is set in the spring and Tokuriki has dotted the hillsides with cherry trees.

title: Roadside Fortune Teller (大道占師 daidō uranaishi)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)

title: Oharame's House (大原女の家 Oharame no uchi)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description: A scene in a typical farm house in Ohara on the outskirts of Kyoto. The women who lived in the village, known as Oharame (woman of Ohara), sold their farm products in Kyoto, travelling there by foot and cart. Wada captures a mother holding her baby and the baby's grandmother wearing the distinctive clothing of Oharame consisting of, most prominently, an indigo blue kimono (sometimes patterned, sometimes not) with a white kerchief.

title: Lemon-Blue, No. 367
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: The artist's signature lemons contained within a blue square. As with many of Funasaka's prints the use of high-gloss inks makes it radiant, something that is lost in an electronic reproduction.

title: Lemon, 347
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: The artist's signature lemons contained within a red rectangle which seems to recede within its black three-sided surround. A feather-like object softens the picture.

title: Bon Dori (盆踊り)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description:
Senpan's rendition of the Buddhist custom of Bon Odori (bon dance) during which one's deceased relatives are celebrated. A high wooden scaffold (yagura) is assembled especially for the festival and it is the center for the dance as well as serving as the bandstand for musicians and singers.
<br>Writing in his seminal book Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn published in the year this print was issued, Statler comments on the artist,"People are his main interest, the ordinary people of Japan, and although he sometimes shows them at work, he likes best to catch them when they are enjoying themselves." He characterizes Bon Dori as one of his best prints. - Source: Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn, Oliver Statler, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1956, p. 47.

title: Autumn Scenery at Takao (高雄秋景 Takao shūkei)
creator: Nomura Yoshimitsu 野村芳光 (1870-1958)
description:
One of six prints in the series Famous Places of Kyoto by the artist Nomura Yoshimitsu (1870-1958). While not the original edition of this print, it was certainly created during the artist's lifetime and likely in the late 1930s, after the completion of the second seminal exhibition of modern Japanese prints in 1936 at the Toledo Museum of Art where the original edition of the print was exhibited.<br>
The original edition of the print was issued in a limited edition of two hundred prints and carried the Sankōkai 三光會 gourd-shaped seal under the artist's name as opposed to the 佐藤版 Satō Shō han gourd-shaped seal used on this collection's print.

title: Moon at Hirosawa (広沢之月 Hirosawa no tsuki)
creator: Nomura Yoshimitsu 野村芳光 (1870-1958)
description:
One of six prints in the series Famous Places of Kyoto by the artist Nomura Yoshimitsu (1870-1958). While not the original edition of this print, it was certainly created during the artist's lifetime and likely in the late 1930s, after the completion of the second seminal exhibition of modern Japanese prints in 1936 at the Toledo Museum of Art where the original edition of the print was exhibited.<br>
The original edition of the print was issued in a limited edition of two hundred prints and carried the Sankōkai rectangular-shaped seal under the artist's name as opposed to the 佐藤版 Satō shō han square-shaped seal used on this collection's print.

title: Oki Province: Takuhiyama Takibi no Yashiro (隠岐国・焚火山 焚火ノ社)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
Print number 48 四十八 in the series Nihon chishi ryakuzu (Simple Illustrations of Places in Japan) consisting of at least 78 prints.  The series formed a type of geographical primer of Japan and the prints were sold individually and bound into albums.
<br>This print pictures the Sea of Japan off the coast of Nishinoshima Island, one of four islands making up the Oki Islands in current day Shimane Province. Takuhiyama, a 452 meter high mountain, on the island of Nishinoshima, is the highest point in the Islands and the Torch Shrine (Takibi no Yashiro), was a well-known sacred place among fishermen and sailors, who, when passing by the island would devote their prayers to the shrine's kami (deities.) The man on the boat in the print is shaking a gohei, a kind of ritual wand that along with offerings of cloth were presented to the kami by attaching them to a staff.

title: Sea, Evening Calm
creator: Iwami Reika 岩見禮花 (1927-2020)
description:
An earlier print from the artist just prior to her starting her signature use of gold foil and embossing in prints. There is a range of subtle color in this print that can really only be appreciated by examining the actual print.
<br>About this print, the artist writes: 
<br>The Ocean, with its limitless breadth and scope
<br> Embraces all deep in its heart;
<br>The anger, too, of the bitter and tempestuous night.
<br>Peace descends silently in the distant horizon.
<br>I love the Ocean
<br>- Reika Iwami
<br>This collection's print appeared in the Portland Art Museum for the exhibition "Joryū Hanga Kyōkai, 1956–1965 Japan’s Women Printmakers," which ran from September 24, 2020 until June 13, 2021.

title: Maiko (舞子)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)

title: Asakusa (浅草)
creator: Ōuchi Makoto 大内マコト (1926-1989)

title: Between Vertical and Horizon-Descended Triangle (A)
creator: Ida Shōichi 井田照一 (1941-2006)
description: "The something 'Between Vertical and Horizontal' is what emerges from the interaction of the forces involved. As an artist I create situations to discover my relationship to substances. The meaning of 'descended triangle' is the idea of penetrating beneath the surface, be it in a vertical or horizontal condition." - the artist Ida Shōichi

title: Print 26 Very Popular Story
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: Print 26 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk.

creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: Print 27 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: Print 28 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. title: Windows
creator: Yoshida Chizuko 吉田千鶴子 (1924-2017)
description: An early geometric abstraction from the artist with wonderful overlays of subtle color.

title: Spring
creator: Yoshida Chizuko 吉田千鶴子 (1924-2017)
description: This collection contains two almost identical prints by the artist using the same woodblocks, with minor modifications, this print titled Spring (IHL.1091), and an untitled version of the print (IHL.1985). In these prints Chizuko presents two tilting city landscapes. As compared with this print, in the untitled print Chizuko has shifted the position of the chain of heart-shaped objects to the right and darkened the background. Additional marks, most noticeable in the lower left of the image have also been made. Known for her later prints featuring myriads of butterflies, there may be one flitting about in the upper left quadrant of both these prints.

title: Conversation of the Winds (風の会話 Kaze no kaiwa)
creator: Uchima Ansei 内間安瑆 (1921-2000)
description:
Swirling winds come together with a face-like appearance in this abstract print.
<br>The work of Ansei Uchima reflects a complex fusion of Western and Eastern artistic traditions. Born in California, Uchima returned to Japan at age nineteen, and after World War II studied painting and traditional Japanese printmaking. His first prints, beginning in 1957, drew from nature and the world around him. After he returned to the United States in 1959, his floating, calligraphic compositions, characteristic of sōsaku hanga, suggested the growing influence of Abstract Expressionism.

title: Kasumigaseki (霞ヶ関)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
The Kasumigaseki (gate of mist) district in Tokyo is the area where the Meiji government chose to build its government. In the early 1940s, when this print was created, it would have been a bustling, densely packed area, so this sparsely populated image, showing only a single building complex and two cars in the background, is a bit of a surprise even during a heavy evening snow.<br>
This collection's print is a publisher's proof print that contains notes as to changes to be incorporated on the released print.

title: Nihonbashi (日本橋)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
All is quiet in a usually bustling part of Tokyo around Nihonbashi as an evening snow falls. 
<br>Nihonbashi Bridge, originally built in 1603, was the point from where all distances were marked along the Tōkaidō Road connecting Edo (now Tokyo) to the old capital of Kyoto. The current stone structure, which was rebuilt in grand Western style during the Meiji era (1868-1912), dates back to 1911. It’s now designated a national important cultural property.
<br>Long obscured by the Metropolitan Expressway, by 2041 Nihonbashi will no longer be in the expressway's shadow when a new tunnel replaces this portion of the expressway.

title: Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Nakamura Sōjūrō, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, Onoe Kikugorō V and Bandō Shiuka in the play Kumo ni magō Ueno no hatsuhana. (岩井半四郎 (八代目)、中村宗十郎、市川団十郎 (九代目)、尾上菊五郎 (五代目)、坂東志う調・天衣粉上野初花)
creator: Morikawa Chikashige 守川周重 (active 1869-January 1882)
description:
From right to left, the actors Iwai Hanshirō VIII 岩井半四郎 in the role of the courtesan Michitose 女房おま; Nakamura Sōjūrō 中村宗十郎 in the role of Jōshūya Sadajirō 上州屋定次郎; Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 in the role of the bogus priest Kōchiyama Sōshun 河内山宗俊; Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上菊五郎 as Kataoka Naojirō 片岡直次郎, nicknamed Naozamurai - the "Faithful Samurai"; and Bandō Shiuka 坂東志う調 as Masume Ofuji (reading unconfirmed) 娘おふぢ in the play Kumo ni magō Ueno no hatsuhana 天衣粉上野初花, performed at the Shintomi-za 新富 theater, Tokyo, on March 31, 1881 (Meiji 14).
<br>"Kumo ni magō ueno no hatsuhana" is a sewamono (a play set in contemporary times) depicting the lives of six bad men. Kawatake Mokuami wrote this work while looking back with nostalgia on the Edo emotional mood which he felt was being lost after the Meiji period started.
<br>This play became popular from its premier performance in which Ichikawa Danjūrō 9th played Kōchiyama and Onoe Kikugorō 5th played Naojirō.

<br> Chikashige has used the Toshidama seal, denoting members of the Utagawa School, as the pattern on the red backdrop of the center sheet.

title: Blue and White Space (with holes), No. 319
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: This print has a companion print without the punched holes, IHL.1097. It is possible that both prints are from the same edition of sixty prints with the artist's signature holes being added to some prints in the edition and not to others.

title: Blue and White Space (without holes)
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: This print has a companion print with punched holes, IHL.1096. It is possible that both prints are from the same edition of sixty prints with the artist's signature holes being added to some prints in the edition and not to others.

title: Niwa - Summer house (庭・夏の家)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description:
While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa.  Also see Niwa (Sunshine), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (Winter Scenery), Niwa (80-K) and Niwa (April) in this collection.<br>
Note that this collection's print from the numbered edition differs from the artist's proof (A.P.) pictured in the artist's catalogue raisonné. For the editioned print, as in this collection, Takahashi did not carry the embossing forward and simplified the bottom oblong element.

title: Seashore at Midday (昼の浜)
creator: Okubo Yutaka 大久保担 (1924-2008)
description: One of many prints picturing small boats along the shore that the artist created. For two other similar prints by the artist see IHL.1476 and IHL.1198.

title: Illustration of Noble’s Imperial Ceremony (高位御大禮之図 Kōi godairei no zu)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: Published on March 27, 1900, six weeks before the wedding ceremony of twenty-one year old Crown Prince Yoshihito to sixteen year old Kujō Sadako, daughter of Duke Michitaka Kujō, head of Kujō branch of the Fujiwara clan, this triptych portrays an unnamed ceremony being conducted at the Imperial Palace with the crown prince, his bride to be, the emperor and empress and military officials in attendance. Three court ladies are seated before the crown prince.

title: Hiroshima Imperial Headquarters 廣島大本營 Hiroshima daihon'ei)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
Print number forty-seven (四十七, as printed in right margin) of the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting an outside wall of Hiroshima Castle in the foreground with the Imperial Headquarters (daihon'ei) in the mid-ground and the castle keep in the background.  Hiroshima Castle originally built in 1590 was destroyed in the atomic bombing.  The keep was rebuilt in 1958.
<br><br>SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
<br>The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.
<br><br>In his commentary on the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

title: Udo Shrine (鵜戸神宮 Udo jingū)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
Print number seven (七, as printed in right margin) of the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting the Shinto shrine Udo jingū built in a cave among the cliffs of the Nichinan Coast in Miyazaki prefecture. It is the mythical birthplace of Emperor Jimmu's father and where the spirits of Jimmu and his father are enshrined. 
<br><br>SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600

title: Kwansei Gakuin University (関西学院大学)
creator: Kawanishi Yūzaburō 川西祐三郎 (1923-2014)
description: View of Kwansei Gakuin University's Nishinomiya Uegahara Campus with the Chapel in the foreground right and Clock Tower in the background. The artist had a lifelong relationship with Kwansei Gakuin University with which he worked collaboratively to design a large number of promotional items.

title: Illustration of the Ceremony for the Promulgation of the Constitution of Great Japan (大日本憲法発布式之圖 Dai Nippon kenpōhappushiki no zu)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)

title: The Whole Nation Living in Perfect Contentment (傳聞萬民鼓腹 denbun banmin kofuku)
creator: Utagawa Fusatane 歌川房種 (active 1854-1888)
description:
This scene depicts Empress Shōken, the Empress Dowager and their court ladies assembling pledgets (large bandages) for the Imperial troops fighting rebel samurai during the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. While this print was issued in June of 1877 when the rebels were on the run and close to defeat, the scene it depicts is set towards the end of February when the rebels were laying siege to Kumamoto Castle and its government defenders were experiencing heavy casualties. The sewing of the pledgets was one of the many charitable tasks that the Empress engaged in and was noted in an 1893 book on the historical role of Japanese women prepared for the World's Columbian Exposition, as follows: "In all these [women led educational and charitable institutions] Her Imperial Majesty, our wise and most gracious Empress, takes the lead. There has not been a notable stand taken by women that has been for the public benefit but that the Empress in the kindness of her heart has not either directly or indirectly given it her patronage.<br> 
"When the Kagoshima war broke out in 1877, she sent an immense quantity of lint pledgets of her own preparation for the use of wounded soldiers." - Source: Japan Women [The Japanese Woman's Commission for the World's Columbian Exposition], multiple unnamed Japanese women authors, A.C. McClurg & Co., 1893, p 150.

title: Mount Daisen, North Wall (伯耆大山北壁 Hōki Daisen hokuheki)
creator: Konishi Seiichirō 小西誠一郎 (b. 1919)
description: A depiction of the north wall of Mount Daisen, also called Hōki Daisen.

title: Siblings compete in sacrificing their lives to avert danger, story 9, page 8 ([九] 兄弟死を争ふて危難を免る [八丁])
creator:
Inano Toshitsune 稲野年恒 (1858-1907)
<br>Tominaga Toshichika 富永年親 (1847-?)
description:
In this print, two brothers are confronted by the robbers. Facing certain death, each brother begged the robbers to kill him and spear the other. The robbers felt compassion for their brotherly love and let them go unharmed. This print, one of ninety-two full-color supplemental prints to the earlier issued six volume textbook titled Brocade Pictures of Moral Education illustrates tory number 9 in volume 1.<br>
In October 1883 a set of ninety-two full-color oban-size prints designed by students of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi were published by Tsuji Keiji and his publishing house Fukyūsha as supplements, or accompaniments, to the six volume set of textbooks titled ""Nishiki-e shūshindan"" 錦絵修身談 (Brocade Prints for Moral Education), published earlier by Tsuji and illustrated by Yoshitoshi. These supplemental prints illustrated the ninety-one short stories contained in the six volumes. A number of the full-color prints issued were based upon Yoshitoshi's black and white illustrations in the texts. Each of the full-color prints carries the textbook's title 錦絵修身談 and volume number across its top and the name of the story and its location in the textbook in a vertical red cartouche.

creator:

title: Crater (噴火口 Funkakō)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description: Sakamoto gives us a view into the active crater of Mt. Aso, the largest active volcano in in Aso Kujū National Park in Kumamoto Prefecture, on the island of Kyūshū. This print is one of five in the series Five Views of Aso, which was first published in a limited edition of 300 in 1950 by Kuga Ichio 久我五千男 (1922-1984) of Sōjinsha, with carving and printing at Katō Hanga Kenkyūsho under the supervision of Katō Junji. The envelope in which the five prints were packaged had a small print picturing two horses grazing affixed to it (see IHL.2379) and the set of prints also contained a cover page which used the same image of two horses grazing (see IHL.2310.)

title: Autumn at Lake Towada (十和田湖の秋) Towadako no aki)
creator: Yasui Sōtarō 安井曾太郎 (1888–1955)
description:
A bold color statement by Yasui, considered one of Japan’s most respected Western-style (yōga) painters from the1930s through his death in 1955, demonstrating his belief that prints were an ideal vehicle for "expressing things by lines and color." - Source: Japanese Wood-block Prints, Shizuya Fujikake, Japan Travel Bureau, 1938 revised 1949, p. 137. 
<br>Yasui designed at least sixteen woodblock prints that he then had carved and printed, under his supervision, by others.

title: Backlit Fuji (逆光富士)
creator: Miyashita Tokio 宮下登喜雄 (1930–2011)
description: Not quite a "red Fuji," Miyashita gives us a view of Fuji at dusk, with the mountain taking on a deep purple hue. One of Miyashita's post-1980s prints, displaying a move back towards realism from the abstraction of his works created in the 1970s. This print is very similar to the artist's 2002 print Daybreak at Mt. Fuji featured in The Library of Congress online exhibition On the Cutting Edge, Contemporary Japanese Prints from the 50th College Women's Association of Japan Print Show. (See https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/cwaj/online/gallery3.html [accessed 8-17-23])

title: Dockyard (造船所)
creator: Miyashita Tokio 宮下登喜雄 (1930–2011)
description: A ship being loaded with freight at a dockyard. One of Miyashita's post-1980s prints  displaying a move back towards realism from the abstraction of his works created in the 1970s.

title: Work 69.5 (作品 69.5 sakuhin 69.5)
creator: Kusaka Kenji 日下賢二 (1936-2020)
description: Approximately three feet high, this print by the artist that epitomizes his continuing series of prints carrying the title Work ( 作品 sakuhin) begun in the early 1960s. This series began with some reference to identifiable objects but quickly became more abstract and dynamic with use of intense primary colors. Starting around 1967 Kusaka introduced the circle form which subsequently morphed into an egg shape. This egg shape counterbalanced his straight lines and angular corners.

title: Ariadne (アリアドネ)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description:
One of 42 prints in the artist's series Greek Mythology.  Hagiwara pictures a sleeping Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, the King of Crete, suspended by a single vine.  She is in her classic sleep pose of one arm raised over her head with a look or exhaustion and despair, as she has been abandoned by her lover Theseus on the island of Naxos.<br>
The entire series was issued as a complete portfolio bound in a black woven material, imprinted in silver. Hagiwara employed both traditional Japanese woodblock technique as well as intaglio on these prints.

"Throughout his working life, Onchi produced many works entitled 'Lyric'. In these works he explored the characteristics of woodcut searching for a union of poetry and visual art." - Source: Art Gallery of New South Wales http://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/collection/works/82.2000/ [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Shimabara District After the Rain (しまばらくるわ雨後 Shimabara kuruwa ugo)
creator: Kamei Tōbei  亀井藤兵衛 (1901-1977)
description:
One of twelve small prints from the portfolio titled New Famous Places of Kyoto designed by Kamei Tōbei  (1901-1977), who used the artist name Kamei Genbei 亀井玄兵衞 starting in 1953, and fellow Kyoto print artist Tokuriki Tomikichirō (1902-2000). The set was published by the New Famous Places of Kyoto Publication Society (新京都名所刊行会), which may have been formed by Kamei and Tokuriki specifically to publish this set of prints.<br>
This print depicts the main gate entrance to Shimabara, Kyoto's former red-light district, after a night rain. When this print was made Shimabara was still a licensed entertainment area.  Japanese art historian Lynn Katsumoto notes: "The sign on the stand to left says 'tako' - the 'yaki' is left off, but I think that's what most people assume. Tako yaki are little bready balls with bits of octopus inside, popular street fare." A crude drawing of an octopus appears to the right on the stand's curtain. For another impression of this print see IHL.2190.

description: The actors, from right to left, Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, Ichikawa Shinjūrō II and Nakamura Nakazō III are depicted below extensive text. It is likely that the publication of this print coincided with the change of ownership in the Kawarazaki theater sometime in 1876 to a new group of investors who renamed the theater the Shinbori. The presence of chrysanthemums indicates that this print is marking an auspicious occasion.

title: Ranking of Wages of Tokyo Actors (東京俳優給金附 Tokyo haiyū kyūkin zuke)
creator: Toyohara Chikamitsu 豊原周光 (active c. 1891- 1896)
description:
A depiction of nineteen actors in character, along with a listing of their salaries and the salaries of other leading Tokyo kabuki actors. The leftmost entry on the scroll running across the top of the print provides a date of Meiji 29 (1896) for the annual salaries that are given above each actor's name.<br>While there is some English language information available on both pre and post-Meiji salaries for kabuki actors, there seems to be little information available in English on salaries for Meiji-era kabuki actors. For the salaries shown on the print's scroll, they are likely yearly salaries as actors contracted with a theater for the entire kabuki season. On this print, the highest annual salary listed is that of Ichikawa Danjurō IX 市川団十郎 at 2,000 yen. As a point of reference, the basic starting pay of a policeman in 1881 was 72 yen per year and for an elementary school teacher in 1886, 60 yen.
<br>In discussing actor salaries at the beginning of the 19th century, Arendie and Henk Herwig state, "[T]op actors’ annual earnings were between 1000 and 1500 ryō."[1]  According to Brandon in Kabuki Plays on Stage: Villainy and Vengeance, "1000 ryō would be the equivalent of 400,000 to 800,000 American dollars today. They did have to pay for their own costly costumes, however.  Popular actors received a formal salary, but they were also supported by wealthy patrons who provided extra revenue or paid for expensive costumes. In return, the patrons could expect favours such as the presence of actors at their parties or private performances. It was common practice for actors to honour their patrons with a visit during the first days of the New Year bringing gifts as tokens of gratitude."[2]

<br><br>[1] Heroes of the Kabuki Stage: An Introduction to the World of Kabuki with Retellings of Famous Plays, illustrated by Woodblock Prints, Arendie Herwig and Henk J. Herwig, Hotei Publishing, 2004, p. 40.
<br>[2] Kabuki Plays on Stage: Villainy and Vengence, 1773-1799, editors James R. Brandon, Samuel L. Leiter, University of Hawaii Press, 2003, p. 288.

title: Moon at Namino (波埜の月)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description: A full moon over Kujū National Park in Kumamoto Prefecture on the island of Kyūshū. The main attraction in the park in Mount Aso, a 1,592 meter (5,223 ft) active volcano, Japan's largest. The white circular ring in the distance might be a formation caused by vapors from the volcano.<br> The print is one of five in the series Five Views of Aso first published in a limited edition of 300 in 1950 by Kuga Ichio 久我五千男 (1922-1984) of Sōjinsha, with carving and printing at Katō Hanga Kenkyūsho under the supervision of Katō Junji. The prints in the series was reprinted a number of times, including a smaller-size version in 1962 by Kyūryūdō under a new title "Sakamoto Hanjiro gashu."

title: Act III - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (三段目 忠臣蔵 sandanme Chūshingura)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Chūshingura Act III: Kampei confronts Bannai and his servants near the gate to the palace of Ashikaga Tadayoshi - This scene is set in the evening outside of Kamakura Castle. Kampei, behind whom stands Ōkaru by the bridge over the moat, across which rise the walls and towers of Kamakura Castle, is about to be attacked by Bannai and his men. Bannai is about to arrest Kampei and take Ōkaru, who has her orange scarf ready to strangle Bannai. The immediate aftermath of this scene, in which Bannai and his men flee Kampei, was portrayed about ten years earlier by Hiroshige II's teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige.
<br><br>Utagawa Hiroshige II created this series of twelve prints under his art name (gō) Shigenobu. His teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I, created several earlier series in the horizontal ōban format depicting the acts in the play Chūshingura, one published by Izumaya Ichibei between 1835-1839 and one published by Arataya Seiemon between 1843-1847. As with Hiroshige I's series, Hiroshige II bordered the prints with the double Tomo-ye crest of Yuranosuke, the hero of the play.  For several scenes, Hiroshige II borrowed heavily from his teacher as he did for this print.

title: Act VIII - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (八段目 忠臣蔵 hachidanme Chūshingura)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description: Chūshingura Act VIII: Konami's bridal journey (michiyuki travel dance) - The scene is set on the road from Edo to Kyoto. Tonase and Konami are on their way to Yamashima to find Rikiya, Yuranosuke's son and Konami's betrothed. They are resting under the shade of a large tree overlooking the seashore and admiring the fine view of Fuji with their porter sitting before them. Behind them rises the wooded island of Enoshima.<br>Utagawa Hiroshige II created this series of twelve prints under his art name (gō) Shigenobu. His teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I, created several earlier series in the horizontal ōban format depicting the acts in the play Chūshingura, one published by Izumaya Ichibei between 1835-1839 and one published by Arataya Seiemon between 1843-1847. As with Hiroshige I's series, Hiroshige II bordered the prints with the double Tomo-ye crest of Yuranosuke, the hero of the play. For several scenes, Hiroshige II borrowed heavily from his teacher, but for his portrayal of this act he chose to depict a different scene than his teacher, though each shows a pause in this bridal journey.

title: Act XI - The Storehouse of Loyal Retainers (十一段目 忠臣蔵 jūichidanme Chūshingura)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Chūshingura Act XI (third episode): Moronao captured and shown Enya's suicide sword by Yuranosuke - The scene is set on a snowy night under a full moon. Moronao is discovered in his hiding-place in an outhouse used to store wood and charcoal. Yuranosuke shows him the dagger with which Enya committed suicide and invites him to do likewise, an invitation which Moronao declines.
<br>Utagawa Hiroshige II created this series of twelve prints under his art name (gō) Shigenobu. His teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I, created several earlier series in the horizontal ōban format depicting the acts in the play Chūshingura, one published by Izumaya Ichibei between 1835-1839 and one published by Arataya Seiemon between 1843-1847. As with Hiroshige I's series, Hiroshige II bordered the prints with the double Tomo-ye crest of Yuranosuke, the hero of the play.  For several scenes Hiroshige II borrowed heavily from his teacher, but for his portrayal of this act he chose to depict the moment before Moronao is seized by Yuranosuke and then killed.

description: One of three woodblock printed postcards (also see IHL.1155 and IHL.1156) packaged in a decorative envelope (see IHL.1153) which display some aspect of interaction or cooperation between the Japanese and their American occupiers following the war. This set of postcards were created under the direction of Wada Sanzō (1883-1967) and the idenities of the artists whose signatures appear on the postcards are unknown. This postcard depicts three G.I.s watch two passing maiko while standing on Sanjō Bridge in Kyoto.

title: Japanese Coming Home on Hakata Pier (博多港の邦人引揚げ Hakata-kō no hōjin hikiageru)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967) - "complemented" by the artist
description: One of three woodblock printed postcards (also see IHL.1154 and IHL.1156) packaged in a decorative envelope (see IHL.1153) which display some aspect of interaction or cooperation between the Japanese and their American occupiers following the war. This set of postcards were created under the direction of Wada Sanzō (1883-1967) and the identities of the artists whose signatures appear on the postcards are unknown. This postcard pictures civilians disembarking from the ship named the "Dockwiler" at Hakata Pier in Fukuoka. The ship is likely the Liberty Ship the S.S. John Dockweiler, launched in January 1944. Hakata was a major processing center for Japanese "displaced persons" who had been repatriated from China, Korea and other former Japanese colonies with the help of U.S. ships following Japan's defeat.

title: A Snowy Sight at Hibiya Junction in Tokyo (東京日比谷交差点の雪 Tokyo Hibiya kōsaten no yuki)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967) - "complemented" by the artist
description: One of three woodblock printed postcards (also see IHL.1154 and IHL.1155) packaged in a decorative envelope (see IHL.1153) which display some aspect of interaction or cooperation between the Japanese and their American occupiers following the war. This set of postcards were created under the direction of Wada Sanzō (1883-1967) and the identities of the artists whose signatures appear on the postcards are unknown. This postcard features an occupation soldier and a Japanese policeman cooperating in directing traffic at busy Hibiya Junction. They seem to be waving to each other in a comradely way, further evidence of the harmonious relations between defeated Japan and the occupation forces depicted in these postcards.

title: Landscape Spring Evening (春宵 A)

description: A semi-abstract landscape with a rising moon in a silver metallic sky. The artist has used deep embossing through the white band beneath the sky. A green field of flowers dominates the foreground. This print was exhibited at the CWAJ Twentieth Annual Print Show, October 1975 at the Tokyo American Club.

title: Katsushika (葛飾)
creator: Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki) 高橋松亭 (弘明) (1871-1945)
description: The artist Takahashi Shōtei (Hiroaki) (1871–1945) is credited with over 750 designs during his lifetime, the majority of which depicted landscapes in the shin hanga style. While he worked with at least one other publisher, most of his work was done for the publisher Watanabe  Shōzaburō, starting in 1907. In this post Great Kantō Earthquake print a fisherman, bent over with his load, carries a heavy basket after a day of fishing. A torii and shrine can be seen in the background. Titled "Katsushika" ("葛飾" above the artist's red square-shaped seal on the right side of the pirnt), Katsushika-gun (now Katsushika City) was a Tokyo ward. The river seen in the print may the Arakawa which bordered Katsushika on the west or the Edogawa bounding it on the east.

title: Tsuta Onsen (蔦温泉)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description:
From Senpan's fourth set of prints picturing Japanese onsens. This print depicts the bus or automobile stop outside of Tsuda (Tsuta) onsen with the sign reading 國鉄自動車 ったおんせん (National Railway bus stop or auto stop. Tsuda onsen). The spa-goers stand, looking perplexed, at the sign.
<br>"Tsuta Onsen is an inn situated at the mouth of Oirase Gorge in Aomori. Records of hot spring resorts here date all the way back to the year 1147." - Source: website of Tsuta Onsen https://tsutaonsen.com/en/ [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>ABOUT THE SERIES HOT SPRING NOTES
<br>One of his most famous series of prints, "Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes" (Hanga yokusen fu), depicts various hot springs around Japan. It was published in five volumes of twenty prints each over an 18 year period, starting in 1941 when Maekawa was evacuated to Okayama in southwest Honshu and ending in 1959.

<br>Merritt states that most of the prints were started during the war but could not be published until the war was over. She notes that although his countrymen are depicted at one of their favorite pastimes, spa going for rest and relaxation, "the feeling is not joyous," due to Maekawa's use of somber colors. The general demeanor of the spa goers is also somber in many of the prints. 
<br>However, writing in 1955, Oliver Statler found Senpan's spa prints "some of his pleasantest prints" and praised Senpan's "connoisseur's selection from the country's hundreds of hot spring resorts."
<br>In 1954 the publisher Ryūseikaku 竜星閣 released a volume containing full size reproductions of the sixty woodblock prints contained in the first three volumes.
<br>The five volumes comprising the entire series are titled are:
<br>Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes  (版画 浴泉譜 Hanga yokusen fu), 1941.
<br>More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1944.
<br>More and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1952.

title: Village in snow with Mount Fuji (untitled)
creator: Okuyama Gihachirō 奥山儀八郎 (1907-1981)
description:
A snow covered village backed by a line of bare trees with a snow covered Fuji dominating the background. 
<br><br>Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) maker and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. His work also crossed over into the new print (shin hanga) genre. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own woodblock prints, such as IHL.1844, and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.

title: Semi Onsen (瀬見温泉)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description:
From Senpan's fourth set of prints picturing Japanese onsens. This print depicts an inn near the Semi hot springs on a winter's day. Two lonely figures sit in the inn on a bleak looking day.
<br> The Legend of Semi Onsen
<br>In 1187, a samurai warrior named Minamoto Yoshitsune, his companion Benkei and their party, were passing by the Semi Onsen hot springs on their way to Hiraizumi in Iwate, pursued by the forces of his brother, Yoritomo. At that time, Yoshitsune's pregnant wife, Kitanokata, suddenly began to feel labour pains, and Kamewakamaru was born.
<br>"Benkei went down the mountain in pursuit of water for the newborn's first bath, and discovered columns of steam rising from beneath rocks. He dug down into the ground using his naginata (bladed pole weapon), and thermal waters gushed out, according to Gikeiki (The Chronicle of Yoshitsune). Since then, these top quality waters have been flowing from the spring, continuously, for over 800 years. Many historical sites and attractions in association with Yoshitsune and Benkei are lovingly preserved in Semi Onsen." - Source: website of Kansyokan Semi Onsen https://kansyokan.co.jp/en/about/ [accessed 8-17-23]
