title: Pottery Works (陶藝工所)
creator: Kotozuka Eiichi 琴塚英一 (1906-1979)
description: A small print showing a potter at work from the portfolio of twelve prints titled Collection of Color-Prints with Views of Kyoto, Nara, Osaka and Kobe offered by the Osaka Railway Division, Japanese National Railways.

title: Kinkakuji (Golden Pavilion) in the Snow (金閣寺雪景)
creator: Kamei Tōbei  亀井藤兵衛 (1901-1977)

title: 897 Eiffel Tower
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: Another one of Funasaka's prints using a silkscreened image of an iconic building as a backdrop for his signature brightly colored vertical forms printed using woodblock technique. This time it's the Eiffel Tower that he has hand pixelated as part of the print process.

creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: Eight of Funasaka's signature brightly colored vertical forms float over a golden grid. The background ink is laced with mica.

title: Aoto Fujitsuna (青砥藤綱)
creator: Inoue Yasuji 井上安治 (1864-1889)

title: Not Aware Man and Aware Man, No. 2
creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)
description:
The top print shows what appears to be a sleeping man (perhaps sleepy with too much drink), being rushed through the nighttime streets in a jinrikisha (note 人力車 jin/riki/sha on the lantern.) He is being moved ahead at great speed by both the jinrikisha drivers and a slew of bad little akudama. A wallet (kamiire) containing money (satsu), that he possibly dropped, can be seen in the lower left of the print.<br>
The bottom print shows a man, who is carrying a box, so possibly some type of vendor, near a sake shop (note the character 酒 on the first shop on the left) whose attention is being drawn to a wallet with its contents lying on the ground by six good little zendamas. Is it his good fortune that he has found this money? Has his abstinence produced his good luck? Will he try to return the wallet to its drunken onwer

title: Gathering Shellfish at Low Tide at Fukagawa Susaki (深川洲崎汐干狩)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
Shiohigari (Shellfish gathering at low tide) a popular beach activity for the people in Edo, was an annual event in March on the beaches such as at Shinagawa, Shibaura, Fukagawa Susaki. Among all, Susaki was especially crowded with many people as a famous spot for shellfish gathering.<br>
The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III, created a number of series of prints depicting meisho (famous places or famous views) in and around the city of Tokyo/Edo. It is interesting to compare his depiction of this popular past time with his predecessors Utagawa Hiroshige I and Utagawa Hiroshige II.

title: Mansei Bridge (萬世橋 Mansei bashi)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)
description: One in a series of prints showing famous places ("prides") in and around Tokyo. The Mansei Bridge, built and destroyed a number of times, spanned the Kanda river and was one of the major gateways to Tokyo. Its current iteration is located in present day Akihabara.

title: Portrait of Saigō Takamori, Former Army General Senior Grade of the Third Court Rank (西郷隆盛像旧陸軍大将正三位) Kyu Rikugun Taishō Shōsanmi Saigō Takamori zō)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description:
Issued in the beginning of November 1877, approximately six weeks after the end of the nine month Satsuma Rebellion and the death of its leader, Saigō Takamori, this print portrays Saigō decked out in all his military finery from the days when he was one of the most powerful men in the new Meiji government. While it was not until the end of February 1889 that Saigō, the rebel, received his official state pardon and the restoration of his imperial court rank, he and his top commanders were portrayed as heroes by printmakers and their publishers as soon as the rebellion was crushed.
<br>Translation of text on print: "Saigō Takamori was born in Satsuma. His former name was Zenbei, and he also used the sobriquet Nanshū. He was naturally endowed with unusual talent and an imposing appearance, such that all who saw him immediately recognized him as extraordinary. Enlisting early in the royalist cause he entered the Capital of Kyoto in the Kaei era [1848-54] and became a follower of the monk Gesshō, incumbent of the Hōjōin at Kiyomizu. Favored by the noble Lord Konoe he grieved at the desuetude into which the royal house had fallen, and plotted with Ijichi Masaharu and Kaieda Nobuyoshi to do great deeds. But then the shogunate sent forces to arrest and confine these idealists. Saigō fled to Kyushu with Gesshō, meaning to return to his own holdings, but when they were prevented, they made a pact to throw themselves into the sea. They leapt into the water in each other’s arms, but others on the boat pulled them out. Saigō was revived, but Gesshō perished. Having thus been returned mysteriously to life, Saigō assumed the name Kikuchi Gengo. His domain shunned his actions and banished him to the Great Island [Amami]. He spent several years there, his aspirations becoming ever firmer even as his learning grew broader. He was pardoned in Bunkyū 3 [1863] and returned to his domain, where he changed his name to Kichinosuke and quickly rose in the domain’s government. In Keiō 1 [1865] he participated in the shogunate’s campaign against Chōshū but affected the release of imprisoned royalists in many domains. Not least of his deeds was done in the spring of Boshin [1868] when as deputee in charge of the imperial forces’ expedition to the East he took Edo Castle. Subsequently he followed the Great Governor General [Prince Arisugawa] in pacifying Hokuetsu, in which action he performed meritoriously. In further quelling brigand forces in Ezo his tactics were uniformly apt for the moment. For all of this the Court elevated him to the post of Councilor, but he refused and returned to his domain. Then on 6/2/Meiji 2 [1869] it was decreed that for his aid in the great work of Restoring the government, for seizing Edo Castle and leading the Hokuetsu expedition, and for his stalwart performance of military deeds, his leadership, and his successful and foresighted planning, all of which had brought much comfort to His Majesty, he would be rewarded with a stipend of 2000 bales of rice. In Meiji 4 [1871] he was elevated to Third Rank, First Grade, at court and made Councilor. In 4/Meiji 6 [1873] he was made Commander in Chief of the Army. In the 10th month of that year he advocated on behalf of an Imperial expedition against Korea, and when that was refused he resigned his position and returned to his home country. He also attempted to refuse all his rewards and emoluments, but the court would not allow this, and so he devoted them to the establishment of private academies in the countryside. He sent several of his students abroad to study, without requiring reimbursement. In this way the young men of the prefecture came to support him. Then in the 2nd month of this year he joined with Kirino [Toshiaki], Shinohara [Kunimoto], and others to raise a great army with himself as commander in order to make inquiries of the Government. With violence they occupied the Higo Road, and the Government moved quickly to mount an expedition against them. By land and sea, forces flying the Imperial flag advanced upon Kyushu. Battles were fought in Bungo, Higo, Satsuma, and Kumamoto. In the 9th month the rebel forces again attacked Kagoshima, but then the Imperial forces surrounded them at Shiroyama with superior numbers. At 3:00 in the morning on 9/24, they began attacking from all sides. There was no way to fend them off now, and he, along with Kirino and Murata [Sansuke], slit his belly, dying at Shiroyama. The remaining rebels were all captured, and by 7:00 that morning the rebellion had been quelled. Once he had held lofty rank and position, but in this way, having enlisted with insurrectionists, he became a traitor to the Realm." - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon

title: Portrait of Kirino Toshiaki: The Former Army Major General of the Fifth Court Rank (桐野利秋像・旧陸軍少将正五位)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description: Issued in the beginning of November 1877, approximately six weeks after the end of the nine month Satsuma Rebellion and the death of its leader, Saigō Takamori, this print portrays Kirino Toshiaki, Saigō Takamori's second in command, not in his former military uniform as a Major General in the new Meiji army (as Saigō is portrayed in the print Portrait of Saigō Takamori, IHL.1171), but in his samurai regalia. This is befitting as Kirino was known as a ferocious swordsman, one of the "Four Hitokiri of the Bakumatsu" 幕末四大人斬り. Kirino was to be slain along with Saigō at the last battle of the rebellion at the end of September 1877.

title: First Chanting of Noh at the New Year (御謡初 O-utai zome)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
This print is from a series of 32 scenes documenting life for the elite during the later days of the shogunate. In this print, samurai have gathered in a large reception hall in the Chiyoda Outer Palace to hear the year's first chanting of noh at Edo Castle. The inscription in the center of the print starts off,  "Every year on the evening of the third of the New Year, the first dance of the year is held in the main hall . . . ."[1] The inscription goes on to tell us that "selections were performed from Oimatsu, Takasago and other plays."[2] The different schools of noh would take turns annually to present the chants.

<br><br>THE CHIYODA OUTER PALACE
<br>The Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) series of 1897, together with Chikanobu's 1895-1896 series Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku), provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868.
<br>While the Chiyoda Inner Palace series focused on women in the private quarters of the palace, Chiyoda Outer Palace focused on the society of men, centered on the shogun, inside and outside the castle. The thirty two prints (including one hexaptych) show "activities which Chikanobu may have participated in when he was part of the shogun's retinue. This set, too, while more authentic because of Chikanobu's personal experiences, is also an artistic representation, and focuses on the elite side of life in the late Edo period."[3]
<br>The activities in the Chiyoda Outer Palace series are set both "in the more public areas and grounds of the castle and beyond the castle precincts...as far away as the shogunal mausoleum at Nikkō."[4]
<br><br>
[1] Princeton University Art Museum https://artmuseum.princeton.edu/collections/objects/50952 [accessed 8-30-23]
<br>[2] The British Museum https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_1906-1220-0-1620-1-3 [accessed 8-30-23]
<br>[3] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 170.
<br>[4] Princeton University Art Museum https://artmuseum.princeton.edu/collections/objects/24904  [accessed 8-30-2333333]

title: Illustration of the National Diet Building (國會議事堂圖 kokkai gijidō no zu)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: On November 29, 1890 the ceremonies for the long awaited opening of the Imperial Diet took place. That morning the emperor left the palace at 10:30 and proceeded toward the House of Peers. He was accompanied by Prince Taruhito, Interior Minister Sanjo Sanetomi, Prime Minister Yamagata Aritomo, President of the Privy Council Oki Takato, and various high officials. On reaching the Diet building, the emperor was met by other dignitaries.

title: Steam Train at Takanawa Seashore, Tokyo (東京高輪海岸蒸気車鉄道走行之全図 Tōkyō Takanawa kaigan jōkisha tetsudō hashiriyuki no sen zu)
creator: Utagawa Yoshitora 歌川芳虎 (active c. 1836-1882)
description: The little steam train from Shinagawa in Tokyo to Yokohama started running in the summer of 1872. This print, however, was issued sometime in 1871 and was likely based on the artist's imagination of a steam train, possibly culled from American or European illustrations. Plans for the rail line between Yokohama and Tokyo were announced in 1870 and it immediately became an emblem of civilization and enlightenment (bunmei kaika). Publishers rushed to represent this modern conveyance and dozens of prints ensued.

title: Rokkasen kyōga no suminuri (六歌仙狂画墨塗)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: Staged in March 1880, at the Shintomiza 新富 in Tokyo, this dance play was a mitate (parody) on the theme of the Six Immortal Poets (rokkasen). Pictured in the roles of the Six Immortal Poets are the actors (from right to left), Iwai Hanshirō VIII 岩井半四郎 as the lady Ono no Komachi 小野小町, Onoe Kigugorō V 尾上菊五郎 as Hōshi [priest] Kisen 喜撰法師, Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 as the evil noble Ōtomo no Kuronushi 大伴黒主, Nakamura Sōjūrō 中村宗十郎 as Sōjō [abbot] Henjō 僧正遍昭, Ichikawa Danjūrō 市川団十郎 as the noble Bunya Yasuhide 文屋康秀 and Bandō Kakitsu 坂東家橘 as the courtier Ariwara no Narihira 在原業平.

title: Bridge (橋)
creator: Oka Shikanosuke 岡鹿之助  (1898-1978)
description: A woodblock rendition of a 1948 oil painting by the artist. This collection's print is likely a proof print for the editioned version which was one of five prints included in the folio titled Oka Shikanosuke Woodblock Print Collection, First Series [岡鹿之助第一輯版画集 Oka Shikanosuke daiichshū hanga gashū]. The folio was issued in an edition of 150 in 1970 by the publisher Katō Hanga Kenkyūsho (Katō Print Institute).

title: Tea Ceremony (茶の湯 chanoyu)
creator: Kasamatsu Shirō 笠松紫浪 (1898–1991)
description: The Japanese tea ceremony is called chanoyu or sado in Japanese and the bitter tea served is called matcha. It is basically a choreographic ritual of preparing and serving tea together with some sweets. Each movement is predefined. The whole process is not about drinking tea, it is about aesthetics. The proper performance requires a long training and the use of certain tools like chasen, a bamboo brush. For an earlier edition of this print see ihl-0008.

title: Remaining Light at Jōshū, Minakami (残燈 上州水上 Zantō, jōshū Minakami)
creator: Kasamatsu Shirō 笠松紫浪 (1898–1991)
description: A later edition of a 1958 print picturing the sun setting behind the distant mountains behind the Alpine village of Minakami, a hot spring and ski resort. The Tone River, seen in the foreground, reflects the last of the sunset's glow.

title: Spring Snow at Maruyama, Kyoto (春の雪 京都円山 Haru no yuki Kyoto Maruyama)
creator: Tsuchiya Kōitsu 土屋光逸 (1870-1949)
description: Three woman in traditional winter clothing, geta on their feet, stroll through snow covered Maruyama Park  in early evening. This collection's print is a later edition of a much-reprinted image by Kōitsu, originally released in March 1936.

title: Still Life of Crystal Vase and Rose (untitled)
creator: Maeda Masao 前田政雄 (1904-1974)
description: One of at least four similar images of a crystal vase done by the artist in various formats.  This impression from an edition of 250 prints is dated 1973, a year before the artist's death, and appears to use the same blocks as the original 1959 edition of 50 prints.

title: Inbanuma, the Desolate Marsh (印旛沼、沼辺の荒涼)
creator: Ishii Hakutei 石井柏亭 (1882-1958)
description:
This print, one of 15 contributed by Hakutei to the 50 print series Japan Scenery Prints, published by Nakajima Jūtarō, pictures a lonely fisherman's hut on Inba marsh, located in current day northeastern Chiba Prefecture on the Shimōsa Plateau about 50 km northeast of Tokyo and about 15 km west of Narita Airport.
<br><br>"The series Nihon fūkei hanga (Japan Scenery Prints) consisted of ten sets of prints, with each set composed of five small landscapes and a cover print giving the name of the series, the name and number of the set, and the name of the artist. In addition, each set was accompanied by a table of contents and colophon sheet. Specific publication dates ranging from January 1917 through April 1920 indicate that each set was issued separately.  As Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958) designed the majority of prints in the series, it seems likely that Hakutei was the spearhead for the project. The artists asked Igami Bonkutsu to carve the blocks and Nakajima Jūtarō to publish the series." - Source: Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 274-276.
<br>In addition to Ishii Hakutei (1182-1958), the other artists who contributed to the series were Sakamoto Hanjirō (1882-1969), see this collection's print Sea of Fire, IHL.0862 and Chikugo River, IHL.2068, Hirafuku Hyakusui (1877-1933), Morita Tsunetomo (1881-1933), Kosugi Misei (1881-1964) and Ishii Tsuruzō (1887-1973), elder brother of Hakutei.

title: Daido Bay (Daidokō 大同江)
creator: Ishii Hakutei 石井柏亭 (1882-1958)

title: Tug of War (つなひき Tsuna hiki)
creator: Ikeda Shūzō 池田修三 (1922-2004)
description: A smaller version, measuring 3 3/4 x 5 7/8 in. (9.4 x 14.9 cm), of a larger 1964 print by the artist, measuring 11.25 x 18.25 in. (28.6 x 46.4 cm), picturing two groups of school children at a game of tug of war. Ikeda Shūzō's best known works are those featuring children, although his later works included landscapes.

title: Iwai Kumesaburō III, Ichikawa Ebizō V and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII in a scene from Koi goromo karigane zome (三代目 岩井粂三郎、五代目 市川海老蔵、八代目 市川団十郎・恋衣雁金染)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description:
The actors (right to left) Iwai Kumesaburō III as the Courtesan (Keisei) Iwasaki, Ichikawa Ebizō V as Bizen'ya Jūbei (びぜんや) and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII as Yamakawaya Gonroku (山川屋権六 ) in a scene from the Kabuki play Koi goromo Karigane zome (恋衣雁金染), staged at the Kawarazaki theater during the first month of 1852.
<br>THE PLAY KOI GOROMO KARIGANE ZOME
<br>The play Koi goromo Karigane zome, written by playwright Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), is based on the story Five Men of Naniwa, about five real-life outlaws who prayed on the residents of Osaka at the turn of the eighteenth century and who were eventually tried and executed in 1702.
<br>While a number of kabuki plays had previously used the Five Men of Naniwa as the basis for their script, Koi goromo Karigane zome "added captivating new twists to the way events unfolded" and left audiences gasping as the five outlaws were executed for killing the samurai Noda Kakuzaemon. In a twist from the real story, the five outlaws are seen as heroes for killing the evil Noda and their punishment is portrayed as an injustice visited upon them by the authorities. - Source: The Merchant's Capital of Early Modern Japan, James L. MacClain and Wakita Osamu, Cornell University Press, 1999, p. 145.

title: The characters Shimanuki Yoso, Akama Genzaemon and Otomi in a scene from Hana to mimasu yayoi no hatsuyaku ((島ぬけ与三、赤間源左衛門、愛妾おとみ・ 花覣宿初役)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description: The actors (right to left) Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII in the role of Shimanuki Yoso, Seki Sanjūrō III in the role of Akama Genzaemon and Onoe Baikō IV in the role of the prostitute Otomi 愛妾おとみ.<br>While only the actor's roles are provided on the print (within the orange cartouches) the website of the Tokyo Metropolitan Library provides the actor's names. The scene pictured in the print was likely from the play titled "Hanato mimasu yayoi no hatsuyaku", which was part of a program of three pieces staged in the third lunar month of 1853 at Edo's Nakamura theater. The signpost in the right panel reads on its right side 大当り／＼, or "big hit, big hit!", and on its left the name of play is posted, 武覣熊ヶ谷領 (Hanato mimasu yayoi no hatsuyaku).

title:
The actors Ōtani Tomoemon IV, Bandō Shuka I, Nakayama Bungorō II, Bandō Kichiya and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII
(in the play Akegarasu Hana no Nureginu)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description:
The actors (right to left) Ōtani Tomoemon IV in the role of Yamanaya Shirōbei, Bandō Shuka I in the role of the courtesan Yamanaya Urazato, Nakayama Bungorō II in the role Yaritenokaya, Bandō Kichiya in the role of Katsumi and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII in the role of Kasugaya Tokijirō in the Kabuki play Akegarasu Hana no Nureginu [明烏花濡衣], staged at the Ichimura theater in Edo during the second month of 1851.<br>

Play Synopsis: Urazato, a courtesan of the Yamana-ya, and her lover, Tokijirō, are the parents of Midori, a child maidservant at the brothel. Since a courtesan’s having a permanent lover is considered an obstacle to the business operations of the Yamana-ya, an attempt is made to separate the pair. One snowy day an employee of the brothel discovers Urazato engaged in a secret rendezvous with Tokijirō. The latter is driven away, and the courtesan is tied to a pine tree in the garden and beaten. Urazato bemoans her ills for a time and weeps. However, Tokijirō steals over the fence and rescues her; the lovers escape with Midori on her father’s back. - Source:  Kabuki Encyclopedia, An English-Language Adaption of Kabuki Jiten, Samuel L. Leiter, Greenwood Press, 1979, p. 12-13.

title: Onoe Kikugorō as Kashiwabara Koheita, Ichikawa Danjūrō as Tokugawa Ieyasu and Ichikawa Sadanji as Kakuya Shichirō in the play Matsu no sakae Chiyoda no shintoku (柏原小平太 尾上菊五郎、徳川家泰公 市川団十郎、 角屋七郎次 市川左団次 ・  松栄千代田神徳)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The three greatest actors of the time (from right to left) Onoe Kikugorō V, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX and Ichikawa Sadanji I in the play Matsu no sakae Chiyoda no shintoku, written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1892) and staged at the Shintomi-za in June 1878. The play, which portrayed the life of first Tokugawa shogun, Tokugawa Ieyasu, was the first commercial production in the Shintomi-za and ran for forty-two days, attracting a total of 49,000 theater goers.

title: Evening Sky at Suwa Shrine, Nippori (日暮里 諏方神社 Yūzora, Nippori Suwa jinja)
creator: Kasamatsu Shirō 笠松紫浪 (1898–1991)
description: A later edition of the original 1932 print depicting the torii leading to Suwa Shrine (諏方神社 Suwa jinja) in the Nippori district of Tokyo. The sunset glow backlights this scene and a lone figure, a woman, perhaps with a baby on her back, is seen heading towards a shrine building.

title: Yotsuya Araki Yokochō (四ツ谷荒木横町)
creator: Tsuchiya Kōitsu 土屋光逸 (1870-1949)
description: One of Kōitsu's most popular designs, reprinted many times by the publisher since its original printing in January 1935. This collection's print is a posthumous edition, likely printed between 1981 and 1995. The artist presents us with two geisha bathed in the light of a teahouse in the early evening. Kōitsu's marvelous handling of light is evident in this print.

title: Nezu Shrine (根津神社)
creator: Tsuchiya Kōitsu 土屋光逸 (1870-1949)
description:
As falling snow covers the ground, a lone woman leaves only the impression of her footsteps at Nezu Shrine, one of the oldest Shinto shrines in Tokyo, established in 1705 when the 5th shogun Tsunayoshi relocated it from Sendagi to Nezu to commemorate the adoption of Ienobu as his successor. Susanoo no Mikoto is the shrine's the guardian deity. 
<br>Originally released in December 1934, this collection's print lacks any publisher seals making its likely printing date sometime between 1960 and the early 1990s. There is at least one other state of this print.

title: Tempura Chef
creator: Mori Yoshitoshi 森義利 (1898-1992)
description: One of Mori's kappizuri-e (stencil prints) depicting craftsmen at work. In this case it's a tempura chef. This print which is unsigned and uneditioned, was also issued in a numbered edition of one hundred.

title: Ships at Night (untitled)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
An unusual subject for Kōgyo. The print exists in several color variations, two of which are in this collection. Print IHL.1193 is the darkest of the color variations. It carries the "Toshihisa" seal of the artist, while other impressions of this print, including this collection's IHL.1716, do not.<br>
"In this composition, a fire in the distance illuminates the sky and creates an effective backdrop to the three moored boats." - Source: The Beauty of Silence: Nō and Nature Prints by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927), Robert Schaap & J. Thomas Rimer, Hotei Publishing, 2010, p. 151.

title: The Sakawa River and Mount Fuji  (酒匂川と富士)
creator: Jōkata Kaiseki 定方塊石 (1882-1966)
description:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print, Fuji rises in the background as the Sakawagawa meanders between the hills and transmission lines. The stone marker in the left foreground reads "the border of Kanagawa and Shizuoka Prefectures" 神奈川縣 静岡縣 界. The foreground shows us the edge of a traditional looking village with electrical and telephone transmission lines punctuating the landscape. This combining of the traditional with the modern is one of hallmarks of this series.
<br>The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

title: A View at the Western Suburb of the Metropolis - Rainy Season (望首都西郊・梅雨 Bo-shuto seikō・baiu)
creator: Yoshida Chizuko 吉田千鶴子 (1924-2017)
description:
Published by the Japan Print Association (Nihon Hanga Kyokai) as part of the series One Hundred Views of Tokyo, Message to the 21st Century, the JPA began the series in 1989, commissioning 100 artists over a ten year period to create their impressions of Tokyo. In 2000, the JPA compiled the prints by all 100 artists into ten volumes. In the preface to the series, the JPA notes that the "Tokyo Hyakkei series will serve as 'a witness of time' by the artists and will consist of one hundred views by print by one hundred artists, which ultimately will take ten years in all [and] will present the changing international megalopolis Tokyo. . . . We are confident that [it] will achieve artistic and historical significance. . . ."<br>
Commenting on the print, in which Yoshida employs both photolithography and wood block technique, she states, "Early on, the Tocho (Tokyo Metropolitan Office) was dismissed as an utter waste of tax money. But now, its 45th floor observatory seems to be popular among visitors. I have been on more than one date to that floor with my husband, Hodaka. There, on clear days, the town where I live can be seen beyond Tokyo's western suburbs of Nakano and Suginami. But because of haze, the view is often obstructed. Though most days are covered with this haze, the viewer can still readily see that Tokyo's western suburbs are packed with large and small buildings, apartments and houses. If an earthquake occurs, it is expected that this area will suffer the greatest damage."

title: Outskirts of Nara (奈良郊外 Nara Kōgai)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description: A view of the rice fields next to Hokki-ji Temple in Ikaruga on the outskirts of Nara. Hokki-ji, a three-storied pagoda, the oldest of its kind in Japan, can be seen in the background. The reflections of the two figures on the right is seen in the flooded paddy. It seems as though Sekino has captured this scene on a moonlit night.

title: The characters Yokosone Heikurō, Shimobe wataru sanpeiI, Gengō Unoki and Yokosone Heitaro in the play Ume yanagi sakigake zōshi (横曽根平九郎、下部弥三平、言号卯の木言号卯の木、横曽根平太郎 ・梅柳魁双紙)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description: While only the actor's roles are provided on the print (within the orange cartouches) the website of the Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum of Waseda University provides the actor's names and the title of the play. The actors (right to left) are Nakamura Nakasuke II in the role of Yokosone Heikurō, Nakamura Fukusuke in the roll of Shimobe wataru sanpei, Nakamura Tomijūrō II in the role of Gengō Unoki and Ichikawa Danjūrō VIII as Yokosone Heitaro in the play Umeyanagi sakigake zōshi 梅柳魁双紙, staged at the Ichimura theater in Edo during the third lunar month of 1854.

title: Fishing Harbor at Noon (昼の漁港)
creator: Okubo Yutaka 大久保担 (1924-2008)
description: One of the artist's many prints picturing small boats along the shore. This print carries the number 4 on its verso, which may indicate that the print is part of an untitled series. See IHL.1476 and IHL.1099 for two other similar prints by the artist.

title: Sakanoshita  (坂ノ下)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
Depicting the 48th of 53 stations along the Tōkaidō Road, which connected Edo (modern day Tokyo) where the shōgun resided, to Kyoto, where the emperor resided, the artist shows us two monks seated before a high ranking samurai. Off to the left we see the distinctive Mount Fudesute, which derives its odd name from an incident in which the celebrated artist Kano Motonobu [1476-1553] threw away (sute) his brushes (fude) when he could not capture the beauty of the mountain in a painting. Perhaps the monks are trying to succeed where Motonobu failed.
<br>One of two series of chūban-size vertical prints designed by the artist, a disciple of Hiroshige I, depicting the stations along the Tōkaidō. This series, titled simply Tōkaidō Road (東海道), was published by Tsutaya Kichizō (the same publisher who published Utagawa Hiroshige I's famous "Vertical Tōkaidō" series) between the 8th month of 1863 and the 12th month of 1867, a period of over three years. It is not known why the publishing period was so extended for these prints. Hiroshige II's other series, titled Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (東海道五拾三駅), was issued by the publisher Maruya Tetsujirō in the 10th month of 1865.

title: Yokkaichi (四日市)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:

The artist presents us with a daimyō and his retainers on the coast near Yokkaichi.  One of his retainers looks out to sea with a telescope and we are shown a veiled scene of a distant land.

title: Hiratsuka (平塚)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:

In the equivalent print of the same place by his master Hiroshige I the scene itself is almost identical, with the round-topped Mount Kōrai dominating the middle-ground, and the snow-capped iconic Mount Fuji just peeping into view behind it." - Source: Comments of Associate Professor Alison Tokita, Monash University on the Monash University website

creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)

title: Horses (馬 Ume)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)

title: Horses in Pasture (Uma sandai 馬三代)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)

title: Imamiya Street, Chōshi, at Dusk (薄暮・銚子町今宮通にて Hakubo・Chōshi machi Imamiyadōri nite)
creator: Ishiwata Kōitsu 石渡江逸 (1897-1987)
description: "This print maintains Koitsu Ishiwata's reputation gained for depicting life in Tokyo and Yokohama's streets. Choshi is a port city in the subprefecture Chiba of Tokyo and is a developing tourist destination as well as a home to many industries in Chiba. This print is a characteristic Koitsu scene at dusk in a neighborhood. The depiction of night, darkness, mist and rain became more prominent after the Meiji era because the European influence taught Japanese artists how better to construct space, depth and shadow in darker conditions. This is one of Koitsu's most well known works and is even today in high demand amongst collectors all over the world." - Source: website of the University of Alberta Art Collection https://search.museums.ualberta.ca/11-15855 [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Rainy Night at Shinobazu Pond (夜雨 不忍池 Yoru ame, Shinobazunoeki)
creator: Kasamatsu Shirō 笠松紫浪 (1898–1991)
description: A solitary figure walks toward Benten Temple under a steady rain. This print was issued in two color schemes, a more common purple-hued tint (see IHL.0019) and a greyish-hued tint as seen here. Both color schemes were first issued in 1938, as both can be found with the Watanabe type-E publishing seal used by the publisher between 1931 and 1941. This print is likely a first edition based upon the presence of the publisher's "E-type" seal in the lower right margin.

title: Portrait of Kido Takayoshi with a transcript of the biographical sketch of Lord Kido Takayoshi from the Day-by-Day News (木戸孝允公略傳日々新聞ヨリ録 Kido Takayoshi-kōryakuden Nichi Nichi Shinbun yori shō)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description: A memorial portrait of the Meiji statesman Kido Takayoshi 木戸孝允 (1883-May 26, 1877), better known as Kido Kōin 木戸孝磯, published nine months after his death by Tokyo publisher Matsuki Heikichi.  The print's scroll contains a short biography of Kido taken from the Tokyo newspaper Nichi nichi Shimbun.<br> This print is most notable for its reproducing, using both traditional and experimental woodblock techniques, the 1872 photo of Kido taken in London. Both the artist Kiyochika Kobayashi (1847-1915) and the publisher were known for their experimentation, and in this print a cross hatching (or net pattern) is used to simulate the wood engraving process that was used for mass reproduction of photographs in the days before half-tone reproduction was invented.

title: The Lament of the Lord appearing in The Ladies' Graphic, Volume 1, Number 3 (おん主の嘆き・婦人グラフ 第1巻第3号 Onnushi no nageki・Fujin gahō)
creator: Fukiya Kōji 蕗谷虹児 (1898-1979)
description: Fukiya, a painter, illustrator and poet, was strongly influenced by Takehisa Yumeji who he was introduced to in 1920 and through whose contacts he would become an illustrator for the magazine The Ladies' Graphic.

title: Takino River, Ōji (王子 滝の川 Ōji Takinogawa)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)

title: Oharame - Carrying Kindling (小原女)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Tokuriki depicts an Oharame (woman of Ohara) carrying a load of kindling on her head. For generations, the women known as Ohara-me, living in the villages of Yase and Ohara at the the foot of Mt. Hiei located in the north of Kyoto, sold bundles of kindling, flowers and charcoal in Kyoto. Today, the tradition continues as a tourist attraction. Their distinctive traditional dress consists of an indigo blue kosode, white underwear, a red and white thin obi belt, a pair of white tekko protectors, a pair of habaki leg protectors, an apron and waraji straw sandals. Her head is covered with a white tenugui towel. Also see IHL.1213 Oharame (seated).

title: Oharame - Seated (小原女)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Tokuriki depicts an Oharame (woman of Ohara) at rest outside a teahouse, her bundle of kindling at her feet.  For generations, the women known as Ohara-me, living in the villages of Yase and Ohara at the the foot of Mt. title: Poppies from the book Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems (詞華集 日本の花・罌粟 Shikashū・Nihon no hana Nihon no Hana・keshi)
creator: Kawanishi Hide 川西英 (1894-1965)
description:
Poppies, a collotype print of an original woodcut by Kawanishi Hide (1894-1965), appears on p. 77 of the 1946 poetry and print book "Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems." It serves as an illustration for a poem of the same name by poet and professor Andō Ichirō (1907-1972).
<br>"Flowers of Japan: Anthology of Poems," was edited and designed by Onchi Kōshirō, a seminal artist in the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement and pioneering book designer. Contributing twelve prints and one poem, Onchi, along with poet Inoue Yasufumi 井上康文 (1897–1973), selected the book's thirty poems by poets such as Satō Haruo (1892-1964), Kitahara Hakushū (1885-1942), Noguchi Yonejirō (1875-1947), Kaoru Maruyama (1899-1974), Tatsuji Miyoshi (1900-1964), Ryuko Kawaji (1888-1959) and Andō Ichirō (1907-1972). 
<br>When this book was published in May 1946 "much of the country, including Tokyo where it was printed, remained in ruins following the previous year’s aerial bombardments. . . . Nihon no hana demonstrated the sophisticated aesthetic sensibility of the Japanese people, while providing a hopeful image for the future rebuilding—or 're-flowering'—of the country and its people." - Source: Commentary by Alicia Volk, https://pulverer.si.edu/node/462/title/1 [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Act VII -The Ichiriki Teahouse (七段目 Nanadanme)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description: One of twelve prints from the series titled Pictorial Siblings to The Treasury of Royal Retainers.  The circular inset on this print depicts the actual scene from act VII of the play Chūshingura (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) in which Rikiya, the son of Yuranosuke, goes to the garden of the Ichiriki teahouse where his father is pretending to live a life of debauchery while he plots revenge against Moronao. Rikiya hands his father a message from Lady Kaoya telling him of Moronao's whereabouts. In the parody of this scene portrayed in the print a wad of tissues are furtively passed to a courtesan by another courtesan, pointing to a night of wild love making.  The young courtesan kneeling by the bamboo fence bites down on her head scarf indicating the passion that the night holds.

title: Dampū 壇風 (The Holy Wind)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 19-21.) -  While in exile on the island of Sado, Mibu no Suketomo has been placed in charge of Homma no Saburō. He has now received a strict order from the authorities in Kamakura thatSuketomoe is to be executed immediately, but just before he dies he is able to say farewell to his son Umewaka who arrives from Kyōto with the priestS otsu.  Umewaka sees Homma as the cause of his father’s death and with the help of Sotsu, revenges his father by killing him.  When they go to escape from the island, however, the boatman refuses to put in to shore for them to board.  In answer to the priest’sprayers, a god from Kumano appears and causes a wind to blow the ship back.  He then give the boat a following wind so that they are able to escape from their pursuers and return to Kyōto.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Senju 千手
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 155-156) - Shigehara, brought to Kamakura after his capture at the battle of Ichi-no-tani, has been given into the charge of Kano-no-suke Munemochi until his fate is decided. To lighten the tedium of his captivity, Senju-no mae has been sent to comfort him. When she comes on this occasion it is to tell him that even his request to be allowed to enter the priesthood has been refused. Shigehira tells of his regret at having burned the Nara temples, but Senju-no-mae entertains him with song and dance, and Shigehira himself plays a piece on his lute. Dawn comes all too soon, however, and Shigehira is taken away to face his punishment in the capital.

title: Blockhead (木偶の坊 Dekunobō)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
This print is one of fifty prints from the first part of the three part series One Hundred Victories, One Hundred Laughs, which presented comic, often racist, parodies of the Chinese enemy. The text on the prints was written by Koppi Dōjin (Master, Skin and Bones), a pseudonym used by the newspaper writer Nishimori Takeki (1861–1913).<br> 
"This print with the title 'pinhead' shows a wooden doll, which looks like a Chinese official. It is modeled on the military commander-in-chief of the Chinese Empire, Li Hongzhang. Next to the doll with the destroyed mouth, a Japanese soldier is also depicted. In the last line, it says 'it's a shame about the mouth', thus, the doll with the destroyed mouth points at the unfortunate loss of Port Arthur. Instead of the port of Port Arthur, the mouth of Port Arthur is mentioned again and again, this is a play with homonyms." - Source: University of Vienna website https://ukiyo-e.univie.ac.at/en/fullview.html?lang=e&docid=941 [accessed 8-17-23]

description: Issued as a promotion for the play Hototogisu Date no kikigaki staged at Tokyo's Shintomi theater in June 1876, this print features, from left to right, Bandō Hikosaburō V 坂東彦三郎 as Harada Kai 原田甲斐, Sawamura Tosshō  II 沢村訥升 as Itakura Naizen 板倉内膳正,  Ichikawa Sadanji I 市川左団次 as Date Aki 伊達安芸 and Onoe Kikugorō V 尾上菊五郎 as Kaminami Sanzaemon 神並三左衛門. The play, written in 1876 by By Kawatake Mokuami 河竹默阿彌 (1816-1893), tells the story of Harada Kai, a Date vassal, and his confederates who are plotting to usurp the power and position of the young leader of the clan, Kamechiyo.

title: Illustration of Garden Cockfight (庭前闘鶏之圖)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: Young samurai, supervised by an elder, watch the beginning of a cockfight in a garden. This print is a 1898 reissue of an 1884 woodblock print of a painting made by Chikanobu for the government sponsored Second Painting Competitive Exhibition, held in April 1884. After the original painting was awarded a bronze prize and then purchased by the Imperial Household Agency, the publisher Morimoto Junzaburō (firm name Entaidō) issued a woodblock print reproduction of the painting in response to public demand.<br>When this collection's print was reissued fourteen years after the original print, the publisher changed the title, removed explanatory text from the left panel, removed the artist's seal below his signature and changed many of the colors used for the samurai's robes. It is not known why the publisher decided to re-issue this print in 1898.

Whether Chikanobu was presenting the viewer with an imagined scene or if these ladies were part of the retinue of the Empress during her and the Emperor's special visit to the exhibition, is unknown.

title: Telegraphic Record of the Russo-Japanese War: Manchurian Mounted Bandits Destroy Railroad (日露戦争電報実記・馬賊満州鉄道ヲ破壊ス Nichiro sensō denpōjikki・Bazoku Manshūtetsudōo hakai su)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)
description: The Trans Siberian Railway gave Russia a huge advantage in the war, allowing Russia to send reinforcements to the war zone in a very short time. In retaliation, Japan engaged honghuzi (Manchurian bandits) to destroy the railway, as illustrated in this print.<br>During the decade earlier Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895), the honghuzi often attacked the Japanese. (See IHL.0081 Foreign-looking Manchurian Horsemen on an Expedition to Observe the Japanese Camp in the Distance Near Sauhoku.) During the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905), "Japanese adventurers backed by the Imperial Army contacted such gangs and led them on harassing missions behind the Russian lines, blowing up bridges and destroying railway lines in the name of the 'Righteous Army of Manchuria' (Manshū gigun).” - Source: Bandits in Republican China, Phil Billingsley, Stanford University Press, 1988, p. 216.

title: Iwai Hanshirō VIII, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX and Bandō Kakitsu in the play Jiraiya gōketsu monogatari (岩井半四郎 (八代目)、市川団十郎 (九代目)、坂東家橘・児雷也豪傑物語)
creator: Morikawa Chikashige 守川周重 (active 1869-January 1882)
description:
The actors Iwai Hanshirō VIII in the role of the princess Tagoto hime 田毎姫; Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 in the role of Jiraiya 田毎姫 and Bandō Kakitsu 坂東 家橘 in the role of Takasago Yūminosuke 高砂勇美之助 in the play Jiraiya gōketsu monogatari 児雷也豪傑物語 ( (The Heroic Tales of Jiraiya), performed at the Shintomi-za 新富 theater, Tokyo, in August 1881.
<br>The play Jiraiya gōketsu monogatari is drawn from an episodic illustrated novel published in multiple volumes from 1839 to 1868. The play, written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), was first performed in July 1852 at the Kawarazaki-za in Edo.
<br>As an infant, Jiraiya’s noble family is slain by Tsukikage, lord of Echigo province and regent of the shogun who has been led astray by his adopted son Orochimaru. Tsukikage adopted Orochimaru after being saved by him from an attack by a giant snake. However, Orochimaru is possessed with the evil snake spirit and eventually kills Tsukikage and comes to rule Echigo.  Jiraiya, who along with Tsunate-hime princess of another noble family killed by Tsukikage, has been saved from death by a mountain hermit who teaches them both magic – toad magic in the case of Jiraiya and slug magic in the case of Tsunate-hime.   They both vow to take revenge upon Orochimaru. Capturing a magical sword they attack Orochimaru, who attempts suicide but is saved by Takasago Yūminosuke, a high ranking officer for the shogun. Yūminosuke wants to visit a harsh punishment on Orochimaru for his evil deeds, but Jiraiya and Tsunate-hime tell him that Orochimaru’s evil spirit has now been exorcised by the sword. Orochimaru departs in peace.<br>
The character princess Tagoto is the unwilling object of Orochimaru’s affection, who wants her for his wife. - Source: website of the Japan Arts Council  http://www2.ntj.jac.go.jp/unesco/kabuki/en/5/5_04_10.html [page no longer accessible 8-17-23]

title: Mera Cape, Izu (妻良岬、 伊豆 Mera-misaki、Izu)

description: A view of Mera Cape on the Izu Peninsula in Shizuoka Prefecture. The time of day is either sunrise or sunset and small fishing boats are on the bay. The rectangular flat object next on the far right of the print may be one of the artificial reefs built to protect the harbor. Hiratsuka was most interested in portraying the essence of objects rather than realistic renderings and he often used the color yellow for both the sea and sky in his color landscapes of the 1920s and 30s.

title: Snow Torture scene from The Pine Tree to which a Colt is Bound on Skylark Mountain (雲雀山駒絆松樹｜雪責)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
Starring Kataoka Gadō III (R), Nakamura Fukusuke IV (C) and Iwai Matsunosuke (L) <br>
"Reminiscent of tales like Cinderella and Snow White, this play partially retold the 8th century legend of Princess Chūjō (center), daughter of a widowed nobleman whose power-hungry new wife (right) plots against her stepdaughter. The stepmother arranges for a cherished object to be hidden in the princess’s quarters, framing her for theft. When it is discovered there, she insists on punishment, ordering her servants to beat Princess Chūjō outside in the snow. That famous scene, depicted here, involves a former maid (left) fired by the stepmother for her fondness of the princess, entering the garden and preparing to toss her straw cloak to the girl. This act of kindness enrages the stepmother who moves to strike the girl with her long tobacco pipe. As the plot unfolds, other servants enter the fray, and the princess falls to the ground, feigning death. Her father appears, remorseful of his wife’s cruelty, and asks the loyal servants to carry the seemingly lifeless Chūjō to Mount Hibari for burial. Instead, they take her to a cottage in the mountains where Chūjō is eventually reunited with her father. The play was a tour-de-force for three male actors of women’s roles, onnagata." - Source: Didactics by Lynn Katsumoto for the exhibition "Ukiyo-e to Shin Hanga: Changing Tastes in Japanese Woodblock Prints" (Portland Japanese Garden, November 20, 2021 - January 30, 2022)

title: Serving Spiced Rice Wine (お流れ Onagare)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
This print is from a series of 40 scenes, published 1895-1896, documenting life inside the women quarters of the shogun's palace in Edo, prior to the Meiji Restoration in 1868. "On the first morning of the new year, a special spiced wine (otosu) is drunk before breakfast and thought to bring good health throughout the coming year. Usually the youngest member of the family or group is served first, and in Chikanobu's print, a young woman raises a red lacquered wine cup to receive the invigorating brew from Inner Palace matron (jōrō toshiyori), while older women solemnly wait their turn in the background. The beverage is made by steeping overnight various flowers, herbs and roots in sweet rice wine (mirin). The two folding screens are painted with pine, bamboo, and plum branches (shōchikubai), the traditional evergreens and early blossoms associated with the new year."[1]
<br><br>THE INNER PRECINCTS OF CHIYODA<br>
 "Chikanobu imagines something he never saw—the inner precincts of Edo Castle, which housed the shogun’s mother, wife, and concubines. The area was off limits to all men other than the shogun himself or his young male heir."[2] "The Chiyoda Inner Palace (Chiyoda no Ōoku) series of 1895-1896, together with his 1897 series Chiyoda Outer Palace (Chiyoda no on-omote) provided detailed depictions of life in and around Edo Castle before the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the Chiyoda Inner Palace set, Chikanobu documented various annual ceremonies in the women’s quarters, especially those at New Year’s, and seasonal activities, particularly those conducted in the palace gardens. While Chikanobu did not indicate specific events or name certain people that would link these images to a single date or time period, the scenes give an overall impression of what the shogun’s private quarters might have looked like in the mid-19th century. "Most women depicted in Chiyoda Inner Palace are portrayed as elegant dignified ideal feminine figures, showing little emotion or excitement. No one seems happy or sad, ebullient or upset. In fact, these imaginary depictions suggest a realm of tranquil harmony, without conflict or illness. Only two old women are shown, and most of the more than 150 featured figures are youthful looking, appearing to be in their 20’s or early 30’s. A few girls are present, but even they are well behaved; no babies or pregnant women are evident. There is a sense of tension among the women, though, as ritual gestures and prescribed ceremonies are carried out with great seriousness. Although some settings are animated by secondary figures (servants, actors, parade participants, etc.) or pet animals, overall the quiet rhythm of life in the Chiyoda Inner Palace is predominant and well described."[3] 

<br><br> [1] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 172.
<br>[2] Portland Art Museum http://portlandartmuseum.us/mwebcgi/mweb.exe?request=record;id=46772;type=101 [accessed 8-30-23] 
<br>[3] Chikanobu – Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p. 169.

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Musashibō Benkei in the play Kanjinchō (九世市川団十郎 武蔵坊弁慶・勧進帳)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the lower left panel, playing the role of the warrior priest Benkei in the kabuki play Kanjinchō (The Subscription List). Above his likeness is an unidentified actor in the role of Togashi 冨樫. 
<br>"Ichikawa Danjūrō VII created this play which he based on a Nō play called 'Ataka.' It was first performed in 1840. Minamoto Yoshitsune is with his followers and his most faithful retainer Benkei, fleeing from the soldier of his nasty and insecure brother, Yoritomo. He has to pass through the Ataka barrier to reach the northern part of Japan. Togashi who was warned by Yoritomo that Yoshitsune and his party would try to get through disguised as mountain priest is immediately suspicious when they arrive. Benkei announces that they are collecting money for the restoration of the Tōdai Temple in Nara but Togashi argues that if they were real priests they would have a subscription list. Benkei immediately produces one and skillfully 'reads' it. Admiring his loyalty and presence of mind Togashi decides at this moment to let them pass through. He is by now enjoying their act and even offers to contribute to their fund. They are allowed to leave but then a guard warns Togashi that one of the priests looks like Yoshitsune. Togashi cannot ignore this and probably hopes that Benkei will save the situation. Benkei initially feebly argues that it is possible for people to look like others but then out of sheer despair strikes Yoshitsune with a wooden stick. In the end Benkei, who was treated to food and drink and performed a dance for Togashi leaves on the hanamichi quietly thanking him since he knows that Togashi will have to commit suicide."[1]
<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
<br>"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series." - Source: website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

<br><br>[1] Kabuki Eighteen Traditional Dramas, Kawatake Toshio, Chronicle Books, 1985, p. 14.
<br>[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

title: Seven Variations in a Kyōka Contest in the Bunsei Era (文政狂歌合七變化)
creator: Unknown
description:
A print designed by an unknown artist signing his name 魁州 which can be read as "Kaishū". The artist presents us with a strange assortment of Bunsei Era (1818-1830) characters engaged in writing comic tanka (kyōka) as part of a poetry contest with the theme of sake. From right to left we see a farmer, a calligrapher, the Thunder God, a child, the poet Hitomaru (one of the Thirty-Six Immortal Poets), an apprentice geisha and a samurai carrying a long sword over which is slung a tsunodaru used for transporting sake.<br>
The print references the Go Gawa (五側) poetry club, active during the Bunsei Era.  Members of the club often wrote poetry on illustrated surimono, and signed their work with the Go Gawa symbol, an hourglass resembling the number five. The Go Gawa symbol appears on the sake bottles in the center panel and on the object in the farmer's left hand.

title: Kabuki Playbill for Plays at the Initial Opening of the Imperial Theater: Yoritomo, Igagoe and Hagoromo (辻番付 帝国劇場初開場番付・頼朝、伊賀越、羽衣)
creator: Torii Kiyotada VII (七代目) 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
The playbill (tsuji banzuke) from the opening performances in March 1911 at the new Imperial Theater (Teikoku gekijō). The three plays illustrated are (from right to left) Yoritomo 頼朝, Igagoe 伊賀越 and Hagoromo 羽衣. In addition to the names of the play given in the illustrations, they appear again with details of their various scenes in the rectangular box at the bottom of the print, along with the names of the cast members and their roles, and the theater name written in kanteiryū, a special calligraphy used in the Kabuki theater. Among the many cast members are the three leading actors of the Imperial Theater's in-house troupe, Onoe Baikō (尾上梅幸) VI, Ichikawa Komazō (市川高麗蔵) VIII and Sawamura Sōjūrō (沢村宗十郎) VII.<br>
The paper used for this playbill appears to be dusted with mica.

title: Illustrations of Noh, Index, volume 1 (能楽図絵 前編  目録 Mokuroku, zenpen)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
The first of five Table of Content prints (mokuroku)  from the series Nōgakuzue (Illustrations of Noh).<br><br>
Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

title: Index, The Kabuki Eighteen (歌舞伎十八番・目録)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
The title page and index (mokuroku 目録) for the series The Kabuki Eighteen.
<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. The eighteen plays are 不破 (Fuwa), 矢の根 (Yanone), 鳴神 (Narukami), 関羽 (Kan'u), 不動 (Fūdō), 七ツ面　(Nanatsumen), 嫐 (Uwanari), 毛抜 (Kenuki), 押戻し (Oshimodoshi), 景清 (Kagekiyo), 象引 (Zohiki), 鎌髭 (Kamahige), 助六 (Sukeroku), 解脱 (Gedatsu), 暫 (Shibaraku), 蛇柳 (Jayanagi), 外郎 (Uirō Uri) and 勧進帳 (Kanjinchō). In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
<br> "This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[1]
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

title: Nakamura Shikan, Sukedakaya Takasuki, Ichikawa Danjūrō and Bandō Kakitsu in the play Sukeroku, Flower of Edo (中村芝翫、助高屋高助、市川団十郎、坂東家橘・助六由縁江戸桜)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: "A new Tokyo theater wecomed Meiji audiences with an updated version of the classic blockbuster about Sukeroku, the samurai-turned-street-fighter (otokodate) who stands up for the little guy, played by Ichikawa Danjūrō IX. He appears, left, with his characteristic purple head wrap, beside his brother, played by Bandō Kakitsu. In the center is the courtesan Agemaki, played by Sukedakaya Takasuke IV, Skukeroku's lover, garbed in magnificence, all of them fending off the evil Ikyū played by Nakamura Shikan IV, who bears the sword that was stolen from Sukeroku." - Source: wallcard from the exhibition "Kabuki: A Revolution in Color and Design," Portland Japanese Garden, July 29-September 3, 2017.

title: The Morning East Wind Clearing the Clouds of the Southwest (西南雲晴朝東風 Okige no kumo harau asa kochi)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: From right to left, the actors Iwai Hanshirō VIII 岩井半四郎 as Aki the mistress of Kishino Toshiaki 岸野の妾おあき (the mistress of Kirino Toshiaki in real life); Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 as Saijō Takamori 西條高盛 (Saigō Takamori in real life) and Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 as Hyakushō Sakuzō 百姓作蔵 in the play Okige no kumo harau asagochi (The Morning East Wind Clearing the Clouds of the Southwest), written by Kawatake Mokuami (1816-1893), produced by Morita Kanya (1846-1897) and performed at Morita's Shitomi Theater beginning in February 1878. The background text is dialogue between Danjūrō's character and Sadanji's character. The play dramatized the recently ended Satsuma Rebellion which pitted rebellious samurai mainly from the Southwest (Satsuma and Chōshū provinces) under the leadership of Saigō Takamori against the vastly superior forces of the new Meiji government. The use of contemporary subject matter, the graphic depiction of the battle scenes (which used fireworks onstage), and the popular sympathy for the defeated hero Saigō Takamori all contributed to the enormous success of the play which ran for eighty days.

title: Bronze Statue of Saigō in Ueno Park (上野 公園 西郷銅像 Ueno Kōen Saigō dōzō)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description:
A spring day in Ueno Park with the cherry trees in bloom and strollers lingering by the recently erected bronze statue of Saigō Takamori, a leader in both the 1867 Meiji Reformation that overthrew the shogun, restoring the emperor and bringing a modern government into power, and the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion which sought to overthrow that same government.<br>
Sitting on a rise near the main entrance to the park, the statue was designed by Takamura Kōun (1852-1934) and unveiled on December 18, 1898. Oriented so that it faces Edo Palace, it promotes Saigō in his earlier role as the hero of the Restoration who led the imperial army in its takeover of Edo Castle, not as the disgruntled leader of samurai interests who had been forsaken by the Tokyo regime. The statue pictures Saigō in informal attire with his dog and conjures the earlier military leader, diplomat and humanist who cherished slogan was 'Revere Heaven, love mankind' and whose spiritual and physical magnanimity earned him the epithet 'Saigo the Great' and the adoration of an entire nation.

title: Kinryūzan Kaminarimon (金竜山風雷門)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: Asakusa Kannon is the popular name of the temple more properly known as Kinryūzan Sensō-ji, dating back to 628. This print pictures the temple's Furai-mon (Wind and Thunder Gate) with its huge lantern reading 志ん橋 Shinbashi (an area in Edo whose constituents contributed funds for the lantern.) This print is marked 古 "old" in the upper right-hand margin, indicating it is a view from the past. It was originally issued as the top half of an ōban size sheet, with the bottom sheet showing a "present" view of the temple grounds. It is one of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, that make up the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present.

title: Yoroi Ferry at Koami-chō (よろひのわたし小阿ミ町  Yoroi no watashi Koamichō)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
This print and its companion print IHL.1290 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. Both prints are views within Nihonbashi, the most densely populated area of Tokyo. This print provides a past (古 old) view of the Yoroi Ferry, which carried passengers across the Nihonbashi canal to at Kabuto-chō to Koami-chō, Tokyo’s mercantile quarter of Nihonbashi, an area filled with warehouses stocked with rice, soy, and oil. It is matched with a present (今 now) view on print IHL.1290, depicting the Yoroi Bridge, built in 1873, that replaced the Yoroi Ferry. In the present view, a gentleman in modern Western-style dress carrying a walking stick is seen in the foreground. Interesting and confusing is how the Yoroi Bridge, built as a Western-style iron bridge, is depicted, showing no modern elements of steel construction.<br>
These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart. They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, that make up the series.

title: The Ebisuya and Hoteiya Dry-goods Store in Owari-chō (尾張町恵比寿や布袋屋呉ふく店 Owari-chō Ebisuya Hoteiya gofukuten)

title: Suruga-chō, Evening View of Mitsui Bank with Mt Fuji (猿る賀町三井銀行夕景の富士 Suruga-chō Mitsui ginkō yūkei no Fuji)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: Pictured is a present (今 now) view, c. 1893, of the Mitsui Exchange Bank building, its flag proudly flying, along Suruga-chō, a street famous for its views of Mt. Fuji and Edo Castle. This now view print was originally paired with an old (古) view print, printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart. The series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present consists of at least 32 past and present views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets.

title: Ōji Paper Company Viewed from Asukayama Park (飛鳥山公園地王子製紙会社 Asukayama kōenchi Ōji seishi kaisha)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: This print and its companion print IHL.1291 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. This print (IHL.1285) presents a present (今 "now") view of Asukayama Park where a group of men gaze out to the Ōji Paper Company founded in 1873 by the industrialist Shibusawa Eiichi (渋沢 栄一, 1840–1931). Its companion print (IHL.1291) presents an old (古) view of Asukayama Park, where women are playing kawarake-nage (throwing unglazed or sun-dried earthenware from a high place with prayers for warding off evil and enjoying watching them flying in the wind).<br>These past and present views were originally printed together as one oban-size sheet and later cut apart. They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut oban-size sheets, in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present. Many of the views are similar to those found in Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei).

title: From Science and Experience: Essential Medicines for Health (學理と經驗とにより・配劑せられたる衛生の要藥)
creator: Unknown
description:
A Taishō era (1912-1936) woodblock printed advertisement (hikifuda) for "medicines for health, based on science and experience." Displayed in the top center of the print is a trademark seemingly made up of the characters 井本 ("Imoto" or "Inomoto"), possibly the trademark of the manufacturer of the five medicines being advertised or a trademark associated with the named pharmacy 磯矢榮壽軒薬房 (possibly reading "Isoya Eijuken pharmacy") located in 伊賀玉瀧 (Tamataki Iga-shi), as printed in the top left corner within the image. The five medicines listed beneath the trademark are,
<br>ヘブリン丸 Heburingan (a cold medicine in pill form)
<br>ヒスミシト丸 (くだりとめ) (possibly an anti-diarrheal in pill form)
<br>五龍圎 (かんぐすり) (possibly a nerve medicine)
<br>胃痛散 (ぬびやりのく〓) (a stomach care powder, also known in Chinese as wèi tòng powder)
<br>腹痛丸 (〓らぐすり) (a stomach ache pill).
<br>In this print, a group of rugged boys are engaged in a strenuous physical activity, which is supplemented with dialogue between the boys. The boy wearing the shirt with the trademark stands his ground against the "frontal attack" of his opponents, while calling the two boys on the left "scaredy-cats." His opponents are in awe telling our boy hero, "your legs are like stone." An interesting choice of illustration to advertise the efficacy of the medicines being sold, cold and stomach medications, but consistent with the statement appearing in the left margin, "The effectiveness of a product depends on the individual's attention to personal health and quality of life." 
<br>Building brand and trust for patent medicines was important in an industry that competed not only with other patent medicine companies but with drug companies providing western and scientifically developed products. This collection's print contains the following assurances from the chief pharmacist 擔當薬製師:

<br>Each product is made from the finest raw materials.

<br>Each product is made to the highest standards of quality.

<br>Our products are the most effective and ready-to-use medicine available.

<br>The best medicines for health and to lose weight.

<br>I hope it will be the best medicine for you.

title: Kawarasaki Kunitarō as Ōkaru (河原崎国太郎 おかる)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: One of a series of prints highlighting individual actors in their roles in the July 1866 performance of the play Kanadehon Chūshingura (variously translated as The Treasury of Loyal Retainers or Revenge of the 47 Ronin or The Revenge of the 47 Loyal Samurai) at the Ichimura-za. This print features the actor Kawarazaki Kunitarō I ( 河原崎国太郎 1849-1867) in the role of Okaru おかる in Act VI of the play.

title: Angry Sumo Fan Demands Refund, No. 1050 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・千五拾號)
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞.  This print tells the story of an angry sumo fan, a Mr. Yamada, attending a sumo match near Hamamatsu station in Tōtōmi Province, who argues with the promoter about a refund of his ticket fee, as the rain has interfered with part of the wrestling match. At one point he jumps into the ring and tears down a curtain and creates quite a commotion. As we can see from the graphic, the promoter is in some pain from returning Mr. Yamada's fee.
<br>The writer for this print is identified as Tentendo Shujin, a pen name for the writer better known as Takabatake Ransen 高畠藍泉 (1838-1885). Takabatake Ransen was a gesaku writer and journalist who joined Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun shortly after its start in 1872 and often worked with the artist Yoshiiku.
<br>At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

title: Akasaka Temporary Place (Akasaka karikōkyo 赤坂仮皇居)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
This print and its companion print IHL.0605 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. This print provides a present (今 now), view in Akasaka, depicting the Akasaka Temporary Palace (Akasaka karikōkyo), which served as the chief imperial residence during the construction of the Tokyo Imperial Palace from 1873 to 1889 IHL.0605 shows a past (古 old), view in Akasaka, depicting a busy street on the Kinokuni slope where the Edo residences of the Kishū Tokugawa family were located.<br>
These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart. They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut oban-size sheets, in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present.

title: Yoroi Bridge at Kabuto-chō (よろひはし兜甼)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
This print and its companion print IHL.1280 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. Both prints are views within Nihonbashi, the most densely populated area of Tokyo. IHL.1280 provides a past (古 old), view of the Yoroi Ferry, which carried passengers across the Nihonbashi canal to at Kabuto-chō to Koami-chō, Tokyo’s mercantile quarter of Nihonbashi, an area filled with warehouses stocked with rice, soy, and oil. This print, IHL.1290, presents a present (今 now) view of the Yoroi Bridge, built in 1873, that replaced the Yoroi Ferry. In the present view, a gentleman in modern Western-style dress carrying a walking stick is seen in the foreground. Interesting and confusing is how the Yoroi Bridge, built as a Western-style iron bridge, is depicted, showing no modern elements of steel construction.<br>
These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart.  They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present.

title: Kawarake-nage at Asukayama Park (飛鳥山かわらけなげ Asukayama kawarake-nage)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: This print and its companion print IHL.1285 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. This print (IHL.1291) presents an old (古) view of Asukayama Park where women are playing kawarake-nage (throwing unglazed or sun-dried earthenware from a high place with prayers for warding off evil and enjoying watching them flying in the wind). Its companion print IHL.1285 is a present (今 "now") view in the same location but now rather than tossing pottery, a group of men at the park gaze out to the Ōji Paper Company founded in 1873 by the industrialist Shibusawa Eiichi 渋沢 栄一 (1840–1931).<br>These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart.  They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present.

title: First Theater District, Shintomi Theater (府下第一の劇場　新富座 Fukadaiichi no gekijō Shintomi-za)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: This print and its companion print IHL.1283 are a pair in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present which compares past and present views of well-known locations in Tokyo. This print (IHL.1292) presents a now (今) view of the Shintomi theater, the re-named Morita theater, established in 1875. Its companion print IHL.1283 presents an old (古) view of  Edo's theater district, giving us a view of the rooftops and banners announcing performances along Saruwaka Street as seen from one of the tea houses on the street.<br> These past and present views were originally printed together as one ōban-size sheet and later cut apart.  They are two of at least 32 views, contained on 16 uncut ōban-size sheets, in the series Famous Places of Tokyo: Past and Present.

creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description: One of three prints commissioned from the artist by Hotta Watchmakers (Hotta Corporation) to commemorate the 95th anniversary of their watch shop. (Also see IHL.2066.) The print was published in collaboration with the Kokugakai (National Picture Association).<br> Carved and printed by Kawakami, this print was printed on paper made by Ichibei Iwano VIII, a Living National Treasure (Preserver of Important Intangible Cultural Properties) of Japan.<br>Ryohei Hotta (1913-1989), ex-president of the Hotta Corporation, was a collector of timepiece ephemera who donated his collection, the "Hotta Collection", to the National Diet Library in 1987. Included in the collection is a privately printed 1971 catalog of colored woodblock prints on watches and calendars titled "Tokei to koyomi no nishikie mokuroku." For a second impression of this print see IHL.2056.
