title: Evacuees in the Suburbs of Tokyo (東京郊外の避難者 Tokyo kōgai no hinansha)
creator: Fukunaga Seihan 福永晴帆 (1884-1961)
description: A poignant scene of young children and their mothers camping on railroad tracks on the outskirts of Tokyo following the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. A single soldier stands guard as the moon rises. The quake was so violent that even the railroad tracks were bent by its force.

title: Tiger and Hare (寅卯)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actors Kawarazaki Sanshō 河原崎三升 in the role of Watōnai Sankan 和藤内三官 matched with the sign of the tiger 寅 and Nakamura Sōjūrō 中村宗十郎 in the role of Kawarazaki mimasu Ashigarayama no yamauba 足柄山のやまうば, matched with the sign of the hare 卯.

title: Torioibune 鳥追舟 (Bird-Chasing Boat)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: The Wisdom of Gassendi (ガセンヂの智)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: In this later edition print issued separately from its original textbook, Yoshitoshi portrays the French astronomer, mathematician, philosopher and priest Pierre Gassendi (1592-1655) as a child proving to his friends that the moon remains stationary while the clouds move. For an earlier edition of this print bound into its textbook see IHL.1541b.

title: Carelessness (麁相 Sosō)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: This print depicting a man drawing water from a well as a passing rider on horseback becomes entangled in a rope, may depict the Japanese proverb Sosō mo toki no ikkyō* (Failure is fun at the time.) *typically written as 粗相も時の一興<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Pilgrims, Number 2 (巡礼  其二 junrei sono ni)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)

title: Former Residence of Ōishi Yoshio in Banshū-Akō (播州赤穂大石良雄旧宅 Banshū-Akō Ōishi Yoshio kyūtaku)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
Print number forty-three (四十三, as printed in right margin) of the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting the house of the Ōishi Yoshio, the leader of the Forty-seven Ronin, famous for their determined effort to avenge their lord's disgrace and death.
<br><br>SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
<br>The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, or the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.
<br>In his commentary on the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

title: Index and Prologue (目録口上 Mokuroku kōjō)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description: The title page providing a list of all twenty-five prints in the series Annual Events of the Edo Theater, originally published in 1897 by Hasegawa Sumi 長谷川寿美 (長谷川スミ).  The list of prints is provided in the form of a stage speech by the publisher. The text is surrounded by the auspicious symbols of pine, bamboo and red plum. This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

title: Evening Sky (untitled)
creator: Inagaki Tomoo 稲垣知雄 (1902-1980)
description: Printed on a very thin and translucent paper, Inagaki gives us a rural farmhouse with a darkening sky as viewed from an intersection of roads. A slightly altered version of this print titled 風景 "Landscape" appeared in the magazine HANGA, Volume 10 issued in July 1926.

title: Snow covered house by a stream (untitled)
creator: Okuyama Gihachirō 奥山儀八郎 (1907-1981)
description:
The prolific and stylistically varied artist Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981), whose work encompassed the sōsaku hanga and shin hanga movements, created many monochrome woodblock prints similar to this untitled print of a snow covered house by a stream under a full moon. His son, Okuyama Gijin 奥山義人 (1934-2020), who studied under his father, created a number of similar monochrome woodblock prints and their work is sometimes conflated.

<br>Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) maker and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own woodblock prints, such as IHL.1844, and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.

title: Picture Book of Modern Figures of Fashion, Volume 1 (絵本時世粧 乾  Ehon Imayō Sugata)
creator: Utagawa Toyokuni 歌川豐国 (1769-1825)
description: A 1916 re-issue of the first of two volumes of Utagawa Toyokuni's illustrated book Ehon imayō sugata (Picture Book of Modern Figures of Fashion), originally issued in 1802. Originally published by Izumiya Ichibei of the publishing firm Kansendō, this 1916 edition was issued in a larger overall format by the Tokyo publishing house Fūzoku emaki zuga kankōkai (Association for Publication of Genre Handscroll Illustrations), specializing in the reprinting of Edo-period illustrated books and scrolls and classic ukiyo-e prints.<br>During his lifetime, Toyokuni illustrated over 400 books and this work may be his masterpiece, depicting Kansei era (1789-1801) women of all classes - from aristocratic and samurai, to servants and courtesans. Published in two volumes, the first volume contains twelve double-page illustrations of women engaging in various past-times and work, dressed in period fashion appropriate to their class. The second volume, not currently part of this collection, contains twelve double-page depictions of women of the "pleasure quarters", from elite courtesans to unlicensed prostitutes. The illustrations are generally arranged in order of perceived popular status rather than by strict class order.

title: The Arrowhead (矢の根 Yanone)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu III 三代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu III 三代 小信 ) (1881-1963)
description:
This print depicts the famous scene from the play "Yanone," based on the play The Soga Brothers Revenge, which Gorō, the younger of the two Soga brothers, is sharpening a huge, V-shaped, arrowhead, hoping that at the time he aims this arrow at the neck of his target Kudō Suketsune, the killer of their biological father, its flight will be true. The Soga Brothers Revenge, one of the most popular vendetta stories in Kabuki, tells of Jurō's and Gorō's suffering for eighteen years before being able to avenge the death of their father who was murdered by Kudō Suketsune.
<br>This print is one of the eighteen prints making up the portfolio titled "Chūkō kabuki jūhachi ban" originally issued in 1941 as a deluxe set of eighteen prints with table of contents and explanatory sheet, each mounted on a decorative shikishiban cardboard sheet and packaged in a wooden box. This collection's print is not mounted on a shikishiban sheet and is a later c. 1950 printing. A number of re-issues of the original eighteen prints are known.

title: Charcoal Seller (炭屋 sumiya)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
By the time this print, showing a charcoal seller cutting charcoal logs into pieces, was issued during the Pacific War, Japanese homes and small industry were demanding more and more charcoal, adding to the degradation of Japan's large forests.
<br>A translation of the artist's commentary originally accompanying this post-war second edition (originally print number 14 in the second series) reads "What would be the reason for the mysterious phenomenon nowadays of the upper-class voices on the street supporting the government, while the lower-class are concentrating all their energy on rice and charcoal? And everywhere you go you hear the polite phrase 'The world has become a strange place, don't you think.' As autumn turns to winter, people's eyes are drawn more acutely to rice and charcoal with each passing day. And people go crazy over charcoal to the extent that a lump that before would have seemed completely insignificant to them, now looks like a black diamond. Some people even pine is prison because of it. Because of the current situation, almost every day new substitutes are invented and them substitutes for substitutes . . . .  I wonder what on earth will happen to Japan's forests and mountains."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3] 
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 54.
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Mount Fuji from Lake Ashinoko at Hakone (箱根芦之湖の冨士 Hakone Ashinoko no Fuji)
creator: Kasamatsu Shirō 笠松紫浪 (1898–1991)
description: This is a later, although lifetime, edition of Kasamatsu's 1935 print of Lake Ashinoko at Hakone with Mt. Fuji in the background.<br>Lake Ashinoko was formed in the caldera of Mount Hakone after the volcano's last eruption 3000 years ago. Today, the lake with Mount Fuji in the background is the symbol of Hakone.

title: Gennosuke as Otomi (源之助切 お富)
creator: Matsuda Seifū 松田青風 (1880-1978)

title: Bicycle Race (競輪 keirin)

title: Niwa -79-C (庭・79-C)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist since his early printmaking days, the word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, NIwa.  Also see Niwa (80-K), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (April), Niwa (Sunshine) and Niwa (Winter Scenery) in this collection.

title: Print 32 Very Popular Story
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: Print 32 in a series of thirty-eight 3M color-in-color magnetic process prints (the entire series issued in a portfolio by the Nantenshi Gallery, Tokyo) created by the artist in 1974. The thirty-eight prints show the progression of an "EVENT", with only the artist in attendance, during which drinks are poured and Ay-O gets drunk.

creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)

title: Conception appearing in Volume 7 of the magazine Hanga Geijutsu
creator: Ida Shōichi 井田照一 (1941-2006)
description: This small print titled Conception appeared in Volume 7, the autumn issue for 1974 of the magazine Hanga Geijutsu (Print Arts). The print was bound into the magazine as a "special attachment." It is a five color offset print, using aluminum and zinc plates, printed on a heavy-weight Japanese paper.<br>Hanga Geijutsu is Japan's foremost magazine dedicated to the art of printmaking. Since 1974, each issue has featured a specially commissioned original print. This print is part of a series of prints and 1974 multimedia installation in which Ida explored the theme of "conception."

title: Hōjō Yasutoki (北條泰時)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
Print number 25 (廿五), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the armor-clad Hōjō Yasutoki 北条 泰時 (1183–1242), the third shikken (regent) of the Kamakura shogunate, being criticized by the seated Taira no Moritsuna 平の盛綱 for wasting valuable time and risking his life in coming to the aid of his younger brother Hōjō Tomotoki 北条 朝時 (1193-1245) who had come under attack. Responding Yasutoki says, “How shall it be called a small affair when my brother is in danger? If I had lost my brother, what consolation would my rank have furnished?"<br>
Devotion to family over personal glory is only one of the reasons Yasutoki is judged by history as a paragon of warrior leadership.<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0611.<br>This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization.  Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

title: Onoe Kikugorō V as Mibu no Kozaru - Rat (三生の小猿 尾上菊五郎 - 子)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
This series of twelve prints depicts actors in roles associated with the twelve animal signs of the Zodiac. The Japanese Zodiac and calendar were introduced from China into Japan in the sixth century. Legend has it that the animals of the Zodiac (子 Rat, 丑 Ox, 寅 Tiger, 卯 Hare, 辰 Dragon, 巳 Snake, 午 Horse, 未 Goat, 申 Monkey, 酉 Rooster, 戌 Dog and 亥 Boar) were named by the Buddha as he lay dying.<br>
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as Mibu no Kozaru, covered in a monkey skin,  in the play Tsuki no Ume Megumi no Kagekiyo.

title: Illustration of Wedding Ceremony of the Noble Couple (高位婚礼式之図 Kōi konreishiki no zu)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: One of a number of similar prints designed by Nobukazu and published in 1900 to popularize the ceremonies around the wedding of twenty-one year old Crown Prince Yoshihito to sixteen year old Kujō Sadako, daughter of Duke Michitaka Kujō.<br>From the time of the decision of the prince's marriage on August 21, 1899 to the marriage ceremony itself on May 10, 1900 , a series of newly fabricated events, including the marriage ceremony itself, had been instituted by the newly formed Imperial Institutions Investigatory Bureau (teishitsu seido chōsa kyoku), which was tasked with studying European monarchy practices in order to "create a modern monarchy that they believed would represent a level of civility equal to that of the West. . . ." - Source: Splendid Monarchy: Power and Pageantry in Modern Japan, T. Fujitani, University of California Press, 1998, p. 118.

title: Illustration of the Imperial National Diet Building - Members of the House of Representatives and Members of the House of Lords (帝国々会議事堂之図・帝国衆議院議員名鑑・帝国貴族院議員名鑑 Teikoku Kokkai gijidō no zu・Teikoku Shūgiin giin meikan・Teikoku Kizokuin giin meikan)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru III 三代 歌川国輝 (active c. 1886-1895)
description: This March 1892 print depicts a meeting of the second Diet, following the February 1892 election of the House of Representatives, along with a complete list of all the Diet members and a view of the exterior of the National Diet Building. The names of the 251 members of the House of Peers appear on the right and those of the 300 members of House of Representatives on the left. This second election resulted from the dissolution of the first Diet in December 1891, due to a budget impasse. The second Diet would be dissolved in December 1893.

creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
A large dai-oban size posthumous print after Yumeji's 1921 original watercolor painted by the artist as part of a group of ten watercolors commissioned by the Nagasaki collector, playwright and art historian Nagami Tokutarō.[1] 
<br>This collection's print is one of a series of ten woodblock prints reproducing the original watercolors titled Ten Subjects of Women issued by the Tokyo publisher Takamizawa. Takamizawa issued a complete set of the ten prints making up the series in a numbered limited edition of 200 copies in 1993. This collection's print is not from that original edition of 200, but from a likely later edition of 280 prints.

<br><br>[1] Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Hotei Publishing, 2015 , p. 52 and Yumeji Modern: Designing the Everyday in Twentieth-Centry Japan, Nozomi Naoi, University of Washington Press, 2020, p. 175.

title: Mirror (鏡 kagami)
creator: Ōuchi Makoto 大内マコト (1926-1989)
description:
A courtesan's reflection and kumadori (stage makeup) for the kabuki stage. The artist comments, "In the Edo Period, mirrors were made from a polished brass plate coated with mercury. I have a pocket hand mirror of this period at home. The reflection on it is not so clear as an image on a modern glass mirror. I recommend an ancient mirror to anybody who wants to see a beauty in the mirror. - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 103.

<br><br>While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

title: Mt Minōo, View from Komorino (水縄山 小森野より望む Minōsan Komorino yori nozomu)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description: This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, picturing the Chikugo River in the foreground with the Minō Mountain Range on the horizon, is from the 1970 set of five prints titled Five Scenes of Tsukushi by the publisher Katō Junji. The five prints are re-issues (using new printing blocks) of the original 1918 prints issued as set six of the ten set series titled Japan Scenery Prints by the publisher Nakajima Jūtarō. The new printing blocks were very carefully recarved for this reissue, resulting in prints that closely match the 1918 releases. For a print from the 1918 original issue see Sea of Fire from the series Japan Scenery Prints, Set 6: Tsukushi District (IHL.0862.)

description: A small untitled print of a mountain landscape that was originally issued as the December page of a 1986 calendar issued by the Miura Bookstore. The bulk of the artist's prints depict brightly colored flowers and mountain landscapes and are generally small format prints and ex-libris.

title: Bijin gazing into garden (untitled)
creator: Kitani Chigusa 木谷千種 (1895-1947)
description:
Kitani Chigusa (1895-1947), was an Osaka based woman nihonga painter and a member of the Four Women Association founded in 1916 which included the female painters Okamoto Kōen, Kitani Chigusa, Shima Seien, and Matsumoto Kayō, who were known as the "Setsu Getsu Ka Sei" (Snow, Moon, Flower, and Star). Excelling at painting bijinga, she was in demand as a designer of bijin kuchi'e for popular magazines of the time.
<br>This chromolithograph print bears a characteristic trifold from its insertion into a popular mass-market magazine of the time.
<br><br>THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E<br>

The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

title: Mibu River from the magazine HANGA (Prints), Volume 14 (版画 第14輯・三峯川)
creator: Moriyama Shūji 森山収治 (1890-?)
description:
This print was created for the dōjin (coterie magazine) HANGA (Print Art), Volume 14, issued in 1928 by the Hanga-no-Ie institute. It depicts a lone figure on a bridge in the mountains near the headwaters of the Mibu River, a tributary of the Tenryu River, in the southern Alps. 
<br><br>Published by Hanga-no-Ie in Kobe under the direction of Yamaguchi Isayoshi, HANGA made its appearance in February 1924 and sold to subscribers for 80 sen each. Sixteen quarterly issues (numbers 9 and 10 combined) were published until April 1930.  Merritt estimates that there were no more than 300 subscribers. As announced in its table of contents, the purpose of the magazine was "to publish, exhibit, and encourage appreciation of sōsaku hanga."

creator: Fujimori Shizuo 藤森静雄 (1891-1943)
description: This print was created for the dōjin (coterie magazine) HANGA (Print Art), Volume 14, issued in 1928 by the Hanga-no-Ie institute. It provides a somewhat bleak landscape of Iizuka in Fukuoka Prefecture about an hour from Fujimori's birthplace in Kurume. Iizuka is in the valley of the upper Onga River. The city developed as a mining center with the opening of the Chikuhō 筑穂 Coalfield and a railway from Wakamatsu (now in Kitakyūshū) in the 1890s. The mines were gradually closed after World War II. title: Fishermen (漁師 ryōshi)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Three fishermen look out to sea on what might be the day before the New Year. This print was originally issued in 1940 by the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin as the fifteenth print in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1.<br>
A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "When I was drunk on New Year's sake, I unsteadily put on my shoes and went to the beach alone. Today is the spring of the 2600th Year of Imperial Rule (1940). Outside the cape that protrudes beyond the shore on which the sun shines warmly, there is no smoke or clouds of the boats going off into the distant haze on the boundless open sea. Among the group of friends talking between the landed boats about the same unchanging topics with the same unchanging faces, and some already have grandchildren. These days, quilted coats and festive dresses have become a rare sight. Their place has been taken by convenient wood sweaters. Boats, too, have been replaced by motorboats."[1] 
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 14.
<br> [2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: The Old Story of Sanshō Dayū, (昔談柄三升太夫 Mukashi-banashi Sanshō Dayū)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description: The highlight of this performance involving kidnap, slavery, revenge and redemption, is the afflicted Osan turning into a fowl, as she is depicted in the left sheet, in the play The Old Story of Sanshō Dayū, as performed at the Kawarazaki theater in the 4th month of 1852. Osan will soon chew the ropes from Kanamenosuke (right sheet), with whom she is in love, and then kill herself. The evil Sanshō Dayū, in the center sheet, looks on.

title: A Great Victory of Our Forces at Kiuliencheng (九連城ニ於テ我軍大勝利)
creator: Tsuneshige 経茂 (active 1894-1904?)
description: The artist has taken some liberties with this scene in portraying a bigger battle than actually occurred as the Chinese troops had previously withdrawn from Kiuliencheng and the fortress was conquered virtually without fighting.

title: A Great Victory of Our Fleet: An Enemy Ship was Attacked and Sunk on the Open Sea off of Haiyang Island (我艦隊大勝利 海洋嶋沖ニ敵艦ヲ撃沈ム Waga kantai daishori ・ Kaiyoto oki ni tekikan o uchishizumu)
creator: Utagawa Toshimasa 歌川年昌 (Shunsai 春斎)(1866-1913)
description: This print depicts the first great naval battle of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) on September 17, 1894 near the islands of Haiyang and Zhangzi, off the coast of the Liaodong Peninsula, midway between Port Arthur and the mouth of the Yalu River. It pitted the Chinese fleet of larger but older ships against newly built and more maneuverable Japanese ships. The Chinese fleet was led by Admiral Ding Ruchang who was injured by his own ship's gunfire early in the battle and the Japanese fleet was led by Admiral Itō Yūkō. Two Chinese ships were sunk in the engagement and the remainder of Chinese ships fled. There was also extensive fire damage to Chinese and some Japanese ships. The New York Times headlines of this battle ran "China's Waterloo in Corea" and "Japan's Great Naval Victory."<br>The artist, who did not witness the battle, must have reconstructed it from newspaper accounts. One error of fact appears on the print. The Chinese ship the Lai-yuen [Laiyuan], shown sinking at the bottom of the center panel, did not, in fact, sink at the battle. It was its sister-ship, the King-yuen, that was sunk.

title: Japanese Forces Conquer Kiuliencheng (大日本大勝利九連城没落之図 Dai Nihon daishōri Kyūrenjō botsuraku no zu)
creator: Yōsai Nobushige 揚斎延重 (active 1894-95)
description: The artist portrays a fictional battle for Kiuliencheng (Jiuliancheng) in Manchuria which was taken without opposition by the Japanese in late October 1894. While the Japanese had prepared for a fierce battle to take the Kiuliencheng citadel, the Chinese forces had withdrawn and the fortress was conquered virtually without fighting. For a second copy of this print see IHL.0350.

title: Yu-no-hama Onsen (湯野浜温泉)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description:
From Senpan's fourth set of prints picturing Japanese onsens. This print depicts a gentleman in a trench coat sitting with two traditionally dressed women on the rocks overlooking the Yu-no-hama hot springs resort along the coast of Yamagata. To quote from a current-day  advertisement about these hot springs:
<br>"Warming yourself up with a soak in this hot spring after swimming in the ocean and playing water sports on a beach of white sand and clear blue skies is a truly unique experience. Because this hot spring is along the ocean, the seafood is exquisite. After you’re done enjoying the hot spring, you can have a romantic evening eating delicious seafood while watching the sun set into the ocean."
<br>ABOUT THE SERIES HOT SPRING NOTES
<br>One of his most famous series of prints, "Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes" (Hanga yokusen fu), depicts various hot springs around Japan. It was published in five volumes of twenty prints each over an 18 year period, starting in 1941 when Maekawa was evacuated to Okayama in southwest Honshu and ending in 1959.

<br>Merritt states that most of the prints were started during the war but could not be published until the war was over. She notes that although his countrymen are depicted at one of their favorite pastimes, spa going for rest and relaxation, "the feeling is not joyous," due to Maekawa's use of somber colors. The general demeanor of the spa goers is also somber in many of the prints. 
<br>However, writing in 1955, Oliver Statler found Senpan's spa prints "some of his pleasantest prints" and praised Senpan's "connoisseur's selection from the country's hundreds of hot spring resorts."
<br>In 1954 the publisher Ryūseikaku 竜星閣 released a volume containing full size reproductions of the sixty woodblock prints contained in the first three volumes.
<br>The five volumes comprising the entire series are titled are:
<br>Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes  (版画 浴泉譜 Hanga yokusen fu), 1941.
<br>More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1944.
<br>More and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1952. 
<br>More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku yokusen fu), 1956.
<br>More, More, More, and More Woodblock Prints, Hot Spring Notes (続続続続版画 浴泉譜 Zoku, zoku, zoku, zoku hanga yokusen fu), 1959.

title: Totems
creator: Hiyoshi Mamoru 日吉守 (1885-?)
description:
One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945.<br>
Five wood totems, jangseung in Korean, which serve as village guardians and are traditionally placed at the edges of villages to mark village boundaries, stand along the edge of a road as children play and villagers pass by. The left totem reads 天下大將軍 "Great General of All Under Heaven" and the totem to its right reads  地下女將軍 "Female General of the Underworld."

title: Castle Gate
creator: Hiyoshi Mamoru 日吉守 (1885-?)
description:
One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945.<br>
This print may be a depiction of Pyongyang's Taedongmun Street with Taedongmun Gate, built in mid-6th century, dominating the background.

title: Asaki Haru (浅き春)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description: This small print titled Asaki Haru after the poem it illustrated was most likely produced by the Katō Print Institute under the supervision of the Yumeji Art Museum.  It is a reproduction of an earlier 1919 work by the artist.

title: Mt. Fuji from the Pass (峠の富士 Tōge no Fuji)

title: Noh mask, Onna : Manbi (能面 女 : 万媚)
creator: Unidentified
description: A depiction by an unidentified artist of what appears to be a onna manbi mask used in the Noh theater to represent a "a mysteriously beautiful young woman. The name manbi, or '10,000 coquetries,' derives from the phrase 'winning over 100 coquetries.' The manbi mask is typically used to represent a demon that has transformed into a beautiful woman." - Source: website of the-Noh.com https://www.the-noh.com/sub/jp/index.php?mode=db&action=e_view_detail&data_id=77&class_id=1 [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Gojō Bridge (五條橋) - untitled
creator: Miyake Katsumi 三宅克己 (Kokki) (1874-1954)
description: Little is known about the production of woodblock prints from Miyake's drawings and paintings, although it is likely he worked closely with the carver and printer who executed the finished prints. This small print with an impressionistic take on Gojō-bashi over the Horikawa River in Nagoya may have appeared in one of the many magazines of the period or as an illustration for a novel.

title: Canal (untitled)
creator: Miyake Katsumi 三宅克己 (Kokki) (1874-1954)
description: Little is known about the production of woodblock prints from Miyake's drawings, although it is likely he worked closely with the carver and printer who executed the finished prints. This small untitled print may have appeared in one of the many journals of the period or as an illustration for a novel. Whether this impressionistic view of a canal and what may be a farmhouse in the distance is a scene from Europe or from the artist's native Japan is unknown.

title: Venice
creator: Miyake Katsumi 三宅克己 (Kokki) (1874-1954)
description: Little is known about the production of woodblock prints from Miyake's drawings, although it is likely he worked closely with the carver and printer who executed the finished prints. This small print, titled Venice, may have appeared in one of the many journals of the period or as illustrations for a novel. Miyake made at least two trips to Europe which included some time in southern Italy and in 1911 his European painting tour book, Ōhshū Ryokō e Angya, was published.

title: Autumn (秋 Aki)
creator: Ōuchi Makoto 大内マコト (1926-1989)
description:
A courtesan holds a cup of sake with the character 亀 "heavy drinker" denoting the courtesan's name, her habits or the artist's admitted love of the drink. And, the artist comments, "Liquor. I like it. I like the atmosphere of drinking parties more than the liquor itself. The refreshing Australian beer in Sydney. Wine at a party in Melbourne. A whisky and water at a back-street bar in Kawasaki, etc. etc." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 103
<br><br>While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

title: Crane (鶴 Tsuru)
creator: Ōuchi Makoto 大内マコト (1926-1989)
description:
The artist comments, "The decorative standard borne by the fireman is called 'matoi'. In the age of chronic civil strife in Japan, from about the middle of the 15th century to the middle of the 16th century, warriors stripped off an enemy's clothes and made it their mark. During the Edo Period 'matoi' became the sign of a team of firemen. It developed into a battle flag in recent times." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 102.
<br><br>While many traditional Japanese themes are depicted in his work, his production technique is not traditional woodblock. Ōuchi work employs "a combination of etching processes as well as embossed effects created by paper blocks. His methods as well as the tasteful dispositions of color and the romanticism of a long-gone past are all creative innovations of Ōuchi, achieved after many years of trial and error, accomplished through his own persistence and desire to be an artist." - Source: Aramusha - Ouchi Makoto: The Artist Warrior, Mary S. Tolman, Norma H. Tolman, ed., Sobunsha, 1982, p. 16.

title: Sumizō in the role of Hōkaibō (壽美蔵 法界坊)
creator: Ogawa Hyōe (Heibei) 小川兵衛 (active c. 1915)

title: Kiyoko in the role of Akagashi Mitsue (京子 赤樫満枝)
creator: Ishii Hakutei 石井柏亭 (1882-1958)

title: A Record of Modern Events, volume 1 (近世紀聞 巻之一 Kinsei kibun, maki no ichi)
creator: Kobayashi Eitaku 小林永濯 (1843-1890)
description: Volume 1 of 12 volumes of a history jitsuroku (歴史実録) co-authored by Jōno Arindō and Somezaki Nobufusa, also known as Tamenaga Shunsui II, published from 1874 to 1882. It took its material from official government proclamations, newspaper reports, and gossip and rumor to create modern histories of Japan in a familiar gesaku form, adopting the language and published format of popular Edo period fictional genres.

title: Gion District (祇園まち Gion machi)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
Standing outside the gate of the Ichiriki teahouse, young Rikiya, son of Yuranosuke, the leader of the Forty-Seven Loyal Samurai, looks warily around.  He has a secret letter for his father with the details of their plot to kill Lord Moronao who they blame for their master's death. This scene is from ACT VII, "The Ichiriki Teahouse," in the play "Revenge of the Forty-Seven Loyal Samurai" (Kanadehon Chūshingura). The full moon will light the way for the Loyal Samurai's subsequent attack on Moronao's mansion and his beheading.
<br>This collection's print is from a bound album, created by the publisher, of the entire series of one hundred prints.

<br><br>ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
<br>One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
<br>"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

<br><br>
[1] Yoshitoshi's One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, John Stevenson, published by Hotei Publishing, Netherlands 2001, p. 53.

title: Onoe Kikugorō V as Torii Tsuneemon and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Okudaira Heihachirō in the play Go fūdoki kabuki no hon'yomi (鳥井弥左衛門 尾上菊五郎・奥平平八郎 市川団十郎・後風土記劇本読)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as the faithful messenger Torii Tsuneemon passing through a moat strung with ropes of warning bells on his return to Mikawa, in the play Go fūdoki kabuki no hon'yomi (Reading a Play on the History of the Region.) The inset in the top left shows the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the role of Okudaira Heihachirō.<br><br>In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

title: Stone Bodhisattva at Datong (Yungang), China (大同雲崗石佛)
creator: Hiratsuka Un'ichi 平塚運一 (1895-1997)
description: The artist's depiction of a stone statue of the Buddha in meditation from the famous Yungang caves in Datong, China, which the artist must have visited during his 1943 stint teaching print classes in Japanese-occupied Beijing.

title: Nakamura Tokizō as Danshichi Shima no Okaji (中村時蔵の団七縞お梶)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)

creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)

title: Sawamura Sōjūrō VII and Nakamura Shikaku II in Wakaki no Adanagusa at the Mitsukoshi Theater
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
This print depicts the actor Sawamura Sōjūrō VII (1875-1949) in the role of Ranchō in the play Wakaki no Adanagusa, a dramatic version of a shinnai bushi musical number Ranchō. The circular inset depicts the actor Nakamura Shikaku II (1900-1981) in the role of Konoito.<br>The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in October 1948. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.<br>
The inscription along the left edge reads らんてふ (Ranchō) followed by 宗十郎 Sōjūrō (Sawamura Sōjūrō VII). The inscription in the inset reads 此糸 (Konoito) and beneath it しかく (Kiya) [as in Konoito of the Wakakiya] and 木屋 Shikaku (Nakamura Shikaku II).

title: Nakamura Moshiho IV as Sodehagi in Sodehagi Saimon at the Mitsukoshi Theater
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)

title: Nakamura Moshio IV and Sawamura Tosshō IV in Onna Goroshi Abura no Jigoku at the Mitsukoshi Theater
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description: This print depicts a scene in the third act from the play Onna Goroshi Abura no Jigyoku, in which Kawachiya Yohei, played by Nakamura Moshio IV (1909-1988), is about to slay Okichi, the wife of the proprietor of the Teshimaya oil store, played by Sawamura Tosshō IV (1908-1975). The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in February 1949. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.<br>Sasajima has hand-applied ink on the verso of this print to provide a subtle coloring when viewed from the front, a technique he learned from the artist Munakata Shikō 棟方志功 (1903-1975).

title: Kataoka Roen V as Yaoya Oshichi in Date musume koi no hikanoko at the Mitsukoshi Theater
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)

title: Ichikawa Omezō IV as Hayase Iori in Katakiuchi tengajaya mura at the Mitsukoshi Theater
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description: This print depicts the actor Ichikawa Omezō IV (1898-1969) in the role of Hayase Iori in the play Katakiuchi tengajaya mura, a classic tale of revenge, at the Mitsukoshi Theater in September 1948.<br> The play was performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in September 1948. The print is one of an unknown number of prints created by Sasajima for the 1948 and 1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater.<br>The inscription in the cartouche reads 伊織 (Iori) and the kana below reads おめぞう (Omezō).

title: Mitsukoshi Kabuki Hanga, Works of Sasajima Kihei, September 1948 (三越歌舞伎版画 昭和二十三年 九月 笹島喜平作)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description: Likely the introductory print for the series of prints Sasajima created for the 1948-1949 kabuki seasons at the Mitsukoshi Theater. The inscription in the top cartouche reads Mitsukoshi Kabuki hanga and in the left cartouche is written 昭和二十三年 九月 (September 1948) followed by 笹島喜平作 (works of Sasajima Kihei) .The actor pictured is not identified in the print, nor is the character he is playing.<br>Sasajima has hand-applied ink on the verso of this print to provide a subtle coloring when viewed from the front, a technique he learned from the artist Munakata Shikō 棟方志功 (1903-1975).

title: Three Dance Performances at the Mitsukoshi Gekijō: Onoe Shōroku II in Sarutori, Ichikawa Omezō IV in Tonbi Yakko, Onoe Baikō VII in Karigane
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description: This print portrays three actors in three dance performances, performed at the Mitsukoshi Theater (三越劇場 Mitsukoshi gekijō) in September 1948.  The actors and their roles are as follows: Onoe Shōroku II 二代目 尾上松緑  (1913-1989) as Tobi no mono 鳶のもの in Sarutori さる酉 ; Ichikawa Omezō IV 四代目 市川男女蔵 (1898-1969) as Yatsutaki taira 奴瀧平 in Tonbi Yakko とんび奴; Onoe Baikō VII 七代目 尾上梅幸 (1915-1995) as Benten Oteru 弁天おてる in Karigane 雁がね.

title: A Sweet Pastry into the Open Mouth. Love Makes No Distinction Between High and Low; The Famous Holy Man of Shiga Temple (あいた口へおはき  恋に上下のへだてなし  志賀寺之名高キ上人 Aito kuchi e ohagi. Koi ni ueshita no hedate nashi, Shigadera no nadakaki shōnin)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: Kyōsai pairs the proverb "A sweet pastry [bean-jam rice cake] into an open mouth," (meaning, an unexpected windfall) with the ancient story of the infatuation of the holy man of Shiga Temple for the Empress Somedomo. In the bottom scene of the print, we see the holy man grasping the hand of the empress while several onlookers giggle. In the story the holy man from the Shiga temple grasped the hands of the Empress Mother (Empress Somedomo) and recited the poem on the Jeweled Broom to liberate himself from obsessive thoughts and worldly desires. In the end he was unable to endure such passion and turned into a blue ghost.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: The Complete Sixteen Divine Generals of the Tokugawa (徳川英勇揃 十六將之圖)
creator: Unsen 雲僊 (active. c. 1874)
description: The artist portrays the Sixteen Divine Generals serving Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616) founder and first shogun of the Tokugawa shogunate of Japan, which ruled Japan until the Meiji Restoration of 1867. It is interesting to ponder why this subject was depicted in 1874, seven years after the emperor was restored to power. 1873 and the beginning of 1874 were rough times for the new Meiji emperor and government, with open revolts by both the masses (over misinterpreted conscription laws and demands for tax reduction) and disaffected samurai, a handful of whom tried to assassinate the Minister of the Right, Iwakura Tomomi (1825-1883), on January 13, 1874.  Perhaps this reminder of the loyalty of these generals to the first shogun was to be a lesson in showing loyalty to the young emperor?

title: The Old Capital in Late Fall (古都晩秋 Koto banshū)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
Depicting the five-story pagoda at Tōji (East Temple) in Kyoto on a late autumn day.
<br>Toji Temple (東寺, Tōji), literally "East Temple", was founded at the beginning of the Heian Period just after the capital was moved to Kyoto in the late 700s. The large temple, together with its now defunct sister temple Saiji ("West Temple"), flanked the south entrance to the city and served as the capital's guardian temples. Toji Temple is one of Kyoto's many UNESCO world heritage sites.
<br>Across from the Kondo (the temple's main hall and largest building) and Kodo (a lecture hall) stands Tōji's five storied pagoda, which was originally erected by Kobo Daishi in 826. It stands 57 meters tall, making it the tallest pagoda in Japan, and has become a symbol of both the temple and Kyoto as it can be seen from many places across the city. The ground floor of the pagoda is irregularly opened to the public and houses four smaller Buddha statues. - Source: website of japan-guidel.com http://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3919.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Fuji (Lake Ashi) B (富士 [芦ノ湖] B Fuji Ashi no ko B)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description: Depicting Mount Fuji as seen from across Lake Ashi, this is one of at least fifteen views of Mount Fuji created by Sasajima. Sasajima used his "takuzuri" process, forcing damp paper into the grooves of a carved woodblock with a press, to give this print a dynamic three-dimensional effect. He has hand-applied black ink directly on the raised areas of the print.

title: Kami Harbor, Distant View of Genkai Sea (神湊 玄海灘を遠望 Kami no minato, Genkai nada oenbō)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description: This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, depicts Kami Harbor in Kōnominato in Fukuoka Prefecture. On the right we see what is  likely Kusasaki, with Katsu Island, seen center, and Jinoshima Island, seen left in the far background. This print is from the 1970 set of reissued prints titled Five Scenes of Tsukushi by the publisher Katō Junji.  This set was originally issued in 1918 as part six of the six set series titled Japan Scenery Prints by the publisher Nakajima Jūtarō. New printing blocks were very carefully recarved for this reissue, resulting in prints that closely match the 1918 releases.

title: Sea of Fire, View from Offshore (火の海 沖の端より望む Hi no umi Oki no hata yori nozumo)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description: This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō, picturing the ancient fortifications along Hakata Bay, is a 1970 reissue of a print originally released in 1918. (See IHL.0862 for the original 1918 print.)  Originally the print was published by Nakajima Jūtarō and the Japan Scenery Prints Association as part of the set of five prints titled Tsukishi District which was part of the ten set series titled Japan Scenery Prints. In 1970, the publisher Katō Junji reissued the five scenes of Tsukushi under the title Five Scenes of Tsukushi (筑紫五景 Tsukushi Gokei.)  New printing blocks were very carefully recarved for this reissue, resulting in prints that closely match the 1918 releases.

title: Enoki Temple Shrine, View from the Direction of Tofurō (榎寺神社 都府樓方面よ Enokidera jinja Tofurō hōmen yori nozomu)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)

title: Boxers, Number 3 (拳闘家 其三 kentōka sono san)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
This first edition 1939 print, issued as the Japanese were ruthlessly continuing their colonization of Asia, depicts two fighters slugging it out in a boxing match. Boxing in Japan is traced back to Commodore Perry's second visit to Japan and shipboard boxing matches. 
<br>The commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "Boxing the sport in which men of equal weight contend in skill and strength, reached its full development in America, and having been introduced into Japan in recent years has made great progress here too. Consequently the number of professional Japanese boxers has gradually increased. Battle of human bodies staged in the blue glare of flood lights under a summer evening sky have a great fascination for the young men and women of Japanese cities. The fighting spirit - no, the killing spirit - of men covered with blood still trying to knock out their opponents might even be called brutal and makes one feel that for the Japanese nature, which ordinarily strives to make fine arts of courtesy and rules even in the coarsest moods and at the most critical moments, this sport may be a little excessively gruesome."
<br>Along with the print title, this collection's print has the series title and the number of the print in the series printed within the image area. The majority of prints in the series carry the series title in the lower right margin, not within the image area, and not all prints show the series number on the print.
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2] 
<br><br>
[1] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[2] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Onoe Kikugorō V as Masaoka supported by Onoe Iwagorō as Senmatsu and Ichikawa Botan as Tsurikyō in the play Precious Incense and Autumn Flowers of Sendai (政岡尾上菊五郎・鶴千代丸 市川ぼたん・千松 尾上きく・伽羅先代萩)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as the nursemaid Masaoka 政岡 in the play Meiboku Sendai Hagi (Precious Incense and Autumn Flowers of Sendai). The inset in the top right shows the actors Onoe Kiku [Onoe Iwagorō 尾上岩五郎 ] as Masaoka's own son Senmatsu 千松  and Ichikawa Botan 市川ぼたん [Ichikawa Sadanji II] as the young lord Tsurikyō, Masaoka's charge.<br><br>n 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

title: By now you must be near Komakata, a cuckoo calls - Takao (たか雄 君は今駒かたあたりほとゝきす Kimi wa ima/ Komakata Atari/ hototogisu - Takao)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
Often assumed to be the first print in the series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, it pictures Takao, one of the eleven famous courtesans of the Yoshiwara in the 17th and 18th centuries.  It is believed Yoshitoshi's print pictures the sixth Takao, known for her poetry.<br>
This print is a modern re-issue of the original 1885 print [see IHL.0970], created from re-cut blocks. It is part of a portfolio of 15 designs from the series issued by the woodblock department 版画部 of the publishing company Nihon Bijutsu Gakai 日本美術画会 and overseen by Japanese art historian and one-time president of the Japan Ukiyo-e Society Yamaguchi Keizaburō 山口桂三郎 (1928-2012) who also provided a commentary for each print. For the original print see IHL.0970.

creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)

title: Takemitsu Kikuchi (菊地武光)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)

title: Takasugi Shinsaku (高杉晋作)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)

title: Sano Tsuneyo (佐野常世)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)

title: Koshikibu no Naishi (小式部内侍)
creator: Kobayashi Kiyochika 小林清親 (1847-1915)
description:
Print number 5 (五), one of 20 contributed by Kiyochika to the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the young poetess Koshikibu no Naishi tugging at the robe of Middle Counselor Fujiwara no Sadayori, who had come to her room to tease her about being chosen to participate in a poetry contest.<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0759.
<br><br>INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
<br>This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter.".

title: Taking Refuge on the Tracks (線路の避難 Senro no hinan)
creator: Igawa Sengai 井川洗厓 (1876-1961)
description:
One of three prints (also see IHL.1406) contributed by the artist Igawa Sengai (1876-1961) to the series Pictures of Taishō Earthquake, issued in 1926 three years after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. This print pictures a family sitting on the streetcar tracks gazing at the city in ruins while fires smolder and refugees flee with their belongings. They are well dressed and without the backdrop of devastation it would look like a picnic.
<br>The series consists of 25 prints by nine, mostly lesser-known, artists, a number of whom, including this print's creator, were students of the Nihonga artist Tomioka Eisen (1864-1905). The nine artists are Katayama Shunhan (fl. c. 1901–1926); Hakuhan Yawata (1893–1957); Noguchi Kōgai (born c. 1899, active c. 1919-1930s); Igawa Sengai (1876-1961); Kirigaya (Kiriya) Senrin (1877–1932); Shibata Kōyō (fl c. 1920s); Hamada Josen (1875-1928); Kondō Shiun (fl. c. 1915–1940) and Takashima Unpō (1894-1987).

Registering at a magnitude of 7.9, the quake struck on September 1, with its epicenter some 50 miles southwest of Tokyo, in Sagami Bay.  The hour was 11:58A.M., just when households everywhere were lighting small charcoal stoves to prepare lunch. <br>"Hot Spring Notes" is one of Maekawa's most famous series of prints. creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Kitaoka's rendering of the Ishizuchi plateau with Mt. Ishizuchi, western Japan's highest peak, in the background.<br>East of the city of Matsuyama is Mt. It is said to protect the city of Saijo to its northeast from typhoons. Dedicated to gongen (deities with both Shinto and Buddhist forms), Mt. title: Komoro Castle and Mount Asayama (小諸城と浅間山 Komoro-jō to Asamayama)

description: The San-no-mon Gate at Komoro Castle (Komoro-jō), designated an Important Cultural Property by the Japanese government, is depicted with the city of Komoro sitting beyond the gate with the active volcano Mount Asama in the background. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

title: Himeji Castle (姫路城 Himejijō)
creator: Kawanishi Yūzaburō 川西祐三郎 (1923-2014)
description: View of Himeji Castle with cherry trees in bloom.<br>Originally built in 1346, Himeji Castle was built for warfare. The walls contain geometrically shaped sama, openings through which archers and gunners shot at attacking troops and ishiotoshi, an opening through which stones or boiling water were dumped on enemy soldiers scaling the wall.<br>  Throughout its history it was owned by thirteen warrior families, including Hashiba (Toyotomi) Hideyoshi, the commoner who rose to become the de facto military dictator of Japan during the Sengoku-jidai (Civil War Era). Lord Hideyoshi reconstructed the castle as a three storied structure in 1581.  In 1601, Ikeda Terumasa, son-in-law of Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogun who defeated the Hideyoshi family, transformed the castle into its present five tiered configuration with three smaller donjons. The castle was designated at UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.

title: Pagoda and pond (untitled)

description:
An untitled small format print by an artist signing his name 福太 (possibly read "Fukuta") depicting what is likely Sarusawa Pond in Nara with the five-story pagoda of Kofukuji Temple in the background. This signature is sometimes attributed to the shin hanga artist Fukutarō Terauchi  寺内福太郎 (1891-1964), who specialized in atmospheric watercolors and designed a small number of woodblock prints for the publisher Shingawa Kyoomi, owner of. Kyoto Hangain in the 1950s and 1960s, but this is conjecture. 
<br><b>Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints</b><br>
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in.
<br>Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
<br>The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
<br>The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints).

title: Jinzhou Castle After Occupation (占領後の金州城内)
creator: Miyake Katsumi 三宅克己 (Kokki) (1874-1954)
description:
From the printed title below the image we know this is a view of Jinzhou Castle after it was occupied by the Japanese. As Jinzhou was fought over and then occupied by the Japanese in both the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) and the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) this scene could have been from either war. However, given the artist's 1874 birth date, it is more likely a scene from the Russo-Japanese War. Jinzhou was taken by the Japanese from the Russians on May 26, 1904.  I can find no information on the artist having been to the front in either of these wars.<br>
It is difficult to tell whether this print is a woodblock or a lithograph. The artist worked in both mediums.

title: Idaten (韋駄天)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
In this print Sasajima depicts the Buddhist deity Idaten (the Indian deity Skanda) who is "faster than the wind."<br>
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with Sasajima's original printing of the work, Yoneda has used the technique of "back coloring" 裏彩色 in his reproduction.

title: Pontochō Through Street 2 (先斗町通りぬけ II)
creator: Konishi Seiichirō 小西誠一郎 (b. 1919)
description: An early morning view of Pontochō alleyway connecting Shijō and Sanjō streets in Kyoto, famous for its shops and restaurants. The street is empty except for a lone geisha. Konishi created two editions of this print, a "private printing" (shikaban) of 200 impressions and this collection's print of 500 impressions, which carries the suffix II after its title.

title: Sukeroku (助六)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu III 三代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu III 三代 小信 ) (1881-1963)
description:
Picturing the kumadori makeup for the kabuki character Sukeroku, this print is one of ten in the second set (or "collection") that the publisher Hangakai hanmoto intended to issue in monthly installments for ten months, making for a total of one hundred prints when complete.<br>
Kumadori is  the stylized exaggerated makeup used in the kabuki theater particularly when performing in the bold and bombastic aragoto style. Kumadori makeup generally consists of brightly colored stripes or patterns over a white foundation, the colors and patterns symbolizing aspects of the actor's character.  The three basic colors, other than black, are red (denoting a hero), blue (denoting an evil character) and brown (denoting a supernatural character).

title:
Reproduction of: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge at Atake,
No. 58, after Hiroshige (複製：大はしあたけの夕立・ 広重後 Fukusei：Ōhashi Atake no yūdachi・Hiroshige no ato)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige 歌川広重 (1797-1858) - after the artist
description:
An undated (c. 1930s) small format reproduction after Hiroshige's 1857 Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge at Atake, No. 58 from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. The original print has been called the "undisputed masterpiece" of the series.
<br>The publisher of this print was Yokohama-based Hideo Takemura (H. Takemura & Co.) who targeted his work at a Western audience, specializing in, as printed on his business card, Christmas Cards, Japanese Old Colour Prints, Famous Modern Colour Prints and Water Colors.
<br><b>Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints</b><br>
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in. 
<br>Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (Doi Hangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
<br>The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
<br>The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

creator: Unknown
description: A print with a portion of its right side and bottom trimmed. A torii reads 天満宮 (Tenman-gū) and the inscription in the lower left partially reads 神社  (Shinto shrine).
