title: The Port Arthur Surrender - Illustration of the Second Meeting Between General Nogi and General Stoessel to Review Prisoners of War (旅順降服・乃木大將トステツセル将軍ノ會見并二捕虜檢閲之図)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)
description: Using the signature Ryūa, as he did for all of his Russo-Japanese War triptychs, Kokunimasa gives us a view of the second meeting between Japanese General Count Nogi Maresuke (乃木 希典), (1849–1912) and the Russian Major-General Baron Anatoly Mikhailyovich Stoessel (1848–1915) on January 7, to discuss the conditions for the transfer of prisoners. In the left sheet we see captured Russian soldiers being led by Japanese officers bearing the Imperial Russian flag as a sign of respect for their vanquished foe.

title: Making Sanbon Sugar [Highly Refined Sugar] in Sanuki Province (同 [讃岐国] 三盆糖製造之図  Dō sanbontō seizō no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the making of sanbon (highly refined sugar) in Sanuki Province, present day Kagawa Prefecture.<br>Sanuki (讃岐国) was an old province of Japan on the island of Shikoku, with the same boundaries as modern Kagawa Prefecture. It faced the Inland Sea and bordered on Awa and Iyo Provinces. Across Naruto strait it bordered Awaji Province too.<br>
Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan, notes that "The chief production of this province of Sanuki are popularly known as ‘the three white things’ (sam-paku), viz, salt, sugar, and cotton.  The sugar industry is modern, having been introduced from Satsuma only half a century ago."

title: Niwa - Birth of the Season (庭・季節の誕生)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: This print Niwa (Birth of the season), along with Niwa (Andante), was one of the first two prints of the artist's acquired by the British Museum.  Lawrence Smith describes the print as having "sober tonalities."<br> While Japanese gardens are a primary source of material for the artist, the word Niwa (庭), Japanese for garden, made its first appearance in Takahashi's 1977 print titled Niwa R (Garden R) and subsequently appeared in at least 97 print titles, the last being two prints published in 1993, each titled, simply, Niwa.  Also see Niwa (80-K), Niwa (Movement) B2, Niwa (April) and Niwa (Winter Scenery), Niwa (Summer house) and Niwa (Sunshine) in this collection.

title: I Love You (Love Letters)
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: I Love You (Love Letters), a silkscreen print with an edition size of 11,111 prints, was the result of discussions between Ay-O, Tokuzo Okabe (founder of the first silkscreen printing studio in Japan), gallery owner Fujio Watanuki and others about expanding the appeal of prints to a wider audience and, particularly, a younger audience. Ay-O suggested adapting his 1973 lithograph Love Letter for this purpose and in 1974 a full run of 11,111 prints was completed.

title: Shinshū Matsushiro-chō  (信州松代町)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description: Two travelers walking through the town of Matsushiro-chō in Shinshū (modern-day Nagano Prefecture.) This print along with another print by the artist, Mitarai Inland Sea Port (Shimozima Ōsaki) 瀬戸内海御手洗港 (大崎下島), were bundled, each in its own separate folder, with the artist's book titled "Kaidō kōryo, Sekino Jun'ichirō gabunshū" (Travels Along Highways: Illustrations and Text by Sekino Jun'ichirō), published by Bijutsu Shuppansha in 1983.

title: Lathe Operator (旋盤工 senbankō)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Five male machinists at work on their lathes in this sixteenth print from the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, 1. This print is one of a small number of prints in the series depicting modern industry in Japan.<br>A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "A machine is formed by a collection of parts. The more complex the individual parts are, the more sophisticated the machine and its function. Nowadays, compared to a carpenter and a potter, the machinist has already become a major occupation. As a major role in heavy industry, light industry, and precision machinery industry, everyone agrees that this profession is a vital cornerstone. There is no doubt that this profession, which requires extraordinary skill instead of manpower, is extremely popular in today's world."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 14.
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Shoe Shiners (靴みがき kutsumigaki)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Wada presents us with his rendition of shoe shiners at work in a park-like setting on a sunny day in this 4th print in the twenty-four print post-WWII series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Continued" (3rd series). The happy picture that Wada presents us with is a much prettier picture than reality. Finding work in the aftermath of the war was tough, especially for veterans many of whom were forced to take this type of labor to survive. Disadvantaged boys also worked shining shoes to survive.
<br>The English language commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "'Shoe-Shine' became so popular in Japan after the war, that the 'shoe-shine boy' became the title of a hit song. Shoe-shine seems now to have become a legal occupation for men, and is a business conducted on the streets of Japan. Originally most Japanese thought it was rather a luxurious service, and a waste of money and time. After the war many people began to wear well-polished shoes as they came to afford well pressed white shirts. I am told that Spain is famous for this skill, and there are many shoe-shiners in its big cities, but this does not mean that all Spanish men are beaus. It seems to me that this profession may be considered as one of the solutions for unemployment. [I do not have much interest in this, so I am not very sure, but it seems.] Shoe-shiners are making their own efforts to make all shoes shine beautifully. Some of them have actually achieved a technique like a craftsman."
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES, CONTINUED (3RD SERIES)
<br>After WWII, the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi issued the third set of prints in the popular pre-war series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures." His former publishing business, Nishinomiya Shoin, being destroyed during WWII, Shinagawa opened a new publishing business in Kyoto, Kyōto Hangain 京都版画院. At first, Kyōto Hangain published re-prints from the pre-war series 1 and 2 of “Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures,” but would go on to publish this new third series consisting of 24 prints between November 1954 and September 1956, working closely with Wada as they did for the first two series.

title: White Fishing Boat (白い漁船)
creator: Okubo Yutaka 大久保担 (1924-2008)
description: Another of the artist's many prints picturing small boats along the shore.  For two similar prints by the artist see IHL.1099 and IHL.1198.

title: Gorō (五郎)
creator: Mori Yoshitoshi 森義利 (1898-1992)
description: One of several stencil prints created by Mori Yoshitoshi portraying a kabuki actor in the role of Gorō who along with his older brother Jurō sought revenge for the death of their father. The story of the Soga brothers' revenge was originally told in the 12th century "Soga monogatari" 曽我物語.

title: Catching Sea Otter in Chishima Province (千島国 海獺採之図 Chishima no kuni rakko to no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It portrays Ainu hunters chasing and harpooning sea otters. In the background we see foreign ships who contributed to the near decimation of the sea otter population in the Kuril Islands (Chishima.)<br>
Records of the Ainu hunting sea otters go back to the 1500s. Traditionally the Ainu hunted sea otters with bow and arrow, leister, and harpoon. Starting in the 1870s, at about the time this print was published, it was reported that most of the hunting was being done by foreign vessels and by 1897 a British sea captain reported that “sea-otter hunting on the Kurils are practically no longer worth considering…” due to their declining numbers. - Source: Notes on the Kuril Islands, Captain H. J. Snow, John Murray, 1897, p. 88.

title: Shipping Ice from Hakodate, Hokkaidō (北海道函館氷輸出之図 Hokkaidō Hakodate kōri yushutsu no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park.  It portrays people in Western-style garments cutting ice from the moat around Goryōkaku fort near Hakodate on the island of Hokkaidō, from where it was shipped, insulated with sawdust, to Yokohama, Tokyo and other southern destinations.  The ice would be held in storage until the summer months when it would fetch the highest prices. Production and transportation of natural water ice first succeeded in 1869.
Hakodate, located on Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaidō, developed as a port town for trade with foreign countries at the end of the 19th century. From December 4, 1868 to June 27, 1869 the Goryōkaku fort was the site of the Battle of Hakodate fought between the remnants of the Tokugawa shogunate army, consolidated into the armed forces of the rebel Ezo Republic, and the armies of the newly formed Imperial government. This was the final battle in the Boshin War.

title: Digging Kudzu [Pueraria] Root in Yamato Province (大和国 葛根堀図 Yamato no kuni kakkon hori zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

title: Producing Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 2 (山城国 宇治茶製之図 二  Yamashiro no kuni Uji cha sei no zu ni)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting women and men sorting, sifting, steaming, drying, and packaging tea in Uji in Yamashiro Province. The Uji district was famed for its tea plantations and its high-quality tea which was unequaled in Japan.  Historically, "the Uji powdered-tea industry was so important that it received bakufu protection, and farmers had to sell their tea through designated channels. [Uji farmers excelled] in the processing of green tea,especially as a result of innovations developed in the 1730’s.  Instead of kettle-firing, they steamed theleaves and then rolled rubbed them over a hearth.  This process produced a flavorful tea highly prized in central markets. [This superior tea] "became especially important with the opening of the ports in 1859, when tea became one of the country's leading export items.  From 1859 to 1867 tea exports increased over eighteen-fold,with more than 7 million pounds being exported in 1867 alone." - Source: Japan's Protoindustrial Elite: The Economic Foundations of the Gōnō, Edward E Prat, Cambridge: Harvard Univ. Asia Center, 1999. p. 52.
<br>For Figure 1 "Picking Uji Tea" see IHL.1495.

title: Abalone Divers in Ise Province (伊勢国 鮑採之図 Ise no kuni awabi tori no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting women divers (ana) bringing abalone (awabi) up to waiting boats in Ise Bay. Cave ruins containing tools the divers used for peeling abalone from the sea bed go back 3,000 years and there are written records of women divers dating to the year 927.<br>
As in this design, the artist based many of his designs on designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

title: Ennosuke in the role of the Exiled King and Tōzō in the role of the Warrior Priest Kōku (猿之助 流離王 東蔵 好苦梵士)
creator: Ishii Hakutei 石井柏亭 (1882-1958)
description:
The actors Ichikawa Ennosuke II in the role of the exiled king and Nakamura Tōzō II as the warrior priest Kōku in the play Washimo Shiranai わしも知らない staged at tje Gekijō, Tokyo on June 28, 1915. One of seven prints by the artist that appeared in the magazine Shin Nigao whose purpose was to advertise the Kabuki theater and renew interest in actor prints.<br>
During the Taishō period (1912-1926), many urban Japanese youth were drawn away from kabuki to more modern forms of entertainment, especially Western imports like cinema and baseball. One notable effort to revive interest in actor prints was the publication of Shin Nigao 新似顔 (New Portraits) magazine in 1915. This art magazine was a collaboration among several well-known Japanese artists, including Natori Shunsen (1886-1960), Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958), and Yamamura Toyonari (1885-1942). The general purpose of Shin Nigao was to advertise for the kabuki theater, but it also gave the artists a chance to express themselves in new ways. A total of 77 prints were published in the magazine over five issues, with each of the first four issues featuring 14 small woodblock prints and the fifth, and last, the "Coronation" issue, featuring 21 prints, including five portraits of officials and entertainers associated with the November 1915 enthronement ceremonies of Yoshihito (Emperor Taishō).

description: A large woodblock print tipped to a backing sheet depicting two women washing clothes along a riverbank below village houses perched above a steep enbankment. No biographical information is available on this artist who, auction records show, created both woodblock prints and watercolors of landscapes.

creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

title: Coal Mine in Iga Province (同国 [伊賀国] 石炭山之図 dōkoku sekitan yama no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting coal miners entering a mine with pickaxes (tsuruhashi) in hand and exiting the mine carrying yoked baskets (sena) of coal, this color woodblock print (nishiki-e) was one of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. As the series’ name implies, each print depicted an economic activity in a province or district of Japan. In addition, each activity was described on the print in a scroll-like cartouche.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0324.
<br>
Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi,Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces. The Saruka mountains which bordered Iga were noted for their coal reserves. An 1878-1879 geological survey describes Iga coal as being "black and shining." The print's scroll mentions that the coal produced is like the color of lacquer.

title: Making Steamed Flatfish in Wakasa Province (同[若狭]蒸鰈製造之図 Dō [Wakasa] mushi karei seizō no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the steaming and drying of flatfish to make mushi-garei.<br>
Wakasa was famous for the flatfish (karei) caught in their offshore waters which were considered a winter delicacy. Wakasa flatfish were often steamed in salt water and then dried, as shown in this print. The mushi-garei from Wakasa were considered the best and known to be offered as gifts to the imperial family.

title: Polishing-sand of Iga Province (伊賀国 磨砂 Iga kuni migakizuna)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, workers are mining a white sand that will be be used in tooth powder, for polishing rice to make uruchi, and other applications using polishing sand. Iga Province was a province in the area that is today Mie Prefecture. Iga bordered on Ise, Ōmi, Yamato, and Yamashiro Provinces.<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0323.

title: Catching Salmon in Echigo Province (越後国 鮭洲走を捕図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. The print depicts men catching salmon which have become stranded on a sandbar during their autumn migration up river.<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0364.
<br>Echigo (越後国, Echigo no kuni) was an old province in north-central Japan, on the shores of the Sea of Japan. It corresponds today to Niigata Prefecture, minus the island of Sado.

The trunks and baskets made in Tajima were especially beautiful and were "sent to the baths at Arima, and further still to Kobe, and also exported." - Source: The Industries of Japan: Together with an Account of its Agriculture, Forestry, Arts and Commerce, J. J. Rein, A. C. Armstrong and Son, 1889, p. 173.

title: Making Stretched Dried Abalone in Ise Province (同国 [伊勢国] 長鮑製之図 dōkoku [Ise no kuni] naga awabi sei no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting men and women cutting abalone (awabe) into long strips and laying them out to dry.<br> 
As in this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

title: Picking Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 1 (山城国 宇治茶摘図 一  Yamashiro no kuni Uji chatsumi zu ichi)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting women and children picking tea in Uji, Yamashiro Province. The Uji district was famed for its tea plantations and its high-quality tea. Historically, the "Uji powdered-tea industry was so important that it received bakufu protection, and farmers had to sell their tea through designated channels. Unlike farmers in other parts of the country, who cultivated tea on the footpaths between fields or on mountain slopes, Uji farmers grew their plants in groves. To produce a high-quality product, they latticed over their groves for superior grades of tea with straw or reed to protect the plants from the elements until the buds appeared." -  Source: Japan's Protoindustrial Elite: The Economic Foundations of the Gōnō, Edward E Prat, Cambridge: Harvard Univ. Asia Center, 1999. p. 52 
<br>Also see IHL.1481 Producing Uji Tea in Yamashiro Province, figure 2.

title: Bear Hunting for Gall in Kaga Province (加州熊并ニ胆ヲ取ル図 Kashū-gama narabi ni kimo o toru zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, the Asian black bear (note the white chest mark) is being hunted for his gall.  Kaga Province (加賀国, Kaga no kuni) was an old province in the area that is today the southern part of Ishikawa Prefecture. Ruled by the Maeda clan, the capital of Kaga was Kanazawa. Kaga bordered on Echizen, Etchū, Hida, and Noto Provinces. It was part of Hokurikudō Circuit.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0272.
<br>The artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" or, as in the case of this print, practiced in the same manner in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

title: Cultivating Wild Silkworms in Tajima Province (同国 [但馬国] 野蚕(蠶)養之図 dōkoku [Tajima no kuni] yasan yō no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting the tending of mulberry trees and silkworm cocoons.  When this print was issued in 1877 silk was Japan's leading export and by 1909 Japan surpassed China as the world's number one silk producer.<br>
In keeping with the importance of sericulture to Japan's economy and industrialization, seven prints in the series are devoted to it. The Exposition was essentially an industrial promotion opportunity providing a meeting place for Western technologies and their Japanese counterparts." "Silk production was the first example of an industry in which European producers deliberately sought out Japanese know-how" and "the source of Japan's first export technology." - Source: "Sericulture and the Origins of Japanese Industrialization", Tessa Morris-Suzuki, appearing JSTOR, Vol. 33, No.1, January 1992, p. 1-2-103; p. 121.

title: Catching Yellowtail in Tango Province (丹後國鰤追網之図 Tango no kuni buri ō ami no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. Boatmen are herding the Yellowtail (albacore tuna, binnega maguro) into nets which are then pulled in from the shore by others who are rotating two axles of winding rollers, which were anchored on the beach.
<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0374.

<br>Tango Province (丹後国, Tango no Kuni) was an old province in the area that is today northern Kyoto Prefecture facing the Sea of Japan. Tango bordered on Tajima, Tamba, and Wakasa provinces.  At various times both Maizuru and Miyazu were the capital and chief town of the province.<br>
As with this print, the artist based many of his designs on the designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued. (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

title: Manufacturing Imari Porcelain in Hizen, figure 1 (肥前伊万里陶器造図 一 Hizen imari tōki tsukuru zu ichi)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park, depicting women preparing porcelain clay to be used by two male potters shaping Imari ware. "Imari" refers to the port near Arita in Hizen from which the pottery was shipped.  Porcelain production, pioneered by Korean potters living in Japan, began in the early seventeenth century. See IHL.1494 Manufacturing Imari Porcelain, figure 2 in Hizen [Province] which depicts the painting of Imari porcelain.<br>
The artist based many of his designs on designs that appeared in the 1799 book Nihon Sankai Meisan Zue (Famous Sea and Land Products in Japan), leaving some question whether everything Hiroshige III portrayed in the series was truly the "state of the art" in 1877 when the series was issued.  (Although for many activities pictured, things would have looked much the same in 1877 as in 1799.) In many cases, the information in the scroll is also copied from the earlier work.

title: Making Sōmen in Noto Province (能登 素麺製造ノ図 Noto sōmen seizō no zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the making of sōmen, very thin, white Japanese noodles made of wheat flour.<br>
Sōmen was introduced to Japan from China during the Kamakura period (1185-1333) and were originally made at Zen monasteries.  In the mid-1400s "sōmen production requiring certain techniques and skill and a wide space, transferred from Zen monasteries to other artisans, marking the birth of the sōmen industry." - website of Kikkoman Company https://www.kikkoman.com/jp/kiifc/foodculture/pdf_17/e_001_004.pdf [accessed 8-25-23]

It depicts a traditional rain hat [sedge hats (sugegasa 菅笠)] maker in Kanazawa in Kaga Province (加賀国, Kaga no kuni) which is now part of Ichikawa Prefecture.

title: Watōnai, Master of Papier Mache (和藤内　はりこの名人 Watōnai hariko no meijin)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: In this print Kyōsai portrays the fierce warrior Watōnai (Coxinga) as a maker of paper mache daruma dolls. Watōnai is staring at paper mache tigers (tora), alluding to the play The Battles of Coxinga in which Watōnai vanquishes the fierce tiger.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Putting Her Husband Under Her Behind; Plastering Mud on Her Husband's Face (亭主を尻に敷く　亭主の顔へ泥を塗る Teishū o shiri ni shiku Teishū no kao e doro o nuru)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: In both the top and bottom scenes Kyōsai portrays a husband dominated by his wife. In the top scene, a wife sits on her husband smoking a pipe, while her husband holds a tabakobon (tobacco tray) for her comfort. The smoke from her pipe is spelling out the words noroma-yarō (のろま やろう), meaning "slow-witted man." To their left, their little girl, dressed in rags, is tracing out in the air (as children often due when learning new words) the characters from the pipe and learning from the bad example her parents are setting. In the bottom print, a wife is putting mud on her husband's face to keep him from seeing her lover hiding behind a hanging kimono, to whom she hands a love letter.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts fishermen on a beach in Tango Province gathering a net with their catch of Yellowtail (amberjack or albacore tuna, binnaga maguro). 
<br>Tango Province (丹後国, Tango no Kuni) was an old province in the area that is today northern Kyoto Prefecture facing the Sea of Japan. Tango bordered on Tajima, Tamba, and Wakasa provinces.  At various times both Maizuru and Miyazu were the capital and chief town of the province.

title: Making Arrowroot Powder in Yamato Province (大和国 葛之粉製図 Yamato no kuni kazura no kona sei zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, kuzu (Japanese arrowroot or pueraria) is being processed into starch.  Kuzu root is the traditional medicine of choice for a host of digestive disorders and it is also used as a cooking starch. Yamato Province (大和国, Yamato no Kuni) was a province of Japan, located in Kinai, corresponding to present-day Nara Prefecture in Honshū.<br>

title: Crane Hawk [falconry] in Iyo Province, figure 2 (伊予国 鶴鷹之図二 Iyo no kuni kaku yō no zu ni)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the capturing of a "crane hawk" using a tame crane hawk and a bird on a lure in Iyo Province. While the title of this print, shown in the leftmost red part of the scroll, does not give the location, the scroll itself tells us that the scene is taking place in Iyo (伊豫) which is now part of Ehime Prefecture on Shikoku in Southeast Japan. The small yellow cartouche informs us that the bird resting on the falconer's gloved hand is tame.

title: Making Dried Bonito Flakes in Tosa Province (同 [土佐国] 鰹節を製ス図 Dō katsuobushi o seisu zu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description: One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. In this print, katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes, a staple of Japanese cookery) are being processed. Tosa Province (土佐国 Tosa no kuni) is a former province of Japan in the area that is today Kōchi Prefecture on Shikoku. Tosa was bordered by Iyo and Awa Provinces. It was sometimes called Doshū (土州). "The waters of the bay [Tosa Bay] made possible a flourishing fishing industry, and dried bonito (katsuobushi) from Tosa found its way from the fishing villages, via the proper guild channels, to the markets of Osaka and Edo." - Source: Sakamoto Ryoma and the Meiji Restoration, Marius B. Jansen, Princeton University Press, 1961, p. 23.

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Teruhi no Miko in the play Uwanari (九世 市川団十郎 照日の神子・嫐)
creator:
Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
<br>Torii Kiyotada VII 七代 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
Ichikawa Danjūrō IX, in the upper left panel, playing the role of Teruhi no Miko in the kabuki play Uwanari. He wears a white hannya mask, denoting a vengeful female spirit of aristocratic background. Below Danjūrō is an unidentified actor playing the role of Kishō 吉聖. 
<br>The play Uwanari is variously translated as “The Mistress,” “The Second Wife,"“Jealousy,” and “Ambush of the Second Wife.” Uwanari was originally staged in 1699. While the original script has been lost, the play was re-written and re-staged in 1936.
<br>Uwanari, which means “second wife” and “jealousy”, is a torrid tale of jealousy, hate, and love. In it, a man divorces his wife and marries another woman. But while the newlyweds enjoy marital bliss, the jilted wife fumes, and plots her revenge on her ex-husband and the woman who replaced her. Passions will flare and dark schemes will bloom in this in riveting play, all told through impassioned dance.[1]
<br>"The Kabuki Eighteen," a collection of plays established by Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, stresses the special aragoto acting art of the Danjūrō line. In the Meiji period other acting families began to gather their most successful plays into similar collections.
<br>"This particular series of prints of Danjūrō VII's famous selection is the most well-known work by Torii Kiyotada (who is also confusingly known as Tadakiyo or Hasegawa Kanpei XIV), and was based on sketches by his father, Torii Kiyosada. Kiyotada was himself an amateur kabuki actor, and probably had a deep personal interest in the series."[2]
<br>The series was first published in 1895-1896 by the publisher Hasegawa Sumi and a second edition was released in 1927 by the publisher Shūbisha. Shūbisha issued the series in nine sets of two prints each, enclosed in an envelope. These reissued prints lack the original publisher's name and related information that appeared in the left column on the original Hasegawa release.

<br><br>[1] https://metropolitant.com/2015/06/22/ebizo-ichikawa-xi-returns-to-singapore-with-japan-theatre-2015/ [accessed 8-23-23]
<br>[2] website of David Bull's Mokuhankan https://mokuhankan.com/collection/index.php?id_for_display=00032 [accessed 8-23-23]

title: Sado Traveler's Journal (佐渡紀行 Sado kikō)

title: Bunraku Samurai
creator: Saitō Kiyoshi 斎藤清 (1907-1997)
description: In a January 2023 email in response to collector Jon Lipka's inquiry about this little known series of bunraku prints, Koko Nakayama of the Adachi Institute of Woodcut Prints wrote, "Adachi produced the Bunraku series of Kiyoshi Saito around the 50s (late Showa 20s). And the red small stamp on the back is ours. It was commission work just for the production, so we did not sell them. They were printed on the dyed in black non washi paper. It is quite an unusual production method for us, but it seems that we were asked to try it that way. Instead of printing with watercolors and letting them soak in the fibers of the washi paper, only this series was printed to let the colors sit on the paper with different types of paints, which creates the thick texture of the print as you mentioned. The black area we see underneath the other colors is the color of the dyed paper. It was ordered by either artist, Kiyoshi Saito or his publisher. After this series, we produced the other series (Children), but they were printed with a standard ukiyo-e style woodcut printing method."

title: Illustration of The Imperial Assembly of the House of Peers (帝国議会貴族院之図 Teikoku gikai kizokuin no zu)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: Picturing a meeting of the Imperial Diet's House of Peers, the upper house of the Imperial Diet consisting of appointed high-ranking nobles, this print was published in September 1890, two months before the actual first meeting of the House of Peers (貴族院 Kizoku-in) on November 29, 1890. This type of portrayal of future events was not unusual, as the Meiji government encouraged publishers to inform the public of new institutions.

title: Rat and Radish (untitled)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description: A small rat (nezumi) nibbles on a bright red radish. One of about fifty kachō-ga (bird and flower prints) in the shikishiban (almost square) format designed by Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927) for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) around the turn of last century. Multiple editions of this print exist. See IHL. 2141 for another impression of this print.

title: Seto Inland Sea, Tomonotsu (瀬戸内海 鞆之津 Setonaikai Tomonotsu)
creator: Tsuchiya Kōitsu 土屋光逸 (1870-1949)
description: The harbor at Tomonotsu in the waning glow of sunset. This image, originally published in the summer of 1940, is one of the artist's most famous and was reprinted numerous times by the publisher, Watanabe Shōzaburō, including one edition using re-carved blocks. This collection's print bears Watanabe's round 7mm seal indicating a later edition. The paper type, the coloration of the print and the presence of the date in the left-hand margin point to a mid-1950s to mid-1960s impression.

title: The Woodcutter from Mino (美濃樵夫 Mino no kikori)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
One of two known prints in the series Selections from Japanese History, issued by the little-known publisher Yazawa Hisakichi 矢沢久吉.  This triptych pictures the tale of a woodcutter from Mino whose filial piety brought about a visit by the Empress Gensho 元正天皇 (reign 715-724). On the left we see the woodcutter and his father in front of Yōrō Falls paying reverence to the Empress in her palanquin who has come to see the reported miracle of the falls' water turning into sake.
<br>As told in the Zenken kojitsu 前賢故実, during the 8th century a poor woodcutter went to the forest for firewood to warm his sick father. While searching, he came upon a waterfall whose water magically turned into sake. Filling his gourd he returns home to his ailing father who drinks the sake and miraculously recovers. 
<br>Hearing about this miracle, Empress Gensho visited the waterfall herself and determined that the miracle was a reward for the filial piety of the woodcutter. In honor of this miracle the Empress renamed the year of her reign "Yōrō", for the location of the waterfall.

title: The Courtesan of Eguchi; A Lotus in the Mud (江口ノ遊君 江口里 でい中乃蓮 Eguchi no yūkun, Eguchi no sato, Deichū no hasu)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description: The top portion of the print parodies the tale in which the bodhisattva Samantabhadra (Fugen), the protector of the Lotus Sutra, takes the guise of the courtesan Eguchi and offers shelter to a travelling monk. The bottom portion of the print, showing a lotus coming out of the mouth of courtesan, parodies the saying "a lotus in the mud", meaning that although the lotus grows in the mud, it is pure, the quintessential flower for Buddhists, as is the courtesan who tries to keep her heart pure although she is in a house of prostitution.<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Distant View of Snow and Komagatake (雪の駒ヶ岳遠望 Yuki no Komagatake enbō)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description: A horse-pulled sled and its driver pause to look out at Lake Onuma on Hokkaidō with Komagatake, an active volcano, in the background.

title: Children Blowing up the Belly of Hotei and Painting It Like a Candy (漢子以布袋腹擬吃飴)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
In this print a raucous group of children are painting the belly of Hotei, the god of happiness. It is one of forty prints (chūban size) which make up the series Sketches by Yoshitoshi (Yoshitoshi ryakuga). The series consists of forty humorous subjects originally printed in pairs on an ōban size sheet.

<br>Lea Baten in Playthings and Pastimes in Japanese Prints provides us with the following description of this print:

<br>"[C]hildren painting Hotei’s belly to look like a giant mochi cake. Hotei, one of the seven gods of good luck, is the Japanese god of happiness, for in his huge sack he carries toys and treasures for the flocks of children who swarm around him everywhere. He is very tolerant and allows the boisterous bevy many liberties, while pondering sleepily and not too seriously on the deterioration of today’s morals. Here, after having received paint and paintbrush, a mischievous youngster is trying out his artistic talents on Hotei’s immense hairy stomach to the joy of the others who are accompanying his efforts with jumping, laughter, and brandishing toys. A plum blossom and a pine needle adorn the patient Hotei’s grotesque belly, which is being blown up through a natural channel, to put it euphemistically, by a daring juvenile delinquent with a long bamboo pipe." - Source: Playthings and Pastimes in Japanese Prints, Lea Baten,Weatherhill, 1995, p. 110-112.

title: Raikō (Yorimitsu) Enters the Treasure Mountain (頼光宝之山入Yorimitsu takara no yama ni iru)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description: In this print Minamoto no Yorimitsu, also known as Minamoto no Raikō, in full armor prepares to lop off the head of the drunken ogre (oni) Shutendōji 酒呑童子 (literally, "drunken child"). Shutendōji, who can change form, here seen in the guise of a giant child, has fallen asleep on an armrest held up by coral legs. An overturned sake bowl (sakazuki) and a ladle lie in front attest to his being drunk and various treasures (takaramono) are scattered about. This print is one of forty prints (chūban size) which make up the series Sketches by Yoshitoshi (Yoshitoshi ryakuga). The series consists of forty humorous subjects originally printed in pairs on an ōban size sheet.

title: Lamps and Pots (洋燈とつぼ)
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description: A collector of old foreign language books, Kawakami loved depicting the objects he found in them. This 1955 print uses two of the artist's favorite objects -  lamps and a jar. In addition to numerous prints depicting these objects, Kawakami devoted an entire book to the lamp titled "ranpu" (ランプ)

title: Apricot in the Night, Nap, Dance of the Three-legged Kettle (夜の梅, 居眠り, 鼎踊り)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description:
Kyōsai gives us two comic scenes and one image of an apricot tree (in the stone-rubbing style) in this harimaze print.  The two comic scenes show us a drunken folk dance and a napping scholar being teased by two courtesans hiding behind a curtain.<br>
This series, consisting of a least ten prints, using "legitimate Kano school subjects as their themes" depicted in comic situations, made Kyōsai quite popular as an ukiyo-e artist. "At the time, these harimaze prints were cut into individual scenes and the small pieces were used to repair the holes in paper sliding doors and screens.  Kyosai’s humorous scenes were thus enjoyed in the everyday lives of the Japanese people." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 32-33, 220-225.

title: Egret, Ofuku, Coiffeur, Holes in Their Abdomen (連封一品, お福, 髪結い, 胴に穴あき)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description:
The three multi-color panels of the print are referred to as Ofuku (goddess of mirth who at the time of creation with her boisterous dance brought the sun goddess Amaterasu from her dark cave, bringing sunshine to the world), Holes in Their Abdomen and Coiffeur. The upper right panel depicting a crane and lotus bears the kanji characters 連封一品. The pairing of a crane (yipin niao) and lotus (lianhua) is a rebus for lianfeng yipin (may you continuously be promoted to the first rank).<br>
This series, consisting of a least ten prints, using "legitimate Kano school subjects as their themes" depicted in comic situations, made Kyōsai quite popular as an ukiyo-e artist. "At the time, these harimaze prints were cut into individual scenes and the small pieces were used to repair the holes in paper sliding doors and screens.  Kyosai’s humorous scenes were thus enjoyed in the everyday lives of the Japanese people." Source: Comic Genius: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Oikawa Shigeru, Clark Timothy and Forrer Matthi, Tokyo Shinbun, 1996, p. 32-33, 220-225.

title: Wind God (風神 Fūjin)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
Picturing the Shinto god of the wind Fūjin, one of the oldest Shinto gods, Fūjin was present at the creation of the world when he first let the winds out of his bag, clearing the morning mists and filling the space between heaven and earth allowing the sun to shine. He is portrayed as a terrifying dark demon carrying a large bag of winds on his shoulders. Fūjin is often seen paired with Raijin, the thunder god.<br>
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. The printer, Yoneda Minoru, has employed Sasajima's takuzuri technique, employed on the original print, of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press and dabbing the raised areas with an ink saturated pad giving the print a sculpted three-dimensional appearance.

title: Stone Path (石径)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
Picturing a pathway through the trees to what is likely a temple building, the printer, Yoneda Minoru, has employed Sasajima's takuzuri technique of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press and dabbing the raised areas with an ink saturated pad giving the print a sculpted three-dimensional appearance. For this print, he appears to have used a dyed kozo paper.<br>
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru.

title: Otonashi River at Ōji, No. 36 (王子音無川・三十六 Ōji Otonashigawa・sanjū roku)
creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)
description: This view of a dam, built in 1657, along the Otonashi River borrows heavily from the more famous print by Utagawa Hiroshige I issued in 1857 by the same publisher as part of the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei). The dam was popularly referred to at the "Great Waterfall."<br>By the 1960's the Otonashi River had been reduced to a concrete channel, but in 1985 a three year construction plan was begun to revive and beautify the 100 meter length of the river. Otonashi Shinsui Park was opened in 1988.

title: Series "Kyoto" No. 22 (シリーズ京都 No. 22)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: It is generally assumed, whether or not the artist has used the Japanese words "Niwa" (Garden) or "Kyoto" as part of a print's title, that the print portrays a Japanese garden.  Whether this print Series Kyoto No. 22 portrays the abstracted elements of a Japanese garden, e.g. rocks, water, trees, moss, plants, buildings, gates, lanterns and fences or the abstracted elements of a Kyoto city scene, the artist's forms and layers of color are left to the viewer to interpret.

creator: Kitagawa Utamaro 喜多川歌麿 (1753-1806) - after the artist

title: Konjiki Pagoda (平泉金色堂)
creator: Kawase Hasui 川瀬巴水 (1883-1957) - after the artist
description:
A small format unsigned print very similar to a design created by Kawase Hasui for the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō. Konjiki-dō (Golden Hall) is part of the Chūson-ji Temple complex. (Reference Hp-47 in "Kawase Hasui, The Complete Woodblock Prints, Volume 1" Hotei Publishing, 2003, p. 143.)
See IHL.0654 for another similar design of Konjiki-dō by another unknown artist.
<br><b>Small Format Prints - Shin Hanga and Ukiyo-e Reprints</b><br>
Small hand-printed woodblock prints started to appear in large numbers in the 1930s to fill the need for inexpensive souvenirs and greeting cards. They are variously referred to as postcard size prints (hagakiban 葉書版), miniature prints and small prints and range in size from approximately 2 x 3 in. to 3.5 x 6 in. 
<br>Publishers who issued small prints included Takemura Hideo, Shōbidō Tanaka, Doi Sasaichi (DoiHangaten), Baba Nobuhiko, Bijutshusha, Shima Art Company, and Watanabe Shōzaburō.
<br>The designs for these small prints were often taken from previously designed ōban-size prints or were newly created by both well-known, little known and unknown artists. Some of the designs bear signatures or seals of known artists, some bear signatures or seals that cannot be read or linked with known artists and some have no signatures or seals at all, making attribution to a specific artist difficult, if not impossible.
<br>The subject matter for the bulk of these small shin hanga prints is landscape, particularly of well-known scenic spots throughout Japan, and kachō-ga (bird and flower prints). The small size reproductions of ukiyo-e prints, copy (or borrow), from Edo-period designs and also feature landscapes along with bijinga (pictures of beautiful women) and kachō-ga. In discussing the small reproductions of ukiyo-e the publisher Watanabe notes, "By 'reproductions' we mean the masterpieces of the great ukiyo-e (color –print) masters reprinted as nearly as possible like the originals, with the same technique and still as in olden times. Such reproductions serve the purpose of enabling us to appreciate the composition and coloring of the originals, which are usually very rare."

title: Peacock and Cherry Blossom
creator: Ohara Koson 小原古邨 (Shōson 祥邨) (1877-1945)
description: This print picturing a peacock and peahen on cherry tree branch was tipped into the 1936 Watanabe sales catalog, Catalogue of Wood-cut Color Prints, of S. Watanabe, p. 39.  On p. 36 of that catalog the print is titled "Peacock and cherry blossom." Postcard size prints were first offered by Watanabe in his 1931 sales catalog.

title: Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Volume 2 (錦絵修身談 巻二 Nishiki-e Shūshindan kanni)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
Volume two of a six volume set of moral instruction textbooks designed for young children. Each volume contains from one to three color woodblock prints by one of the most popular artists of the time Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), who also designed the black and white illustrations that accompanied the short stories written by Yamana Tomesaburō, based upon the morally illustrative actions of adults and children from Japan, China and the West.<br>
This volume contains three color woodblock prints by Yoshitoshi titled The Loyalty of Kusunoki Masashige 楠正成の忠 (IHL.1539a), Wang Lan Harmony Between Siblings 王覧の悌 (IHL.1539b) and The Benevolence of Harry Lane エリーレーンの仁  (IHL.1539c) along with fifteen short stories and eight black and white illustrations.

title: The Loyalty of Kusunoki Masashige (楠正成の忠)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
In this print, one of three color prints in Volume 2 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays Kusonoki's parting speech to his son at Sakura Station on his way to the Battle of Minatogawa, telling his eleven year old son Masatsura "I feel this is the last time I will see your face in this life."  He orders him  to return home to Kawachi to continue the family line and to support the emperor until death, ending by saying "This will be your most important filial duty to me."
For the other two color prints in this volume see IHL.1539b and IHL.1539c.

In this print, one of three color prints in Volume 2 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays a young Wang Lan (206-278) protecting his older half-brother Wang Xiang (185-269) from the wrath of his mother, who favored her own son. After her husband's death, she vowed to remain chaste thereby fulfilling the "li" of a woman. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1540b.

title: The Frugality of Kuroda Josui (黒田如水の倹)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi 月岡芳年 (1839-1892)
description:
In this print, one two color prints in Volume 4 of Brocade Pictures for Moral Education, Yoshitoshi portrays the samurai and Christian convert Kuroda Jusoi (1546-1604) who was known for his frugality and his generosity. Here he has instructed his servant to remove the flesh from some tai he had been sent as a present and make soup of the bones for he and his guests, who had borrowed money from him. His guests seeing this severe economy worried that they would be charged high interest on their loan but Kuroda would not even take the principal. The print's large cartouche provides an explanation suitable for a child of elementary school age to understand. For the other color print in this volume see IHL.1541b.

title: Sponsored by the Votive Women's Association, print 18, Lake Hamana and  Futaminoura (納札 婦人會 催主, 十八・濱各湖・二見浦)
creator: Takeda Keihō 竹田敬方 (1873-1942)
description:
One of a set of at least eighteen votive prints (nōsatsu 納札 or senjafuda 千社札) picturing various scenic places designed by the painter Takeda Keihō, a student of the Meiji  era nihonga painter and woodblock designer Mizuno Toshikata (1866-1908) for an unknown women's votive association. Over the years votive temple offerings evolved from small wood plaques, to small paper slips bearing the names of pilgrims, attached by pilgrims to Buddhist and Shinto shrine buildings, to woodblock printed designs called kōkanfuda (交換札), to be shared among members of votive associations (nōsatsukai) at nōsatsu exchange meetings. The various motifs of kōkanfuda were inspired by nishiki-e themes: kabuki actors, famous landscapes, scenes from popular literature, and legendary and mythical figures.  
<br>This print provides views of Lake Hamana and  Meoto Iwa (Wedded Rocks) at Futaminoura.

title: Asakusa Kinryūzan (浅草金龍山 )
creator: Utagawa Kunitoshi 歌川国利 (1847-1899)
description: Kunitoshi did a number of quick sketches for a few Meiji-era publishers which were turned into sloppily produced prints, including this print. This print pictures part of the grounds of Kinryūzan Sensoji Temple, which dates back to 628, including the Five-Storied Pagoda (Gojūnotō) first built in 942, Hozomon Gate to its right and Hondō, the main hall, on the left in the foreground. The area around the temple was filled with shops and was a popular entertainment center, as it is today.

title: Onoe Kikugorō V as Shinohara Kunimoto and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Saigō Takamori in the play Mikawa gofūdo-ki (篠原国幹尾上菊五郎・西郷隆盛 市川 團十郎・三河後風土記)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) as the pro-government soldier Shinohara Kunimoto (1836-1877) and, in the top inset, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Saigō Takamori, the leader of the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion, in the play The Morning East Wind Clearing the Clouds of the Southwest (Okige no Kumo Harau Asagochi) performed at the Shintomi-za in March 1878.  According to Brandon and Leiter, "The scenes of modern warfare, with exploding artillery shells (simulated by fireworks) and gunfire, were a great success" and were "an extremely important step toward contemporary realism." Source: Kabuki Plays on Stage: Restoration and Reform, 1872-1905, ed., James R. Brandon, Samuel L. Leiter, University of Hawaii Press, 2003, p. 91.
<br><br>In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

title: Autumn Moon at Takanawa, No. 35 (高輪秋月 三十五 Takanawa shūgetsu)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description:
A view of Edo Bay at Takanawa with wild geese flying under an autumn moon. Takanawa at Shiba bordered Edo and the evening travelers going about their business would have to pass through a checkpoint at the town gate (machikido) into Edo. The town gate would close at about 10 PM and re-open at daybreak.<br>
As with many of Hiroshige II's prints, the prints comprising the series Forty-Eight Famous Views of Edo borrowed from the designs of his teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I.

title: Hollyhock Slope, No. 41 (葵坂 四十一 Aoi-zaka)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige II 二代 歌川広重 (1826-1869)
description: A view of the dam along the Hollyhock Slope in Minoato-ku. According to Edo Meisho Zue, a gazetteer of Edo published in the 1810s, "Beside the dam on the other side of the corner checkpoint, which is on the north side of the reservoir, is an area which has been planted with aoi, hollyhocks. This area is called Hollyhock Hill, and the slope that runs downwards to the east from here is called Aoizaka, Hollyhock Slope." The tiled hut in the foreground and the other tiled hut on the hill to the left seem to be the corner checkpoints, or tsujibansho, mentioned in the gazetteer. These checkpoints were set up in this area where samurai and noblemen resided to maintain surveillance and keep order. The road sloping to the left is probably Aoizaka; the reservoir and the dam are on the right.<br>As with many of Hiroshige II's prints, the prints comprising the series Forty-Eight Famous Views of Edo borrowed from the designs of his teacher, Utagawa Hiroshige I.

title: End of Summer (夏の終り)
creator: Yuki Rei 由木礼 (1928-2003)
description:
One of Rei's semi-abstract landscapes created from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. "The texture of the woodblock itself creates dappled tones and fragile shades. The works are light, yet the source of the light is hidden behind fences and arches.  It is a light defined by shadows, creating a mood of timeless suspension.<br>
"Leafless branches cast foreground shadows, mysteriously real and abstract, stark and delicate. The texture of the block, structural unity of the geometric ground figures, subdued coloration and shading, and magical, waving forms together create a locus, a place that is both definite and infinite, haunting and unassuming, vague and too vivid to be mere fantasy." - Source: Who's Who in Modern Japanese Prints, Francis Blakemore, Weatherhill, 1975, p. 247.

title: Sukiya Bridge (数寄屋橋 Sukiyabashi)
creator: Hiratsuka Un'ichi 平塚運一 (1895-1997)
description:
One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Last Tokyo. This print was one of eight designs for the series which originally appeared in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This 1945 print was made from recut blocks. It is one of two designs that Hiratsuka contributed to Scenes of Last Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955).<br>
The building in the centre is the main office of Asahi Shimbun, one of Japan's biggest newspapers, completed in 1927. The bridge was demolished in 1957, and the canal filled in.
<br><br>SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
<br>Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. -  Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

title: Tiger (寅)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
Picturing a tiger with his prey, a parrot, in his mouth, and representing the third sign of the zodiac, this print was published on January 1, 1903, as dated in its left margin.  Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals, the series which this print is a part of, was originally issued c. 1901, again in 1903 and then reissued by Unsōdō Publishing several times into the early 1940s. As this print has a centerfold, it may have been issued as part of a folding album with the other eleven prints representing the animals in the zodiac, or it may have been issued as a stand-alone print. 

<br>Each of the prints in Seihō's Album of the Twelve Calendrical Animals is essentially a woodblock facsimile of what must have been an original watercolor created by Seihō, a nihonga, Maruyama-Shijō school painter. In describing an earlier book of prints by the artist, also published by Unsōdō Publishing, Jack Hillier notes that the Meiji printmakers responded to the challenge of reproducing Seihō's watercolors, with "marvelous interpretive skills" and goes on to say “There is, in truth, a complete abnegation of the medium qua woodcut; its own virtues of bold line and flat wash are sacrificed in the cause of a facsimile rendering of a water-colour: this was a fundamental change in technique which led to incredible feats of reproduction…”

title: Fish (folding fan design)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description: A silver-yellow fish swims across this design for a folding fan by Seihō.

title: Peacefully Sleeping Couple
creator: Kondō Kōichiro 近藤浩一路 (1884–1962)
description: This print is one of at least forty prints created by the painter/manga artist Kondō Kōichiro 近藤浩一路 (1884–1962) and the poet/journalist Inoue Kenkabō 井上剣花坊 (1870-1934) in 1930, which pair a senryū (short humorous verse), almost all of which were written by Kenkabō, with an illustration by Kondō.<br>In this print the senryū is, for now, unread - and the illustration pictures a couple sleeping peacefully.<br>All the titles assigned to prints in this series are more-or-less descriptive of the images, enhanced, on occasion, by isolated words translated from the senryū on the print. They are in no way translations of the senryū, which are extremely difficult to translate.

title: Blue and White Space
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description: This print was included in the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, published in 1973.  Using woodblock for the irregular shapes defining the trapezoid, silkscreen for the yellow and the blue patterns and some type of hole punch to create a grid pattern of 5/16" circular holes Funasaka gives us another eye-pleasing print in his long-running series Blue and White Space.

title: Birth of Shakyamuni Buddha (untitled)
creator: Unidentified
description: In this print by an unidentified artist, Shakyamuni receives his first bath, the water of which is said to have been poured down from the heavens. He is pointing to the heavens with his right hand and to the earth with his left. He is naked apart from a cloth wrapped around his waist, which makes it clear that this is as a depiction of the baby Buddha. - Source: Global Nepali Museum, from a description of a sculpture depicting the birth of the founder of Buddhism, Shakyamuni.

title: Four image harimaze-e: Old Story (昔咄 Mukashi banashi), Rape Blossoms and Crane (菜の花に鶴 Nanohana ni tsuru), Sumida River (すみた川 Sumidagawa), Okina (翁)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
The artist Utagawa Hiroshige III, a disciple of the great Utagawa Hiroshige I (1797-1858), created these sketches (manga) in 1879, which were arranged three, four or five to a single sheet as a harimaze-e. Titled "Sketches by Ryūsai," Ryūsai being an artist name (gō) of Hiroshige III, they were very much in the tradition of his master Hiroshige I, who is sometimes credited as the inventor of the print genre harimaze, which can be literally translated as "paste and mix pictures" and is commonly translated as "cut-out pictures."
<br>The height of their popularity was in the mid-1800s and these inexpensive prints were purchased and then often cut-apart and pasted onto Japanese screens or into scrapbooks. Harimazi-e could include the work of multiple artists or just a single artist, as in the case of these harimaze-e. For other examples of harimazi-e in this collection see Kawanabe Kyōsai (1831-1889) and his works from the series Kyōsai Manga.

<br>The Four Panels:
<br>top right: Old Story 昔咄 (The illustration appears to relate to the folktale the Tongue-Cut Sparrow 舌切り雀.)
<br>top left: Chrysanthemum Flower and Crane 菊の花に鶴
<br>bottom left: Sumida River すみた川
<br>bottom right: Okina 翁

Saigō is pictured brush in hand having just completed one of his many instructive verses. Saigō adopted the pen name Nanshū, meaning "south," during his five years in exile on the island of Oshima.

title: The Maiden at Dōjō Temple  (京鹿子娘道成寺 Kyōkanoko Musume Dōjōji)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: This print advertises the March 1890 performance at the Kabuki-za of one of the greatest works of dance in Kabuki, Kyōkanoko Musume Dōjōji, starring Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Hanako the shirabyōshi dancer, as seen in the center sheet. In this scene, Hanako, wearing a tall eboshi hat, dances for three priests at the temple. The temple bell, that figures prominently in the story, can be seen in the upper right hand corner and the  signboard on the left sheet reads "Women forbidden at the present time" (‘Nyonin kinsei toji’, 女人禁制 当時).<br>The actors  and their roles depicted in the print are, from right to left, Ichikawa Sumizō 市川寿美蔵 as the priest Kurokumobō 黒雲坊, Ichikawa Shinzō 市川新蔵 as the priest Shirakumobō 白雲坊, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX 市川団十郎 as the shirabyōshi dancer Hanako 白拍子花子 and Ichikawa Gonjūrō 市川権十郎 as the priest Jōeibō 浄永坊.

title: Raising a banner (untitled)
creator: Igawa Sengai 井川洗厓 (1876-1961)
description:
A rough looking man appears to be raising a banner on tall tree. Likely an illustration for a book. 
<br>The designer of this woodblock print, Igawa Sengai, is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as <i>Kingu</i> (King), <i>Fujin gahō</i> (Graphic Magazine for Women) and <i>Kōdan Kurabu</i> (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).

title: Flying Cloud Around Mt. Fuji・E (飛雲富士・E Hiun Fuji・E)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description: One of at least three different prints by Sasajima bearing the same title of Hiun Fuji [Flying Cloud(s) Around Mt. Fuji]. Sasajima has used a heavier paper for this print and it bears a much lighter embossing than other prints in this collection printed using his "takuzuri" process, whereby damp paper is forced into the grooves of a carved woodblock with a press, to give a print a dynamic three-dimensional effect. He has hand-applied black ink directly on the raised areas of the print.
