title: Shakkyō 石橋 (Stone Bridge)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br> Summary of the play Shakkyō: "A priest [the Monk Jakushō] goes to China to visit famous Buddhist places. One day he is about to cross a stone bridge across a ravine when child appears. He hears from the child that since the land on the other side of the bridge is the Paradise of the deity Monju Bosatsu [Manjusri Bodhisattva], even famous priests in olden times could only cross it after long and severe religious training. Telling the priest that if he waits by the bridge he will see something wonderful, the child disappears. After a while, a lion emerges and gambols and dances among the peony flowers - the king of beast enjoying the most majestic of flowers." -  A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 158-159.

title: Kumasaka 熊坂 (The Robber)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume three of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br>Summary of the play Kumasaka: "A travelling priest stops at Akasaka in Mino Province and meets another priest who, after talking with him, gives him lodging for the night.  This second priest is in reality the ghost of Kumasaka no Chōhan, a robber, and in the dream of the real priest that night the spirit appears and describers how he was killed by the young Ushikawa." -  A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 89.

title: Funa Benkei 船弁慶 (Benkei in the Boat)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br> Summary of the play Funa Benkei: "Benkei explains that in an attempt to clear himself of the suspicion which Yoritomo has about his younger brother's intentions, Yoshitsune has left the capital and come down to Daimotsu Bay.  There Shizuka Gozen joins her lover Yoshitsune, but as Benkei insists that she must return to the capital, they have a farewell party at which Shizuka dances, and then she goes off alone. Yoshitsune and his men then put out to sea in a boat, but suddenly black clouds form, the seas rise, and the ghost of Taira no Tomomori comes upon them. It tries to seize Yoshitsune and carry him down into the sea to suffer the same fate as Tomomori himself, but is eventually driven off by the priestly poser of Benkei." -  A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 35-36.

title: Kamo 加茂
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume three of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br> Summary of the play Kamo: "A priest from the shrine in Muro in Harima province makes a pilgrimage to the sister shrine of Kamo Myōjin and there sees a white-feathered arrow set up beside the river. He learns from a woman who, with a companion, comes there to draw water, that when long ago a woman of the Hata family picked up such an arrow floating in the river and carried it home, she miraculously conceived and gave birth to a son. The child was the god Wake-ikazuchi and he, his mother and the arrow are now revered as the three gods of the Kamo Shrine. Telling the priest that she is one of these gods, the woman disappears with her companion. Later the goddess and her son Wake-ikazuchi come forth to dance and promise to protect the land and its people."- A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 67-68.

title: Yoroboshi 弱法師 (The Priest with the Faltering Tread)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br>Summary of the play Yoroboshi: "Believing some gossip he heard about his son Shuntoku, Michitoshi turned him out of his house. Deeply regretting his cruelty now, he goes on a pilgrimage to the Tennō-ji temple and there sees his son again - but he has become a beggar and having lost his sight as well, is known as 'the priest with the faltering tread.' He sings a song about the temple and then, when the other people go and leave the two of them alone, Michitoshi tells his son who he is and, full of happiness at having found him again, takes him by the arm to lead him home." -  A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 217-218.

title: Hanagatami 花筐 (The Flower Basket)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume four of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br> Summary of the play Hanagatami : "The Crown Prince Ōatobe having suddenly left his country retreat to go to the capital to succeed his father, a servant gives Teruhi-no-mai, the lady who has been the Prince's constant companion, a letter and a flower basket which he has left for her. Some time later Ōatobe, now the Emperor Keitai, is viewing the maples in autumn when a mad woman comes along carrying a flower basket. This is Teruhi who, distracted by her love for the Prince, has come to try to see him. Happy now that she has met him again, Teruhi is once more taken into the Emperor's favour and returns with him to the capital." -  A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 49-50.

title: Semimaru 蝉丸
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume five of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br> Summary of the play Semimaru: "On the order of the Emperor Daigo, a Court official takes Prince Semimaru, who has been blind since he was a child, to Ōsaka-yama and leaves him there with only his lute to comfort him. The Prince accepts his lot with resignation, feeling that his blindness is the result of some failure of his in a previous existence, and that the present apparent cruelty of his father is only due to a desire to help him gain a happier fate in a future life. Meanwhile, his sister Princess Sakagami has gone out of her mind and is now a wild-haired figure, wandering aimlessly from place to place. She comes one day to Ōsaka-yama and, attracted by the sound of Semimaru's lute, finds her brother again. For a while they forget their loneliness as they talk together and comfort each other, but then the Princess leaves him and continues her sad wanderings." -  A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 154-155.

title: Sumidagawa (隅田川)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume five of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934. The woodblock prints were created by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963), the photographs by Genzō Kitazumi (1898-1982), the album's text was written by Kanze Sakon (1895-1939), the 24th head (sōke) of the Kanze School and Nō actor, and the preface was written by Sasakawa Rinfu (active 1920s-1930s).<br>Synopsis of Play Sumidagawa: "A ferryman on the Sumida-gawa is told by a traveller about to cross the river that following close behind is a woman whose mind has been unbalanced ever since her son was taken from her. He therefore waits for her to arrive, and then begins to cross the river. On the way, the traveller asks the reason for the crowd of people on the other bank. The boatman tells him that they are there to perform a mass for a boy of about eleven years of age, the son of one Yoshida from the capital, who died there a year ago after being taken from his home. At this, the woman weeps bitterly, and reveals that the boy was the son she is seeking. The ferryman takes her to the grave and when they recite prayers there, the boy's voice is heard. The mother prays again and her son appears to her. But when she reaches out for him he is no longer there, and with the coming of dawn he disappears again forever." - source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 173-174.

title: Shōjō 猩々 (The Tippling Elf)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: From volume five of a twenty volume album titled Nō Sugata consisting of text, photographs, illustrations and color woodblock prints published by Unsōdō Publishing over the period 1931-1934.<br> Summary of the play Shōjō: "A man named Kō-fū, living in ancient China, explains that by following a dream which he had in reward for his filial piety and which told him to sell wine in the market, he has become a prosperous man. At the market, there is one particular person who always comes to him to buy wine, and since he told the dealer that he is an elf living in the sea, the man has come down to the estuary to wait for him to appear. creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Kitaoka depicts the lower level gardens and Ogonchi Pond at Kokedera (Moss Temple), also known as Saihoji.<br>Saihoji Temple belongs to the Rinzai school of Japanese Buddhism. In 1994 the site was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The gardens built by Muso Soseki (a nationally designated scenic and historic site) consist of an upper level of dry karesansui-style rock arrangements and a lower level built around Ogonchi Pond, which is shaped like the Chinese character meaning "heart."  Blanketed by more than 120 species of moss, the temple is popularly and affectionately known as Kokedera ("Moss Temple").

title: Treasure of Saruwaka (猿若の宝物 Saruwaka no Takaramono)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description: This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print)  picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō explaining the origins of the gold military baton given to Saruwaka Kanzaburō (1597?-1658, the founder of Edo-style kabuki and its first licensed kabuki theater in 1624.)  The baton was one of the rewards given to Kanzaburō by the Shogun as a reward for entertaining the Shogun while he was on his pleasure boat Atakmaru in Edo bay in 1633. This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

title: Listening to Rumors (風聞きゝFūbunkiki)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts a soba (buckwheat noodle) stand in front of the Ichimuraza Theater, one of the three officially recognized Kabuki theaters of Edo. The word "nihachi" (二八, literally 'two-eight'), written on the noodle stand, came from the noodles that cost sixteen (two times eight) mon a bowl and also from the proportion of 20 parts udon flour to 80 parts soba flour.
<br>"With the excitement of the experience still in the air, fellow theatre aficionados might pass time after the performance exchanging opinions about what they had seen, as depicted in this print of men standing around talking in front of the theatre while slurping noodles from a food cart. Collecting this gossip was useful to the theatres. Spies would be sent out to listen in, and according to what they heard, acts might be replaced or play content might otherwise be modified. This print depicts a time before the three licensed Edo theatres (Edo sanza) were forced to move to Saruwaka-chō in Asakusa as a result of the Tenpō Reforms (1841-1843)." Source: Art Research Center, Ritsumeikan University https://www.arc.ritsumei.ac.jp/lib/vm/kabuki2015_e/2015/11/post-17.html [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

title: Auspicious Plays (ワキ狂言 Waki kyōgen)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description: This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts an annual waki kyogen performance starting at dawn, announced by the banging of the large drum, consisting of auspicious dances such as the Dance of the Seven Lucky Gods and the Sanboso dance.  Reference is made in the scroll to both the Ichimura-za and Nakamura-za theaters in Edo. <br>This print is a later undated edition of IHL.0673. This later edition is characterized by an embossed border.

title: Curtain-Raiser Performance (序開きJobiraki)

title: Praying to the Ōtsu Inari Shrine in 3rd Floor Dressing Room (大津稲荷 Ōtsu Inari)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts an actor praying at an Inari shrine in the third floor dressing room of a Kabuki theater.  Chief of the pantheon of gods worshiped under the name Inari, Ame-no-uzume-no-mikoto (the heaven-alarming-female whose dance for the Sun Goddess, Amaterasu, helped restore light to the world) is the "patron deity of all professional actors, for, as she does, they lighten the hearts of men, comfort them in distress, and make the sun shine again.  An Inari shrine, large or small, is installed in every Kabuki theatre . . . ." - Source: The Kabuki Theatre, Earle Ernst, University Press of Hawaii, 1974, p. 164.
<br>This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

title: Front Entrance Ticket Sellers (木戸羽織 Kido haori)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description:
This print, part of a series of twenty-five prints (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater, depicts kidoban, employed by the theater, at the front entrance encouraging passerby to purchase tickets. Sometimes kidoban would imitate actors to entice people to buy tickets. "Their attire included a small towel (tenugui) wrapped around the face and a long outer garment (haori), which was a gift from the troupe's top female-role actor and was therefore marked with that actor's crest. The small towel and folding fan were provided by the troupe leader (the top male-role actor) and carried his crest, so passersby would know right away who the troupe's top stars were." - Source: Art Research Center, Ritsumeikan University http://www.arc.ritsumei.ac.jp/lib/vm/kabuki2015_e/2015/11/b09.html [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>This print is a later undated edition characterized by an embossed border.

title: Bijin in brown kimono (untitled)
creator: Igawa Sengai 井川洗厓 (1876-1961)
description:
Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as <i>Kingu</i> (King), <i>Fujin gahō</i> (Graphic Magazine for Women) and <i>Kōdan Kurabu</i> (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).
<br> This untitled offset-printed color lithograph bijin kuchi-e (frontispiece illustrations of beautiful women) with its characteristic tri-fold, appeared in an unknown magazine. 

<br><br>THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E<br>

The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

title: Kanadehon Chūshingura, Act VI (仮名手本忠臣蔵、六段目)
creator: Yūsai Toshiaki 幽斎年章 (1864-1921)
description: One of a series of twelve prints portraying a Kabuki version of the play Kanadehon Chūshingura. This particular print was likely part of an album as it bears a vertical centerfold and has remnants of being mounted along the left edge verso. Prints in this series are dated either 1896 or 1897.<br>In this scene two of the rōnin, Gōemon and Yagorō, visit Kanpei (seated with his head bowed) to return the money he contributed to erect a monument to their dead master, saying: "It would not please his spirit if we paid for the monument with money taken from a man who had proved disloyal and faithless to his lordship." In the background on the left we see Okaru (Kanpei's lover) being carried by a palanquin to a brothel and behind Kanpei sits Okaru's mother weeping.

title: Morning Mist, Burning Fields  (三十六富士朝霧野焼  Asagiri noyaki)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description: Hagiwara’s Thirty-Six Fujis series is the artist’s only excursion into landscape. It is his homage to the sacred mountain and to past ukiyo-e artists, such as Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1848) and Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858). Living near Mount Fuji, Hagiwara gathered his impressions of the mountain for over fifteen years before beginning work on this series. Toward the end of the project he wrote: “Just when I think I have grasped [Fuji], it slips through my hands. Let's pick up this ‘slippery Fuji’ and keep on going.” Hagiwara captures a view of Fuji from the town of Ōhara on a spring morning, during the annual burning of grasslands (noyaki) on the northern foot of the mountain.

title: Remains of Flowers (三十六富士名残の花 Nagori no hana)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description: Hagiwara’s Thirty-Six Fujis series is the artist’s only excursion into landscape. It is his homage to the sacred mountain and to past ukiyo-e artists, such as Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1848) and Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858). Living near Mount Fuji, Hagiwara gathered his impressions of the mountain for over fifteen years before beginning work on this series. Toward the end of the project he wrote: “Just when I think I have grasped [Fuji], it slips through my hands. Let's pick up this ‘slippery Fuji’ and keep on going.”  In this print Hagiwara pictures the remnants of the moss phlox (shibazakura) that surrounds Mount Fuji in spring.  The flowers begin to bloom at the end of April with most of them dying at the end of May.  Hagiwara masterfully employs his unique color overlay technique to intensify his abstract coloration and a subtle dusting of ground mica highlights the colors.

title: Sayama Motosuke from the novel The Gold Demon  (狭山元輔・金色夜叉)
creator: Igawa Sengai 井川洗厓 (1876-1961)
description:
One of eight prints, seven of which are woodblock prints, appearing in the 1920 "pocket edition" (shukusatsu 縮刷), published by Shunyōdō 春葉堂, of The Gold Demon 金色夜叉 by the popular novelist and poet Ozaki Kōyō 尾崎紅葉 (1868-1903).<br>
Sengai's illustration is that of the character Sayama Motosuke, the true love of O’Shizu (really Aiko of the Kashiwaya geisha house), who makes a suicide pact with her. Pictured are the rings they exchanged the night of their planned suicide, which was interrupted by the novel's main character, Kan’ichi.
<br>For other prints appearing in the novel see IHL.1642, IHL. 1643 and IHL.1644.
<br>Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to such popular magazines such as Kingu (King), Fujin gahō (Graphic Magazine for Women) and Kōdan Kurabu (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) A Pair of Pines (Hiyoku no matsu), Lady Shizuka (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and The Gold Demon (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).

<br>Shunsen's illustration is that of the character Kamata Tetsuya, a high school friend of the main character Hazama Kan'ichi. Kamata has become a successful attaché in the Diplomatic Service and Hazama a usurer. Kamata pays off a debt owed to Hazama by one of their mutual friends, but hard feelings result.
<br>For other prints appearing in the novel see IHL.1641, IHL. 1643 and IHL.1644.
<br>Ozaki Kōyō, born in Tokyo, became a novelist at an early age, publishing his first novel Love Confessions of Two Nuns (Ninin bikuni irozange) in 1889. His subsequent novels were all serialized by the newspaper Yomiuri shinbun which Ozaki was the literary editor for. When he died in 1903, his most successful novel The Gold Demon was not yet complete, although already in serialization.

title: Mochizuki 望月
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
The print depicts the climatic scene in the play Mochizuki sometimes attributed to the playwright Sa-ami (15th c.). "Thirteen years ago, the evil Mochizuki no Akinaga had killed Yasuda no Tomoharu. Now Mochizuki is staying at an inn, having just returned from Kyoto where he claimed Yasuda’s property. Unbeknownst to the murderer, the innkeeper Kozawa had been a retainer of Yasuda. Also at the inn are Yasuda’s widow and son. The three plot revenge: they offer to entertain Mochizuki. While the widow sings, her son plays a drum and then dances. Kozawa appears dressed as a lion dancer and is able to approach and stab Mochizuki to death." - Source: Ruth Chandler Williamson Gallery, Scripps College http://web-kiosk.scrippscollege.edu/Obj21710?sid=83782&x=1666787 [accessed 8-17-23]
<br><br>Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. Its 261 prints include 221 depicting Noh plays, 27 depicting kyōgen plays and 13 miscellaneous prints, e.g. props, costumes and five illustrated tables of content. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

title: Kashihara Shrine, Yamato  (大和橿原神宮 Yamato Kashihara jingū)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
Print number thirteen (十三, as printed in the right margin) in the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi shiseki meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941, depicting the large plaza in which sits the shrine's first gate (Kashihara jingū daiichi torii). The obelisk to the right is engraved with the shrine's name 橿原神宮.
<br>Kashihara jingū is a Shinto shrine located in the city of Kashihara, Nara Prefecture, Japan. The shrine's vast precincts cover an area of roughly 500,000 square meters. It was built in 1889 at the site of the Kashihara-gū where Japan's mythical first emperor, Emperor Jimmu, is said to have acceded to the throne on February 11, 660 BC.
<br>The use of the word Yamato 大和 in the print's title references the national foundation story embodied by Emperor Jimmu and the Kigen 2600 celebrations, starting in 1940, that marked the mythical 2,600th anniversary of Japan's founding. These celebrations which were years in the planning, were used to build popular support for Japan's territorial ambitions. More than 12,000 events were held to commemorate the anniversary including the publishing of this print series. Commenting on the series the artist writes that his devotion to the sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the "dignity of the national polity," going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.
<br><br>SCENES OF SACRED AND HISTORIC PLACES and THIRTY-SIX VIEWS OF MOUNT FUJI - A CELEBRATION OF KIGEN 2600
<br>The print artist Tokuriki and the publisher Uchida created two series of prints to mark Kigen 2600, or the 2600th year of Japan's mythical founding as a nation. The first, a paean to Mount Fuji, a sacred site of pilgrimage and worship, titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, harkened back to Hokusai’s famous 1831 series of the same name. The second series, Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, capitalized on the nationalist ideology that Japan was a divine land, presenting overtly nationalistic landscapes including shrines, temples, castles, places associated with the divine origins of Japan, Meiji era history and samurai culture.
<br><br>In his commentary on the series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places, the artist wrote that his devotion to these sites is intended to demonstrate to the people the dignity of the national polity, going on to say that he advocates prints as a means of providing comfort and pleasure to the wholesome citizens of the nation.

title: Usa Shrine 宇佐神宮 (Usa jingū]
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
Print number nineteen (十九, as printed in the right margin) in the fifty print series Scenes of Sacred and Historic Places (Seichi Shiseki Meisho) published by Uchida Art Co. Ltd. in 1941. Tokuriki gives us a view of the sacred bridge [神橋 shinkyō], leading to the main entrance of the shrine, on a moonlit evening. 
<br>The shrine was founded in Kyūshū during the Nara period. Ancient records place the foundation of Usa jingū in the Wadō era (708-714). A temple called Miroku-ji was built next to it in 779, making it what is believed to be the first shrine-temple (jingū-ji) ever. From 1871 through 1946, Usa was officially designated one of the Kanpei-taisha (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. The shrine is the main sanctum of over 40,000 hachiman shrine locations. The Emperor Ojin, who was deified as Hachiman-shin (the god of military power) and worshiped as the protective deity of the Imperial City, is enshrined in these shrines.

title: Kawarazaki Gonjūrō, Nakamura Ganpachi, Arashi Kangorō, Seki Sanjūrō, Sawamura Tanosuke, Nakamura Ichō and Bandō Hikosaburō in the play Imayō Shuten Dōji (河原崎権十郎、中村鴈八、嵐冠五郎、関三十郎、沢村田之助、中村いてう、坂東彦三郎・ 當世酒呑童子)

description:
Picturing the actors (from right to left) Kawarazaki Gonjūrō as Minamoto no Yorimitsu, Nakamura Ganpachi as the demon Shiyatsuki, Arashi Kangorō as the demon Metsuki, Seki Sanjūrō III as Shuten Dōji, Sawamura Tanosuke III as Jijo (lady attendant) Keiko, Nakamura Ichō as Hanazono Hime and Bandō Hikosaburō V as Hirai no Yasumasa (a retainer of Minamoto no Yorimitsu) in the play A Modern Shuten Dōji (Imayō Shuten Dōji), performed at the Nakamura-za in February 1863.
<br>"One of Japan's most popular stories was the legend of the destruction by Minamoto no Yorimitsu (who actually lived AD 948-1021) of the ogre called the Shuten Doji ('The Drunken Boy'). This flesh-eating, drunken giant lived in the mountains, where he kept young women captive, some of whom he ate. Yorimitsu and his four companions gained access to his lair disguised as travelling priests, got the monster intoxicated, and cut off his head. The real Yorimitsu was a warrior who helped the court rid Japan of bandits and pirates, hence the attachment of this legend to him." -  Source: website of The British Museum https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_1881-1210-0-383-416-a [accessed 8-27-23]

title: Electrical Linesman (電線工)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Linesmen installing electrical lines and transformers during the era when electrical power, its generation, transmission and distribution, were under state control. This print is number twenty-one in the series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures.<br>A translated version of the original Japanese language commentary accompanying this print reads, "Looking down from a high place upon the crowds of a busy city, the profession of the electrical linesman, always wearing blue and working beneath the blue sky, is a happy one. The work that from our earthbound perspective looks like it is no trouble at all, is in reality truly nerve-racking, because their life depends on how they handle the so-called 'lifeline' and 'death line.' The difference between them is whether electricity runs through them or not.<br>
"Tokyo is gradually becoming more distinguished, but I will not go into detail here about how it fills me with pride when I see the above ground utility poles standing closely together, which major cities in the west do not have."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3] 
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 14.
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Kamo Monogurui 加茂 物狂 (Madness at Kamo)
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)
description:
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 68-69) -  A man from the capital who has been away in the eastern provinces for more than three years returns to the capital on the day of the Kamo Festival and there sees his wife.  She, however, has lost her reason and although they talk together and she dances for him, she does not realize who he is.  She tells how, unable to bear her husband's absence any longer, she set off to the east on a fruitless search for him, and how loneliness and disappointment have made her mad.  They then recognize and acknowledge each other, but because of the curiosity of the onlookers they pretend to be strangers and leave separately, to be reunited in their home.

<br><br><b>Nōga Taikan (Encyclopedia of Noh Plays)</b>, made up of 200 prints, was published in Tokyo between 1925 and 1930 in five volumes. The original designs for Volumes 2 through 5 were drawn by Kōgyo, but the drawings for twenty-four of the prints in Volume 1 were created after Kōgyo’s death by Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963), Kōgyo’s very talented protégé. <br>"Each print is a scene from the noh play represented, similar to the same scene as it appeared on stage. Of Kōgyo’s three sets of noh prints, the Nōga Taikan prints seem to show the plays more accurately than either Nōgaku zue or Nōgaku hyakuban. In fact, if he sketched plays in the noh theater using brush and black ink, as his daughter Gyokusei said he did, he must have made notes to himself somewhere about what colors and designs to use on the costumes and stage props. The prints are very simple: the main actors at an important moment in the play, the artist’s signature, and the artist’s seal. The prints reveal at most few parts of the stage and its backdrop, and when so, only faintly. The focus is on the actors qua actors. The prints do not reveal the name of the plays represented, but each print in all five volumes is preceded by a piece of translucent paper on which the title of the play, the actors by type (shite, waki, tsure, kyōgen, kokata) and name of character in his role appear in Japanese." - Source: "Kōgyo, The Art of Noh," University of Pittsburgh https://exhibit.library.pitt.edu/kogyo/noga_taikan.html [accessed 8-17-23]

description:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print Fuji is barely visible from the rice planting area around Bentenjima. Three bi-planes along with four birds fly through the sky, while a traditionally dressed rice-farmer and old-fashioned fishing boats go about their business. Again, the artist juxtaposing the traditional with the modern.

<br>The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. He was mourned as a peerless warrior, artist, and poet, even by his enemies, and a chapter of the Heike monogatari is devoted to his death.

<br><br>ONE HUNRED ASPECTS OF THE MOON
<br>One Hundred Aspects of the Moon "is a series of one hundred single-sheet woodblock prints with the moon as its unifying motif. It illustrates a wide range of figures from Japanese and Chinese history, literature, and folklore. Apart from the moon or references to it (the moon is not always visible in the print), the subjects are unrelated.
<br>"Like most of his contemporaries, Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1839-1892) was fascinated by the world elsewhere, but as the decades passed he became increasingly concerned at how much his countrymen had lost by abandoning their traditions. He therefore took as subjects for his prints stories from Japan’s glorious and colorful past. Though they looked backwards in the sense that they illustrated historical events, Yoshitoshi’s prints were revolutionary in their representation of individual human emotion and in their psychological sensitivity. The supreme example is his last great series of prints, Tsuki hyakushi, One Hundred Aspects of the Moon."[1]

title: Washing Clothes
creator: Hiyoshi Mamoru 日吉守 (1885-?)
description:
One of at least six prints in a series depicting various aspects of Korean life. While published in the 1950s, the scenes are reminiscent of the time of the artist's residency in Korea from 1909 through the end of its colonization by Japan in 1945. In this idyllic scene, women are washing or carrying laundry. Isabella Bird, in writing about her visit to Korea at the end of the 19th century, painted a less idyllic picture, at least of clothes washing in Seoul, as follows:
<br>"She washes in this foul river, in the pond of the Mulberry Palace, in every wet ditch, and outside the walls in the few streams which exist. Clothes are partially unpicked, boiled with lye three times, rolled into hard bundles, and pounded with heavy sticks on stones. After being dried they are beaten with wooden sticks on cylinders, till they attain a polish resembling dull satin. The women are slaves to the laundry, and the only sound which breaks the stillness of a Seoul night is the regular beat of their laundry sticks."

creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)
description: Miyata depicts a very spare Lake Tōya with its islands in pink light (a sunrise or a sunset?) and the active volcano Mount Usu looming ominously in the background in solid black. This print is from one of the volume of prints, likely a volume of scenes of Hokkaidō where Lake Tōya is located, from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.<br><br>Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

description: The actor Ichikawa Sadanji 市川左団次 in the role of Okawa Tomoemon in the sensational act IV, Tsuta moyō chizome no goshuin, of the play Hosokawa no chi-daruma. In this scene the hero Tomoemon, his clothes on fire, has just rescued the title deed to his master's, the daimyo Hosokawa, fiefdom from the treasury room in Hosokawa's burning palace. Hemmed in by the fire and having no escape he is about to slit-open his belly and place the document inside to save it. The final scene will show Tomoemon's burnt corpse being carried before Hosokawa and the discovery that the deed, and therefore his master's fortune, has been saved, as the blood-stained document is drawn from Tomoemon's bosom. The title deed clutched in Tomoemon's mouth in the print bears the characters 御朱印, goshuin, a letter bearing the shogun’s scarlet seal.

title: Horse (馬 Uma)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description:
This print of a horse in a barn, simply titled Horse, was one of a set of two woodblock reproductions of paintings by the artist issued by Okamoto Studio in 1983, as supervised by the Sakamoto Hanjirō Institute (坂本繁二郎研究所). Hanjirō began painting horses at about the time he moved to the city of Yame in 1931. "He would head out to Aso, Unzen, and other parts of Kyushu in search of a horse that appealed to him, sketch it, and then work on the painting back in his studio in Yame. He was enthralled by the forms of horses, bathed in the sunlight, dappled with so many colors." - Source: website of the Bridgestone Museum.

title: Four Bridges, frontispiece appearing in the magazine Bungei Kurabu (Literary Club), Volume 2, No. 10 (文芸倶楽部, 第二巻, 第 十編・井字橋 Bungei kurabu, dai 2-kan, dai 10-hen・Ijibashi)
creator: Tomioka Eisen 富岡永洗 (1864-1905)
description:
Although he studied with the Kanō school painter Kobayashi Eitaku (1843-1890), Tomioka Eisen was primarily an illustrator creating frontispieces and illustrations for serialized novels published by various newspapers and magazines, such as this print for the literary magazine Bungei Kurabu illustrating the story "Four Bridges" by the writer of popular fiction Takeda Gyōtenshi 武田仰天子 (1854-1926).
<br>In this print Oshun, in the circular opening, the love of Genshichi, has just read a letter held by Genshichi from her malicious sister-in-law who wants her to marry her nephew rather than Genshichi. In the tragic ending, Genshichi and Oshun will commit suicide.
<br><br>THE LITERARY MAGAZINE BUNGEI KURABU
<br>Bungei Kurabu 文芸倶楽部 was a very popular literary magazine published from 1895-1933 by Hakubunkan. It was one of the most dominant venues for Meiji literature, publishing noted authors such as Izumi Kyōka, Kunikida Doppo, Higuchi Ichyō, and Kawakami Bizan.  In the magazine's later years, post 1907, it became a less elevated popular entertainment magazine.

title: Brief History of Japan Pictorial Gameboard, top left sheet (皇国史畧雙録 Kōkoku shiryaku sugoroku)
creator: Yōsai Nobushige 揚斎延重 (active 1894-95)
description:
The top left sheet of an e-sugoroku (pictorial game board) with its top panel depicting Nintoku Tennō, who is considered to have reigned from 313 to 399. This top panel is the goal or finish of the game. Each of the four sheets comprising the game, depicts three or four scenes of famous stories and historical figures demonstrating moral actions to be emulated. Brief explanatory texts appear in the scrolls on each panel. Note that one of the sheets making up the complete game is missing from this collection, but is shown with a red border in the image to the left for reference.

<br><br>E-SUGOROKU
<br>The earliest surviving examples of e-sugoroku date from the 17th century. Starting as Buddhist teaching tools, by the end of the 17th century they had become popular entertainment for the common people. The increasing popularity of e-sukoroku is tied to the development of woodblock printing, with the "game-boards" being composed of multiple standard oban size sheets after the advent of multicolor woodblock print technique towards the end of the 1700s. "Game-boards were often assembled from two, four or nine sheets joined together, so that the sizes of the finished products vary, up to a size of about 90 x 70 cm. They were sold in folded form (rather like modern maps), in envelopes or wrappers into which they could be easily inserted again after use."[1]
<br>
"In order to play, players needed a die and markers or figures with which to play. . . All sugoroku games have a starting square usually called furidashi and a goal called agari."[2] In this collection's e-sugoroku, a tobi sugoroku or "jumping sukoroku," "[e]ach field or square in the game gives instructions as to which square players must proceed to, when a given number is thrown. Sometimes, fewer than 6 numbers are given; in this case, players who fail to come up with one of the stipulated numbers have to wait for the next round in order to make a move."[3]
<br><br>
[1] "Playing with Filial Piety – Some Remarks on a 19th-Century Variety of Japanese Pictorial Sugoroku Games," by Susanne Formanek and Sepp Linhart appearing in the magazine Board Game Studies, Volume 5, International Journal for the Study of Board Games, CNWS Publications, 2002, p. 40.

title: 71-1 (Haniwa)
creator: Maki Haku 巻白 (1924-2000)
description: One of at least a half-dozen prints of haniwa (ancient Japanese funerary clay figures) created by Maki. It is assumed that this print's title "71-1" would make it the first print that Maki created in 1971.<br>Maki made his own printing blocks by carving a motif onto a piece of plywood, filling the carved-out areas with cement paste, and passing the print several times through a press to achieve various textures. Calligraphy is central to his works; he sometimes manipulates calligraphy to defy reading, thereby drawing attention to the form of Chinese characters.

title: Poem 71-5 (仁)
creator: Maki Haku 巻白 (1924-2000)
description:
Maki presents us with the Chinese character for ren, "仁", the Confucian concept of benevolence. Maki's "poem" prints may be a tribute to his teacher, the pioneering abstract print master Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), who used "poem" as a title for a number of his prints and was often inspired by poetry. While he had no formal art training, Maki studied for two years with Onchi, attending meetings of the Modern Print Study Society (Gendai Hanga Kenkyūkai 現代版画研究会), founded in 1950 by Onchi and Kitaoka Fumio (1918-2007) under the auspices of the Nippon Hanga Kyōkai.

creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
This print appeared in the October 1924 issue of "The Ladies' Graphic" (Fujin gurafu), a magazine targeted to women covering "international news, matters relating to the lifestyle of the 'contemporary' woman as well as information about cuisine and current styles in clothing, hair and make-up." - Source: Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Brill, 2015, p. 108. 
<br>Yumeji contributed illustrations to the magazine starting with its first issue in May 1924.  Yumeji's designs were printed separately by woodblock and tipped onto a page in the magazine.

title: Actors' New Year’s Party (俳優新年筵会 Haiyū shinnen enkai)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: Twenty-six kabuki actors at a New Year's party. The actor Bandō Kichiroku I, "a low-ranking travelling actor" is costumed as a turtle (a symbol of longevity) in the center panel, paired with the actor Nakamura Tsuruzō II, a supporting tachiyaku actor, in a dance. They are being watched with critical eyes by their more famous colleagues such as Ichikawa Danjūrō IX in the plaid-patterned kimono in the center of the right sheet, Ichikawa Sadanji I sitting over the brazier to Danjūrō's right and Onōe Kikugorō V in the left sheet holding the red fan.

title: Asakusa, Tenth Month (浅草・十月)
creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)
description:
In this print we see what appear to be vendors selling sake, fish and other delectables on Azuma bridge, while a strange looking gentlemen in a red coat performs. In the background we see Asakusa and its Buddhist temple Sensō-ji and the five-story pagoda Asakusa Shinto shrine. The yellow title cartouche of this print remains largely unread, except for the first two characters 十月, 10th month, and the characters 浅草, Asakusa.<br>
Each print in this twelve print series is a comic riff on famous places or sites in Tokyo. Twelve Months at Famous Places in Tokyo was created during the same year that the artist created his more famous comic series Thirty-Six Famous Views of Tokyo: A Comic Selection. In discussing this larger comic series of prints, a parody of Hiroshige's famous 1856/1859 series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, Johnathan Solomon notes that Shōsai "found comic expression a suitable response to the chaos and uncertainty" of the early Meiji Era. - Source: "Bridging Edo and Meiji, Shōsai Ikkei's Comic Views of Early Tokyo" appearing in Impressions: The Journal of the Ukiyo-e Society of American, Inc., Number 21, 1999, p. 45.

title: The Heroine Osai in Gonza the Lancer (鑓の権三重帷子のおさい Yari no Gonza kasane katabira no Osai)
creator: Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972)
description:
In this print Osai, the wife of a tea ceremony teacher, who secretly longs for Sasano Gonza, her intended son-in-law, holds the sash she has just torn from Gonza after a struggle. The sash displays his crest and a reverse chrysanthemum joined in a lover's knot. After tearing off the sash she cries "Are you so devoted to that sash? Here, I know you won't like it, but wear my sash instead. It will become a vengeful snake, wrap itself around you waste, and never let you go." While jealous, she smiles sweetly, looking over her shoulder with a tender expression of affection. When Gonza throws her sash into the garden it is taken by the samurai Bannojō, hiding there, as proof of their adultery, the penalty for which is death. - Source: The Major Plays of Chikamatsu, translated by Donald Keene, Columbia University Press, 1961, p. 291.<br><br>
One of 18 prints published from 1922 to c. 1925 as part of the celebration of the two-hundredth anniversary of the death of Chikamatsu Monzaemon (1623-1724), perhaps the greatest dramatist in the history of the Japanese theater. Each design illustrates a scene or character from one of Chikamatsu’s famous works which were compiled into 16 volumes by Chikamatsu researcher Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950). The prints were inserted into the volume containing the story they illustrated and were also separately sold.

title: Dancing Ladies (fan design sample)
creator: Unknown
description: A fan design sample created as a marketing tool for deluxe fan makers. While this fan design was likely created during the Taishō or early Shōwa eras (c. 1912-1940), fan design samples date back to the Meiji era. They showed the season's available designs, commissioned from some of the most eminent artists of the day. Once the season was over, the sample fans and books of fans were sold. Most samples in this collection do not carry a signature or seal and the artists will be forever unknown, but some famous names do appear on several of the prints. The designs range from Art Deco to traditional genre scenes. The shape of these prints indicate they were designs for folding fans (sensu 扇子, or ōgi 扇 as they are also known.) While often described as "woodblock prints", most of these sample designs appear to be hand painted or inked rather than printed.

title: Monster Reforms Mayor, No. 8 appearing in the Ōsaka Nichinichi Shinbunshi (大阪日々新聞紙・第八号)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description: At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability. Following their introduction in Tokyo, nishiki-e shinbun made their appearance in Osaka. The Osaka issued prints differed from their Tokyo counterparts in being half-size (chūban rather than ōban size).<br>In this print, "the fearful-looking monster was in fact a good spirit. It made its appearance before a [Mr.] Nakayama, who was so captivated by a certain widow' s charms that he neglected his duties as the chief of a certain district in what is now Hyogo prefecture. The monster is shown trying to reform the man." The text is signed Bun Sanjin 文山人記, certainly a pseudonym of an unknown writer. - source: website of Waseda University Library http://www.wul.waseda.ac.jp/kosho/bunko10/b10_8068_6/index.html [accessed 8-17-23]<br>The red cartouche in the upper left hand corner provides the name of the paper 大阪日々新聞紙  (Ōsaka Nichinichi Shinbunshi) and the print number 第八号 (8).

title: Autumn in Ohara (大原の秋)
creator: Kamei Tōbei  亀井藤兵衛 (1901-1977)
description:
A chuban size print depicting two woman in traditional dress in the town of Ohara (Oharame - maidens of Ohara) in present day Sakyo-ku, Kyoto.  Oharame (maidens of Ohara) were once a frequent sight, carrying flowers or other merchandise on their towel-wrapped heads and wearing traditional dress.
<br>
There is an annual Oharame Festival in Ohara, in late April and early May, during which time the Oharame experience, dressing in costume, can be had for about 1,000 yen.

<br>This print is part of a set of five prints by the artist created for the famous soba shop Owariya 尾張屋 in Kyoto, which has been in business since 1465.  Four of the prints depict scenic views in and around Kyoto and the fifth depicts the Owariya. Originally published in the 1930s, this set was reprinted for the celebration of the 15th generation household head of Owariya during the 1980s. The Owariya name in kana をはりや or kanji 尾張屋, within a rectangular cartouche, appears on each of the prints.

title: Mallards in Coastal Scene
creator: Ohara Koson 小原古邨 (Shōson 祥邨) (1877-1945)
description:
Originally issued in 1931, this collection's print is a later edition c. 1946-1957.<br>
"Less successful are Koson's attempts at integrated landscape compositions such as "Mallards in a coastal scene," one of the few dated prints by the artist (1931), in which the groupings of ducks appear wooden and stolid in an equally lackluster landscape setting. The forms of the diving and swimming ducks in this print are clearly borrowed from other prints like "Mallards and lotus" or visa versa. title: Bijin in brown haori over green kimono (untitled)
creator: Ikeda Terukata 池田輝方 (1883-1921)
description:
Ikeda Terukata, primarily known as a bijinga artist, began his career as an illustrator and would go on to win prizes as a nihonga (modern Japanese-style) artist at the Bunten, the annual Ministry of Education art exhibition. <br>This bijin kuchi-e, reproduced using a color offset lithographic process, displays the characteristic tri-fold of prints inserted into popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi).
<br><br>THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E<br>

The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

title: Act XII [The Treasury of Loyal Retainers] (十二段目 [假名手本忠臣蔵])
creator: Utagawa Yoshitora 歌川芳虎 (active c. 1836-1882)
description:
Act XII: The deed has been done, revenge achieved, Moronao (the historical figure protocol officer Kira Kōzuke-no-suke Yoshinaka) has been slain, and his head, washed and wrapped with a purple cloth, is being presented by forty-six of the "loyal forty-seven rōnin" at the grave of their master, Enya Hangan (the historical figure Asano Takumi-no-kami Naganori, the daimyō of Akō [Lord Asano]) in Segakuji temple. The dirk by which Lord Asano disembowled himself is held aloft by Hazama Jūjirō, one of the rōnin who discovered where Moronao was hiding.
<br>The gravestone seen in the print contains the following inscriptions:
<br>源長矩朝臣 (Lord Asano Naganori)  吹く毛玄利大居士 (Asano's posthumous Buddhist name, alluding to his passing in the spring of life)
<br>元禄十四年三月十四日 (Genroku 14th year, 3rd month, 14th day - April 21, 1701, the day when Asano Naganori drew his sword in a corridor of Edo Castle and slashed at the senior bakufu protocol official, Kira Yoshinaka.)

<br>The names of sixteen of the loyal ronin are shown in the red cartouches, including the names of Hazama Jūjirō 間十次郎, who is seen holding the dirk before the grave of his lord; Ōishi Kuranosuke 大石内蔵助 (the leader of the loyal forty-seven rōnin), seen holding the manuscript laid upon the tomb of their master and Takebayashi Tadashichi 竹林唯七, offering incense.

The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

title: Nostalgia 7
creator: Amano Kunihiro 天野邦弘 (1929-2020)
description: A largely self-taught artist, Amano first exhibited his work in 1955 and his work would later appear in numerous international exhibitions. His prints range from the representational to the abstract and he is best known for his abstract and semi-abstract works, such as Nostalgia 7. At least 20 of the artist's prints carry the word "Nostalgia" in their title followed by their number (likely chronological) in the series. In the words of Gaston Petit, a great fan and promoter of post-war avant-garde woodblock print artists in Japan, "Amano works in a series, though not in the sense of repeating the same image in a loosely realted manner . . . but in a more systematic permutational sense." - Source: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Gaston Petit, Kodansha, 1973, p. 56.

title: Taiwan War: Illustration of the Battle of Baguashan (臺灣戰争・八卦山激戰占領圖)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)

title: The Moon: A Modern Meiji Beauty, a supplement to the magazine Shufu no tomo (The Housewife's Friend), Volume 19, Number 1 (主婦之友、附録・月 明治風俗美人、第十九巻 第一號)
creator: Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972)
description:
This chromolithograph was one of three long pillar-format bijin prints titled Snow, Moon and Flower issued as special supplements to the January 1935 issue of the magazine The Housewife's Friend (Shufu no tomo). The other two artists contributing designs were Yamakawa Shūhō (1898-1944), "Flower: A Modern Meiji Beauty," (IHL.2103) and Itō Shinsui (1898-1972), "Snow: A Modern Meiji Beauty," (IHL.2104). 

<br>Shufu no tomo began publishing in 1918 using the slogan "Once you're married, it's Shufu no tomo." Print runs for the magazine were in the tens of thousands, hitting over 300,000 in some months.

<br> Printed on the top margin is this paean to Kiyokata (as translated by art historian Lynn Katsumoto): "No one but a great artist like Kiyokata could have captured the lyrical mystery of an exceptional beauty, one whose countenance evokes the mysterious luminosity of a misty moonlit night. This work exceeds even the superb artwork that Kiyokata had previously submitted (perhaps the reader knows that the jury awarded it a top prize) to the Imperial Art Exhibition."
<br>Kaburaki Kiyokata, a successful illustrator for newspapers and novels, turned to nihonga (Japanese-style) painting in his early twenties becoming one of its 20th-century luminaries.

title: Woman Combing Her Hair
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: This collection contains two impressions from the same edition of Tokuriki's portrait of his wife combing her hair.  (See IHL.0098.) This is one of Tokuriki's iconic sōsaku hanga prints. While a number of sources, including the Honolulu Academy of Arts, date the original publication of this print to 1935, Statler dates it to 1947, as do the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston and The British Museum. In commenting on Tokuriki's technique Statler writes "the best of his creative prints, like Woman Combing Her Hair . . ., show a resolute effort to design with the knife. 'I want to break away from the brush,' says Tokuriki," referring to moving away from his Japanese-style painting (nihonga) background. - Source: Modern Japanese Prints: An Art Reborn, Oliver Statler, Charles E. Tuttle Company, 1956, p. 122.

title: Ukiyo-e World, Volume 5, No. 1 (浮世絵界 第五卷 第一号 Ukiyo-e kai, dai go-kan, dai ichi gō)
creator: Yamakawa Shūhō 山川秀峰 (1898-1944) - cover design
description: Sixty-seven issues of the magazine Ukiyo-e kai were published from March 1936 through June 1941. Each issue featured a woodblock printed cover. Initially, the magazine, a successor to the magazine Ukiyo-e geijutsu, both edited by the print scholar Muneshige Narazaki, sometimes featured modern designs, such as the February 1937 issue with a work by the sōsaku hanga artist Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960) as a frontispiece, but subsequent to that issue the focus was on traditional ukiyo-e design, such as this issue's woodblock print cover by the shin hanga artist Yamakawa Shūhō 山川秀峰 (1898-1944), in keeping with the mission of the Society for Ukiyo-e Enthusiasts (ukiyo-e dōkōkai).

title: Idaten (韋駄天)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
In this print Sasajima depicts the Buddhist deity Idaten (the Indian deity Skanda) who is "faster than the wind."<br>
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with Sasajima's original printing of the work, Yoneda has used the technique of "back coloring" 裏彩色 in his reproduction.

title: Guardian of the South (増長天 Zōjōten)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
Picturing Zōjōten the Guardian of the South, one of Four Heavenly Kings who protect the four cardinal directions (shintennō),  adapted by Japanese Buddhism from Hindu deities. Shintennō exist between the heavenly and the earthly panes in which mankind and bōhisattvas live. Zōjōten's companion guardians are Jikokuten, Guardian of the East who links heaven and earth; Kōmokuten, Guardian of the West; and Tamonten, Guardian of the North.<br><br>
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with the original printing  by Sasajima, Yoneda has colored this print from the verso, a technique known as "back coloring" 裏彩色.

title: Thunder God (雷神 Raijin)
creator: Sasajima Kihei 笹島喜平 (1906-1993)
description:
Picturing the Shinto god of thunder Raijin who holds a circle of hand drums over his shoulder to produce thunder. Most often pictured as a pair with Fūjin, the wind god, Raijin and Fūjin are portrayed as oni (demons), though in Buddhism both are attendants of Kanno, the Goddess of Mercy, and neither are inherently good or evil, capable of displaying both characteristics.<br>
This print is one of twenty comprising the portfolio "Woodblock Prints by Kihei Sasajima" issued in an edition of 300 copies by the Tokyo publisher Bijutsu Shuppan-sha in 1964. The prints in the portfolio are woodblock reproductions, almost all of them reproduced in a smaller size than the original prints created by the artist. The woodblocks for the reduced-size prints (縮写復刻 shukusha fukkoku) were carved by Iokibe Kin’ichi and printed by Yoneda Minoru. In keeping with the original printing  by Sasajima, Yoneda, in his reproduction, has employed Sasajima's takuzuri technique of forcing paper into a deep-cut block with a press and dabbing the raised areas with an ink saturated pad giving the print a sculpted three-dimensional appearance.

title: Empress Dowager Eishō’s Imperial Funeral from the Kyoto Ōmiya Palace to the Imperial Tomb (京都大宮御所ヨリ陵月縄新御陵ヘ御送柩心圖)
creator: Harada Kōkyo 原田耕挙 (1863-1925)
description: The Empress Dowager Eishō (consort of Emperor Kōmei, 1831-1867), who was suffering with catarrhal pneumonia, died at on the evening of January 11, 1897 after a visit earlier in the day from Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken. Her funeral was held on February 7.  This print published on February 5, two days before the funeral, is an announcement of that event. The illustration was likely created from details provided by the Imperial Household Ministry. The black bordered inscription on the top of the center sheet starts with the words "Imperial Funeral Bulletin" 御大葬彙報.<br>The funeral arrangements for the Empress Dowager were to be the model for those of Emperor Meiji when he died in 1912. (See IHL.1683, Illustration of the Main Gate at Aoyama During the Imperial Funeral Ceremony, 1912.)

title: The Occupation of the Fortress at Niuzhuang: The Battle of Lieutenant Colonel Imada (牛荘城占領今田中作戰闘之圖 Gyūsōjōsenryō: Imada chūsa sentōno zu)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description: Depicting Japanese troops taking a Chinese battery above the strategic town of Newchwang (Niuzhuang), the battle was fought in brutally cold weather during the first week of March 1895.  Frostbite claimed more casualties than the actual fighting, although before the town was taken by the Japanese they would encounter fierce resistance and house-to-house fighting.  Involved in the fighting for the Japanese were their 3rd and 5th Divisions attacking from different directions.  Japanese losses were 70 killed and 319 wounded, while the Chinese lost over 2,000 men with 635 soldiers taken prisoner.

title: Captain Higuchi, in the Midst of the Attack, Personally Holds a Lost Chinese Child (樋口大尉進撃之途次自抱持清民遺兒之圖 Higuchi taii shingeki no toji mizukara Seishi no ishi o hōji suru no zu)
creator: Ogata Gekkō 尾形月耕 (1859-1920)
description:
"One of the most celebrated Japanese heroes of the Sino-Japanese War was Captain Higuchi, who reportedly rescued a Chinese infant in a crucial battle near Weihaiwei. As the story was told, Captain Higuchi heard the abandoned child crying on the battlefield, scooped him up in his left arm, and led his forces to victory flourishing his sword with his right arm. After the battle, Higuchi returned the child to his parents." Source: MIT Visualizing Cultures  https://visualizingcultures.mit.edu/throwing_off_asia_02/visnav_ii_d.html [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>This print was one of a number of Sino-Japanese war prints on display in the "posters" section at the 1895 Nineteenth Triennial Exhibition of the Massachusetts Charitable Mechanic Association. They were contributed by the famous importer and purveyor of Japanese goods Bunkio Matsuki.1 In the report of the judges for foreign and American posters they note, "Your jury further wish to highly recommend the artistic and graphic nature of the Japanese War series of bulletins."2
<br>For other depictions of Captain Higuchi rescue of a Chinese infant see IHL.1343 "Captain Higuchi" by Mizuno Toshikata (1866-1908) and IHL.2163 "The Attack on Weihaiwei: The Taking of the Hundred Foot Cliff [Captain Higuchi saves a child]" by Watanabe Nobukazu (c.1872-1944).

title: Tenko 天鼓 (The Drum from Heaven)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu III 三代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu III 三代 小信 ) (1881-1963)
description:
This print depicts a scene from the play Tenko, attributed to the playwright Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443).<br>
Play synopsis (A Guide to Kyogen, Don Kenny, Hinoki Shoten, 1968, p. 188-189.) - A boy name Tenko has a wonderful drum which had come down from Heaven, but when this was taken from him to be presented to the Emperor he drowned himself. An Imperial envoy tells this story and explains that as no one has been able to make any sound come from the drum since it was taken to the Palace, he has been sent to fetch the father of Tenko. Together they go to the Palace, and when the father strikes the drum it gives out such a miraculous sound that he is promised a rich reward and a musical performance is arranged to placate the soul of his son. When this is done, the ghost of Tenko comes and dances before them.

Done largely in shades of gray, the print comes alive with Kitaoka's reserved splashes of red, brown, green and yellow.

title: Cape Tachimachi (立待岬 Tachimachi Misaki)
creator: Maeda Masao 前田政雄 (1904-1974)
description: The artist's rendering of Tachimachi Cape in Hakodate, Hokkaido. The cape sits at the southeastern end of Mount Hakodate and overlooks the Tsugaru channel. Late in the eighteenth century the shogunate built a fort there which is now only noted with a marker. It is known for its wildflowers and its views. This print is one of the three different states of this landscape created by the artist.

title: Portrait of Shiga Nayoa  (肖像画　滋賀直哉)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description:
The fourth state of this print, originally created by Sekino in 1968. Sekino has captured the novelist Shiga Nayoa (1883-1971) from rough sketches, his own photograph and impressions of his meeting with the novelist, who would not agree to sit for his own portrait.<br>
Sekino comments: "One who is famous for disliking to sit for his portrait was the novelist Shiga Naoya. I asked him if I could sketch him, but the request was turned down. I heard that another painter tried to sketch him too, but he apparently ended up fighting with Mr. Shiga. When I visited Mr. Shiga, I was at least allowed to take his photograph; but I am only an amateur photographer, and unfortunately the picture did not turn out well. Later I made his portrait using my rough sketch, photo, and my impression of him."

title: W-396 (Wandering Heart) (漂白 (さすらひ) のハート)
creator: Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (1937-2019)
description: While Kurosaki has written "W - 396", "W" followed by a number (a type of inventory number he gave to almost every print), he has omitted, intentionally or otherwise, the descriptive title "Wandering Heart" appearing on other impressions and listed in his catalog raisonné.

title: Illustration of the Disastrous Flood (大洪水之図)
creator: Ōkura Kōtō 大倉耕涛 (1873-1910))
description:
In September 1896, devastating floods hit the Tokyo area after several weeks of heavy rain. Multiple rivers in the Tokyo area, including the Arakawa, Tone, Tama, Naka, Edogawa and Sumida overflowed their banks causing severe flooding. Water levels rose over 24 feet in some places leading to the collapse of a number of embankments and dams. The flooding, which continued for several weeks, effected a broad area of Tokyo.
<br>As the print's inset in the right sheet explains, the flooding was the worst in fifty years. The embankment of the Nakagawa collapsed and the entire area of Mukojima became a lake that could only be navigated by boat. Officials and police officers rescued people and did what they could to mitigate the disaster.

Saruhashi is one of "Japan's Three Odd Bridges."  It is 33 meters high, 3.3 meters wide and 31 meters long. The bridge is built over a narrow ravine, with four stacked haneki, or cantilevered members, embedded to the rock wall of both banks. The structural support is similar to architectural roofing. The construction year is unknown, but there are records of this bridge style existing in 1676. The oldest estimation is that it was completed over 500 years ago. The bridge was restored in 1984.

creator: Yamaguchi Gen 山口源 (1896-1976)
description:
Yamaguchi pictures the torii at the entrance to the Meiji Shrine, a Shinto shrine in Shibuya, Tokyo, that is dedicated to the deified spirits of Emperor Meiji and his wife, Empress Shōken. It is identified by Laurence Smith as one of the six prints in this series depicting "places with serious imperial resonances."<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.0121.
<br><br>SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
<br>Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. -  Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

title: Onshi no musume (恩師の娘)
creator: Igawa Sengai 井川洗厓 (1876-1961)
description:
Having just read the card on the table, she clutches her handkerchief in this illustration for a story titled "Onshi no musume" (My Teacher's Daughter), as printed in red kanji charachters below the artist's signature and seal. This offset-printed color lithograph bijin kuchi-e (frontispiece illustrations of beautiful women) displays the characteristic tri-fold resulting from its insertion into a popular culture magazine (taishū zasshi).
<br>Igawa Sengai is considered “one of the pioneers of book and magazine illustration,” contributing to popular magazines such as <i>Kingu</i> (King), <i>Fujin gahō</i> (Graphic Magazine for Women) and <i>Kōdan Kurabu</i> (The Storytelling Club) and creating illustrations for novels such as Gotō Chūgai’s (1868-1938) "A Pair of Pines" (Hiyoku no matsu), "Lady Shizuka" (Shizuka Gozen) by the female writer Hasegawa Shigure (1879-1941) and "The Gold Demon" (Konjiki Yasha) by Ozaki Kōyō (1868-1903).

<br><br>THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E<br>

The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined. 
<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

title: Portrait of Yoshida Shōin, sensei (吉田松陰 先生之像)
creator: Okuyama Gihachirō 奥山儀八郎 (1907-1981)
description:
In this woodblock print titled "Portrait of Yoshida Shōin," Okuyama has copied a well-known photo of Yoshida Shōin (1830-1859), a samurai from the Chōshū domain who was executed in 1859 for the attempted assassination of Ii Naosuke, the shogunate Tairō (prime minister). Yoshida had a profound impact on a number of key figures in the Meiji Restoration, including Hirobumi Ito and Aritomo Yamagata.

<br>Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) maker and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own woodblock prints, such as IHL.1844, and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.

<br>When this print was produced in 1943, Okuyama was one of many print artists who had joined the wartime nationalist print organization Nihon Hanga Hōkōkai. This portrait of Yoshida Shōin (1830-1850), whose Tokugawa-era writings were used as justification by nationalist supporters of Japan's military and colonization of Asia was created to bolster Japan's war effort.

<br>For another impression of this print see IHL.2187.

title: Imperial Palace and Mount Fuji (宮城と富士)
creator: Jōkata Kaiseki 定方塊石 (1882-1966)
description:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print we see the Imperial Palace grounds in the foreground (with the palace's outer moat in the immediate foreground), the National Diet Building, which would have been under construction at the time behind the palace grounds on the left and a very white Mount Fuji standing as a beacon in the background. Cars and people dot the scene and hazy clouds, reddened by the setting sun, streak the sky.
<br>The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

<br>
Play synopsis (A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 95-96.) - Feeling that he will die in the coming battle with Ashikaga Takauji, Masashige calls his son Masatsura to him in the town of Sakurai and gives him his last words of advice. At the farewell party Onchi Mitsukazu dances to entertain them. Masashige then sends his faithful retainer away with his son to take him back to their home, while he himself prepares for battle. 
<br><br>Illustrations of Noh, issued between 1897 and 1904, is Kōgyo's first series of Noh theater prints. The prints show the primary actor (shite) often accompanied by one or two other performers (known as the waki, tsure, or aikyōgen), stage props, and sometimes the larger milieu including musicians or stage architecture. In the right margin Kōgyo gives the title of the play and, for Noh plays only, a list of the roles and a brief synopsis of the story.

He adds that he himself is Taki-matsuri no Kami, the protective god of the shrine, and then disappears. That night, while the official is resting, a goddess comes to the place and dances, and then the god himself appears, carrying the spear.
