title: Tokyo, Konishiki Yasokichi (東京 小錦八十吉)
creator: Utagawa Toshimasa 歌川年昌 (Shunsai 春斎) (1866-1913)
description:
Yasokichi I 小錦八十吉 (1866-1914) was a sumo wrestler from Musha District, Kazusa Province. Konishiki made his professional debut in May 1883 and reached the top makuuchi division in May 1888. He won 39 bouts in a row after his makuuchi debut. Konishiki was promoted to ōzeki in May 1890, and awarded a yokozuna licence by the house of Yoshida Tsukasa in March 1896. He was the sport's 17th yokozuna. 
<br>As we see in this print an impressive part of sumō-e are their depictions of the kesho-mawashi (ceremonial brocaded aprons) worn by wrestlers. These aprons, originally bestowed by daimyō upon the professional wrestlers they retained as a "badge of accomplishment," became increasingly splendid in appearance as daimyō competed with each other in this display of ornamental finery used in classical sumō ritual in the ring.

A transcript of the text on illustration no. 25 can be found at https://www.lib.iii.u-tokyo.ac.jp/collection/ono_sn/17.html#N015 [accessed 8-17-23]
<br><b> Brief Overview of Nishiki-e Shinbun</b><br>
At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written (using furigana and katakana to enhance readability), by popular writers of light novels and the pictures were drawn by woodblock print artists of the day.
<br>While the "Tokyo nichinichi shinbun" was the first paper to publish news nishiki-e, many other print publishers in Tokyo and Osaka jumped into the news nishiki-e market adopting a similar masthead design, featuring the name of their news nishiki-e on an unfurled banner held in the air by a pair of fat cherubs.
<br>At their brief height, around forty nishiki-e shinbun were in publication. While nishiki-e shinbun were largely gone by the late 1870s, challenged by the rise of faster and cheaper letterpress newspapers, they played an important role during their short life in spurring the growth of the Japanese press during its formative years.

title: Sake Brewing at Itami in Settsu Province (摂津国伊丹酒造之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts the brewing of refined sake at Itami in Settsu Province (摂津国, Settsu no kuni) which is now part of Hyōgo Prefecture.<br>
Settsu Province (摂津国 Settsu no kuni) was a province of Japan, which today comprises the southeastern part of Hyōgo Prefecture and the northern part of Osaka Prefecture. It was also referred to as Tsu Province (津国 Tsu no kuni) or Sesshū (摂州). Osaka and Osaka Castle were the main center of the province. Most of Settsu's area comprises the modern day cities of Osaka and Kōbe.

title: Viewing the Cherry Blossoms on the Sumida River at Night (隅田川夜櫻)
creator: Imae Shunkin 今江春近 (active 1881-1895)
description: A mounted folding fan print picturing courtesans on a pleasure boat during an evening viewing of the cherry blossoms along Tokyo's Sumida River, still billed as the "ultimate spring experience" while in Tokyo.

title: Pagoda at Yanaka Tennōji Temple at Shitaya,View 78 (下谷・谷中天皇寺之塔 ・七十八景)
creator: Koizumi Kishio 小泉癸巳男 (1893-1945)
description: In this print, Koizumi presents us with a view of the main road leading into the Yanaka cemetery and the five-story Tennōji pagoda that once stood there. A woman with baby and young child, a peddler and a figure dressed in a light blue kimono walk along a path.<br>The pagoda which survived the 1923 earthquake and the allied bombing was burnt down in 1957. The artist comments, “In the middle of the Yanaka cemetery stands a five-story pagoda made of plain, unpainted wood.”<br><br>Print number seventy-eight in the one hundred print series Shōwa dai Tokyo hyakuzue (One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo During Shōwa). Koizumi started this series in 1928 and completed it twelve years later in 1940. In the preface to the compiled boxed set of prints issued in the autumn of 1940 after the completion of the series, Koizumi comments, "My One Hundred Pictures of Great Tokyo in the Shōwa period are sōsaku hanga, and are carved and created with my own hands . . . . With your permission I would like to become the Hiroshige of the Shōwa era to achieve my dream of making a life's work out of one hundred landscape prints featuring Tokyo in the Shōwa period. Even if it seemed to be somewhat economically dead during its production, it was a labor of love and a lot of effort  . . . .”  - Source: Great Tokyo One Hundred Views by Koizumi Kishio, Maureen de Vries, Nihon no Hanga, 2019, p. 5.

title: Pagoda
creator: Saitō Kiyoshi 斎藤清 (1907-1997)

title: Mitsuke: Stone Embankment Along the River (見附 川石垣)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description: Sekino's rendition of station number 29, Mitsuke, along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. The print is the 12th, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekino created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō, originally made famous by Andō Hiroshige (1794-1858).<br>"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching for a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . In 1975, after the completion of the modern Tōkaidō series, the Ministry of Education Award was granted to Sekinō because of his outstanding achievement 'in using every possible technique in woodblock printing, Japanese traditional art, and the recreation of the old fifty-three stations on the Tōkaidō highway in a present-day light.'" - Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p.241-242 and Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 259-260.

title: White Herons and Willow (柳に白鷺 Yanagi ni shira-sagi)
creator: Ohara Koson 小原古邨 (Shōson 祥邨) (1877-1945)
description: Two little egrets (Egretta garzetta) are depicted in flight past a green willow. Later printings, such as this collection's print, utilize a brighter green and lack the subtle grey shading of the background of the first edition.<br>Ohara Koson was one of the most important and prolific kachō-ga (bird and flower) woodblock prints artists of the early 20th century shin-hanga (new print) movement.

title: Old Elementary School Building in Komono (菰野小学校旧校舎)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: In 1973, on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Komono Elementary School in the small city of Komono about 90 miles due east of Kyoto in Mie Prefecture, Tokuriki issued two prints to mark the occasion. This collection's print depicts the old administrative building built in 1934. The second print, not part of this collection, depicts the site of the castle ruins located next to the school.<br>Today, this beautiful building is gone, as are the other early structures, replaced by unattractive and blocky white buildings.

title: Hiragata Harbor (平潟港 Hiragatakō)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)
description: Miyata depicts Hiragata harbor in the city of Kitaibaraki, Ibaraki Prefecture. As with so many of his prints, all is calm, serene and quiet, and no people can be seen. This print is from one of the volume of prints, likely a volume of scenes of Hokkaidō where Lake Tōya is located, from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.<br><br>Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

title: Pasture Scene (牧場の風景 Bokujō no fūkei)
creator: Takagi Shirō 高木志朗 (1934-1998)
description: This pastoral scene of horses in a field is one of a number of similar themed prints by Takagi, a mostly self-taught artist whose work became more representational as he aged.

title: Pulling Up a Whale (同 [壱岐] 神楽桟にて引揚図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. This crêped print version depicts the hauling onto shore of a whale for processing. The whale has been taken close to shore by a hunting party in fast chase boats (seko-bune 勢子船).<br>
When this print was issued in 1877 near-shore whaling had given way to offshore, or open sea, whaling.  By 1877 Japanese whaling was undergoing a transformation from traditional to modern practices forced upon them by declining near-shore whale populations. In traditional active whaling, whalers belonged to a specific whaling group (ōnaya) based out of a coastal village that had space on the beach for processing whales taken near shore (shore-based whaling). As inshore whale populations declined, larger open sea whaling ships were used to haul whales back to processing plants on shore and ownership of whaling operations passed to larger business groups, such as the massive Masutomi group, able to provide the bigger ships and on-shore facilities. By the 1920s factory ship whaling had begun in which harpooned whales taken on the open seas were towed to a centralized factory ship for processing.

title: Mandarin Orange Plantation in Kii Province (紀伊国蜜柑山畑之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. This crêped version of the print depicts workers harvesting mandarin oranges in a terraced grove in Kii province. Kii Province (紀伊国, Kii no Kuni), or Kishū (紀州), was a province of Japan in the part of Honshū that is today Wakayama Prefecture, as well as the southern part of Mie Prefecture.  Kishū has been a major orange growing area for centuries.  Basil Hall Chamberlain, British Japanologist, in his 1907 Handbook for Travellers in Japan describes a scene much as depicted in this print. "We are now in the district of Arida [in Kishū province], notable as the greatest orange-producing centre in Japan; and as we proceed, we find all the lower slopes of the wide sheltered valleys covered with orange-groves."<br>
This crêped version of the print was made by the chirimen process, resulting in a cloth-like, smaller dimensioned, irregularly shaped print. See IHL.0540 for the non-crêped version of the print.

It depicts the planting of rush (igusa) in Bingo Province (備後国, Bingo no kuni) which is now part of Hiroshima Prefecture.<br>
This crêped version of the print was made by the chirimen process, resulting in a cloth-like, smaller dimensioned, irregularly shaped print.

creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)

title: Haniwa [4] (埴輪 [四])
creator: Saitō Kiyoshi 斎藤清 (1907-1997)
description:
One of at least fifteen prints by Saitō picturing one or more haniwa, ancient clay funeral sculptures from the Kofun era (approximately 200-552CE). Saitō's rendering of a haniwa warrior in this collection's print makes the figure look monumental, but comical, with its lopsided face.  

<br>Writing in 1957, Oliver Statler called the artist's haniwa prints "adventures with straight lines and curves, stimulated by his study of the nude" and "an exercise in deformation." - Source: Saitō Kiyoshi hangashū, Oliver Statler and Chisaburō Yamada, Kodansha International, 1957.

title: Actor Onoe Tamizō Playing the Role of Nakanori [Kaminari] at the Age of Eighty from the magazine Bijutsu Sekai Vol. 16 (俳優尾上多見蔵頽齢八十にして中乗を演ずる図 美術世界 巻十六)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description:
Adoring fans watch Onoe Tamizō II 尾上多見蔵 二代目 (1800-1886) at the age of 80, playing the thunder god, raijin, [Nakanori Kaminari], in the play Hatsuharu no kotobuki iwau kokonobake, in this double-bookplate by Kyōsai appearing in the 16th volume of the arts magazine Bijutsu Sekai (World of Art), published in February 1892, three years after Kyōsai's death in 1889. Note the candles at the end of bamboo rods that the kurogo (black-clad stage assistants) would have held to illuminate the actor at critical times in the play.<br>
It is one of four prints designed by Kyōsai appearing in volume 16, all of which feature older characters - the kabuki actor Onoe Tamizō II at the age of 80; the warrior Ōkubo Hikozaemon 大久保 彦左衛門 (1560-1639) at the age of 82; the Confucian scholar Kō Gentai 高玄岱 (1649-1722) at the age of 78; and a prostitute at the age of 89.

title: Takachiho (高千穂)
creator: Kuroki Sadao 黒木貞雄 (1908-1984)
description:
Kuroki captures the colors of terraced rice fields and a blazing sunset in this semi-abstract rendering of the town of Takachiho in the Nishiusuki District of Miyazaki Prefecture located about 40 km west from his birthplace of Nobeoka. Surrounded by the Kyūshū Mountains, Takachiho is located in a forest-enclosed environment where flat land is rare.

Takachiho has been known since ancient times as a sacred ground where the gods descended to earth. The area is also famous for yokagura, sacred dance rituals reenacting the legends, which are performed in the fall and early winter.

title: New Year at the Lakeshore and Mount Fuji (湖畔の正月と富士)
creator: Jōkata Kaiseki 定方塊石 (1882-1966)
description:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print Fuji is blanketed with snow as villagers prepare for a New Year's festival which includes paying honor to the goddess of Mount Fuji, Sakuyahime (traditional name: Sengen). Her name 咲耶姫 appears on the white banner which has been brought to the festival by parishioners from a local shrine. A taiko drum is in the center of the print which will herald in the New Year and a pole festooned with prayer slips and colorful decorations dominates the right side.
<br>The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

title: Imperial Japanese Army Emperor Banzai Tank Death Squad
creator: Unknown
description:
A color lithograph patriotic fan sample print, likely dating from the early years of the Asia-Pacific War (1931-1945), extolling the brave warriors of the suicide tank squads. The print carries the sample catalog number そ印 參百五拾參號 So jirushi (or in) 353 Sanbyaku go jū san gō. (Also see IHL.1936.)
<br>These numbered fan prints (uchiwa-e 団扇絵), were used as samples to show wholesale customers the range of available designs. The sample prints were gathered into a sample book (uchiwa mihonchō 団扇見本帳, or uchiwa gachō 団扇画帖.)
<br>The first two columns of text on the print read, 戰車ヲマモル勇士 | 決死隊ノ勇士夕テハ extolling the "warrior who guards the tank" and the "brave soldier of the suicide squad."

title: Japanese National Defense Women Association (大日本國防婦人会)
creator: Unknown
description:
A color lithograph patriotic fan sample print, likely dating from the early years of the Asia-Pacific War (1931-1945), promoting the Japanese National Defense Women Association which, at its height,  boasted over 9 million members. The two women wear white aprons over kimono, with a sash bearing the association's name 大日本國防婦人会. The red text to the left of the women reads, 興亞長期建設, a reference to the government's long-term national policy on East Asia, whose stated purpose was to unite Asian nations and solidify and create a continental identity to defeat the designs of the Western nations to perpetuate hegemony.
<br>
<br>The print carries the sample catalog number そ印 參百五拾貳號 So jirushi (or in) 352 Sanbyaku go jū ni gō. (Also see IHL.1935.)
<br>These numbered fan prints (uchiwa-e 団扇絵), were used as samples to show wholesale customers the range of available designs. The sample prints were gathered into a sample book (uchiwa mihonchō 団扇見本帳, or uchiwa gachō 団扇画帖.)

title: Around Ueno (上野附近)
creator: Takashima Unpō 高島雲峰 (1894-1987)
description:
One of two prints contributed by the artist Takashima Unpō (1894-1987) to the series Pictures of Taishō Earthquake, issued in 1926 three years after the 1923 Great Kantō Earthquake. This print pictures the Ueno district ablaze in the aftermath of the earthquake. Takashima has captured a cross-section of Tokyo-ites running for their lives as the fires swirl around them.
<br>The series consists of 25 prints by nine, mostly lesser-known, artists, a number of whom, including this print's creator, were students of the Nihonga artist Tomioka Eisen (1864-1905). The nine artists are Katayama Shunhan (fl. c. 1901–1926); Hakuhan Yawata (1893–1957); Noguchi Kōgai (born c. 1899, active c. 1919-1930s); Igawa Sengai (1876-1961); Kirigaya (Kiriya) Senrin (1877–1932); Shibata Kōyō (fl c. 1920s); Hamada Josen (1875-1928); Kondō Shiun (fl. c. 1915–1940) and Takashima Unpō (1894-1987).
<br>In his recollections of the fires, playwright and theater historian Kawatake Shigetoshi describes "scenes of frenzied panic and terror." Fleeing his home in Honjo in eastern Tokyo, he recalls looking north to a "blazing inferno."  He writes, "I was speechless, watching the whirlpools of fire and the undulating waves of flames. It was utterly beyond description." Kawatake's son perished in the disaster. - Source: website of Smithsonian.com https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-great-japan-earthquake-of-1923-1764539/ [accessed 8-29-23]
<br>"The Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923 stands in memory as one of the most terrifying calamities in Japanese history.  Registering at a magnitude of 7.9, the quake struck on September 1, with its epicenter some 50 miles southwest of Tokyo, in Sagami Bay.  The hour was 11:58A.M., just when households everywhere were lighting small charcoal stoves to prepare lunch. Fires broke out instantly in the densely populated cities of Tokyo and Yokohama and were spread by high winds.  Since the earthquake had broken the water lines, both cities were reduced to smoldering ruins within a few hours. . . . The earthquake and its aftermath caused well over 140,000 deaths and left nearly 700,000 people homeless." - Source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 273.

title: Evening Shore (夕浜 Yūhama)
creator: Tadashige Ono 小野忠重 (1909-1990)
description: An evocative night time scene of seaside village.<br>To realize his dark atmospheric prints, Tadashige uses a water-based-pigment technique called inkoku tashoku-zuri mokuhan (color negative woodblock printing) that he developed in 1948. This process involves first dying the paper with black bokujū, made from dissolving and grinding sumi in water, then printing a thick opaque white gouache beneath the areas to be colored to keep the black from absorbing the colors.

title: The Glory of the Imperial Flowers (花の都御代乃榮 Hana no miyako goyo no sakae)
creator: Nagashima Shungyō 永嶌春暁(active 1870-1905)
description:
This scene of courtly ladies and imperial regalia first appears as if it’s out of the Heian era (794-1185), when court ladies painted eyebrows high up on their foreheads after shaving their real eyebrows. But, these lady’s eyebrows are not shaved, suggesting an elaborate dress-up, and who is the man sitting high-up in the left panel?  Could it be Emperor Meiji? Donald Keene tell us that in June of 1880 the emperor embarked on a journey to understand the local conditions of his subjects. Included in his journey was a stop in Kyoto in July, when this print was issued. While in Kyoto he visited his aunt, Princess Sumiko, who had arranged a program of plays for his entertainment. “The performance was attended also by members of the nobility still living in the old capital, a momentary revival of their former glory.”<br>
While the artist would certainly not have attended the performance, details of the emperor’s journey were widely reported allowing Nakashima to construct this scene using his artistic license.

title: Index to Thirty Subjects of Kyoto
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: This print, mounted on its original stiff board, serves as the index to the portfolio of thirty prints titled Thirty Subjects of Kyoto published by the Uchida Art Store (Uchida Woodblock Printing Company) in 1936.

title: Shipping New Brew Sake in Settsu Province (同 [摂津国] 新酒荷出之図)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. It depicts laborers moving vats of sake in preparation for loading onto boats in Osaka Bay. The Cambridge History of Japan notes in discussing the governments 1874 survey of physical production in Japan that "The value of sake produced was astonishingly large, more than the value of all silk and cotton textiles and three times value of raw silk output."<br>
This crêped version of the print was made by the chirimen process, resulting in a cloth-like, smaller dimensioned, irregularly shaped print. See IHL.0540 for the non-crêped version of the print.

title: Illustration of Military Review Outside [Osaka] Castle (城外観兵式之圖)
creator: Hayashi Motoharu 林基春 (1858-1903)
description: The Emperor reviews troops as they parade outside of Osaka Castle in this color lithograph, part of a twenty print portfolio published in April 1895 to coincide with the opening of the Fourth National Industrial Exhibition in Kyoto.<br>This portfolio of color lithographs 色石版画, issued by the Osaka publisher Furushima Takejirō in 1895, consists of ten well-known scenes in Kyoto and ten scenes in Osaka. The portfolio is likely the earliest use of color lithography, most likely using zinc plates, for the production of meisho-e, or pictures of famous places. The portfolio was sold in shops in the exposition hall and in souvenir/gift shops around Kyoto. The selling price and number of total copies is unknown, but it appears that at least two editions of this portfolio were produced. As over 1.3 million people attended the exposition, the print runs must have been quite large.

title: View of the West Gate of Shitennō-ji Temple (四天王寺西門の景)
creator: Hayashi Motoharu 林基春 (1858-1903)
description: Visitors in traditional and Western dress near the stone torii leading to the West Gate (Gokuraku mon) of Shitennnōji, Japan's first Buddhist temple, located in Osaka. The five-storied pagoda (Gojūnotō) can be seen in the background. The yellow sign pillar to the right of the torii reads 従是東公園地 大阪府, telling us that we are at the affiliated East Park area in Osaka prefecture.<br>This portfolio of color lithographs 色石版画, issued by the Osaka publisher Furushima Takejirō in 1895, consists of ten well-known scenes in Kyoto and ten scenes in Osaka. The portfolio is likely the earliest use of color lithography, most likely using zinc plates, for the production of meisho-e, or pictures of famous places. The portfolio was sold in shops in the exposition hall and in souvenir/gift shops around Kyoto. The selling price and number of total copies is unknown, but it appears that at least two editions of this portfolio were produced. As over 1.3 million people attended the exposition, the print runs must have been quite large.

title: Valiant Battle at Jiuliancheng (九連城勇戦図 Kyūrenjō yūsen zu)
creator: Hōei 峰栄 (active 1894)
description: On October 26, 1894 the Japanese army, having crossed the Yalu River into Chinese territory on the morning of the previous day, engaged the Chinese forces at Hushan and on the banks of the Ai River. The Japanese then marched west, surrounded Jiuliancheng, a fortified town guarding the Yalu and a gateway to Manchuria, and launched a full-scale offensive.  The Chinese forces, rather than defend this strategic town which served as their headquarters, retreated to defensive positions leaving the Japanese to enter the town without opposition.

title: Illustration of The Sino-Japanese War, Ansong Crossing, Korea (朝鮮安城渡日清戦争ノ図)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description:
The legendary Captain Matsuzaki (松崎大尉 as printed in the small red cartouche), front and center with sword drawn, leads his men in the Advanced Column across the Ansong (Anjō in Japanese) River in Korea attacking the enemy. The captain was felled by several bullets and died. Lieutenant Colonel Fukushima (福嶋中佐 as printed in the small red cartouche) on his white horse with his troops attacks.
<br>The large scroll in the print begins, "On the night of July 29th, 1894, at half-past twelve, our army crossed the Ansong." The crossing of the Ansong was the beginning of the battle to take the Chinese stronghold of Songhwan, Korea, which the Japanese would take later that day.

title: Illustration of a Scouting Patrol in a Skirmish in the Vicinity of Port Arthur (旅順口附近我斥候進撃之図 Ryojunkō fukin waga sekkō shingeki no zu)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)
description:
Port Arthur fell on November 21, 1894. Prior to its capture there were major engagements on the Liaotung (Chinchou) Peninsula where the Port Arthur forts were located. This print, from the artist's imagination, depicts a skirmish between a Japanese Army scouting party (likely a part of the Second Army) and Chinese troops. As usual, the casualties are all Chinese.<br>
The print is a wonderful composition of movement. Kokunimasa was one of the more talented artists of the later years of the Meiji Era.

title: A Courtly Mirror of Ashiya Dōman (蘆屋道満大内鑑 Ashiya Dōman Ōuchi Kagami)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)

title: Nikko Senjōgahara from the book Nihon no sansui (日本の山水・日光戰場原)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description: Picturing the Senjōgahara marshlands in Nikko National Park, this print was originally published as part of the 1946 book titled Nihon no sansui (Mountains and Waters of Japan.) This collection's print was either issued separately from the book or removed from the book, designed and compiled by Onchi Kōshirō 恩地考四郎 (1891-1955). The book contains poetry by twenty-one poets, three color woodblock prints by the artists Yamaguchi Susumu 山口進 (1897–1983), Azechi Umetarō 畦地梅太郎 (1902-1999) and Maekawa Senpan, and a cover print presumably designed by Onchi.

title: Akasaka Palace (赤坂離宮  Akasaka gosho)
creator: Hiratsuka Un'ichi 平塚運一 (1895-1997)
description:
One of fifteen prints from the 1945 series Scenes of Last Tokyo. This print was one of eight designs for the series which originally appeared in the 1929-1932 series Shin Tokyo hyakkei (One Hundred Views of New Tokyo). This 1945 print, made from recut blocks, is one of two designs that Hiratsuka contributed to Scenes of Lost Tokyo, the publication of which was orchestrated by Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955).<br>Hiratsuka's view of Akasaka Palace is rather bleak - trees without leaves, absent of people, an ochre hued sky, foreground and palace itself. The palace was lightly damaged during the allied bombings of Tokyo on the night of April 13-14, 1945.
<br><br>SCENES OF LAST TOKYO (TŌKYŌ KAIKŌ ZUE)
<br>Tōkyō kaikō zue 東京回顧圖會, a portfolio of fifteen prints created by nine artists, is variously translated as Scenes of Last Tokyo ("last" likely being a typographical error appearing on the folder accompanying the complete collection), Recollections of Tokyo, Retrospective Scenes of Tokyo, and Scenes of Lost Tokyo. Though the target audience for the portfolio was the Occupation forces, the portfolio, according to Lawrence Smith, contained "a coded message to Japanese readers" in the subjects depicted in some of the prints and in its introductory message. This coded message, composed shortly after the surrender of the Japanese in August 1945, by the leading sōsaku hanga (creative print) artist Onchi Kōshirō (1891-1955), was a hope for the retention of some of the imperial institutions in the remaking of Japan. -  Source: Japanese Prints During the Allied Occupation 1945 – 1952, Lawrence Smith, The British Museum Press, 2002, p. 23–24.

title: View of Ikejiri, Setagaya (世田谷 池尻 風景)
creator: Hiratsuka Un'ichi 平塚運一 (1895-1997)
description: A view, seemingly of a formal garden, possibly leading to a temple, in Ikejiri, Setagaya. This print was issued in 1922, a year before the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. Today, Setagaya has the largest population and second largest area (after Ōta) of Tokyo's special wards.

title: Aridōshi 蟻通
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Hakurakuten 白楽天
creator: Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (1869-1927)

title: Picture of the Famous Kōbe Steam Train (神戸名所鉄道蒸気車之図 Kōbe meisho tetsudō jōkisha no zu)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description: One of fifteen prints originally created by Hasegawa Sadanobu II in the early to mid 1870s that were re-carved and reprinted as part of a 1936 collection of prints of famous sights in Kobe issued by an organization called the Kobe Old Print Association.<br>The railroad connection between Kobe and Osaka was opened in May 1874 (Meiji 7). It took 70 minutes to travel the 32.7 kilometer route. The first Osaka Station, popularly known as Umeda Teishajo (梅田停車場), was located in Umeda, Osaka and was opened on May 11, 1874 (Meiji 7).<br>Two English-made steam locomotives were imported by the Imperial Government Railway of Japan for use on the Kobe-Osaka Line and Hasegawa's rendition of the engine is a fair rendering of the actual locomotives.

title: Vive La (ヴィヴ・ラ)
creator: Kawanishi Hide 川西英 (1894-1965)
description: This print is marked 見本 "sample print" in the upper left margin. The black ink marks (printer marks) in the lower left of the image area and the absence of  "ひで" (Hide in kana) in the circular area of the artist seal in the lower right corner of the image are consistent with a trial print not meant to be sold. This design was originally issued in a different color scheme in 1957 and then reissued for the second volume of the Kawanishi Hide Print Collection containing five "original" woodblock prints issued in 1980 by Keishōsha and edited by Hide's son Kawanishi Yuzaburō 川西祐三郎 (1923-2014).

title: Wang Xiang, No. 7 [Catching Fish for His Stepmother in Winter]  (第七號王祥)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)

title: Tanzi, No. 10 [He Fed His Parent's Doe's Milk] (第十號剡子)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
"These two pictures seem to be only tangentially related. At top Tanzi is dressed in deer hide so he could sneak into a herd of deer to get milk for his ailing parents. However, when a hunter was about to shoot the deer, Tanzi revealed his identity, shouting, “Don’t shoot!’ The larger image shows a boy being scolded by his mother for having upset the desk items, including brushes, books and a paper weight.  What connects the two scenes is that both boys are wrapped in fur, but from the mother’s gestures and the little boy’s expression, the Japanese narrative seems unrelated to proper behavior."[1]

<br>"[I]n the 1890s, Chikanobu began to show increasing concern for teaching moral values to the new generations, especially to women. Increasingly, women were seen as the protectors of Japanese customs and virtues, while men were expected to cope with Western influences and the modernization process taking place. Beginning in 1890-1891 with Juxtaposed Pictures of Twenty-four Paragons of Filial Piety [Nijūshi ko mitate awase) . . .  Chikanobu created a series of didactic images that encouraged traditional values found in filial piety, social hierarchies and restrained behavior."[2]

<br><br>
[1] Chikanobu: Modernity and Nostalgia in Japanese Prints, Bruce A. Coats, Hotei Publishing, 2006, p.156.
<br>[2] Ibid., p. 46.

title: Hotei from the book Kaiga kōshū roku (布袋・繪画講習録 第六回 第十二号)
creator: Utagawa Yoshimune II 二代 歌川芳宗 (1863-1941)
description:
The god of good fortune, happiness and laughter, Hotei, one of the seven shichifukujin (gods of good fortune), resting in his sack filled with toys and treasures for the flocks of children who swarm around him everywhere.<br>

This print was included in the 6th book of the 12th volume of Kaiga kōshūroku (Painting training book), a series of correspondence training books teaching subscribers how to paint. Each issue contained five examples of paintings reproduced as woodblock prints, along with an explanation of each painting.  The books were issued on a quarterly basis by Dai Nihon Kaiga Kōshūkai 大日本絵画講習会.

title: Miyajima in Rain (雨の宮島)
creator: Ogyū Tensen 荻生天泉 (1882-1947)
description: The artist's rendering of Itsukushima on Miyajima with Gojunoto (the Five-storied Pagoda) in the background and the famous Sika deer in the foreground during a gentle rain. The print was included in a portfolio titled 瀬戸内三題 (Three Subjects of Setouchi), issued by Watanabe Publishing in 1935, which included three woodblock prints designed by Ogyū.

title: In Praise of the Harmonious Soga at Mount Fuji (和合曽我誉富士 Wagō Soga Homare no Fuji)
creator: Utagawa Yoshitaki 歌川芳滝 (1841-1899)

title: Kikugorō in the role of Jūjirō (菊五郎 十次郎)
creator: Yamamura Toyonari 山村豊成 (Kōka 耕花) (1885-1942)

title: Utaemon in the role of Agemak (歌右衛門の揚巻 Utaemon no Agemaki)
creator: Natori Shunsen 名取春仙 (1886-1960)

title: Terukuni (照國)
creator: Okuyama Gihachirō 奥山儀八郎 (1907-1981)
description:
The sumo Terukuni Manzō 照國万藏 (1919-1977) from an untitled series of sumo portraits by the prolific and stylistically varied artist Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981), whose work bridged the sōsaku hanga and shin hanga movements. The wrestler pictured in this print, Terukuni Manzō, was promoted to the highest rank of yokozuna in 1942 and retired in 1953. 
<br>While this impression is not signed or sealed by the artist, other impressions carry both Gihachirō's signature and seal.

title: Gamō Kunpei (蒲生君平)
creator: Isoda Chōshū 磯田長秋 (1880-1947)
description:
Isoda constructs this fictional scene showing the writer and imperialist Gamō Kunpei (1768-1813) castigating the shogun, Tokugawa Ienari (1773-1841), on the poor state of the Imperial Tombs he surveyed in the late 18th century. Gamō subsequently published the "Sanryō shi" (Record of the Imperial Tombs) in 1808. His work prompted "members of the Sonnō Movement at the end of the Edo period to pressure the bakufu for better treatment of the tombs." - <font size="-1"> Source: "Contested Access: The Imperial Tombs in the Postwar Period" by Walter Edwards appearing in the Journal of Japanese Studies, Vol. 26, No. 2 (Summer, 2000), p. 377.</font>
<br><br>The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

title: Hashimoto Sanai (橋本左内)
creator: Shimada Bokusen 島田墨仙 (1867–1943)
description:
Shimada depicts the samurai philosopher Hashimoto Sanai (1834-1859) shortly before his execution at the age of 25. He sits at his desk reading his treatise Keihatsuroku 啓發録 (A Book of Resolutions or Treatise on Enlightenment) which he wrote at the age of 15 in 1848. Written on the panel against his bookcase in the upper right is 急流中底之柱、即是大丈夫之心 , a saying that Hashimoto treasured.
<br><br>The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

title: Rai San'yō (頼山陽)
creator: Ōta Chōu 太田聴雨 (1896-1958)
description:
Ōta portrays the Confucian scholar, historian and calligrapher Rai San'yō (1781-1832) with his widowed mother Baishi viewing the cherry blossoms at Mount Yoshino in Yamato in 1827. This fulfilled her desire to once more see the cherry blossoms before her death. While there, he pointed out to his mother Emperor Go-Daigo's (1288-1339) tomb, lamenting Go Daigo's  failed attempt tin 1331 to overthrow the Kamakura Shogunate (1185-1333) and restore Imperial rule.
<br><br>The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

title: Thomas Carlyle (カーライル)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description:
One of fourteen prints in the series of color woodblock educational prints titled Legends of Great Westerners issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print depicts a distraught Thomas Carlyle, the English writer, historian and philosopher, rushing towards his burning manuscript, the first volume of his history of the French Revolution, while his dog looks on.<br>
While the text on the print blames the burning of the manuscript on his dog knocking over a candle, it was in fact John Stuart Mill's maid who thought the manuscript, given to Mill by Carlyle, was scrap and burned it for kindling. Carlyle would go on to rewrite the first volume and complete two more volumes, publishing the three-volume work The French Revolution: A History in 1837, and establishing his reputation and one of the great intellectuals of the time.<br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued full-color woodblock prints for childhood education between 1873 and 1885. The Ministry advertised these prints "As an aid to the education of the young child (yōdō) 幼童) within the home… use these pictures as a toy when the child is sitting or lying down. And when the child reaches the age to enter elementary school, the effect will be no small matter.” - Source: "Raising Subjects: The Representation of Children and Childhood in Meiji Japan," Rhiannon Paget an article from New Voices: A Journal for Emerging Scholars of Japanese Studies in Australia and New Zealand, Volume 4, 2011.

title: Richard Arkwright (アークライト)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description:
One of fourteen prints in the series of color woodblock educational prints titled Legends of Great Westerners issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print depicts an angry Richard Arkwright (1732-1792), British inventor and industrialist, casting his wife out of house for destroying his model of the spinning frame.<br> 
Arkwright's 1768 spinning frame was the first textile machine designed to be water powered. There are various versions and embellishments to the story of Arkwright's wife smashing his model. Some have his wife, in fact his second wife Margaret Biggins, smashing many of his models, but they all mention that she was angered by the time and money he was spending on his models and wanted him to return to his earlier profession as a barber and wig-maker.<br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued full-color woodblock prints for childhood education between 1873 and 1885. The Ministry advertised these prints "As an aid to the education of the young child (yōdō) 幼童) within the home… use these pictures as a toy when the child is sitting or lying down. And when the child reaches the age to enter elementary school, the effect will be no small matter.” - Source: "Raising Subjects: The Representation of Children and Childhood in Meiji Japan," Rhiannon Paget an article from New Voices: A Journal for Emerging Scholars of Japanese Studies in Australia and New Zealand, Volume 4, 2011.

title: Sōnosuke in the role of Koharu (宗之助の小春 Sōnosuke no Koharu)
creator: Yamamura Toyonari 山村豊成 (Kōka 耕花) (1885-1942)

title: Dance (Odori) - (untitled)
creator: Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972)
description: An untitled and undated print of a dance performance. The dancer on the left may be portraying the legendary Izumo no Okuni 出雲の阿国, the woman who founded kabuki in the early 17th century. On the right is her attendant.

title: Kagoshima Shinbun: Illustration of the Battle of Yamagaguchi (鹿兒嶋新聞 山鹿口戰之圖 Kagoshima Shinbun・Yamagaguchi sensō no zu)
creator: Adachi Ginkō 安達吟光 (1853-1902)
description: At least a dozen woodblock triptychs depicting various battles during the Satsuma Rebellion, issued by various publishers using the drawings of various artists, carry a cartouche reading "Kagoshima shinbun" (Kagoshima Newspaper) accompanied by the title of the battle being depicted and a descriptive scroll.  While an actual newspaper called the Kagoshima shinbun would come into existence in the late 1880s, it had no relationship to these earlier prints and their publishers.<br>In this print by Adachi, one of several prints of the rebellion he designed, the battle of Yamagaguchi is depicted. The engagement being referenced is most likely the March 12 battle in the Nabeta-Yamaga area, about 30 km due north of Kagoshima Castle.<br>Translation of text on print: "As the Western insurgents made a name for themselves they stood momentarily poised to make good on their rebellion by resisting the Government forces. One of their fiercest commanders was no doubt Maehara Issei, a brigand chieftain and traitor to the nation who brought many a disturbance to the realm. This Issei’s youngest brother was Maehara Ikkaku. In the retreat from Hagi, he hid himself, and when the time came he joined the Kagoshima rioters. Wearing a white cloth over one shoulder with his name written on it, he rode at their head, attacking at Yamagaguchi. Perhaps the brigands’ luck had yet to run out, for he was unharmed even as he galloped around alone amid the vortex of Government soldiers, going back and forth under a rain of bullets. It was a ferocious battle truly Ikkaku may be called a mighty warrior. - Ōta Jō, editor"<br>Note: Maehara Ikkaku is the figure  on horseback in the center of the composition. Hagi, in Yamaguchi Prefecture, was the site of a failed samurai rebellion in late 1876, a precursor to the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, of which the fighting at Yamagaguchi described here was a minor part. Despite the rebel heroics depicted in this print, the Government forces prevailed here as elsewhere. - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon)

title: Ichiriki Teahouse (一力茶屋 Ichiriki chaya)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)

title: Untitled abstract print
creator: Unknown
description: An abstract composiion by an unkown artist, employing woodblock technique with the addition of various objects to the blocks such as plant forms. The grain of the woodblock is put to effective use as the "eye" of the composition.

title: Glaring Contest  (睨シ子)
creator: Unknown
description:
Two figures square off against each other in a glaring contest ( 睨ッ子)* accompanied by a verbal battle recorded in the upper left of the print between the "man on the right" (人ノ右) and the "man on the left" (人ノ左), perhaps a reference to their political positions. The print is neither signed or sealed and is not dated. It appears to be a ponchi-e (political cartoon). 
<br><br>* 睨ッ子 is a slang term originating from the Kansai dialect. It is typically read as "niramikko" and refers to the act of glaring at someone to intimidate or express anger. It is used to describe the action of furrowing one's brow or narrowing their eyes while staring.

title: Illustration of [The Emperor’s Carriage] Departing the Imperial Palace [over] Nijūbashi (宮城御出門貳重橋圖)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: While the red sky may seem glaring, red became the color of modernity during the early years of the Meiji era, and this print's red sky heralds the departure of the Emperor and Empress from the Imperial Palace after the promulgation of the constitution ceremony in the main hall of the Meiji Palace on February 11, 1889. The Emperor and Empress are headed for the military parade at the Aoyama Drill Hall. In the center of the print is Nijūbashi Bridge and in the upper right is the Imperial Palace.

title: Nizaemon in the role of Gonpachi (仁左衛門 権八)
creator: Ishii Hakutei 石井柏亭 (1882-1958)

title: Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Sendo Tonbei in the play Miracle and Yaguchi Ferry (市川団十郎・ 船頭頓兵衛・ 神霊矢口渡)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description:
The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) as the evil ferryman Tonbei in the play Shinrei Yaguchi no watashi (Miracle and Yaguchi Ferry). In keeping with the rest of the series, extensive embossing is employed in the background and mica was applied to the upper black background and Tonbei's hair and beard.<br>
In the play's most famous scene, Yoshimine Nitta, who was escaping from pursuers sent by his enemy, and his lover, Utena, visited the house of Tonbee [Tonbei], a ferryman, for a one night stay. Tonbee had betrayed the Nitta family, which he used to serve, and killed one of Yoshimine’s older brothers, Yoshioki. Now Tonbee saw his chance to also kill the younger brother. But, despite Tonbee’s scheme, his daughter, Ofune, fell in love with Yoshimine at first sight. She betrayed her father and let Yoshimine and Utena get away in order to protect the one she loved. Her outraged father than killed her.<br><br>One Hundred Roles of Danjūrō, featured the major roles of Ichikawa Danjūrō IX (1838-1903) in a set of half-length portraits.  A square cartouche in the upper register of each print contains a verse or illustration, and the series title cartouche is backed by peonies, a flower associated with Danjūrō IX. The publisher Fukuda Kumajiro (together with Gusokuya Kahei) commissioned Kunichika to begin work on the series in 1893. It was completed posthumously in 1903, the year of the actor’s death. The prints in the series were sumptuously printed using expensive materials and techniques. - Time Present and Time Past: Images of a Forgotten Master: Toyohara Kunichika (1835-1900), Amy Reigle Newland, Hotei Publishing, 1999

title: Rough Tales of the Floating World told on Eastern Brocades:  Araki Mataemon Yoshimura, Sekiguchi Yatarō,, Kimura Matazō, Musashibō Benkei (東錦浮世稿談・荒木又右エ門吉村・関口弥太郎・木村又藏・武蔵坊辨慶)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)
description:
Four small prints depicting four heroic and fierce figures from Japanese history printed on a single ōban-size sheet, intended to be cut apart. Toshikata's four small prints model his teacher's, Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), earlier full ōban-size designs published as part of a 50 print series bearing the same title Azuma nishiki ukiyo kōdan ("Rough Tales of the Floating World told on Eastern Brocades") as do these four small prints. 
<br>The four figures pictured are, as follows:
<br>top right: Mataemon Araki Yoshimura 荒木又右エ門吉村 (1599-1638), a master of the art of the sword, with the head Kawai Matagorō at his feet.  
<br>top left: Sekiguchi Yatarō 関口弥太郎 (1640-1729) staring down a pack of wolves in the Hakone Mountains.

<br>bottom right: Kimura Matazō  木村又藏 (lived c. 1600) holding a yari (straight-headed spear), looking at distant fighting.
<br>bottom left: Musashibō Benkei 武蔵坊辨慶 (1155-1189) pretending to read the contents of an empty scroll to be allowed safe passage through the Ataka barrier.

title: Zen-2
creator: Maki Haku 巻白 (1924-2000)

title: Soba Deliveryman (蕎麦の出前もち Soba no demae-mochi)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
In this second edition of the print Soba Deliveryman from Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Series 2, a soba deliveryman, his delicious hot and cold soba dishes stacked to the sky, peddles down the street on his way to his customers.
<br>The English language commentary accompanying this post-war edition reads, "A Delivery Boy (Demai-mochi). The Japanese like 'Soba' and 'Udon' which are something like spaghetti and macaroni [sic]. The udon shop delivers the dishes when ordered, and several kinds of containers are used. You see a delivery boy on his bicycle, holding a stack of bowls or trays, cases, sauce-bottles and cups with his left hand, and steering the bicycle with a single hand, just like trick-riding seen in the circus. Depicted by Sanzo Wada. Printed by KYOTO-HANGA-IN."
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[1] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[2]

title: Illustrated Account of the Sino-Japanese War, Volume 2 (日清戦闘畫報 第四編 Nisshin Sentō Gahō, daini hen)
creator:
Kubota Beisen 久保田米僊 (1852-1906)
<br>Kubota Beisai 久保田 米齊 (1874-1937)
description: Volume 2 of a total of eleven bound volumes forming a pictorial account of the first Sino-Japanese War, from its outbreak in the summer of 1894 to Japan's sea-victories at Weihaiwei, Japan's advance into Manchuria and finally the peace treaty ending the war in April 1895. The eleven volumes were published at irregular intervals between October 21st 1894 and June 6th 1895.  Each volume has an introduction written by a well-known figure of the time. The books were produced from carved woodblocks and are bound in the usual method of "bound-pocket books" (fukuro toji 袋綴じ). Volumes 5 through 11 have English captions above the illustrations.

title: Spring (untitled)
creator: Yoshida Chizuko 吉田千鶴子 (1924-2017)
description: This collection contains two almost identical prints by the artist using the same woodblocks, with minor modifications, IHL.1091, titled Spring, and this untitled print IHL.1985. In these prints Chizuko presents two tilting city landscapes. In this untitled print (IHL.1985), Chizuko has shifted the position of the chain of heart-shaped objects to the right and darkened the background.  Additional marks, most noticeable in the lower left of the image have also been made. Known for her later prints featuring myriads of butterflies, there may be one flitting about in the upper left quadrant of both these prints.

title: Kamigata shumi (Kamigata Taste), 1921, Autumn Issue  (上方趣味 大正十年 秋の巻 Kamigata shumi, Taishō jūnen, aki no maki)
creator:
Ogami Nanryō 小上南嶺 (1893-1966)
<br>Gion Seitoku 祇園井特 (active 1789-1830)
description:
Featured in this October 1921 issue of the magazine "Kamigata shumi" (Kamigata taste) were works of the Ōsaka artist Ogami Nanryō 小上南嶺 (1893-1966) and the long dead Kyōto bijinga painter Gion Seitoku 祇園井特 (active 1789-1830). Ogami designed the magazine's woodblock printed cover of an ant crawling on an andon (Japanese paper lamp) titled "Autumn Night" (秋の夜) along with an inserted woodblock print titled "Otsuta" (お蔦). Gion was represented by an inserted woodblock reproduction of what must have been his original painting, simply titled "Kyōto Bijin" (京美人). 
<br><br> KAMIGATA SHUMI (source: website of the Osaka Prefectural Library https://www.library.pref.osaka.jp/nakato/shotenji/24_shumi.html [accessed 8-17-23]
<br> "Kamigata shumi," edited and published by Watanabe Ryō (渡邊亮), was a long running (146 volumes) small magazine filled with "content related to customs, legends, traditions, specialties, travelogues, and performing arts from various places in Kamigata [the Kyōto-Ōsaka area]." 
<br>Setting out the intent of the magazine in its first issue in April 1915, Watanabe wrote, "We intend to publish this magazine with the aim of igniting the passion of Kamigata taste against Edo taste . . . ." The magazine's small size made it easy to carry and read, and to make it easier on the reader the main text was annotated with furigana. 
<br>A diverse group of authors including Watanabe himself, writing under the name Watanabe Shisen 渡辺紫染 (birth and death dates unknown), Udagawa Bunkai 宇田川文海 (1848-1930), Ema Tsutomu 江馬務 (1884-1979), Kitani Hōgin 木谷蓬吟 (1877-1950), Takaya Shin 高谷伸 (1896-1966) and Takayasu Gekkō 高安月郊 (1869-1944), contributed stories and articles.

title: Matsushima (松島)
creator: Okuyama Gihachirō 奥山儀八郎 (1907-1981)
description:
Okuyama's rendering of Matsushima's Godaidō Temple 五大堂 (temple of Five Great Wisdom Kings) in snow. This small temple sits on a small island in Matsushima Bay, attached to the mainland by Sukashibashi bridge. It has been named an Important Cultural Property. As written in the right margin of the print, the printer of this image was the artist's son Okuyama Gijin 奥山義人 (1934-2020), who took over management of his  father's studio in 1973.
<br><br>Okuyama Gihachirō (1907-1981) was a creative print (sōsaku hanga) artist and a graphic designer for the Japan Wool Company and Nikka Whiskey. He was the founder of the Japan Print Institute (Nihon Hanga Kenkyshū) in 1946, to be followed by the establishment in 1954 of his own workshop, Okuyama Hanga Kōbō, where he produced his own landscapes such as this print and woodblock copies of famous paintings by Western artists. He created over 1,000 prints during his career and dedicated the later part of his life to the study and revival of the traditional woodblock techniques of ukiyo-e production.

title: A Brief Description of World Geography (Compiled by Uchida Masao),  Africa, first of three, vol. 8 ([內田正雄纂輯]・輿地誌略 三篇上 巻八 亜非利加州 Yochi shiryaku・Uchida Masao sanshū, 3-shū, jō, kan 8, Afurica shū)
creator: Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1827-1881) - copper plate prints attributed to the artist. Artist's name does not appear in this volume.
description:
Volume 8 of an eventual 13 volumes of the geography textbook Yochi shiryaku (1870-1880). Volume 8 covers Africa.

<br><br>Yochi shiryaku was the most widely used world geography textbook in the early Meiji era, compiled by former Edo Government officer, Uchida Masao. Uchida was sent to Europe from 1862 to 1866 by the Tokugawa government, to gather information to compile these lavishly illustrated textbooks. He returned to Japan with oil paintings, photographic albums, and hundreds of pictorial natural history images. Based upon the sources he collected on his travels, Uchida began to compile the Yochi Shiryaku in 1870, a thirteen-volume of encyclopedia of world geography. Its success was primarily due to the huge number of illustrations that Uchida called "shashin (photography)," the images copied from the Western photographic albums and traveling magazines by the artist Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1827/1828-1881/1882) who turned them into copperplate illustrations. Yochi shiryaku was published in various editions over ten years and used in schools all over Japan, as well as being widely read as the book of "enlightenment." After Uchida's death, volumes 10 through 13 were compiled by the educator Nishimura Shigeki 西村 茂樹 (1828-1902), a colleague at the Ministry of Education, based on Uchida’s draft.
<br> A premise of Yochi shiryaku was the existence of "a finely ordered hierarchy of peoples and states," with racial differences [the physical features and geographical dissemination of the "five human races" being described] being an "important factor underlying this hierarchical arrangement." - Source: "The Race and Racism Discourses in Modern Korea, 1890s—1910s," Vladimir Tikhonov, appearing in "Korean Studies, 2012, Vol. 36," University of Hawai'i Press, 2012, p. 41.

title: Maru-maru chinbun 團團珍聞, No. 937 (Blue Pencil News of the Weird)
creator: Honda Kinkichirō 本多錦吉郎 (1850-1921), cover design
description:
Maru-maru chinbun was a popular satirical journal published weekly from 1877 to 1907. It was founded by Nomura Fumio 野村文夫 (1836-91), a former official of the Meiji government and journalist, in the style of the British weekly magazine of satire and humour, Punch. Maru-maru chinbun satirised the government with its editorial articles, comic tanka and haiku poems, and caricatures and promoted the Movement for Civil Rights and Freedom in the 1880s.
<br>Like Tokyo Puck and Jiji manga, Maru-maru chinbun was a landmark in the history of manga. Published weekly from 1877 to 1907, it was patterned after the British Punch in its mixture of satirical essays, poems, and cartoons. The famous cover design, too, was reminiscent of Punch, but with Japanese twists everywhere. The horse and deer, for example, were meant to suggest the word baka – written with the characters for “horse” and “deer” but meaning “idiot.”
<br>The title itself involves several puns. Maru-maru literally means “circle-circle,” and refers to the empty circles often printed in lieu of words deemed offensive by censors. Chinbun puns on shinbun or “newspaper,” with “outlandish” substituted for “new.” Thus the title may be thought of as “[censored] News of the Weird.” (“Blue Pencil News” is scholar W. Puck Brecher’s solution.) The magazine was subtitled Odoke-e or “clownish pictures,” but written with characters that mean “Pictures of Tokyo,” a reference to the new capital’s status as the center of the nation’s political life and the magazine’s mission to lampoon it.<br> source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon)

title: Stone Pagodas (石塔)
creator: Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (1937-2019)
description: The series title Eight Views of the Land of the Morning Calm is a reference to the famous Eight Views of Korea, consisting of areas of scenic beauty or historical importance. Kurosaki takes a different tack with his eight views, providing us with "views" encompassing traditional Korean dress to pagodas.

title: Shichimenzan and Mount Fuji (七面山と富士)
creator: Jōkata Kaiseki 定方塊石 (1882-1966)
description:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. In this print the sun rises above Fuji as a family who has made the climb up Mount Shichimen looks on. During the equinoxes, it appears as though the sun is rising out of Fuji's crater and this view may be set during the autumn equinox. Two pilgrims can be seen in the bottom left heading down the mountain. The signboard on the right reads 日天子 遙拝所 月天子 七面山 and there is a round directional finder to the left of the family indicating the four cardinal directions.
<br>The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

title: Spring Field A (春の野 A)
creator: Fujita Fumio 藤田不美夫 (b. 1933)
description: A combining of abstract organic forms, discernible as a freshly plowed field, and a grouping of trees, make for a lovely composition.

title: The Rural Cottages in Onuma and Mount Fuji (小沼の田家と富士)
creator: Jōkata Kaiseki 定方塊石 (1882-1966)
description:
One of twenty-five prints in the series Twenty-Five Views of Mount Fuji: A Woodblock Collection, published by the artist Jōkata Kaiseki in 1931. When this print was published, cottages such as the one depicted in this print, with its small shrine and waterwheel, were common. Today the area around Onuma, located in Nishikatsura, Minamitsuru-gun (Yamanashi) about 49 mi (or 78 km) west of Tokyo, is a bustling suburb.
<br>The table of contents for the series included three laudatory commentaries by well-known artists, Kurushima Takehiko (1874-1950), one of the best-known authors of children's literature of the period; Yūki Somei (1875-1957), a Japanese-style and Western-style painter and member of the Imperial Art Academy and Kanokogi Taskeshirō (1874-1941), a Western-style painter and print artist, also a member of the Imperial Art Academy. Titles for each of the three commentaries can be loosely translated as "On the Occasion of a Close Friend's Outstanding Achievement," "A Marvelous Work that Opened up the Frontier's Unexplored Boundary" and "Exquisite and Excellent Work for Future Generations."

title: Asakusa Battledore Fair (浅草羽子板市 Asakusa hagoita ichi)
creator: Koga Misao 古賀操 (active c. 1960s-1980s)
description:
The artist's rendering of the annual three-day Battledore Fair that takes place each year in Asakusa starting on December 17. Koga gives us a view of the bottom tiers of the Five Story Pagoda of Sensoji, the stalls selling hagoita 羽子板 and the crowds.<br>
This print was one of twenty five included in a portfolio of woodblock prints titled Lyricism of Shitamachi 下町抒情 published by Han no kai, the print society formed by Tadashige Ono (1909-1990) to encourage and support young artists. Tadashige contributed three prints to the portfolio and twenty-one other little-known artists contributed prints.<br>Shitamachi was the name used to designate Tokyo's "low city," an area associated with the common people before the war. In post-war terminology it designates everything east of the Imperial Palace. It is also used more generically to refer to those areas of modern Tokyo that maintain the flavor of the old city.

title: Village Blacksmith
creator: Mori Yoshitoshi 森義利 (1898-1992)
description: A kappizuri-e (stencil prints) depicting a village blacksmith or farrier at work while a horse looks on.

title: The Wheel of Causation, Volumes 21 and 22 (編童謡妙々車 21編, 22編 Warabeuta myōmyō guruma)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada II 二代 歌川国貞  (1823-1880)
description: Volumes 21 and 22 of the 25 volume illustrated novel (kusazōshi 草双紙) Warabeuta myōmyō guruma, originally published between 1855 and 1871 by the Edo/Tokyo publisher Tsutaya Kichizō of the firm Kōeidō. While volumes 21 and 22 were originally issued in 1867 this collection's edition was issued in 1874. Commonly translated as The Wheel of Causation, the story revolves around the romantic adventures of Princess Uzuki and the hero Shidoroku. While written for the masses, the heavily illustrated kusazōshi have been called "a crucial element in the production of modern literary idiom" and "a unique form of verbal-visual art" deserving "to be treated as a national cultural heritage." - Source: "Eyes of the Heart: Illustration and the Visual Imagination in Modern Japanese Literature" [a dissertation], Pedro Thiago Ramos Bassoe, University of California, Berkeley, 2018, p. 1.

title: Scenic View of Tokyo, Ueno Park Tōshō-gū Shrine (東京名所上野公園地東照宮 Tōkyō meisho Ueno kōenchi Tōshō gū)
creator: Yamada Toshitada 山田年忠 (Yamada Keichū 山田敬中) (1868-1934)
description: It is spring and the cherry trees are in bloom as two women and a child all dressed in Western fashion are  strolling through Tokyo's Tōshō-gū Shrine. The shrine dedicated to shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616) and founded  in 1627, has been spared the many natural and man-caused disasters that have visited Tokyo and today remains largely unchanged from its renovation in 1651. The trio likely entered the grounds through Karamon gate, seen in the left sheet. Five small figures, three priests and two groundskeepers, can also be seen. While the print is a "scenic view" of this Tokyo landmark, the real scenic view is the high-fashion Western dress of the women and child.

title: Sarusawa Pond (猿沢池)
creator: Itō Nisaburō 伊藤仁三郎 (1905-2001)
description: Sarusawa Pond in Nara on a rainy day. One of the most popular subjects for shin hanga print artists. "This pond is located within Nara Park, and has a circumference of 360 meters. The five-storied pagoda of Kofuku-ji Temple, as well as the willow trees surrounding the pond reflect beautifully in its surface, and are recognized as one of the Eight Views of Nara."- website of Nara Travelers Guide https://narashikanko.or.jp/en/spot/nature/sarusawaike/ [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Play A Board Game of the Road to Iga Pass, Act IX  (伊賀越道中双六, 九 Igagoe dōchū sugoroku, kyū)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru I 初代 歌川 国輝 (active c. 1820-1860)
description:
This print depicts Act IX of Igagoe dōchū sugoroku, one of the three great revenge plays, along with Kanadehon Chūshingura and Soga no Taimen, in Japanese literature. In this scene we see Otani おたに, ill and clutching her baby, outside of her husband's (Karake Masaemon 唐木政右衛門 - the real life Araki Mataemon) house in Okazaki. Seated beside Masaemon is the wife of samurai Sawai Matagorō, who is the object of revenge. The orange rectangular cartouche in the upper left reads 岡崎の浪宅に政右衛門不計妻お谷に廻逢図, describing the scene being illustrated.

<br>This play was originally written for the bunraku theater in 1783 by Chikamatsu Hanji (1725-1783) and is often seen titled as Numazu after its often performed Act VI. The sugoroku in the title references a board game that incorporated the stations along the Tōkaidō highway running from Edo to Kyoto. Samuel Leiter in his "New Kabuki Encyclopedia: A Revised Adaptation of Kabuki Jiten" provides the following commentary on the play:
<br>"Igagoe deals with the vengeance wrought by Araki Mataemon. The original play’s most distinctive feature was that each of its ten acts represented another stage on the journey along the Tokaido Highway from Edo to Kyoto. Only Act VI’s “Numazu” scene and the VIII’s “Okazaki” scene are still regularly performed.

<br>"The actual vendetta was carried out in 1634 at Iga Ueno, located between Nagoya and Nara, on Kawai Matagorō by Watanabe Kazuma and his master swordsman brother-in-law, Araki Mataemon. The deed occurred four years after Kazuma’s father, Watanabe Yukie of the house of Lord Tadao Ikeda of Okayama, was killed by Matagorō, a retainer of lord of Koremori. The dramatists, as usual, have taken liberties with names, places, and events. The play is a complexly woven tragedy in which numerous loyalties and obligations crisscross with one another among a host of characters." - Source: New Kabuki Encyclopedia: A Revised Adaptation of Kabuki Jiten, Samuel Leiter, Greenwood Press, 1997, p. 211-212

title: Oirasegawa (奥入瀬川)
creator: Yasui Sōtarō 安井曾太郎 (1888–1955)
description:
In the summer 1932 Yasui, considered one of Japan’s most respected Western-style (yōga) painters from the1930s through his death in 1955, stayed at Lake Towada and produced several works under the auspices of the Kokuritsu Kōen Kyōkai (National Park Association.) On his way back home he created a number of sketches of the Oirase River which drains Lake Towada.

<br>This woodblock print is likely a reproduction of one of the sketches of the river he created on this trip.

title: Karuizawa Station (軽井沢駅)
creator: Koga Misao 古賀操 (active c. 1960s-1980s)
description: The artist's rendering of the old Karuizawa Station built in 1910 and closed c. 1999 to make way for the new station handling high speed shinkansen services from Tokyo. The old building was relocated and turned into a museum. Recently, there has been discussion of using the building for new station facilities.

title: Former Mikasa House (旧三笠ハウス)
creator: Koga Misao 古賀操 (active c. 1960s-1980s)
description: The artist's rendering of the 1905 Mikasa Hotel in Karuizawa in Nagano, now a museum.

title: Karuizawa Kōgen Church (軽井沢高原教会)
creator: Koga Misao 古賀操 (active c. 1960s-1980s)
description: The artist's rendering of Karuizawa Kōgen Church built in 1921.

title: Saruwaka Performance by the Descendants of Nakamura Kanzaburō (猿若狂言 Saruwaka kyōgen)
creator: Torii Kiyosada 鳥居清貞 (1844-1901)
description:
One of two prints designed by Torii Kiyosada for this twenty-five print series (plus a prolog/index print) picturing events in a typical year in an Edo theater. This print depicts the comic dance pantomime known as saruwaka kyōgen.
<br>Saruwaka kyōgen is a dance in the style of the kyōgen of the No theatre that found its way into Kabuki. The earliest kabuki saruwaka involved the actor’s participation in chaya asahi (“visit to a teahouse”) scenes, in which a dashing fellow (played by Okuni) went to a teahouse accompanied by his servant, the saruwaka, who wore a tenugui kerchief covering his cheeks; a rough, wide-sleeved, single layer kimon (hitoe), and leggings (kyahan). The plot involved the star’s encounter with the teahouse proprietress (kaka), played by a kyōgen actor (the kyōgenshi). There was a banquet and the characters sang and danced a kouta.
<br> Kiyosada copied this design from one of the earlier Torii masters, Torii Kiyonaga (1752-1815).

title: Bird (鳥)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description: The first of ten prints in the first of five sets of prints comprising the series Outdoor Sketches created by the artist between 1928 and 1935.  In this print a man relaxes on a hillside as a flock of birds flies by. Maekawa created this series of five sets (ten prints each set) of black and white linoleum cuts as, in the artist's words, prints of affection (shin'ai ban).  Each small print, its image area measuring approximately 5 x 5 in. (12.7 x 12.7 cm), depicts a figure engaged in outdoor work or recreation.

title: Parasol (パラソル)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description: The sixth of ten prints in the first of five sets of prints comprising the series Outdoor Sketches created by the artist between 1928 and 1935.  In this print a woman in a bobbed haircut leans against a railing on what might be a boardwalk with a parasol resting lightly on her shoulder. Maekawa created this series of five sets (ten prints each set) of black and white linoleum cuts as, in the artist's words, prints of affection (shin'ai ban).  Each small print, its image area measuring approximately 5 x 5 in. (12.7 x 12.7 cm), depicts a figure engaged in outdoor work or recreation.

title: Music at Winter Garden in New York
creator: Yamagishi Kazue 山岸主計 (1891-1984)
description: An Art Deco style portrayal of a lively singing performance, accompanied by a live orchestra, at New York's Winter Garden, the iconic venue for musical reviews and theater in the Broadway theater district. Dispatched on a three year around-the-world print fact finding mission in 1926, New York certainly would have been on Yamagishi's itinerary. While the date 1930 is written in pencil on this print's verso, Yamagishi presents us with a scene, imagined or real, prior to 1928, before the theater was brought under the management of Warner Bros. (1928-1933) and used exclusively for cinema.

title: February (二月) calendar page from the 1941 Japan Print Association Calendar
creator: Fujimori Shizuo 藤森静雄 (1891-1943)
description:
Fujimori, a founding member of the Nihon Hanga Kyōkai (Japan Print Association) in 1931, contributed this print of a cricket on a branch to the 2601 calendar issued by the JPA. 2601, counting since the mythical beginning of Japan in 660 BCE, translates to 1941, a year that would find Japan attacking Pearl Harbor in December.<br>
The JPA calendars were issued from Showa 11 (1936) through Showa 19 (1944).

title: Shinjuku Imperial Gardens (新宿御苑 Shinjuku Gyoen)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description:
Kitaoka presents us with one of the many tree-lined promenades in this now public garden that contains over 10,000 trees. This undated artist's proof, signed in pencil by Kitaoka, likely dates from 1950 and was released as part of the 1950-1951 five-part portfolio (each portfolio containing five prints), titled The Face of Tokyo 東京の顔.
<br>This artist proof appears identical to the print in the collection of The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo. However, it is printed on different paper than the other four prints from The Face of Tokyo in this collection which are printed on a distinctive mica-impregnated paper.
<br>This beautifully designed and, unfortunately, overlooked series portrays post-war Tokyo in the social-realist style that Kitaoka embraced after the war and later rejected.  For other prints in this series see IHL.0626 "Around Ochanomizu (Kanda River)", IHL.0640 "Playing Bingo", IHL.0641 "Outside Shinjuku Station, the West Exit" and IHL.0642 "Behind the Stage".

title: Work '66 (作品 '66)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: A tiny print with an image area measuring 2 1/4 x 2 5/8 in. (5.7 x 6.7 cm). Takahashi's compositions work well at this small size, inviting even closer scrutiny than his better known large works.

title: B3
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: A tiny print with an image area measuring 2 1/4 x 2 5/8 in. It's amazing that Takahashi's compositions work so well as this small size, inviting even closer scrutiny than his better known large works.

title: Portrait of a Woman (watercolor on paper)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description: While most famous for his prints, Hagiwara trained as a painter and continued to produce paintings, both small (as in this painting) and large, in both oil and watercolor (as in this work) throughout his printmaking career.

title: Nanban Dining (untitled) an Ex-Libris for S. Kagayama
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description: Like a number of other sōsaku hanga artists, Kawakami created numerous bookplates for collectors. In this ex libris 蔵書票 created for the collector S. Kagayama, we see five Nanban gentlemen seated around a table eating and drinking, as they're being waited upon.  Kawakami was fascinated by Nanban (southern barbarians, i.e., Portuguese) culture, producing many woodblock prints on the subject.

title: Woman with Apples (untitled) an Ex-Libris made for  S. Kagayama
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description: One of five small book plates in this collection that were created for a collector of ex libris 蔵書票 with the name of S. Kagayama. Three of the bookplates show the collector's name in kanji characters, either 加賀山 (Kagayama) or 加賀山 蔵書 (Kagayama library) and the other two provide the collector's name in English, either Kagayama or S.
