title: Saihō-ji Western Kyoto (洛西 西芳寺 Rakusei Saihō-ji)
creator: Itō Nisaburō 伊藤仁三郎 (1905-2001)
description:
A depiction of the moss garden at Saiho-ji Temple. While this collection's print is neither signed nor sealed, another impression of this print carries the seal of the artist Itō Nisaburō in the lower right corner of the image.
<br>Saihoji Temple belongs to the Rinzai school of Japanese Buddhism. In 1994 the site was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Tradition holds that after being founded by the monk Gyoki in accordance with an edict from the emperor Shomu during the Nara Period [AD 710-794] and briefly occupied by Kobo Daishi during the Heian Period [1794-1185], Saihoji was revived during the Kamakura Period [1185-1333] by the priest Honen, who restored the temple and converted it into a training hall for Jodo Shinko (the Pure Land faith). The facility was subsequently devastated by military conflict before being rebuilt in 1339 as a center of strict Zen ascetic training by the priest Muso Soseki with the staunch backing of the emperor Godaigo and the shogun Ashikaga Takauji.
<br>
The garden (a nationally designated scenic and historic site), built by Muso Soseki, consists of an upper level of dry karesansui-style rock arrangements and a lower level built around Ogonchi Pond, which is shaped like the Chinese character meaning "heart."  Blanketed by more than 120 species of moss, the temple is popularly and affectionately known as Kokedera (Moss Temple.) - Source: Kyoto City explanatory plaque at site.

title: Triangular Hood (三角頭巾 Sankaku zukin)
creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)
description: Maekawa produced a number of prints of Japanese country women in similar poses.

title: Hello, Ms Mao (毛さん今日は)
creator: Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (1937-2019)
description: "This series is like a report on China. Woodblock printing originated in China, and I had wanted to visit there for a long time, but due to the unstable political situation I was unable to do so. In these prints, I could make good use of video and photographic print techniques while also using Chinese history, culture, written characters, seals, and traditional Chinese composition to establish a new style and changes in my work." - the artist Kurosaki Akira

title: Roof Landscape (屋根の風景 Yane no fūkei)
creator: Konishi Seiichirō 小西誠一郎 (b. 1919)
description: Rooftops of one of the stately neighborhoods in Kyoto. If we need a hint that this view is of Kyoto roofs, the copula on the left carries the characters 西陣, telling us these roofs are in Kyoto's famous Nishijin district, known for its townhouses, machiya, and traditional weaving and textiles.

title: Scenes of the Inner Provinces, Yamato (Nara), Volume 2 (畿内見物 大和の卷 Kinai kenbutsu Yamato no maki)
creator:
Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
<br>Asai Chū 浅井忠 (1856-1907)
description: Volume two of the three volume set of "sketch tour" books titled Kinai kenbutsu (Scenes of the Inner Provinces), published by Kanao Tanejirō (1879-1947) (the publishing house Bunendō) in 1911 and 1912.1 Volume 1, subtitled Kyōto, and volume 2, subtitled Yamato (Nara), were issued in 1911 and the third volume, subtitled Ōsaka, in 1912. The three volumes contain 57 stitched-in woodblock prints, as well as woodblock printed covers, end papers and slipcases, all but one of the woodblock designs by the Western-style artist Nakazawa Hiromitsu (1874-1964). While photogravure, and halftone and heliotype (collotype) reproductions of paintings and sketches by Hiromitsu, and a single heliotype of a painting by Asai Chū (1856-1907), far outnumber the woodblock prints, the quality of these reproductions varies and the true highlight of these volumes are the woodblock prints. See IHL.2398 for volume 1.

title: I Love You B
creator: Ay-O 靉嘔 (b. 1931)
description: Ay-O derived I Love You B from his own silkscreen work of 1974 titled I Love You (Love Letters) (see IHL.1472), and Marcel Duchamp's Étant donnés (1946-1966), an assemblage containing a headless woman mannequin. The Artist Comments, "I love you B combines the Mexican fellow's garments, a nude and a gas lamp said to be made of pig hide held in the hands of a headless woman's torso suggested by Duchamp's last work [Etant donnés] owned by the Philadelphia Art Museum, repeated in a pattern along with parallel lines. A part of this work I titled Portrait of Yoshiaki Tono [art critic]." - Source: AY-O’s Rainbow Prints Catalogue Raisonne 1954-1979, Sadajirō Kubo, Sohbun-sha, p. 160.

title: Shade of a Tree
creator: Ida Shōichi 井田照一 (1941-2006)
description: This color lithograph was issued at the same time as Measure and Pig (IHL.2037), picturing a pig, possibly prior to a trip to slaughter house. The yellow pig in this print, standing among the foliage, seems quite unaware of what fate may hold in store.

title: Measure and Pig
creator: Ida Shōichi 井田照一 (1941-2006)
description: Issued at the same time as Shade of a Tree (IHL.2036), which pictures a seemingly contented pig under green foliage, one wonders if Ida is presenting us with that pig's fate, being measured for the slaughter.

title: Battleship Island (軍艦島 Gunkanjima)
creator: Unknown
description:
The caption on the inside of this New Year's greeting card, signed S. Takagi, Mitsubishi Mining Co., Ltd., President, reads:
<br>"A view of the 'Battleship Island.' 500,000 tons of best coking coal annually are produced here from the working faces 2,400 feet below the sea. The island [Hashima] is a part of the Mitsubishi's Takashima Coal Mine, one of the oldest coal mines in Japan and yet being developed on the most modern lines." 
<br>Left unmentioned is the use of forced labor during wartime by Mitsubishi, including the use of forced Korean labor during World War II to extract coal. At least 800 Koreans were sent to Hashima during the war, 134 of whom reportedly died while working there.
<br>Even for the Japanese who worked at the mine it was a harsh environment and by the end of the war in August 1945 about 1,300 laborers had died on the island, some in underground accidents, others of illnesses related to exhaustion and malnutrition and some drowning while trying to escape from the island which lies in the East China Sea some fifteen kilometers from Nagasaki.
<brBattleship Island (Gunkanjima or 軍艦島) was registered as a Unesco World Heritage Site in 2015 and guided tours began in 2009.

title: New Skin (新膚 Shin hada)
creator: Onchi Kōshirō 恩地孝四郎 (1891-1955)
description: This print was originally created for the dōjin (coterie magazine) Han geijutsu (Print Art), Volume 1, No. 5 published in August 1932 in Tokyo by Shiro to Kurosha, the company of the artist Ryōji Chōmei (Kumata) (1899-1982). This collection's print was re-printed in 1933 for Ryōji Kumata's compilation of prints from Han geijutsu, titled simply 版畫 (Hanga). All the prints were re-printed for this volume from the original blocks created by the artists by the master printer Takahashi Kobo 高橋春正.

title: Bamboo (untitled)
creator: Ide Gakusui 井出岳水 (1899-1978)

title: Pine branches and poem (surimono)
creator: Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1807-1891)
description:
Being a painter of the Shijō school, Zeshin's surimono have been referred to as "Shijō surimono." Robert Schapp writes, "Shijō surimono seemed to have flourished mainly after the gradual disappearance of their ukiyo-e counterparts in the 1830s. And based on his sound Shijō education the talented Zeshin soon became one of the leading designers for Shijō surimono in Edo." He notes that while the total number of surimono designed by Zeshin is unknown, it may run into the thousands.[1]

<br>In this print, auspicious pine branches and the edge of a stream are pictured. Ten haikai (seventeen syllable poems) are written to the left of the image with the names of their composers.

<br>The Art Institute Chicago notes, "Many examples of large-scale [and smaller] surimono by Shibata Zeshin exist; he must have set up a large establishment in order to cater to orders from poets and intellectuals. Since Zeshin was engaged in many official commissions in other media and had a large group of apprentices, he probably left most of the details of surimono production to his apprentices."[2]

<br><br>

[1] "Zeshin's Shijō surimono and his later shikishiban prints," by Robert Schapp, Andon 102, Journal of the Society of Japanese Arts, October 2016, p. 55-67.

<br>[2] Art Institute Chicago https://www.artic.edu/artworks/43726/the-cup-of-long-life [access 8-17-23]

title: Morning glory flowers, calligraphy brush and poems (surimono)
creator: Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1807-1891)
description:
Being a painter of the Shijō school, Zeshin's surimono have been referred to as "Shijō surimono." Robert Schapp writes, "Shijō surimono seemed to have flourished mainly after the gradual disappearance of their ukiyo-e counterparts in the 1830s. And based on his sound Shijō education the talented Zeshin soon became one of the leading designers for Shijō surimono in Edo." He notes that while the total number of surimono designed by Zeshin is unknown, it may run into the thousands.[1]

title: Illustration of Komatsu-hiki (小松引図)
creator: Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1807-1891)
description:
Zeshin's drawing of a samurai and courtier out for a day of "pulling pines," the popular custom in which Heian period nobles took pines home during the fondly-held event called the Komatsu-hiki (pulling out small pine trees on the first day of the Rat), using them to pray for longevity. 

<br>This woodblock print appearing in the 12th issue of the magazine Bijutsu Sekai 美術世界 (World of Art) was published three months after Zeshin's death.

title: Illustration for Chapter 13 Akashi (明石)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
A color woodblock illustration from the first volume of Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari, Yosano Akiko's 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942) translation into modern colloquial Japanese of The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), written by Murasaki Shikibu 紫式部著 in the early 11th century.<br> 
The color woodblock illustrations for the four books comprising Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari were stitched into the books and it is likely, though no definitive proof exists, that the publisher Kanao Tanejirō printed additional copies of the woodblock illustrations to be sold as single sheet prints. This collection's three stand-alone prints (IHL.2046, IHL.2101 an IHL.2270) would be examples of this, as they do not display any evidence of having been removed from a bound volume nor do they display any of the toning present on many of prints bound into the books due to contact with their acidic translucent protective sheets also bound into the original volumes.

title: Birds from the book Simplified Forms of Drawing Birds and Animals (鳥獸略画式 Chōjū ryakugashiki)
creator: Kitao Masayoshi (Kuwagata Keisai) 北尾政美 (鍬形蕙齋) (1764-1824)
description: A single page from Kitao Masayoshi's drawing manual. Kitao was a pioneer of a new style of drawing manual called ryakugashiki, which marked an important point in the development of this style of illustration and he strove, in his work, to simplify forms and capture the spirit of the animals he was depicting. The drawing manuals were reprinted many times and it is not known which edition this single page is from.

title: Work・73-112 (Snow)
creator: Maki Haku 巻白 (1924-2000)
description:
The character for snow 雪, balanced with a pink teardrop, a white circle and Maki's seal, which he always handles as a design element of his print.
<br>In the early 1960s Maki developed his own process of relief printmaking using woodblocks and cement. He first carved a conventional woodblock and then placed a cement mixture around the areas raised in relief on the block. Before the cement was set, Maki would texture it and after it dried he carved and chiseled the cement into the desired shape. After the cement completely dried, the entire surface of the plate was shellacked.

title: The Fight between Hideyoshi and Ito Hyuganokami (秀吉伊東日向守を打取る図)
creator: Utagawa Toyonobu 歌川豊宣 (1859–1886)
description:
This diptych print is from a series of 31 diptych prints plus a table of contents commemorating the rise to power of Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537-1598), one of the three great unifiers of Japan who rose from humble origins to become the second unifier of Japan who, after 100 years of war, brought stability and peace. This print depicts Toyotomi, when he was known as Kinoshita Tokichirō, arriving at Fujikawa for his first battle. Arriving when the battle is almost over, he hides in the reeds along the river and ambushes the commander of the enemy forces, Ito Hyuga no Kami, with a spear. Mt. Fuji rises in the distance. 
<br>Born in 1538, as the son of a peasant foot soldier from a village in Owari province, Toyotomi Hideyoshi was the loyal vassal of Oda Nobunaga. By consistently showing political cunning and strategic skills during military campaigns Hideyoshi eventually assumed the mantle of Nobunaga and became a powerful warlord. By 1591 he had brought order to the country, becoming the second of "the three unifiers," the others being Oda Nobunaga (1534-1582) and Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616).
<br>Multiple publishers were involved with this series.

title: Symbol No. 2 (象徴 Shōchō)
creator: Maki Haku 巻白 (1924-2000)
description: "Maki Haku is known for using the established tradition of calligraphy and abstracting kanji characters—the Chinese ideographs that are used in Japanese writing—into quirky images. At first glance, the top portion of this print seems ambiguous; some may see a twirling figure holding round bells. In fact, the figure is the character for gaku/raku (樂), meaning “music” and “enjoyment.” The etymology of gaku comes from the word for a hand instrument with bells and ornamental strings that was shaken to make music for the enjoyment of the gods. When the bells were not in use, they were hung on wooden stands (as represented by the 木 character, meaning “tree,” which appears at the bottom of the gaku/raku character)." -  Source: Yale University Art Gallery website https://artgallery.yale.edu/collections/objects/110323 [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Frontispiece, Robinson hyōkō kiryaku 魯敏孫漂行紀略 (An Abridged Account of Robinson’s Shipwreck)
creator: Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1828-1881)

title: Onoe Kikugorō V as Yashio and Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Masaoka in the play The Precious Flowers and Autumn Incense of Sendai (八汐尾上菊五郎・政岡 市川団十郎・伽羅先代萩)
creator: Toyohara Kunichika 豊原国周 (1835–1900)
description: The actor Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903) in the role of Yashio and, in the top inset, Ichikawa Danjūrō IX as Masaoka in the play Meiboku sendaihagi (The Precious Flowers and Autumn Incense of Sendai).<br><br>In 1893 Kunichika undertook a commission for this series of 100 single-sheet portraits, dedicated to Onoe Kikugorō V (1844-1903). One Hundred Roles of Baikō (the haiku pen name of Kikugorō V), featured the major roles of Onoe Kikugorō V and included an inset on the top of each print depicting a supporting actor.

title: Onoe Kikugorō V as Washi no Chōki and Kawarazaki Kunitarō as Tōgokuya musume (鷲の長吉尾上菊五郎・東国屋娘およし 故初代河原崎国太郎)

title: Benjamin Franklin (仏蘭克林)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description:
One of fourteen prints in the series of color woodblock educational prints titled Legends of Great Westerners issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print describes how to make Benjamin Franklin's lightning conductor to protect a building in a storm. Inside this steepled building a couple can be seen reacting to the violence of the storm by covering their ears.<br>In 1750, two years before his famous kite and key experiment which proved lightning to be a form electricity, Ben Franklin had "theorized that lightning might be preventable by using an elevated iron connected to earth to empty static from a cloud." - Source: website of the Franklin Institute https://www.fi.edu/history-resources/franklins-lightning-rod [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued full-color woodblock prints for childhood education between 1873 and 1885. The Ministry advertised these prints "As an aid to the education of the young child (yōdō) 幼童) within the home… use these pictures as a toy when the child is sitting or lying down. And when the child reaches the age to enter elementary school, the effect will be no small matter.” - Source: "Raising Subjects: The Representation of Children and Childhood in Meiji Japan," Rhiannon Paget an article from New Voices: A Journal for Emerging Scholars of Japanese Studies in Australia and New Zealand, Volume 4, 2011.

title: Wheel and Axle (輪軸 rinjiku)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description: The right sheet only of one of eight diptych prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of mechanics issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). (For the complete diptych see IHL.0765.) This print discusses and demonstrates the principles and practical uses of the axle and wheel. (For other prints in this series see IHL.0766 and IHL.0767.) <br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

title: Timepiece and Lamp (時計とラシプ Tokei to ranpu)
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description: One of three prints commissioned from the artist by Hotta Watchmakers (Hotta Corporation) to commemorate the 95th anniversary of their watch shop. (Also see IHL.2066.) The print was published in collaboration with the Kokugakai (National Picture Association).<br> Carved and printed by Kawakami, this print was printed on paper made by Ichibei Iwano VIII, a Living National Treasure (Preserver of Important Intangible Cultural Properties) of Japan.<br>Ryohei Hotta (1913-1989), ex-president of the Hotta Corporation, was a collector of timepiece ephemera who donated his collection, the "Hotta Collection", to the National Diet Library in 1987. Included in the collection is a privately printed 1971 catalog of colored woodblock prints on watches and calendars titled "Tokei to koyomi no nishikie mokuroku." For a second impression of this print see IHL.1299.

title: The Charred Ruins of the Hongōza Theater (本郷座の焼跡 Hongōza no yakeato)
creator: Tamura Saiten 田村彩天 (1889-1933)

title: Young Boys' Rough Behavior (粗暴の童男 Sobō no warabe)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)
description: From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) showing examples of children's good (moral) and bad behavior. In this print two children are harassing a horse, pulling its tail and hitting it with a switch, while an adult witnesses their bad behavior which he is sure to report to their parents. <br>In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

title: Little Girls Showing Concern (心切なる童女 Shinsetsunaru warabe)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)
description: From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) showing examples of children's good and bad behavior. In this print two young girls pull an old blind man out of the path of a galloping horse and carriage, leading him to safety. <br>In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

title: Children Who Like Fights (争闘を好む童男 Sōtō wo konomu warabe)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)- attributed to the school of the artist.
description: From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) which show examples of children's good and bad behavior. In this print a boy who has gotten into an unprovoked fight with another boy is confronted by a policeman.<br>In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

title: Business Trip to Saga, Hizen Province, No. 913 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・九百十三号・肥前国佐賀へ出張)
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞.  This print tells the story of three men who were sent to Saga on business and then run off with the business money. They are arrested while splurging in a brothel in Hyogo as pictured in the print.
<br>The writer for this print is identified as Tentendo Shujin, a pen name for the writer better known as Takabatake Ransen 高畠藍泉 (1838-1885). Takabatake Ransen was a gesaku writer and journalist who joined Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun shortly after its start in 1872 and often worked with the artist Yoshiiku.
<br>At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

title: A Geiko in Niigata, Echigo Province, Loses Savings, No. 708 appearing in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun (東京日々新聞・七百八號・越後の国新潟の芸妓に)
creator: Utagawa Yoshiiku 歌川芳幾 (1833-1904)
description:
At the top of this "news nishiki-e" is a banner held aloft by two cherubs containing the name of the sponsoring newspaper, the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun 東京日々新聞.  This print tells the story of a geigi 芸妓 named Imagawaya Hina who has just found out that the 1000 yen she saved is not there. It turns out it was stolen by her lover Tsurugaya Kiemon.
<br>The writer for this print is identified as Sansantei Arindo 山々亭有人, a pen name of the writer Jono Saigiku 条野採菊 (born Jono Denpei 條野伝平). Born in Edo in 1832, by his late teens he had decided to become a writer of gesaku (collective term for prose fiction during the middle to late-Edo period) stories. He published his first story in 1860, and during the 1860s first Yoshiiku, then Yoshitoshi, created illustrations for some of his books. He went on to found the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shinbun, the Keisatsu Shinbun and the Yamato Shinbun and continued to write fiction until his death in 1902.
<br>At the same time that the daily newspapers were trying to increase circulation, the woodblock industry, consisting of publishers, book/print stores, artists and craftsmen, were looking for ways to revive their flagging sales. One way that served both industries was to take the juiciest stories from the dailies and illustrate them with colorful single sheet woodblock prints designed by popular artists and published under the auspices of the newspapers. These woodblock prints called nishiki-e shinbun (“brocade picture newspapers”) included both text and pictures and sold for between 1.6 to 2 sen (a sen is 1/100 of a yen), making them affordable to ordinary working people. The text was mostly written using furigana and katakana to enhance readability.

title: True View of Asakusa Park, Around Twelve-Story Tower: Famous Places of Tokyo (東京名所 淺草公園十二階附近之真景)
creator: Unknown
description:
This lithograph by an anonymous artist, brings us a "true view" of the area near the twelve-story Ryōunkaku (Cloud Surpassing Pavilion) in 1921. Strolling along the Gourd Pond in Asakusa Park is a family dressed in their Sunday best. From the carp leaping up from the pond, to the spring cherry blossoms, to the airship and two bi-planes overhead, all signs are auspicious. Two years later, on September 1923, the Great Kantō Earthquake would devastate not only the 12-story Ryōunkaku but much of the city. 
<br>For a similar view see IHL.2129.

title: Evening View of Hamaōtsu (濱大津夕景 [浜大津夕景 Hamaōtsu yukei)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: Evening scene of the boardwalk at the ferry landing in the harbor at Hamaōtsu on Lake Biwa in Shiga prefecture. This print is part of the series titled New Eight Views of Ōmi, an updated set of views of the classic Eight Views of Ōmi (the area around Lake Biwa in Omi Province).

title: Okunikkō (奥日光)
creator: Maeda Masao 前田政雄 (1904-1974)

title: Timepiece and Lamp [with mug] (時計とラシプ  [マグ] Tokei to ranpu [magu])
creator: Kawakami Sumio (川上澄生; 川上澄夫) (1895-1972)
description: One of three prints commissioned from the artist by Hotta Watchmakers (Hotta Corporation) to commemorate the 95th anniversary of their watch shop. (Also see IHL.2056.) The print was published in collaboration with the Kokugakai (National Picture Association).<br> Carved and printed by Kawakami, this print was printed on paper made by Ichibei Iwano VIII, a Living National Treasure (Preserver of Important Intangible Cultural Properties) of Japan.<br>Ryohei Hotta (1913-1989), ex-president of the Hotta Corporation, was a collector of timepiece ephemera who donated his collection, the "Hotta Collection", to the National Diet Library in 1987. Included in the collection is a privately printed 1971 catalog of colored woodblock prints on watches and calendars titled "Tokei to koyomi no nishikie mokuroku."

title: Illustration of a Sawyer (木挽の図 Kobiki no zu)
creator: Unknown
description:
This print is a 1915 woodblock reproduction of likely an Edo-period anamorphosis print, known as a  "scabbard print" 鞘繪 (saya-e) in Japanese, picturing a sawyer pulling a saw. This reproduction appeared in the July 1915 issue of 浮世絵 "Ukiyo-e" magazine, accompanied by an article discussing saya-e.
<br>The text appearing next to the circle and dashed line in the bottom of the print reads 所へ鞘をあてて見るべし, telling the viewer to look at the print's reflection in a lacquered scabbard. The circle and the dashed line mark where the scabbard (or any reflective cylinder) should be placed and the line of viewing.
<br>Anamorphosis pictures were called saya-eさや絵 or kyōchū zu 鏡中図. When the distorted picture is reflected on a curved surface, such as that of a sword case (saya), it can be seen in its true proportions. Saya-e were a new type of pictorial representation that first appeared in Japan in the eighteenth century as anamorphosis pictures arrived in Japan from Europe (likely from the Dutch) and interest grew in acquiring new knowledge about optics and perspective from the West.

title: Chikugo River (筑後川 Chikugogawa)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description:
This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō from the series Japan Scenery Prints, Set 6: Tsukushi District, presents a semi-abstract view of the Chikugogawa in a heavy rain. The Chikugo River flows through Kumamoto, Ōita, Fukuoka and Saga prefectures in Japan. With a total length of 143 kilometres (89 miles), it is the longest river in Kyūshū. It flows from Mount Aso and empties into the Ariake Sea. 
<br>"Tsukushi is the ancient name of the area north-west of Kyushu [in the area of Chikuzen and Chikugo provinces] where Sakamoto was born. Sakamoto was rarely involved with sheet-prints, but like his colleagues on this series he had worked as a cartoonist and illustrator and had been a collaborator on the magazine Hōsun hence he was well used to graphic techniques. Indeed, his set [Tsukushi district] is the most strikingly designed in the series, combining impressionist, abstract and Expressionistic elements into a characteristically forceful blend." - Source: Modern Japanese Prints 1912-1989, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 1994, p. 42.
<br><br>JAPAN SCENERY PRINTS<br>
"The series Nihon fūkei hanga (Japan Scenery Prints) consists of ten sets of prints, with each set composed of five small landscapes and a cover print giving the name of the series, the name and number of the set, and the name of the artist. In addition, each set was accompanied by a table of contents and colophon sheet. Specific publication dates ranging from January 1917 through April 1920 indicate that each set was issued separately.  As Ishii Hakutei (1882-1958) designed the majority of prints in the series, it seems likely that Hakutei was the spearhead for the project. The artists asked Igami Bonkutsu to carve the blocks and Nakajima Jūtarō to publish the series." - Source: Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p. 274-276.
<br>In addition to Sakamoto Hanjirō (1882-1969), the other artists who contributed to the series were Ishii Hakutei (1182-1958), see IHL.1182 and IHL.1183, Hirafuku Hyakusui (1877-1933), Morita Tsunetomo (1881-1933), Kosugi Misei (1881-1964) and Ishii Tsuruzō (1887-1973), elder brother of Hakutei.

title: Okina (翁)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description:
In this print for the month of January, we see the ritual dance being performed by Okina.
<br><b>The Play - Okina</b> (Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 132-133.)
<br>Okina is a piece quite distinct in character from any other Nō play. Consisting of little more than a group of dances which are said to have been in existence in the tenth century, its history is certainly much older than that of any other Nō.  Throughout its history it has had a religious significance which still exists today. With words and dances designed to win the help of the gods in obtaining peace and prosperity in the land and long life for its people, Okina is performed only at times of special celebration or commemoration. When it is given, it is always performed first and the part of Okina is usually played by the iemoto, the head of the school. Before the players come on to the stage a ceremony of purification is performed in the dressing-room from which women are strictly excluded.  The performance consists of four main parts:
<br>1. Sung part by Okina and chorus
<br>2. Dance by Senzai
<br>3. Dance by Okina
<br>4. Dance by Sambasō - First part, unmasked; Second part, with mask and bells."
<br><b>Twelve Months of Noh Pictures</b>
<br>From a series of twelve prints depicting twelve Noh plays, one play for each month, published by Unsōdō Publishing in 1970. Six of the prints (for the months of January, February, June, September, November and December) were designed by Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963) and the other six (for the months of March, April, May, July, August and October) were designed by his son Matsuno Hideyo (1936-2002). As Sōfū died in 1963, his prints must have been created from existing designs.
<br>As originally issued, the prints were sold as a set with each print placed inside its own mat, which was overlaid with a commentary sheet on the play in Japanese and English. The matted print and commentary were then placed inside an envelope  and all twelve envelopes were then placed into a cloth folio.
<br>Interestingly, the artist seals appearing on the prints, each one being different, relate to the play being pictured, such as in the square red seal on this print whose characters, according to the commentary sheet accompanying the print, read "All's Right With the World."

title: Stonemason (石工 ishiku)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
A first edition by the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin showing stonemasons at work.
<br>A translation of the artist's commentary originally accompanying this first edition print reads, "The Stonemason. It is said that in the capital stone masons are in high demand for tombstones and other stone monuments. As for the kinds of raw material in Tokyo, it seems that average quality products come from Ibaraki, Gunma and Sagami in the Kantō region, and excellent quality granite comes from the Okayama region. For superior red granite one should rely on Nara Prefecture. We ordinary people would worry about how we would be able to handle such heavy objects, but because they do it professionally stonemasons do it with unexpected ease. Nowadays the apprenticeship system is hardly used anymore, during which seven or eight years are focused on handling the stones, and the following two or three are spent learning how to polish. Only after that the apprentice starts practicing engraving and finally immerses himself completely in the study of calligraphy and its forms and elegance."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]
<br><br>
[1] Source of translation: Memories of Shōwa: Impressions of Working Life by Wada Sanzō, Maureen de Vries and Daphne van der Molen, Nihon no hanga, 2021, p. 53.
<br>[2] Pacific Asia Museum website http://www.pacificasiamuseum.org/_on_view/exhibitions/2004/occshowa.aspx [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>[3] Light in Darkness: Women in Japanese Prints of Early Shōwa (1926-1945), Kendall H. Brown, et. al., Fisher Gallery, University of Southern California, 1996, p. 18.

title: Girls Playing Otedama (untitled)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description: Wada captures four young girls, one caring for a sleeping baby brother in a onbuhimo おんぶひも, playing the children's game of otedama お手玉 in which bean bags are tossed accompanied by varied tasks. They appear to be playing in a room used for weaving. Coloring books lay scattered about.

title: Toys (玩具)
creator: Hatsuyama Shigeru 初山滋 (1897-1973)

title: Illustration of Battalion Military Drill (大隊調練圖 Daitai chōren [no] zu)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)
description: Issued during the last months of the reign of the Tokugawa shogunate, in September 1867, this print shows a modernized battalion of Western-style infantry units undergoing field drills, likely on one of the parade grounds newly re-opened by French military advisors.

title: Illustration of the Silver Wedding Celebration (銀婚式御祝典之図)
creator: Utagawa Toshimasa 歌川年昌 (Shunsai 春斎)(1866-1913)
description: A depiction of one of many ceremonies that took place on the day of the silver wedding anniversary of the emperor and empress on March 9, 1894.  In this print we see Emperor Meiji, Empress Haruko and the crown prince, the future Emperor Taishō, receiving felicitations from an official dressed in military attire.

title: Illustration of President Grant Being Entertained at Ueno Park (於上野公園地 グランド君與應ノ図)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: Conceived in early July 1879, over a month before the actual celebration for former President Grant in Ueno Park on August 25, this print was the artist's invention, based upon the announced festivities. In this print we see Mr. and Mrs. Grant seated on the viewing platform with Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken, while displays of kendo, horsemanship and fireworks entertain them. While the artist depicts the presence of the Empress, there is no record of her attending the actual festivities in Ueno Park, although she did meet the Grants on another occasion during their Tokyo visit.

title: Raiden 雷電 (Thunder and Lightning)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description:
Print number thirty in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color depicting the wrathful ghost of Michizane in the play Raiden. <br>Play Synopsis, Raiden: "The ghost of Michizane, who died unforgiving while in exile, appears to the head priest and after thanking him for his past kindnesses, confides to him his intention to crash down on the Imperial palace in the form of a thunderbolt and in this way take vengeance on the nobles who wronged him in the past. He then warns the priest not to go to the Palace if summoned, but he replies that although he could ignore a summons once or even twice, if he were called a third time he would have to go. At this the ghost grows angry and, biting into a pomegranate which it seizes form the altar, spits out the pips at a door of the temple which immediately bursts into flames. The priest quells the flames with a motion of his hand and an incantation, but the ghost emerges into the smoke and is gone. When the priest is later summoned to the Palace, which is being laid wasted by the Thunder God, he succeeds in vanquishing the angry spirit by means of his holy power." Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 139-140.
<br>Each print in this series depicts a main character from a Noh play and is tipped to the top edge of a solid-colored woodblock-printed backing sheet featuring the three small pines appearing along the higashigakari  橋掛 (bridgeway) stretching from the main stage to the kagami-no-ma (mirror room) where the performers gather before going on stage. The trees are printed with a dark gold metallic pigment, a deluxe printing technique.

title: Funa Benkei 船弁慶 (Benkei in the Boat)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description: Print number fifteen in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts the ghost of Taira no Tomomori holding his long sword. He intends to send Yoshitsune to a watery grave. <br>Play Synopsis, Funa Benkei from A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 35-36: "Benkei explains that in an attempt to clear himself of the suspicion which Yoritomo has about his younger brother's intentions, Yoshitsune has left the capital and come down to Daimotsu Bay. There Shizuka Gozen joins her lover Yoshitsune, but as Benkei insists that she must return to the capital, they have a farewell party at which Shizuka dances, and then she goes off alone. Yoshitsune and his men then put out to sea in a boat, but suddenly black clouds form, the seas rise, and the ghost of Taira no Tomomori comes upon them. It tries to seize Yoshitsune and carry him down into the sea to suffer the same fate as Tomomori himself, but is eventually driven off by the priestly poser of Benkei."<br>Each print in this series depicts a main character from a Noh play and is tipped to the top edge of a solid-colored woodblock-printed backing sheet featuring the three small pines appearing along the higashigakari  橋掛 (bridgeway) stretching from the main stage to the kagami-no-ma (mirror room) where the performers gather before going on stage. The trees are printed with a dark gold metallic pigment, a deluxe printing technique.

title: Tamanoi 玉井 (The Jeweled Well)
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description:
Print number eleven in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts the dragon god of the sea, the nochi-shite from act 2 of the play Tamanoi.
<br>Play Synopsis, Tamanoi: "As the god Hōdemi has angered his elder brother by borrowing his fishing-hook and then allowing it to be carried away by a fish, he goes down into the sea in an effort to retrieve it. He is standing beneath a tree surveying the scene when two princesses come to a beautiful well nearby to draw water. They take him to the palace of their father, the dragon-king, who entertains him hospitably for three years and then, on his return, presents him with the hook he was seeking. The princesses each give him a magnificent jewel and, after he has been entertained with dancing, take him to the shore on the back of a huge fish." Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 183-184.
<br>Each print in this series depicts a main character from a Noh play and is tipped to the top edge of a solid-colored woodblock-printed backing sheet featuring the three small pines appearing along the higashigakari  橋掛 (bridgeway) stretching from the main stage to the kagami-no-ma (mirror room) where the performers gather before going on stage. The trees are printed with a dark gold metallic pigment, a deluxe printing technique.

title: Yorimasa 頼政
creator: Matsuno Sōfū 松野奏風 (1899-1963)
description:
Print number seventeen in the fifty print series Fifty Noh Figures in Color. This print depicts Yorimasa telling the story of his last battle, his defeat and his death.<br>Play Synopsis, Yorimasa: "A travelling priest stops at Uji and is admiring the view there when an old man approaches and, after telling him about various historical spots in the neighborhood, leads him to the Byōdō-in. There he shows him the patch of turf cut in the shape of a fan to commemorate the warrior Yorimasa who laid his fan down and killed himself there after being defeated in battle. Revealing that he is the spirit of the warrior, he then disappears. After the priest has prayed for the repose of his soul, Yorimasa comes to him in his true form and tells him about the battle. He asks the priest to continue to pray for him and again fades from sight." - Source: A Guide to No, P.G. O'Neill, Hinoki Shoten, 1929, p. 215-216.
<br>Each print in this series depicts a main character from a Noh play and is tipped to the top edge of a solid-colored woodblock-printed backing sheet featuring the three small pines appearing along the higashigakari  橋掛 (bridgeway) stretching from the main stage to the kagami-no-ma (mirror room) where the performers gather before going on stage. The trees are printed with a dark gold metallic pigment, a deluxe printing technique.

title: Flower on a Withered Tree; Strolling Like a Dog on the Riverbank (かれ木ノ花 犬の川ばた Kareki no hana, Inu no kawabata)
creator: Kawanabe Kyōsai 河鍋暁斎 (1831-1889)
description:
The top portion of the print shows a doctor with his medicine box, along with the patient's family (the patient lying behind the screen in the upper left) looking in amazement at flowers blooming on a dead tree, an expression used when a sick person, near death, suddenly regains his health.<br>
The bottom portion of the print depicts two hapless parents with their children coming across two wandering dogs, illustrating the Japanese expression "that when one goes for a walk without a goal, not knowing what to do, but with the firm intention of not spending a penny; no more than a dog walking on the banks of a river has a fixed goal or money to waste."<br>These very popular prints were issued as part of the series Kyōsai hyakuzu consisting of more than 200 pictorializations of proverbs and depictions of famous subjects unrelated to proverbs. The prints were published continuously as single-sheet prints from c. 1863 to 1866 by the publisher Wakasaya Yoichi and the works were later reprinted in album form by the publisher Ōkura Magobei (Ōkuraya) in 1881 and 1886. Many different color schemes were employed in the various editions and reprintings. Most of the prints in this collection are likely from one of Ōkura Magobei's later reprint editions, as they show evidence of their original album backings.

title: Biographies of Brave and Loyal Retainers, Act 1 (忠雄義臣傳 [忠雄義臣伝] 巻之一 Chūyū gishin den, maki no ichi)
creator: Utagawa Kunisada I 歌川国貞 (1786–1865)
description:
Depicting a scene in Act 1, "Examining the Helmet," from the play Biographies of Brave and Loyal Retainers, a version of  the vendetta tale commonly referred to as Chūshingura or Kanadehon Chūshingura (The Treasury of the Loyal Retainers). In this scene, we see Lady Kaoyo, the wife of Lord En'ya, identifying the helmet of the dead Nitta Yoshisada, an enemy of shōgun Ashikaga Takauji, which is to be enshrined in Kamakura's Hachiman shrine. The four other figures in the print are Lord En'ya, Lord Wakanosuke, Lord Moronō and Naoyoshi Ashikaga, the younger brother of the shogun.
<br>At least two editions of this print exist, published by different publishers. This print is considered a second edition and was published by Izumiya Ichibei who must have purchased the original woodblocks from the publisher Yamadaya Shōbei. This second edition by Izumiya Ichibei is framed by a solid blue border inset with circles containing bats. The first edition published by Yamadaya Shōbei is framed with the saw-tooth pattern associated with Chūshingura. (See IHL.2213 for the first edition print.)

title: Rice Planter
creator: Inagaki Toshijirō 稲垣稔次郎 (1902-1963)
description:
A bold design of a farmer in a rice field, all floating within a handmade sheet of tan-colored paper. 
<br>Inagaki Toshijirō (or Nenjirō) was a graduate of the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts. For almost nine years (1922-1931), he was a designer of stencil patterns for fine kimonos at a Kyoto department store. Later he studied dyeing technology. In 1948 he began to carve stencils and became a dye artist working on both cloth and paper. In the 1950s he designed woodblock prints with the stylized quality of his textile designs which were printed from single woodblocks at Mikumo Mokuhansha in Kyoto. In 1962, Inagaki was designated as a Living National Treasure by the government of Japan for his kataezome (artworks made using the traditional techniques of stencil dyeing called katazome.)

title: Tenjin Bridge (天神ばし Tenjin bashi)
creator: Akamatsu Rinsaku 赤松麟作 (1878-1953)
description: Print number 18 in the series Thirty-Six Views of Osaka depicting Tenjin Bridge originally constructed around 1594. Tenjin Bridge spans the eastern end of Nakanoshima Island and was one of the "three great bridges of Naniwa," together with Tenma Bridge and Naniwa Bridge. The current bridge dates from 1934.

title: Nawa Nagatoshi (名和長年)
creator: Mizuno Toshikata 水野年方 (1866-1908)
description:
Print number 23 (廿三), one of 16 prints designed by Toshikata for the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition, picturing the fourteenth-century samurai and military leader Nawa Nagatoshi (d. 1336) weeping at the sight of the ruined imperial palace of the Emperor Go-Daigo after the attack by the Hōjō forces. 
<br><br>This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

title: Ritsurin Park (栗林公園 Ritsurin kōen)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)

title: Ōboke Gorge (大歩危 Ōboke)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)
description: Miyata depicts Ōboke Gorge with the Yoshino River running below and winding Highway 32 on the left. This print is number 10 from volume 4, Shikoku, from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan.<br>Ōboke Gorge (大歩危, Ōboke) in Tokushima Prefecture on Shikoku, is a steep sided ravine where the Yoshio River flow, surrounded by spectacular scenery, near the entrance to the Iya Valley, Its name means "big dangerous steps" as its jagged, rocky walls can be perilous to navigate.<br><br>Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

title: Kotohira Shrine (金刀比羅宮 Kotohira-gū)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)

title: Beauties Gazing at a Waterfall (untitled)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: Three bijin look out at a waterfall while a traveler contemplates the beautiful scene before him. Nobukazu designed only a handful of pillar prints (a long narrow format) including this print.

title: Gathering Shellfish at Low Tide (汐干狩り)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description:
Gathering shellfish at low tide was a popular family pastime during the Edo and Meiji eras, as can be seen by its many representations in prints by artists such as Hiroshige and Hokusai and in this collection's prints Gathering Shellfish at Low Tide at Fukagawa Susaki (IHL.1169) and Shiohi, Women of the Bunka Era from the series Thirty-six Elegant Selections (IHL.0666).<br>In this print, we have the artist Watanabe Nobukazu, a disciple of Yōshū Chikanobu (1838-1912), depicting a well-heeled mother, daughter and son, accompanied by a young servant, gathering shellfish. Mt. Fuji rises in the background and the little boy is shown grasping for a flounder mired in the low tide.<br>
The top few inches of this long "pillar" print appear to have been cut off and It may well be that this collection's impression was a proof print, given the differences in color with other impressions of this print.

title: Poster announcing the Celebration of the Heian (kyō) [Kyōto] Capital Relocation (平安遷都紀年祭) and the Fourth National Industrial Exhibition (第四回内國勧業博覧會) in the  28th Year of Meiji Era [1895] (明治廿八年之京都 Meiji 28-nen no Kyōto)
creator: Unknown
description:
Likely a modern reproduction of an announcement of the celebration of the 1100 year anniversary of the relocation of the capital to Heian-kyo (Kyōto) from Nagaoka-kyo in the year 794 and the 4th National Industrial Exhibition held in Kyōto to honor, in part, the city's anniversary. It is unknown whether this collection's reproduction is of a period work or a modern design. 
<br>
The main headlines on the poster in front of the seated calligrapher read,
<br>平安遷都紀年祭 - Celebration of Heian(kyō) Capital Relocation
<br>第四回内國勧業博覧會 - 4th National Industrial Exhibition
<br>時代品展覧會 - Exhibition of Historical Items

title: Illustration of Meeting at the General Staff Headquarters (參謀本部會議之圖)
creator:
Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
<br>Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)
description: Inside the General Staff Headquarters, with the Emperor in his military regalia presiding, a telegram is received from Major General Ōshima announcing victory over Chinese forces near Asan in Korea. The Battle of Asan 牙山作戦 at the end of July 1894 was the first major battle in the first Sino-Japanese War. Nobukazu created the interior scene while Kokunimasa created the outdoor scene framed by the pink curtains.

title: Illustration of the Imperial Procession through the Streets after the Ceremony of the Promulgation of the Constitution and Illustration of the Phoenix Carriage at the Great Celebration of the Constitution Ceremony  (憲法発布式後　市街御幸之図 Kenpō happushiki ato shigai miyuki no zu - 憲法式　大祭鳳凰御輦之図 Kenpōshiki daisai hōō gosha no zu)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: Five days before the February 11, 1889 promulgation ceremonies for the new Meiji constitution, Chikanobu provided his audience with a preview of the announced public festivities. Fireworks and balloons adorn the sky over the Imperial Palace and a royal entourage, with the Emperor and Empress in the lead in the Phoenix Carriage, is seen crossing Nijubashi and headed towards the Aoyama Military Parade Field where the emperor will inspect the troops. Thousands were to line the parade route. The red and white banner in the lower right reads l寳柞万歳 "Banzai Treasured Jewel," referencing the new constitution.

title: Quai St. Ann (Bruges)
creator: Brangwyn, Frank (1867-1956)
description: One of six prints in a 1919 portfolio of woodblock prints depicting the Belgium city of Bruges. The prints were designed by Brangwyn, who grew up in Bruges, to illustrate a series of poems by Lawrence Binyon and were printed by Japanese carver and print artist Urushibara Mokuchu 漆原木虫 (1888–1953), a.k.a. Urushibara Yoshijirō 漆原由次郎. This print pictures Quai St. Ann, a canal running through Bruges, with a row of poplar trees along the embankment. This portfolio was the first collaboration between Brangwyn and Urushibara, who worked with a number of British artists, making woodblocks from their drawings and watercolours. Urushibara moved to London in 1910, moving between London and Paris, and later took a position at the British Museum. He stayed in England and France until 1934, producing his own prints and teaching woodblock printmaking to many artists. Brangwyn gave a great deal of credit to Urushibara, saying "He did a good deal of work with me - made coloured woodcuts after my watercolours - so good were some of 'em that it was difficult to tell the difference between the originals."

title: Poppy Flower (けしの花 keshi no hana)
creator: Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972)
description: Originally issued in 1913 as one of four woodblock illustrations (kuchi-e) for the novel Uzumaki (Whirlpool) by Watanabe Kakei (1884-1926), this collection's print is a woodblock reproduction of the original kuchi-e in a larger format issued c. 1975, possibly by the publisher Kyoto Hanga-in. This reproduction has retained the embossed cheesecloth-like background of the original along with burnished highlights in the bijin's hair.

title: November - Balmy Autumn Weather (十一月 小春日 Jūichigatsu koharubi)
creator: Ikeda Shōen 池田蕉園 (1886-1917)
description: This woodblock reproduction of the original 1924 print was most likely issued by the small Tokyo publisher Sodosha as part of a set consisting of twelve woodblock and twenty-seven lithographs of earlier prints of bijin (beautiful women). The print was originally published by the Shin ukiyo-e Bijinawase Kankōkai (新浮世絵美人合刊行会), as part of the multi-artist series Collection of New Ukiyo-e Style Beauties (新浮世絵美人合 Shin ukiyo-e bijin awase).

title: Enryaku Temple on Mount Hie
creator: Sekino Yowsaku 関野洋作 (b. 1944)
description:
While there is no title on the print itself, the artist, Sekino Yowsaku, the youngest son of Sekino Jun'ichiro, confirmed the title as Enryaku Temple on Mount Hiei. Yowsaku presents us with a quiet courtyard in Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei in Ōtsu, overlooking Kyoto. According to the artist, the print was "made on behalf of Japan's Postal Services, who used the design to decorate a corner of a letter writing pad they sell. It is a fairly common practice in Japan and my father [Sekino Jun’ichirō (1914-1988)] did it often as well."<br>

Enryaku-ji Temple, a Unesco World Heritage site, is a complex with more than 200 halls, pagodas and other buildings atop Mt. Hiei, at an elevation of about 2,600 feet. Founded in 788 by Saicho, the priest who founded the Tendai school of Buddhism, it was established to protect Kyoto from demons traveling from the northeast and was the center of Buddhism in Japan for 800 years. At its height the temple contained 3,000 buildings, ruling monks more powerful than the Imperial family and warrior monks that supported them.

title: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building No. 1 (東京都庁第一本庁舎 Tochō-Daiichi-Honchōsha)
creator: Sekino Yowsaku 関野洋作 (b. 1944)
description:
A rendering of Tochō (都庁), the number 1 Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building. The building stands 48 stories above ground, with a height of 243 meters. Its 45th floor contains the North and South observatories. While there is no title on the print itself, the artist, Sekino Yowsaku, the youngest son of Sekino Jun'ichiro, confirmed the title as Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building No. 1.<br>
While best known for his still life prints of flowers in vases, Yowsaku designed a handful of prints depicting contemporary Tokyo. This print is a monumental (approximately three feet high by two feet wide) tribute to this imposing skyscraper that defines the new Shinjuku, once a red-light entertainment district.

title: Mystic Aura, W295 (眤りの風)
creator: Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (1937-2019)
description:
The pyramid, or isosceles triangle shape, made its first appearance in Kurosaki's work in 1976 and recurred in many of his 1982 prints, finding continuing use in the 1990s. Here they act as sentinels as Akira's forms float in front of them.
<br>Though traditional in technique, Kurosaki set his goal "to re-animate their [traditional woodblock prints] style in modern form through strong color contrasts and radical compositions."[1] In the artist's words, "I combine shapes and aspects to create a world reminiscent to that found in ukiyo-e prints" and his favorite shapes originated from his own imagination.[2]
<br><br>[1] Akira Kurosaki Woodblock Prints, 1965-1983, Hideo Tomiyama and Akira Kurosaki, Shirota Gallery November, 1984, p. 16.
<br>[2] The Complete Works of Akira Kurosaki: Catalogue Raisonne: Woodcuts & Paper Works 1965-2006 黒崎彰の全仕事. Tokyo, Abe Shuppan, 2006.

title: Hagi (萩)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description:
Sekino focuses on the stone foundation of one of the remaining buildings in the castle town of Hagi. The main five story castle building and other wood construction were torn down in 1874 and only foundations and a few smaller buildings remain.<br>
The coastal city of Hagi on the Sea of Japan flourished as a castle town after Mori Terumoto (1553-1625) built Hagi Castle in 1604 at the base of Mt. Shizuki (and a smaller fortification on the mountain's top) and is one of the most historic cities in Japan. The impressive samurai and merchant residences lining its narrow streets, the summer oranges peeking out of earthen walls, and the namako patterned walls, harken back to the characteristic streets of the Edo period. In 2015 the town was registered as a World Heritage Site.

title: Futakawa: Moon at Zenith (二川：月天心)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description:
Sekino's rendition of station number 34, Futakawa (Futagawa), along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. This print is the 24th, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekino created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō, originally made famous by Andō Hiroshige (1794-1858). Sekino gives us a masterful print with a shimmering full yellow moon (but only the bottom half) casting its light off the traditional tile roofs of those few houses remaining from the Edo era.<br>
Today, the original Edo period honjin, the official inn for the daimyo, is preserved as part of the Futagawa Syuku Honjin Museum.<br>"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . title: Illustration for Chapter 6 The Saffron Flower (未摘花 Suetsunu hana)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
A color woodblock illustration from the first volume of Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari, Yosano Akiko's 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942) translation into modern colloquial Japanese of The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), written by Murasaki Shikibu 紫式部著 in the early 11th century.<br>
The color woodblock illustrations for the four books comprising Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari were stitched into the books and it is likely, though no definitive proof exists, that the publisher Kanao Tanejirō printed additional copies of the woodblock illustrations to be sold as single sheet prints. This collection's three stand-alone prints (IHL.2046, IHL.2101 an IHL.2270) would be examples of this, as they do not display any evidence of having been removed from a bound volume nor do they display any of the toning present on many of prints bound into the books due to contact with their acidic translucent protective sheets also bound into the original volumes.

title: New Year's Supplement to the Niigata Nippō (元旦新潟日報 付録)
creator: Ikeda Terukata 池田輝方 (1883-1921)
description:
Ikeda Terukata, primarily known as a bijinga artist, began his career as an illustrator and would go on to win prizes as a nihonga (modern Japanese-style) artist at the Bunten, the annual Ministry of Education art exhibition. 
<br>This bijin kuchi-e, reproduced using a color offset lithographic process, with its characteristic tri-fold, appeared as a New Year's supplement on January 1, 1917 to the newspaper Niigata Nippō.
<br><br>THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E<br>

The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.
<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.
<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

title: Flower: A Modern Meiji Beauty, a supplement to the magazine Shufu no Tomo (The Housewife's Friend) (主婦之友附録 明治風俗美人・花)
creator: Yamakawa Shūhō 山川秀峰 (1898-1944)
description:
One of a set of three, forty-two inch long, color lithographs titled Snow, Moon and Flower, by the illustrious artists Itō Shinsui (1898-1972), see IHL.2104, Kaburaki Kiyokata (1878-1972), see IHL.1803 or IHL.2105, and Yamakawa Shūhō (1898-1944), see IHL.2103, depicting three beauties, issued as a New Year's supplement to the popular women's magazine The Housewife's Friend (Shufu no tomo). The prints are part of a long tradition in ukiyo-e using the theme of setsugekka (snow, moon, flowers) as visualized through images of beautiful women. The word setsugekka is derived from a poem by the famous Tang Dynasty poet Bai Juyi containing the phrase, "I remember you especially when the snow, moon, and flowers are beautiful," 雪月花の時 最も君を憶う. 
<br>Each print provides a commentary on the artist and print in the top margin. 
<br>Shufu no tomo began publishing in 1918 using the slogan "Once you're married, it's Shufu no tomo." Print runs for the magazine were in the tens of thousands, hitting over 300,000 in some months. 
<br>Magazine supplements, along with product giveaways, reader contests and even magazine sponsored beauty pageants were all part of increasing circulation. In the early 1930s two competing women's magazines, Shofu no tomo and Fujin kurabu 婦人倶楽部 (Women's Club), entered into what has been called the "supplement wars" 付録合戦. Subscribers could be sure of receiving frequent supplements ranging from reproduced photographs of famous places; to instructions on child rearing, sewing or knitting; to paper board games (sugoroku); to reproduced original artwork, often featuring beautiful women.

title: The Moon: A Modern Meiji Beauty, a supplement to the magazine Shufu no tomo (The Housewife's Friend), Volume 19, Number 1 (主婦之友、附録・月 明治風俗美人、第十九巻 第一號)
creator: Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972)
description:
This chromolithograph was one of three long pillar-format bijin prints titled Snow, Moon and Flower issued as special supplements to the January 1935 issue of the magazine The Housewife's Friend (Shufu no tomo). The other two artists contributing designs were Yamakawa Shūhō (1898-1944), "Flower: A Modern Meiji Beauty," (IHL.2103) and Itō Shinsui (1898-1972), "Snow: A Modern Meiji Beauty," (IHL.2104). 

<br>Shufu no tomo began publishing in 1918 using the slogan "Once you're married, it's Shufu no tomo." Print runs for the magazine were in the tens of thousands, hitting over 300,000 in some months.

<br> Printed on the top margin is this paean to Kiyokata (as translated by art historian Lynn Katsumoto): "No one but a great artist like Kiyokata could have captured the lyrical mystery of an exceptional beauty, one whose countenance evokes the mysterious luminosity of a misty moonlit night. This work exceeds even the superb artwork that Kiyokata had previously submitted (perhaps the reader knows that the jury awarded it a top prize) to the Imperial Art Exhibition."
<br>Kaburaki Kiyokata, a successful illustrator for newspapers and novels, turned to nihonga (Japanese-style) painting in his early twenties becoming one of its 20th-century luminaries.

title: Fuji, a supplement to the magazine The Housewife' Friend, New Year Issue, volume 18, number 1 (主婦の友附録・第十八卷 第一號・富士 Shufu no tomo furoku・dai jūhachi-kan dai ichi-gō・Fuji)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
A chromolithograph reproduction of an ink painting of Mount Fuji by Seihō that appeared as a supplement to the 1934 New Year issue of the magazine Shufu no tomo (The Housewife's Friend). I have not been able to determine if the original painting is extant and, if so, where it resides.
<br>The Honolulu Museum of Art has a reproduction of this ink painting in their collection (Object number: 2.1440), which they identify as being published by Shimbi Shoin and date to c. 1920. It is likely that their information is incorrect, including the publishing attribution to Shimbi Shoin, as this collection's reproduction appears identical (allowing for differences in photography) to the HMA's, including the image dimensions. Note that the right margin providing the publishing details of the print is absent on the Honolulu copy.

title: Portrait of Emperor Jimmu, a supplement to the magazine The Housewife' Friend,  volume 16, number 2 (主婦の友附録・第十六卷 第二號・神武天皇御尊像 Shufu no tomo furoku・dai jūroku-kan dai ni-gō・Jinmu tennō gosonzō)
creator: Maeda Seison 前田青邨 (1885-1977)
description: A chromolithograph reproduction of an ink painting of Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor of Japan, by the nihonga-style painter Maeda Seison. It was issued to "commemorate the birth of His Imperial Highness the Crown Prince (皇太子殿下御降誕奉祝記念)." The print was issued as a supplement to the February 1934 issue of the magazine Shufu no tomo (The Housewife's Friend). I have not been able to determine if the original painting is extant and, if so, where it resides.

creator: Kitani Chigusa 木谷千種 (1895-1947)

creator: Y. Maru (?-?)
description: A watercolor on stiff paper of the Keihan Uji Electric Train running on a 7.6-km long commuter rail line in Kyoto, Japan, operated by the Keihan Electric Railway.

title: Mount Asama Eruption (浅間山噴烟)
creator: Unidentified
description:
A watercolor painting of smoke pouring out of Mount Asama, an active complex volcano in central Honshū, one of the 100 famous mountains in Japan.  Two Edo or Meiji period farmers stop their work to look at the smoking mountain, whose 1783 (Tenmei 3) three month eruption caused widespread damage.
<br>An unread seal of the artist is in the lower right corner and the painting is undated. A price of 25 sen is handwritten on the print's verso, indicating that the work was completed before the retiring of the sen in 1953.

title: Nitta Myōjin Shrine from the book Picture Book of Souvenirs of Edo, Volume 3 (畫本江戶土産 第三巻・新田明神社 Ehon Edo miyage, dai sankan・Nitta Miyojinja)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige 歌川広重 (1797-1858)
description:
This double-page print picturing Nitta Myōjin Shrine was previously removed from volume 3 of the 10 volume set titled Picture Book of Souvenirs of Edo, issued between 1850 and before 1865. The first eight volumes were designed by Utagawa Hiroshige I and volumes 9 and 10, published in 1864, were designed by his student Hiroshige II. Over ten publishers were involved in the production of these popular illustrated books which went through multiple editions.

<br><br>Nitta Shrine (新田神社) is a Shinto shrine located in Ōta-ku, Tokyo. The shrine is dedicated to the memory of the 14th-century [the Nanboku-cho period] samurai, Nitta Yoshioki. He was enshrined there because his death was believed to have been caused by treachery, and those responsible were believed to have suffered a cursed fate. [He met his end at the Yaguchi Ferry crossing in current day Ōta-ku.] The shrine was built to calm his spirit. In addition to its historical and spiritual significance, the shrine has become a popular destination for worshippers seeking love. - Source: Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitta_Shrine [accessed 8-17-23]

Over ten publishers were involved in the production of these popular illustrated books which went through multiple editions.
<br><br>The name of the Senzoku-Ike Pond [located in Ōta-ku, Tokyo], comes from a legend where The Venerable Nichiren stopped and washed his feet to heel fatigue out of travelling on the way from Kuon-ji Temple on Mt. Minobu to Ibaraki for medical treatment. The pine tree onto which he hung his Kesa (Buddhist monk's robe) after taking it off at such a moment is the "Kesagake-no-Matsu". - Source: Tokyo Metropolitan Library

title: Illustrated Guidebook for Travellers Round the World, Vol 1, North America (世界旅行 萬國名所圖繪、巻一、米利加洲の部 Sekai ryokō bankoku meisho zue、1-kan、Amerikashū no bu)
creator: Copperplate engravings 銅版画 are attributed to 中井利山 (Nakai Toshiyama - reading of name is unclear) and 長瀬盛松 (Nagase Morimatsu - reading of name is unclear)
description:
The first of seven armchair traveler guide books edited and published by Aoki Tsunesaburō 青木恒三郎 (1863-1926), a.k.a. T. Awoki, between May 1885 and December 1886. Aoki, owner of the publishing company Suzandō 嵩山堂 (publishing house, printer, and retailer of Japanese and Western books), introduced the history, geography, and customs of the world in detail to a Meiji period Japanese readership and made it possible for them to experience a virtual trip around the world through text and etched copper plate illustrations and maps, each illustration in the first six volumes carrying both an English and Japanese title. For these travel books, Aoki drew on both his own travels and Western literature. Aoki's associate on the project was Minamieda Jun 南枝醇 (?-?), a.k.a. Jun Susuka, about whom little seems to have been recorded. 
<br>This first volume 亜米利加洲の部 takes us to the United States. The first plate in the guide is titled "The Table of Hours of the Situation of Every Cities Around the World" and shows us the time in various cities around the world printed on a rotating paper wheel. We are then introduced to the United States with plates of the Brooklyn Bridge (completed in 1883), world and US maps, and "The Bartholdi Statue of Liberty." To transport the reader to the United States, Aoki provides views of Nihonbashi, Shinbashi Station and Yokohama Bay and finally a three-masted steamship to take us across the Pacific, first stopping in Hawaii and then on to San Francisco. Over eight plates follow, ending with "The Sentinel and the Spectre and the Gaanp Gulch" depicting the caves at Luray, Virginia. The listed price for this first volume was 定價三拾銭 (fixed price thirty sen).
<br>The seven volumes cover the United States (volume 1, 亜米利加洲の部 Amerika-shū no bu ), Europe (volumes 2, 3 and 4 欧羅巴洲の上 Yōroppa-shū no jō, 欧羅巴洲の中 Yōroppa-shū no chū, 欧羅巴洲の下 Yōroppa-shū no ge), Africa and Oceania (volume 5, 阿弗利加洲及阿西亜尼亜洲 Afurika-shū oyobi Oseanina-shū) and Asia (volumes 6 and 7, 亜細亜洲上 Ajia-shū ue and 亜細亜洲下 Ajia-shū ge).
