title: Rainy Antwerp (雨のアントワープ)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description: Looking so much like the zinc rooftops of Paris, the title on a label accompanying the print tells us it is "Rainy Antwerp."  Sekino traveled extensively through Europe, leading to a number of atmospheric prints of the cities he visited. A wonderful marbling technique (perhaps the grain of the wood?) is used on the walls of the houses.

title: Seiho's Guide to Drawing, Vol. 3 (栖鳳 習畫帖 第三 Seihō shūgachō)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
Published just after Seihō's return from Europe, Seihō's Guide to Drawing was exhibited at the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition, held in St. Louis, Missouri, as part of the Japanese government's display of Books and Publications.<br>"Printed on deluxe paper with specially designed covers and bindings, Seihō’s Painting Instruction Album is more of a luxury object than a tool for the would-be self-taught painter. Nevertheless, the designs progress from the simplest monochrome ink sketches, in volumes 1 and 2, to more complex motifs with color, in volumes 3 and 4." - source: The Artist's Touch, The Craftsman's Hand: Three Centuries of Japanese Prints from the Portland Art Museum, Maribeth Graybill, Portland Art Museum, Oregon, 2011, p. 248.
<br>See IHL.0783 for Volume 1, IHL.0784 for Volume 2, IHL.2225 for Volume 3 and IHL.0785 for Volume 4.

title: Bird Resting On a Bamboo Carrying Device
creator: Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1807- 1891)
description: A master of everyday things, Zeshin depicts a sparrow sitting on a bamboo carrying pole tenbinbō 天秤棒 with two roped trays at either end. This print was designed as one of twenty prints for the two volume illustrated book Ehon Yamato Nishiki: Shibata Zeshin sensei gafu 繪本大和錦: 柴田是真先生畫譜 , commonly referred to as Shibata Zeshin Gafu 柴田是真画譜.

title: Two Stacks of Bamboo Baskets and a Spray of Purple Iris
creator: Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1807- 1891)
description: A master of everyday things, Zeshin depicts two stacks of baskets with what appears to be water splashing out of a few of them forming rivulets and a bouquet of purple irises. This print was designed as one of twenty prints for the two volume illustrated book Ehon Yamato Nishiki: Shibata Zeshin sensei gafu 繪本大和錦: 柴田是真先生畫譜 , commonly referred to as Shibata Zeshin Gafu 柴田是真画譜.

title: Wooden Rice Tub and Nori
creator: Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1807- 1891)
description: A master of everyday things, Zeshin depicts a wooden bench, a hangari (bamboo rice tub) and sheets of nori (dried seaweed) for one of twenty prints in the two volume illustrated book Ehon Yamato Nishiki: Shibata Zeshin sensei gafu 繪本大和錦: 柴田是真先生畫譜 , commonly referred to as Shibata Zeshin Gafu 柴田是真画譜.

title: Picture Card Show, Behind Meritorious Deeds (紙芝居 殊勲の蔭に Kamishibai Shukun no kage ni)
creator: Nonoguchi Shigeru 野々口重 (1912-?)
description:
A twenty print (all color lithographs) kamishibai (picture card show) authorized and sponsored during the Pacific War by the Nihon Kyōiku Kamishibai Kyōkai (Japanese Association for Educational Kamishibai), "a quasi-governmental organization charged with producing plays in support of Japanese government policies, to be performed domestically and throughout the Japanese Empire and conquered territories." - Source: https://networks.h-net.org/node/20904/discussions/10774246/kamishibai-database [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>During a picture card show, the presenter would show each image while reciting, sometimes ad-libbing, the accompanying text on each card's verso. For wartime propaganda picture card shows the presenter was required to carefully follow the script and not ad-lib.
<br>While a picture card show associated with children's street entertainment, may seem innocent enough, picture card shows used for war propaganda purposes were targeted not only at children but also at "adults, particularly those of lower classes: factory workers, farmers and other agricultural workers, inhabitants of poor urban neighborhoods, and small business owners, among others." - Source: Propaganda Performed, Kamishibai in Japan's Fifteen Year War, Sharalyn Orbaugh, Brill, 2015, p. 2.

<br>Post-war, wartime kamishibai were the subject of an investigation by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East (IMTFE), better known as the Tokyo War Crimes trial. During this investigation into Japanese wartime propaganda, Akio Saki, President of the Nihon Kamishibai Association, was called as a prosecution witness. The investigation briefly traced the development of educational kamishibai 教育紙芝居 which were originally used, according to Akio, "to make children be honest, kind and to study their lessons," but would later be used as war propaganda (a wartime kamishibai titled "Japan Is Now Fighting" was referenced) "made on direct orders from various branches of the government and many others also by orders from Imperial Rule Assistance Association." Source: website of the University of Virginia School of Law The International Military Tribunal For The Far East Digital Collection, Transcript of proceeding of June 21, 1946 p. 1129- 1187 http://imtfe.law.virginia.edu/collections/morgan/4/1/trial-transcript-june-21-1946 [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Yanagi Bathhouse (柳湯 Yanagi-yu)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description: A modern large-format woodblock reproduction by the publisher Yūyūdō of a design originally appearing in Takehisa Yumeji's 1915 book of poetry titled Samisen-kusa (Shamisen Leaves), published by the Tokyo publisher Shinchōsha.

title: Fishing Village (漁村)
creator: Okubo Yutaka 大久保担 (1924-2008)
description: In keeping with the artist's focus on traditional fishing along the Japanese coast, he portrays a street, absent of villagers, in a small fishing village. Compare Okubo's print with that of his contemporary, Kitaoka Fumio's (1918-2007) print titled Fishing Village in the Afternoon (IHL.0194).

title: Tokyo Asakusa Park: Picture of the Ryōunkaku Building (東京浅草公園凌雲閣之図)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru III 三代 歌川国輝 (active c. 1886-1895)
description:
As Tokyo's, and Japan's, first Western-style skyscraper, Ryōunkaku 凌雲閣 ("Cloud-Surpassing Pavillion") was subject of a number of depictions in woodblock and lithograph prints, posters and postcards. The colors of modernity, red and purple, dominate, as is befitting this architectural marvel which opened in late 1890.<br>
This twelve-story 170' tower stood in the Asakusa district of Tokyo from 1890 until its demolition following the Great Kantō Earthquake on September 21, 1923. Designed by Scottish engineer W. K. Burton, the Asakusa Jūnikai 浅草十二階 (Asakusa Twelve-Stories), as it was affectionately called by Tokyoites, was the most popular attraction in Tokyo, and a showcase for new technologies, housing Japan's first electric elevator.

title: Highland Flowers (高原の花)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: In this print, Kitaoka showcases a "skunk cabbage" on the high moors and peatlands in Hokkaidō's Sarobetsu wilderness. Through the rain we see Mount Rishiri, a stratovolcano on Rishiri Island off the coast of Hokkaidō in the Sea of Japan.<br>This print's image was turned into a large porcelain mural titled 春のサロベツ原野, 1990 (Spring Sarobetsu Wilderness) by the ceramics manufacturer Iwao Jiki Kogyo Co., Ltd. in 1990 and hangs in the Town Hall of Horonobe, Hokkaidō.

title: Mochizuri Stone (信夫文字摺石 Shinobu Mojizuriishi)
creator: Sakamoto Isamu 坂本勇 (b. 1931)
description:
Autumn and the maple trees are aflame in this depiction of the Mochizuri Stone (the "dyeing stone" or "pattern-pressing stone") and a small temple in the Mochizuri Kannon temple grounds in Mojizuri (formerly Shinobu Village) on the outskirts of Fukushima City.<br>

The stone was visited by the haiku poet and traveler Matsuo Bashō during his Narrow Road of Oku journey, which he began in 1689, and appears in a famous poem titled Kawara no Sadijin by Minamoto no Toru (822-295) about unrequited love.

title: Hattachi no kai (波立の海)
creator: Sakamoto Isamu 坂本勇 (b. 1931)
description: A view of Bentenjima and its torii from the Hattachi coast in Iwaki City, the southernmost city along the Fukushima coast. The island was inundated when the tsunami hit on March 11, 2011 but recovered, as has Iwaki City.

title: Aso noyaki (阿蘇野焼き)
creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description: Sekino has captured the many colors of grassland burning on the meadows of Aso, the largest active volcano in Japan. Noyaki 野焼き is the name given to the process of the controlled burning of the grasslands of Aso. Grassland burning has been documented for over a 1000 years in and around the Aso caldera. The burning prevents shrubs and trees from taking over the land and so preserves the grasslands not only for the cattle and horses that graze there but also as a unique landscape for Aso’s visitors.

title: Pokhara (ポカラ)
creator: Saitō Noriko サイトウノリコ (b. 1973)
description: A drypoint and aquatint by the artist Noriko Saitō whose work has been described as "playful," "whimsical" and "expressive."  This print titled Pokhara pays homage to this Nepalese city on Phewa Lake, in central Nepal. Noriko's husband is Nepalese.

title: Eagle Perched on Cliff (untitled)
creator: Ohara Koson 小原古邨 (Shōson 祥邨) (1877-1945) - attributed to the artist
description: This untitled print of an eagle perched on a cliff on a gray wind-swept day in winter, is attributed to Koson by the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art and is stamped as such on the presentation folder for this print, as sold by Robert Muller's Robert Lee Gallery. The print is also seen attributed to the shin hanga artist Shoda Kōhō (1870-1946), but I think this unlikely. It does not appear in Crows, Cranes & Camellias: The Natural World of Ohara Koson 1877-1945, the closest we have to a catalog raisonné for the artist. This print has a small MADE IN JAPAN ink stamp on verso.

title: Musician Greenwich Village (グリニッジビレッジの音楽家)
creator: Takahashi Rikio 高橋力雄 (1917-1998)
description: It is always fascinating to look at an artist's proof print (IHL. 2240) and the final edition of the print (IHL.0238). While the editioned version is of very poor quality with severe toning and horizontal and vertical "burn" marks on the paper, we can see that the biggest change from the artist proof to the editioned print was the addition of the orange markings in the lower right of the print.<br>Created the year following Takahashi's 1963 visit to the United States, this print captures the feel of the Greenwich Village jazz scene in the early 60s.

title: Tale of the Wind, W376 (風のメルヘン)
creator: Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (1937-2019)
description:
Kurosaki's squiggles bring three-dimensionality to this print, wrapping around a granite-like cone. A scarlet and black spearhead stands guard over these dream shapes of the artist.
<br>Though traditional in technique, Kurosaki set his goal "to re-animate their [traditional woodblock prints] style in modern form through strong color contrasts and radical compositions."[1] In the artist's words, "I combine shapes and aspects to create a world reminiscent to that found in ukiyo-e prints" and his favorite shapes originated from his own imagination.[2]
<br><br>[1] Akira Kurosaki Woodblock Prints, 1965-1983, Hideo Tomiyama and Akira Kurosaki, Shirota Gallery November, 1984, p. 16.
<br>[2] The Complete Works of Akira Kurosaki: Catalogue Raisonne: Woodcuts & Paper Works 1965-2006 黒崎彰の全仕事. Tokyo, Abe Shuppan, 2006.

title: Sumidagawa (隅田川)
creator: Matsuno Hideyo 松野秀世 (1936-2002)
description:
In this undated painting of an actor in the role of the mother of Umewaka-maru in the Noh play Sumidagawa, the actor wears a fukai (middle-aged woman’s mask) and carries a sasa (bamboo) branch to suggest her madness at the loss of her son Umewaka-maru. In the last scene "the boy appears (or seems to appear) twice before the mother. She tries to touch him but he slips away back into the grave. What seemed to be her child is but the wild grasses of the tomb. With only sorrow remaining, the woman weeps." - Source: website of noh-kyogen.com http://www.noh-kyogen.com/story/english/Sumidagawa.pdf [web page not active 8-17-23]
<br>One of six siblings and son of the print artist and painter of the Noh theatre Matsuno Sōfū (1899-1963), Hideyo followed in his father's footsteps. He is best known for his paintings of stage backdrops (kagami-ita) for the Kanze Noh Theater in Tokyo, the Nagoya Noh Theater (名古屋能楽堂 Nōgaku-dō) and the Noh theater at the MOA Museum of Art, Atami, Shizuoka and a series of wall paintings at Itsukushima Shinto shrine.

creator: Suga Tatehiko 菅楯彦 (1878-1963)

title: Mother's Short-Sleeved Kimono (母の小袖)
creator: Kikuchi Keigetsu 菊池契月 (1879-1955)
description:
The twentieth print appearing in Volume 3 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>On the first day of the twelfth month in 1702, Tominomori Suke’emon Masakata 富森助右衛門正因, one of the Righteous Samurai, accepted his mother's kosode to wear under his clothing to protect him from the cold after death, as was done by warriors in days gone by to protect themselves from arrows on the battlefield. On December 14, the night of the revenge attack on Lord Kira Yoshinaka, he was one of the first gishi to enter Kira's mansion through the main door. After the deed was done, he was ordered by Ōishi Yoshio to go with Yoshida Chūzaemon 吉田忠左衛門 to report their actions to the bakufu's Inspector General Sengoku Hisanao and surrender. They would be joined by their fellow gishi to await the verdict of the shogunate.
<br><br>GISHI TAIKAN 義士大観
<br>First published in a limited edition of 200 copies in March 1920 (Taishō 9) by Gishikai Shuppanbu 義士會出版部, the publishing house of the Chūō Gishikai 中央義士会 (Central Office of the Righteous Samurai Society), Gishi taikan 義士大観 [義士大觀] is the story, “according to historical facts,” of the 1701 to 1703 Akō Incident 赤穂事件, popularly known as Chūshingura 忠臣蔵 (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) and Shijūshichishi 四十七士 (The Forty-Seven Rōnin), told through eighty woodblock prints and accompanying text. The historical persons and incidents portrayed in the prints include both those involved in the Akō Incident itself and related events, both real and fictional.

title: Official Opening of Sumida River Cherry Blossom Sightseeing (開仕之花隅田ノ遊覧)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description: This print depicts Emperor Meiji in his military uniform and an entourage of court ladies on the phoenix boat viewing the cherry trees along Tokyo's Sumida River. It's unclear whether this print was commemorating an actual event that the emperor took part in the spring of 1883, or was just displaying a popular theme to sell prints. It is known, however, that in April 1883, the month before this print was published, the emperor and his entourage paid a visit to Suzuki-shinden to view the cherry blossoms, about which he later composed several haiku. - Source: Native and Newcomer: Making and Remaking a Japanese City, Jennifer Robertson, University of California Press, 1991, p. 176-177.

title: Inscribed Poem set above Landscape of either Kyoto or Nara
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description: This poem by the poet Kawai Suimei 河井 酔茗 (1874-1965) set above a landscape, possibly designed by Nakazawa Hiromitsu (1874-1964), was added to the second edition of Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces published in 1946 by Kanao Tanejirō. The original 1925 edition, also published by Kanao Tanejirō, included this landscape, without a poem, as one of two end pieces in the album. (See this collection's print IHL.2413.59 Landscape from the Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces.)

title: Meine Liebe ist Grün  (我が恋は緑なり)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
This song sheet (Senow song sheet No. 341) for Johannes Brahms' (ブラームス) Opus 63, No. 5, "Meine Liebe ist Grün" (My Love is Green), with lyrics by the poet Felix Schumann (1854-1879), was issued in 1924 by the music publisher Senow Ongaku Shuppansha. The lyrics were translated into Japanese from the German by the composer and lyricist Keizō Horiuchi 堀内敬三 (1897-1983). The cover illustration (a color lithograph) was designed by Takehisa Yumeji (1884-1934), a leading figure in the Taishō Romanticism movement.<br><br>
In 1910 the music publisher Senoo (Senow) Ongaku Shuppansha, headed by Senoo Kōjirō 妹尾幸次郎 (1891-1961), also known as Senoo Kōyō 妹尾幸陽, began issuing musical scores, the majority of them by Western composers. Over 1000 scores for classical and popular music, including children’s music, were issued, many under the titles “Senoo Gakufu” (セノオ楽譜) and “Senoo Shin-kouta" (セノオ新小唄). From 1916 until 1929, Yumeji designed over 280 covers for Senoo’s published scores and contributed the lyrics for 24 songs of his own, the most famous of which is “Evening Primrose” (Yoimachigusa), published in 1918. The scores became very popular although few people could read or play the scores. They were bought because of their cover art.

title: Tomochidori (友千鳥)
creator: Utagawa Kuniaki II 二代 歌川国 (1835-1888)
description:
Print number 四十 (40) in the series Instructive Models of Lofty Ambition picturing the famous rikishi (sumo) Tanikaze Kajinosuke (1750-1795) outside the home of the younger, and less accomplished, wrestler Tomochidori (b. 1756). Tomochidori, who is struggling financially, is seen feeding delicacies to his sick father, who is only seen in silhouette. His sacrifices to buy food and medicine for his father and forego his own well-being is a demonstration of shikō, or supreme filial piety. Tanikaze is reaching into the sleeve of his robe, perhaps to retrieve money to give to Tomochidori.
<br>Kuniaki contributed a single print to this series and it is fitting that it involves sumo, as Kuniaki's most famous print is that of a sumo and he is best known for his sumo prints.
<br>To see another edition of this print go to IHL.1036.
<br><br>INSTRUCTIVE MODELS OF LOFTY AMBITION
<br>This didactic series was published between October 1885 and November 1890 and featured a long list of heroes and heroines, from antiquity to contemporary times, who were regarded as standards of moral leadership and self-realization. Originally envisioned as a 50 print series, it would grow to 58 prints. Seven artists contributed to the series and upon its completion the publisher, Matsuki Heikichi, was singled out for special recognition by the government for having sponsored such "noble subject matter."

title: Kiyokawa Hachirō (清河八郎)
creator: Kawabune Misao 川船水棹 (1887-1980)
description:
Kiyokawa sits, ink brush in hand, before a fuzukue on which lies a fan he is inscribing. Known as a scholar and an exceptional writer, he wanted to "turn the realm upside down" and restore power to the emperor.
<br><br>The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

title: The Unbreakable (不破伴左衛門 Fuwa Banzaemon)
creator: Torii Kiyotada VII (七代目) 鳥居清忠 (1875-1941)
description:
One of the eighteen prints in Kiyotada's second series of prints picturing the eighteen plays that make up Ichikawa Danjūrō VII's "Kabuki Jūhachiban" (The Kabuki Eighteen). In this print we see an actor in the Danjūrō line in the role of Fuwa Banzaemon in the thunder bolt pattern kimono in the play "Fuwa." The tale of the rivalry between Nagoya Sanzaburō and Fuwa Banzaemon for the love of Katsuragi, a courtesan of the Shimabara quarter in Kyoto (as told in the "Nagoya Sanzaburō monogatari"), is one of the oldest themes in popular theater in the Edo period and is known to have been performed in versions for the puppet theater as early as the Kambun era (1661-1673).
<br>Kiyotada's better known first series of the eighteen plays in "Kabuki Jūhachiban" was published in 1896. (See IHL.1272, IHL.0805, IHL.0991, IHL.0723, IHL.1510, IHL.0722, IHL.0724, IHL.0990, IHL.0471, IHL.0992, IHL.1255.)
<br>For the preparatory painting used as a guide to create this print see IHL.1906.

title: View of Uji Bridge, 4 (宇治橋之景・四)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description:
The fourth print in a set of twelve color lithographs depicting famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print pictures Uji Bridge, leading to Naikū shrine, the inner sanctum of Ise Jingū. Crossing over the bridge takes you from the secular to the sacred world. The inset in the upper left, titled 内宮神苑正面ノ景, depicts the entrance to Naikū, the main sanctuary of Ise Grand Shrine (Isejingū), in evening. A lone figure is seen and a signpost on the right has the characters 下馬 (geba), a prohibition against entering on horseback.
<br>This collection contains two copies (IHL.2257 and IHL.2343) of this print, issued two weeks apart. The impressions for these two prints show significant differences in coloration, with IHL.2343 using softer, a little less saturated, colors. While the dates of printing for these two prints, as printed in their left margins are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2343 and February 25, 1897 for IHL.2257.

title: View of Magatama Pond, 5 (曲玉池之景・五)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description:
The fifth print in a set of twelve color lithographs depicting famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print pictures Magatama Pond 曲玉池 on the grounds of Gekū, the outer sanctum of Ise Jingū. The print shows both Japanese visitors in Western and traditional dress, and a single figure dressed in the traditional garb of a pilgrim, around the pond with cherry trees blooming and dusk approaching. The round inset in the upper right of the print is a nighttime scene of a small bridge and pathway leading through an Ise (jingū) torii on the grounds of Gekū.
<br>This collection contains two copies of this print (IHL.2258 and IHL.2344) , issued two weeks apart. The impressions for these two prints show significant differences in how the evening scene in the inset is handled and in overall coloration, with IHL.2344 using less saturated colors. While the dates of printing for these two prints, as printed in their left margins are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2344 and February 25, 1897 for this print IHL.2258. The artist seals are also different on the two prints.

title: View of Futamigaura, 6 (二見浦之景・六)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description:
One of two copies (see IHL.2345) of print number six (the two prints being issued two weeks apart) in a set of twelve color lithographs of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print depicts pilgrims and visitors viewing the sunrise between the Wedded Rocks (meoto iwa), a natural torii, offshore of Futamigaura in Mie Prefecture. Mt. Fuji is visible in the distance. The buildings on the right are Futami Okitama Shrine, dedicated to the deities Sarutahiko Ōkami and Ukanomitama. Pilgrims often visit this shrine and purify themselves before proceeding to Ise Shrine.
<br>The inset in the upper right presents us with a "View of Hinjitsukan" 賓日館及海水景 at night. The famous Hinjitsukan was built as a luxury inn which hosted Emperor Meiji's mother-in-law in March 1887, followed by other royals and the well-healed.
<br>
The printer has used his discretion, perhaps at the behest of the publisher, in how he printed the insets on the two prints, changing both the coloration and the dappling on the ground. While the dates of printing for these two prints are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2345 and February 25, 1897 for this print IHL.2259. The artist's seal is also different on the two prints and other small differences in the use of color can be seen.

title: A Young Boy Studying (勉強する童男 Benkyō suru warabe)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)
description: From a set of twenty-eight educational prints issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (Monbushō) which show examples of children's good and bad behavior. In this print a young boy is dutifully studying in his parents' open-air store which advertises rice crackers with salt 塩せんべい while other young boys are playing. A gentleman walking by notes the boy's good behavior.<br>In October 1873, the Ministry of Education proclaimed that it would “improve the education of families with young children” by producing “a variety of art and toy products appropriate for children soon entering schools.” It then issued over 100 nishiki-e (color woodblock prints) as an aid for the education of young children and for adults.

title: Day Laborers (日雇労働者 nikoyon)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)

title: Nuns (シスター shisutā)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
Sisters and children at work preparing food at one of the Catholic social institutions in Japan. This print is the last print in the twenty-four print post-WWII series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures, Continued (3rd series).
<br>The English language commentary originally accompanying this print reads, "These nuns belong to a world-wile [sic] religious organization which has done much beneficial social work in Japan. Their self-sacrificing sincerity is appreciated by everyone. [Since ancient times, Roman Catholic nuns have formed communities in the nunneries attached to Catholic churches where they have created a solemn world and lead lives of abstinence.] They run the kindergardens, orphanages, hospitals and even universities. [After the war, the nuns became especially popular in this country, and they have enthusiastically bought half of Japan's social education. I think that there is no one who is not sincerely grateful for this.] The history of these nuns goes back to the 6th century when Saint Benedict established convent in Europe. The Japanese school girls adors [sic] the nuns and are especially teken [sic] by their simple and neat clothing. [It seems only natural that the prim and proper nuns appear in many a girl's dream and that they are a source of admiration for them.]"
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES, CONTINUED (3RD SERIES)
<br>After WWII, the publisher Shinagawa Kyoomi issued the third set of prints in the popular pre-war series "Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures." His former publishing business, Nishinomiya Shoin, being destroyed during WWII, Shinagawa opened a new publishing business in Kyoto, Kyōto Hangain 京都版画院. At first, Kyōto Hangain published re-prints from the pre-war series 1 and 2 of “Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures,” but would go on to publish this new third series consisting of 24 prints between November 1954 and September 1956, working closely with Wada as they did for the first two series.

title: Dollmakers (人形師 Ningyōshi)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)

title: Kintai Bridge (錦帯橋 Kintai bashi)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)
description: Miyata depicts, using black ink only, 500 year old Kintai-bashi, a wooden arch bridge below Iwakuni Castle in Yamaguchi Prefecture. This print is from an unknown volume from the artist's 240 print, 12 volume compendium Miyata Saburō Collection of Woodblock Prints Scenery of Japan. <br><br>Consisting of twelve volumes, each containing twenty woodblock prints depicting scenic locations around Japan, Miyata spent fourteen years from 1970 to 1984 producing the series, which he carved and printed himself in a limited edition of 100 prints each. Most, if not all, the places depicted were actually visited by the artist. Miyata followed this massive series of 240 prints with a printed compendium of the prints titled Miyata Saburō mokuhanga zenshū 宮田三郎木版画全集 (The Complete Woodblock Prints of Miyata Saburō), release in limited edition in five volumes in 1983-1984.

title: Illustration of the Record of the Rise and Fall [of the Heike and Genji clans] in Renga (盛衰記連歌之圖 Seisuiki renga no zu)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874)
description: While the Tokyo Metropolitan Library references the kabuki play Hiragana Seisakuiki ひらがな盛衰記, all of the print's cartouches reference historical figures rather than  character names in the play. Of course this is an imaginary scene, but renga (linked verse) in the title suggests a poetry session among these important Kamakura era personages.

title: Three Crows Flying at Sunset
creator: Shibata Zeshin 柴田是真 (1807–1891)
description: Three crows are passing through the frame of this design as the sun sets (some say, as the sun rises) in gradations of red, achieved through the printing technique known as bokashi. Zeshin's best known, and perhaps best loved, woodblock print design. Originally designed for an 1887 surimono, the design was edited and re-purposed after the artist's death for a shikishiban (square format) version sometime around 1900, and possibly as early as 1888, and subsequently issued numerous times at least through the 1930s and possibly continuing after WWII.<br>In his article dedicated to this print appearing in the journal Andon 95, Robert Schaap notes, "One of the highlights of Meiji period (1868-1912) printmaking is without doubt Zeshin's print of crows flying across the sky in the red glow of a rising sun."<br>Crows were a common subject of Japanese prints and they figured prominently in Shibata's oeuvre, the crow being generally associated with auspicious things, most importantly as part of the official mythology of the nation, in which the three-legged sun-crow Yatagarasu served as a messenger of the sun goddess, assisting the first (legendary) Emperor Jimmu (Jinmu tennō 神武天皇) in pacifying Japan.

title: Illustration of Depth of the Sea (海中高低之図)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description:
The top print in a three scene harimaze-e from a series of prints based on the 13 volume encyclopedia titled A Compilation of Geographical Knowledge (Yochi shiryaku 輿地誌略) by the multi-talented scholar of the West, Uchida Masao 内田正雄 (1839-1876), who traveled throughout the world to compile this encyclopedia. This top portion of the harimaze-e depicts a ship doing a sounding of the ocean bottom using a lead-line to determine depth. Various topographical formations are called out on the print and the red vertical cartouche on the right explains how ocean depth is measured as explained by "Uchida Sensei" (Uchida Masao) in Yochi shiryaku.<br>
In the case of this collection's image, Sadanobu has largely copied the image from Volume 1, Asia of Uchida's encyclopedia, first published in 1870.

title: 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, Deluxe Edition Book, 2 Volumes, and Portfolio, "The Original Prints," containing five original prints
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939);Fukita Fumiaki 吹田文明 (b. 1926);Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (b. 1937);Tamura Fumio 田村文雄 (b. 1941); Yoshida Hodaka 吉田穂高 (1926-1995)
description:
Two volumes bound in the publisher's original cloth over boards (volume one in green cloth with yellow stamping on the spine, volume two in purple cloth red stamping on the spine). Illustrated throughout with 90 plates printed in 4-color and 268 in double-tone offset. Includes a descriptive list of plates. All housed in a matching slipcase. The five artists contributing prints were Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939) (see IHL.2269b), Fukita Fumiaki 吹田文明 (b. 1926) (see IHL.2269a), Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (b. 1937) (see IHL.2269c), Tamura Fumio 田村文雄 (b. 1941) (see IHL.2269d), Yoshida Hodaka 吉田穂高 (1926-1995) (see IHL.2269e).
<br> The author Gaston Petit is a French Canadian Dominican priest who went to Japan as a missionary; painter, printmaker and collector and continues to reside there and create art, including prints, stained glass and paintings, in his Atelier Petit in Tokyo. "He experiments with different styles and incorporates Christian, Shintoist, and Buddhist beliefs in his works." - Source: "The Varsitarian," Student Publication of the University of Santo Tomas, by Tomas U. Santos -Number 8, November 30, 2010, Vol. LXXXII

title: Sun and Water (太陽と水) from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"
creator: Fukita Fumiaki 吹田文明 (b. 1926)
description:
This print is part of the print portfolio accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists, published in 1973. Many of Fukita's works are described as ethereal and this brilliant red sun setting into water is no exception.
<br>Noted on the folder for this print is the following technical information: 1 block of rawan-faced plywood; 5 printing stages using both baren and press; paper: torinoko; pigment: Japanese water-based color; oil-base ink.

title: Blue and White Space from the portfolio "The Original Prints - 44 Modern Japanese Print Artists"
creator: Funasaka Yoshisuke 舩坂芳助 (b. 1939)
description:
This print is part of the print portfolio, "The Original Prints," accompanying the deluxe limited edition (limited to 300 copies) of Gaston Petit's "44 Modern Japanese Print Artists," published in 1973. Using woodblock for the irregular shapes defining the trapezoid, silkscreen for the yellow and the blue patterns and a hole punch to create a grid pattern of 5/16" circular holes Funasaka gives us another eye-pleasing print in his long-running series Blue and White Space. The print contains a centerfold as issued, allowing it to fit into the portfolio. (See IHL.1579 for another copy of this print.)
<br>Noted on the folder for this print is the following technical information: 1 screen frame; 15 blocks of shina-faced plywood; paper: torinoko hanga yōshi; pigment: vinyl-base screen-print ink, Japanese water-base color.

title: Illustration for Chapter 2 The Broom Tree (Hahakiji 帚木)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
A color woodblock illustration from the first volume of Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari, Yosano Akiko's 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942) translation into modern colloquial Japanese of The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), written by Murasaki Shikibu 紫式部著 in the early 11th century.<br>
The color woodblock illustrations for the four books comprising Shin'yaku Genji Monogatari were stitched into the books and it is likely, though no definitive proof exists, that the publisher Kanao Tanejirō printed additional copies of the woodblock illustrations to be sold as single sheet prints. This collection's three stand-alone prints (IHL.2046, IHL.2101 an IHL.2270) would be examples of this, as they do not display any evidence of having been removed from a bound volume nor do they display any of the toning present on many of prints bound into the books due to contact with their acidic translucent protective sheets also bound into the original volumes.

creator: Shōsai Ikkei 昇斎 一景 (active 1860-late 1870s)

title: Saigō Takamori (西郷隆盛)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)
description: Portraying Saigō Takamori, the leader of the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. Above the seated Saigō is a white banner reading "Shinsei kotoku" (New Government rich in virtue), a slogan attributed to the Rebellion but likely concocted by the press.<br>Saigō was a revered figure to many Japanese. Physically he was imposing, standing six feet tall and weighing 200 pounds. He was a key player in the formation of the Meiji government, both as a military leader against the Tokugawa shogunate and as a politician shaping foreign and domestic policies. After leaving service with the Meiji government, largely over differences on Japan’s Korea policy, he returned to his home province of Satsuma. While not actively engaged in politics he remained politically involved through the Shigakkō (private samurai schools), where he was celebrated as the spiritual leader. After a raid on the government arsenal by Shigakkō students, his hand was forced and on February 7, 1877 he announced his decision to “confront the central government.” Nine months later the rebellion was over, Saigō was dead and his outmanned and out-gunned rebels decimated.<br>This print  is one of six in the series titled "Kagoshima eimei kurabe," loosely translated as "Kagoshima Competition for Glory." Each of the six prints portrays an important rebel figure in the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. For other prints in the series see IHL.2273 and IHL.2274.

title: Murata Shinpachi (村田新八)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)

title: Shinohara Kunimoto (篠原国幹)
creator: Utagawa Kunimasa IV 四代 歌川国政 (1848-1920)

title: WAN_16B
creator: Maki Haku 巻白 (1924-2000)
description:
One of Maki's heavily textured ceramic tea bowl (chawan) prints from a series of prints that use the characters 禅味 zenmi (taste of Zen) in a cartouche within the plate. Above the beautiful black tea bowl is the Zen circular form ensō. 
<br>In the early 1960s Maki developed his own process of relief printmaking using woodblocks and cement. He first carved a conventional woodblock and then placed a cement mixture around the areas raised in relief on the block. Before the cement was set, Maki would texture it and after it dried he carved and chiseled the cement into the desired shape. After the cement completely dried, the entire surface of the plate was shellacked.

title: Sawamura Tosshi in the role of Matsudaira Yoshimine (澤村訥子 松平吉峯)
creator: Sakamoto Hanjirō 坂本繁二郎 (1882-1969)
description:
This print by Sakamoto Hanjirō is one of six he created for the twelve print series Sketches from the Stage, conceived by Yamamoto Kanae (1882-1946) who also contributed six prints. In this print we see the actor Sawamura Tosshi VII (1860-1926) in the role of 松平吉峯, which can be read Matsudaira Yoshimine. All of the prints in the series were of actors appearing at the Imperial Theater (Teikoku Gekijō) which had opened in March 1911.
<br>Yamamoto Kanae, the artist who conceived of this series, is credited with creating the seminal work launching the sōsaku hanga (creative print) movement, a self-carved and self-printed woodcut portrait known as Fisherman (Gyofu 漁夫) in 1904.
<br>In an attempt to revitalize Japanese prints he formed the Tokyo Print Club in 1911 along with Sakamoto. To create this series of actor portraits, consisting of three sets, each set made up of two prints by Yamamoto and two by Sakamoto, Kanae first photographed actors in performance. He and Sakamoto then drew actors from life at the new Imperial Theater which had recently opened on the moat opposite the Imperial Palace. Kanae hoped this series would be a money maker by "appealing to  the stylish audience" that would be attending the modern plays at the Imperial Theater. He intended to issue actor portraits from thirty-four new plays, but only twelve prints were produced of the June, July and September performance at the Imperial Theater before the project was abandoned. - Source: Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 123.

title: Kyūshū  Mamehon, vol. 7 (九州 まめほん 第七集)
creator:

description:
The cover engraving for this issue of Kyūshū Mamehon was designed by Sekino Jun’ichirō (1914-1988) whose model, according to his son Junpei, was "undoubtedly my sister who was only 8 at the time." (Also see IHL.2278.) (?-?).
<br><b>Mamehon "Bean Book"</b><br>
Literally "bean book", the term mamehon "is used by Japanese bibliophiles for a book smaller than an ordinary pocket book, which has been artistically printed and bound, issued in a limited edition, and made exclusively to appeal to the refined taste of a collector."[1] Although miniature books have a history going back to the Edo period, modern mamehon date from the post-War period, with the first books issued in 1953. title: Palanquin bearers (untitled)
creator: Morita Kakō 森田華香 (active 1904-1930)
description: Two palanquin bearers arrive in a village at night with their customer, a man in a brown wrap. One of a number of prints created by Morita for the publishing house Kokkeidō sometime between c. 1910 to c. 1930.

title: Sparrow Feeding an Insect to its Chick (untitled)
creator: Ohara Koson 小原古邨 (Shōson 祥邨) (1877-1945)
description: Koson's prints designed for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) date from approximately 1905 until 1926 and were targeted for the overseas market. This collection's print was originally printed with two other designs on a single sheet and the crop marks can still be seen along the print's left edge.

title: Barn Swallow on Branch of a Flowering Weeping Cherry Tree (untitled)
creator: Ohara Koson 小原古邨 (Shōson 祥邨) (1877-1945)
description: Koson's prints designed for the publisher Daikokuya (Matsuki Heikichi) date from approximately 1905 until 1926 and were targeted at the overseas market. title: Illustration of Our Army’s Triumphal Return and Distinguished Service Awards (我軍凱旋勲功賞賜ノ図 Wagagun gaisen kunkō shōshi no zu)
creator: Utagawa Kokunimasa 歌川小国政 (1874-1944)
description: While there is no month of publication on this 1895 print, it was likely issued not too long after the signing of the Treaty of Shimonoseki on April 17 which ended the first Sino-Japanese War. In this print an army officer receives an award from the emperor. Some 2000 awards were given to both military personnel and civilians for their service and sacrifice during the war.

title: Illustration of Celebration Banquet at the New Imperial Palace (新皇居御拜賀之圖 Shin kōkyo goahiga no zu)
creator: Sekisai Kuniyasu 石斎国保 (active 1880–1890s)
description:
Published in 1877, this print presents us with Prime Minister Count Yamagata Aritomo (named in the red cartouche on the center panel) presenting New Year's wishes to the emperor (directly opposite Yamagata and the only figure not named on the print) in the temporary Akasaka Detached Palace. Present in this depiction of, perhaps, an imaginary event, are ministers of the Army and Navy and the Metropolitan Police Commissioner.
<br>While the print's title reads "New Imperial Palace" (shin kōkyo), its location is the emperor's temporary residence in the Akasaka Detached Palace, where he hastily moved after a major fire in the Imperial Palace in 1873. The new Imperial Palace (kyūjō 宮城, a term used from 1888 to 1946) would not start construction until 1884 and was not completed until 1888. In order to accommodate state functions, the Akasaka Detached Palace had undergone renovations, including the addition of Western design elements such as fireplaces, hanging lamps, and carpets. Coffered ceilings, as we see in the left panel of this print, were also installed.

title: Illustration of Silver Wedding Anniversary (銀婚式御祝典之図 Ginkonshiki goshukuten no zu)
creator: Hasegawa Chikuyō 長谷川竹葉 (active c. 1870-1890s)
description: While there were ceremonies marking the March 9, 1894 Silver Wedding Anniversary (also known as "The Great Imperial Wedding Anniversary") of Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken which the public could attend, the ceremonies occurring in the public rooms of the Imperial Palace pictured in this print, and two other prints in this collection (IHL.0383 and IHL.2074), were not open to the public. They were for invited dignitaries only. While it is likely that a few members of the press were invited, it is very unlikely that any of the artists who designed woodblock prints of the event attended, leaving their depictions to their imagination and knowledge of previous prints depicting ceremonies in the palace.<br> "Those who fashioned Japan's modern monarchy borrowed the idea of celebrating the twenty-fifth wedding anniversary of the emperor and empress directly from the practice of Western royalty.<br>"The core ceremonies followed closely the pattern established at the Constitution's promulgation. They began within the sacred and invisible confines of the Palace Sanctuary, continued into the public rooms of the palace where Japanese and foreign dignitaries observed them, and culminated with an imperial military review at the Aoyama Military Parade Field." - Source: Splendid Monarchy: Power and Pageantry in Modern Japan, T. Fujitani, University of California Press, 1998, p. 111, 114.

title: Illustration of Citizens Greeting the Return of His Imperial Majesty's Carriage (聖駕還幸市民奉迎之圖 Seiga kankō shimin hōgei no zu)
creator: Yūsai Toshiaki 幽斎年章 (1864-1921)
description: The Emperor Meiji's procession through the Hibiya Triumphal Arch in Tokyo on May 30, 1895 following the end of the Sino-Japanese War in April. The arch measured 110 meter in length, 18 meters in height with its main tower over 30 meters high and 8 meters wide.

title: Emperor and Empress Leaving the Palace after the Silver Wedding Anniversary (御出門之圖 銀婚式 Ginkonshiki goshutsumon no zu)
creator: Hasegawa Chikuyō 長谷川竹葉 (active c. 1870-1890s)
description:
After the commemoration ceremonies marking the March 9, 1894 Silver Wedding Anniversary (also known as "The Great Imperial Wedding Anniversary") of Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken were completed in the Imperial Palace, (see IHL.2285), the emperor and empress left the palace in their carriage to attend  an imperial military review at the Aoyama Military Parade Field.
<br> "Those who fashioned Japan's modern monarchy borrowed the idea of celebrating the twenty-fifth wedding anniversary of the emperor and empress directly from the practice of Western royalty.<br>"The core ceremonies followed closely the pattern established at the Constitution's promulgation. They began within the sacred and invisible confines of the Palace Sanctuary, continued into the public rooms of the palace where Japanese and foreign dignitaries observed them, and culminated with an imperial military review at the Aoyama Military Parade Field." - Source: Splendid Monarchy: Power and Pageantry in Modern Japan, T. Fujitani, University of California Press, 1998, p. 111, 114.

title: New Translation of The Tale of Genji, 1st Volume (新訳源氏物語 上巻  Shin'yaku Genji monogatari, jōkan)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)

title: New Translation of The Tale of Genji, 2nd Volume (新訳源氏物語 中巻 Shin'yaku Genji monogatari, chūkan)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
The second of four volumes, containing chapters 22 through 39, of Yosano Akiko's 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942) translation into modern colloquial Japanese of Lady Murasaki Shikibu's 紫式部著 (973-1025?), The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), an account of court life in Heian period Japan, written in the early 11th century. Her translation, originally published in 1912 (the first two volumes) and 1913 (the last two volumes) by Kanao Tanejirō (1879-1947), through his publishing house Kanao Bun'endō, was illustrated with sixty-one woodblock prints (including four frontispieces) designed by the Western-style (yōga) artist Nakazawa Hiromitsu (1874-1964). 
<br>Yosano, in writing Shin'yaku Genji monogatari, is credited with transforming "Genji [perhaps the world's first novel] into a modern novel, thus making it part of modern Japanese literature." - Source: Envisioning The Tale of Genji Media, Gender, and Cultural Production, ed. Haruo Shirane, Columbia University Press, p. 7.
<br>For the other volumes see IHL.2288 (vol. 1), IHL.2290 (vol. 3, part 1), IHL.2219 (vol. 3, part 2), IHL.2221 (vol. 4, last volume)

creator: Maekawa Senpan 前川千帆 (1888-1960)

title: Snake (巳)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)

title: Miyuki (深雪)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
This print is one of twenty posthumous large-format woodblock prints created between 1978 and1980 by the publisher Kyōto Hanga-In, after earlier Yumeji paintings and illustrations. Each print was accompanied by a commentary written by curator and art critic Ogura Tadao 小倉忠夫  (1929-?).
<br>This print, titled "Miyukij," depicts the blind heroin Miyuki of The True Tale of Asagao (Shōutsushi Asagao Banashi), who has gone blind from weeping over her separation from her lover.
<br>As in this case, the majority of Yumeji's woodblock-printed designs were released after his death in 1934 and were based upon his paintings or previous designs for song sheets and postcards. They were often rescaled to accommodate standardized sizes of paper used for woodblock prints. Major publishers involved with producing these posthumous prints were Kyōto Hanga-in under the direction of Shinagawa Kiyoomi 品川清臣 (1907-?) and Katō Junji 加藤潤二 (1885-1961) and his Katō Print Workshop (Katō Hanga Kenkyūjo.)

creator:
Mutō Kan'ichi 武藤完一 (1892-1982)
<br>Kagawa Tokio 香川軍男 (1915-2002)
<br>Hatsuyama Shigeru 初山滋 (1895-1972)

title: Shiga Kōgen Lotus Pond (志賀高原 蓮池 Shiga Kōgen hasuike)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)
description: From a collection of twenty prints of scenic areas in Shinsū, a former name of Shinano Province. Shiga Kōgen is a highland area in Yamanouchi town in the northern region of Nagano Prefecture and part of the Joshinetsu Kōgen National Park. The lotus pond serves as a gateway to the area. Shiga Kōgen was host to some of the events of the Nagano Winter Olympics in 1998.

title: Togakushi Mountain Range (戸隠連峰 Togakushi renpō)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)
description:
Miyata created at least three prints depicting the Togakushi Mountain Range in Nagano Prefecture 長野県. Two of the prints depicting the same autumn view of Togakushi were issued in two sizes. This collection's print is the smaller size with an image area measuring approximately 6 x 8 1/4 inches (15.2 x 21 cm) issued in an edition of 300 prints. The larger size print has an image area of appoximately 12 x 16 in. (30.5 x 40.6 cm) and was issued in an edition of 100 prints. The artist also created a summer view of Togakushi in the smaller size, likely using the same woodblocks as were used to print this collection's work. 

<br>Mount Togakushi is a 1,904 meter (6,247 feet) high rocky mountain located about 20 km northwest of Nagano city. It is a sacred mountain, said to have taken its current shape when Amano-Iwato, the Cave of the Sun Goddess, fell to Earth in ancient times. Togakushi Shrine sits at its base. In 2015 a new national park, Myoko-Togakushi Renzan, was established which incorporated Togakushi.

title: Kurobe Dam (黒四ダム Kuroyon damu)
creator: Miyata Saburō 宮田三郎 (1924-2013)
description:
Miyata created two prints displaying the identical view of Kuroyon (Kurobe) Dam in Toyama Prefecture 富山県, but in two different sizes. This collection's print is the smaller size with an image area measuring approximately 6 1/2  x 8 1/4 inches (16.5 x 21 cm) issued in an edition of 300 prints. The larger size print has an image area of appoximately 12 x 16 in. (30.5 x 40.6 cm) and was issued in an edition of 100 prints. 
<br>The Kurobe Dam (黒部ダム) or Kuroyon Dam (黒四ダム), is a 186 m (610 ft) high variable-radius arch dam on the Kurobe River in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. The tallest dam in Japan, it supports the 335 MW Kurobe No. 4 Hydropower Plant and is owned by Kansai Electric Power Company. It was constructed between 1956 and 1963 at a cost of ¥51.3 billion yen. The project was a difficult engineering feat for the rapidly growing post–World War II Japan, and claimed the lives of 171 people. - Source: Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurobe_Dam [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Bird, Fish and Haniwa-like Figures (untitled)

title: A Beautiful Story About a Parent and Child Drawing Water to Make their Way, number 10 from the Authorized Brocade Picture News of Everything (官許  錦画百事新聞  10号・ 水汲渡世の親子美談 Kankyo nishiki-e hyakuji shinbun ・Mizukumi to sei no oyako bidan)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description: The tenth issue of the Ōsaka newspaper Authorized Brocade Picture News of Everything  (Kankyo, Nishiki-e Hyakuji Shinbun.) <br><br>Translation of text on print: "In Heiemon-chō, Asakusa, Tokyo, one Shibamura Kyūzō, a water-carrier by trade, had three children including his heir Kyūtarō, ten, and two daughters. They were poor but the parents doted on their children and could not choose a favorite. Then came the smallpox and they lost one of their daughters. Kyūzō lost heart under the hardship of having his child plucked from him like a cherry blossom in a harsh wind, leaving neither flower nor seed behind. He drowned his desperation in drink; he drank more by the day, becoming increasingly deranged under the influence sake. He fell down the well, jumped from the second story, and ended up losing the use of his legs. His wife remonstrated with him, but to no avail, and so she left the children to care for their father while she took her man’s place to carry water from place to place. Working in this way she ensured their survival in destitution. The children exerted themselves mightily for their father’s sake, and when their mother came home she would give them supper, pained by her children’s sufferings. When rumors of their circumstances –– a chaste woman and her filial children banding together to carry on the family trade –– eventually make their way to the higher-ups, they are bound to praise them, according to the Hōchi Shinbun [News Dispatch]." - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon.

title: A Dutiful Geisha, number 2 from the Authorized Brocade Picture News of Everything (Kankyo Nishiki-e Hyakuji Shinbun 官許  錦画百事新聞  2号・ 孝行な芸妓くら Kankyo nishiki-e hyakuji shinbun・kōkō na geiji kura)
creator: Hasegawa Sadanobu II 二代 長谷川貞信 (Konobu I 初代小信) (1848-1940)
description: The second issue of Osaka's most popular nishiki-e shinbun (color picture newspaper), picturing a dutiful geisha attending to an elderly geisha. <br><br>Translation of text on print: "In Osaka-fu Dai-2-ku 14-shōku Nanba Shinchi 2-banchō, a geisha known as Kura worked in an an establishment popularly known as Sada. Although she had immersed herself in its muddy water her heart and soul were pure with the spirit of filial piety, for she served her mother faithfully. For nine years she toiled in suffering, for ten she endured a world of hurt, and more. Even her customers, as they summoned her in her flowery robes, tugged her sleeves in admiration. Her reputation soared for both beauty and substance as this geisha strove to make her name synonymous with the utmost in filiality." - Source: Glynne Walley, Associate Professor of East Asian Languages & Literatures, University of Oregon

title: The Duel at Takadanobaba (高田馬場の決闘)
creator: Matsumoto Fūko 松本楓湖 (1840-1923)
description:
The fourteenth print appearing in Volume 1 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).<br>Nakayama Yasubei 中山安兵衛 (1670-1703), later to become Horibe Yasubei 堀部安兵衛 , was considered the finest swordsman of the Righteous Samurai (Forty-seven Rōnin). Orphaned as a child, he was raised by a master swordsman in Edo who became his adoptive uncle. In 1694 he came to the aid of his uncle who was ambushed by his rival at Takadanobaba after being lured there for an honorable duel. Yasubei avenged his uncle’s death by slaughtering at least three of the attackers. Impressed by his swordsmanship, Horibe Yahei, a samurai of the Akō domain, offered the young man the hand of his daughter and the honor of adoption into the Horibe family. Later, both father and adopted son were among the Forty-seven Rōnin who avenged their lord, Asano Naganori, Lord of Akō, and were sentenced to commit seppuku. The print pictures the aftermath of the fight witnessed by a crowd of onlookers, which included Yahei's daughter.<br>Horibe Yasubei became the leader of the radical faction of the Forty-seven Rōnin who, after the death of Lord Asano by seppuku, advocated for immediate direct attack on Kira, the shogun's master of ceremonies and the target of Asano's attack at the shogun's castle. Ōishi Yoshio 大石良雄 (1659-1703), Lord Asano's chamberlain, argued for a more cautious approach at first before seeking revenge, but would eventually reconcile with Horibe and the radical faction to mount their fatal attack on Kira.

<br><br>GISHI TAIKAN 義士大観
<br>First published in a limited edition of 200 copies in March 1920 (Taishō 9) by Gishikai Shuppanbu 義士會出版部, the publishing house of the Chūō Gishikai 中央義士会 (Central Office of the Righteous Samurai Society), Gishi taikan 義士大観 [義士大觀] is the story, “according to historical facts,” of the 1701 to 1703 Akō Incident 赤穂事件, popularly known as Chūshingura 忠臣蔵 (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) and Shijūshichishi 四十七士 (The Forty-Seven Rōnin), told through eighty woodblock prints and accompanying text. The historical persons and incidents portrayed in the prints include both those involved in the Akō Incident itself and related events, both real and fictional.

title: Yamaga Sokō's Inspiration (山鹿素行の感化)
creator: Tomita Keisen 富田渓仙 (1879-1936)
description:
The eighth print appearing in Volume 1 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>The artist, Tomita Keisen, presents us with a view of the Confucian scholar, philosopher and military strategist Yamaga Sokō 山鹿素行 (1622-1685), credited with developing the concept of shidō "the way of the samurai", teaching a group of Akō domain retainers. Yamaga came to Akō in 1652 at the invitation of its daimyō, Asano Naganao 浅野長直 (1610-1672), grandfather of Asano Naganori 浅野長矩 (1667-1701), to train the Asano clan in military science. In 1660, after nine years, he resigned from his position going to Edo to open his own school. Running afoul of the shogunate by contradicting prevailing doctrine on the role of the samurai, in 1666 he was sent into exile, back to Akō in the custody of Asano Naganao, where he remained until pardoned in 1675, when he returned to Edo.
<br>In building the legend surrounding the Righteous Samurai vendetta and its leader Ōishi Yoshio (大石 良雄, 1659-1703), Yamaga and his teachings have been positioned as a motivating driver of, and justification for, the vendetta. Fukumoto Nichinan's commentary accompanying this print indicates that Yamaga's impact on Ōishi enabled him "to create a group of forty-seven warriors that attracted the attention of the nation."  In John A. Tucker's words, "Yamaga was early on implicated in the whole [revenge] incident as if he and Ōishi were co-conspirators." In Section 32 of Genroku kaikyoroku, Fukumoto tell us that , "From an early age, he [Ōishi] aspired to the path of literature and martial arts, and studied hard under Yamaga Sokō [during Sokō's exile to Akō]."
<br>While Yamaga's teachings were widely disseminated throughout Japan, many historians cast doubt on the influence he had on Ōishi's actions in taking revenge against Kira, the shogun's master of ceremonies, attacked by Ōishi's lord Asano Naganori. Objections center around the improbability of Ōishi ever having been taught by Yamaga, even when Yamaga was in exile, Ōishi's actions not being consistent with Yamaga's teachings and Ōishi's lack of any mention of Yamaga in his writings.
<br>The propagation of the myth of Yamaga's influence on Ōishi by adherents of Yamaga's teachings, many of whom rose to positions of power after the Meiji Reformation, was instrumental in young Emperor Meiji's 1868 imperial rescript praising Ōishi and the righteous samurai and the public veneration of the vendetta.

title: Village Scenery - Scene 4 (里げしき、其四)
creator: Kaburaki Kiyokata 鏑木清方 (1878-1972)
description:
The fourth print appearing in Volume 2 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).<br>It is the spring of 1702 and Ōishi Yoshio has moved to Yamashina, a rural area southeast of Kyoto, and is spending time in Kyoto's pleasure quarters in Gion and Shimabara and in Shumoku-chō in Fushimi. Here he plays one of his own compositions, perhaps Satogeshiki, on the shamisen at the Sasaya brothel where he has been spending time with the courtesan Ukihashi.<br>Previously, he has divorced his wife Riju and sent his younger children to safety, hoping to spare them punishment for his planned actions.<br>Lore has it that Ōishi's pleasure pursuits were a ruse to make the bakufu and Kira's clan believe that he was not capable of carrying out the vendetta. Tucker points out that "Ōishi, a Genroku samurai who enjoyed life" would have normally been drawn to Kyoto's entertainment districts and that the extent of his debauchery as part of his plan to keep Kira off-guard was likely exaggerated in building the legend of the Righteous Samurai.

The publisher Unsōdō notes, "For the reprint, we used the 'original woodblock' published as a woodblock print in the Meiji period, and hand-printed it as it was at that time by a master printer living in Kyoto." <br>Pictured is one of the Seven Lucky Gods, Daikoku, the god of fortune and wealth, and a god of fertility. Often, as he is here, Daikoku is pictured with a split root daikon, a symbol of his fertility.

title: Air and Water (空気と水)
creator: Utagawa Kuniteru II ニ代 歌川国輝 (1830-1874) - attributed to the school of the artist
description:
One of possibly five prints from a series of color woodblock educational prints covering various aspects of the natural sciences issued in 1873 by the Ministry of Education (文部省 Monbushō). This print discusses the basic properties of air and water and was issued with two differing texts, with the text from this collection's print being edited from Chapter 2 of Yukichi Fukuzawa's 福澤諭吉 (1835-1901) Kunmō Kyūri zukai 訓蒙窮理図解 (Illustrations of Natural Science), published in 1868, in which Yukichi distills the scientific knowledge he gained from books in England and the U.S. - Source: website of SANSEIDO Co., Ltd. Publishers https://dictionary.sanseido-publ.co.jp/column/mono15 [accessed 8-17-23]
<br>Using simple illustrations, the top scene shows a child's wonderment as a fan creates wind to move the box on the go board as he learns that "wind is air" and the bottom print shows an even younger child watching the ripples created in the tub of water by the stirring stick as he learns that when water is disturbed waves are generated.
<br>The newly formed Ministry of Education issued over 100 full-color woodblock prints for childhood and adult education between 1873 and 1885.

title: Yōrō 養老 (Nurturing the Aged)
creator: Taniguchi Tōsen 谷口桃僊 (?-?)
description:
One of 100 prints by the little known artist Taniguchi Tōsen, issued in twelve sets, each set in a decorative envelope with a colophon printed on its verso, between May 1918 and October 1920. This print presents a scene from the noh play Yōrō (Nurturing the Aged) written by Zeami Motokiyo 世阿弥元清 (c. 1363 – c. 1443). For another print depicting this play see IHL.0207. 
<br> PLAY SYNOPSIS (The-Noh.com website http://www.the-noh.com/en/plays/data/program_017.html [accessed 8-17-23])<br>
It was the time of the twenty-first Emperor Yūryaku. His majesty was informed of a rumor of a miraculous spring in Motosu of Mino Province (Present-day Gifu Prefecture) and dispatched an imperial investigator to find out about it. At the site, the investigator meets an old woodcutter and his son who had found the spiritual spring. When the imperial investigator asks, they tell the story of how they found the spring and how they started to call it "Yōrō no Taki Waterfall." When the parents drank the water that his son had found, the old parents felt mentally and physically refreshed and vigorous. They therefore named the fall "Yōrō (taking care of elders)." In addition, the old man points the imperial investigator to the basin of the fall, introduces historical stories related to longevity and water, and praises the medicinal benefits of the waters of the Yōrō Fall. When the investigator is pleased to be able to give a great report to His Majesty, music is heard from the sky and flowers start to fall.
<br>With these auspicious signs, a deity of a mountain, who claims to be an incarnation of Willow Bodhisattva, appears and dashingly dances to bless the peace of the world.

title: A Brief Description of World Geography (Reprinting), Europe, vol. 4, two parts in one, ([飜刻]・輿地誌略  二篇一 巻四, 歐羅巴州 Yochi shiryaku, honkoku, nihenichi, kan 4, Yōroppa shū)
creator: Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1827-1881) - copper plate prints
description:
Volume 4 of an eventual 13 volumes of the geography textbook Yochi shiryaku (1870-1880). Volume 4 covers Europe.

<br><br>Yochi shiryaku was the most widely used world geography textbook in the early Meiji era, compiled by former Edo Government officer, Uchida Masao. Uchida was sent to Europe from 1862 to 1866 by the Tokugawa government, to gather information to compile these lavishly illustrated textbooks. He returned to Japan with oil paintings, photographic albums, and hundreds of pictorial natural history images. Based upon the sources he collected on his travels, Uchida began to compile the Yochi Shiryaku in 1870, a thirteen-volume of encyclopedia of world geography. Its success was primarily due to the huge number of illustrations that Uchida called "shashin (photography)," the images copied from the Western photographic albums and traveling magazines by the artist Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1827/1828-1881/1882) who turned them into copperplate illustrations. Yochi shiryaku was published in various editions over ten years and used in schools all over Japan, as well as being widely read as the book of "enlightenment." After Uchida's death, volumes 10 through 13 were compiled by the educator Nishimura Shigeki 西村 茂樹 (1828-1902), a colleague at the Ministry of Education, based on Uchida’s draft.
<br> A premise of Yochi shiryaku was the existence of "a finely ordered hierarchy of peoples and states," with racial differences [the physical features and geographical dissemination of the "five human races" being described] being an "important factor underlying this hierarchical arrangement." - Source: "The Race and Racism Discourses in Modern Korea, 1890s—1910s," Vladimir Tikhonov, appearing in "Korean Studies, 2012, Vol. 36," University of Hawai'i Press, 2012, p. 41.
