title: Souvenir Pictures of Famous Places in Ise - Twelve Prints [envelope for the set] (伊勢みやげ名所画・拾二葉)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This is the envelope enclosing the twelve print set, published by the Osaka publisher Furushima Takejirō in 1897, titled Famous Places in Ise (Souvenir Pictures). The envelope's design was the work of the artist Hirose Harutaka (1870-?) as were all the prints in this set of color lithographs 色石版画. On the front of the envelope Hirose has depicted the famous cedar trees of Ise Grand Shrine and the buildings of Naikū Shrine all bathed in the glow of the rising sun. The back of the envelope contains the names and addresses of the publisher and distributors of the print set.

title: The Sanctuary Aramatsuri-no-miya of Naikū Ise Shrine, 1 (天照皇太神宮 内宮・壱)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph of Aramatsuri-no-miya, a sanctuary which enshrines Amaterasu's (The Sun Goddess) aramitama (rough or fierce spirit), located in the Naikū grounds, the inner sanctum of Ise Jingū, is the first 壱 in a set of twelve prints of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine. If you look closely at this early evening view of the sanctuary, you'll see a Shinto priest in the lower right and two small figures at the top of the stairs offering prayers.

title: Toyouke Daijingū Shrine, 2 (豊受太神宮 外宮・二)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: In this color lithograph of Toyouke Daijingū Shrine (Gekū), two Shinto priests can be seen raking leaves in early autumn. It is said that Toyouke no Ōmikami, provider of companionship and sacred foods, goddess of agriculture, was enshrined here some 1,500 years ago. This print is the second in a set of twelve prints of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture including Ise City and Ise Shrine.

title: Illustration of Daidai-Kagura, 3 (大々神楽之図・三)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph depicts the sacred Shinto ritual (music and dance) Daidai-Kagura, a prayer for a bountiful harvest and good health. At Ise Naikū (Inner Shrine), the ritual is performed in Kagura Hall, (shown in the print's inset titled View of the Main Shrine Garden of Naikū 御神楽殿之図), built in 1882. This print is the third in the twelve print set titled Famous Places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine.

title: View of Uji Bridge, 4 (宇治橋之景・四)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description:
The fourth print in a set of twelve color lithographs depicting famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print pictures Uji Bridge, leading to Naikū shrine, the inner sanctum of Ise Jingū. Crossing over the bridge takes you from the secular to the sacred world. The inset in the upper left, titled 内宮神苑正面ノ景, depicts the entrance to Naikū, the main sanctuary of Ise Grand Shrine (Isejingū), in evening. A lone figure is seen and a signpost on the right has the characters 下馬 (geba), a prohibition against entering on horseback.
<br>This collection contains two copies (IHL.2257 and IHL.2343) of this print, issued two weeks apart. The impressions for these two prints show significant differences in coloration, with IHL.2343 using softer, a little less saturated, colors. While the dates of printing for these two prints, as printed in their left margins are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2343 and February 25, 1897 for IHL.2257.

title: View of Magatama Pond, 5 (曲玉池之景・五)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description:
The fifth print in a set of twelve color lithographs depicting famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print pictures Magatama Pond 曲玉池 on the grounds of Gekū, the outer sanctum of Ise Jingū. The print shows both Japanese visitors in Western and traditional dress, and a single figure dressed in the traditional garb of a pilgrim, around the pond with cherry trees blooming and dusk approaching. The round inset in the upper right of the print is a night time scene of a small bridge and pathway leading through an Ise (jingū) torii on the grounds of Gekū.

<br>This collection contains two copies of this print (IHL.2258 and IHL.2344) , issued two weeks apart. The impressions for these two prints show significant differences in how the evening scene in the inset is handled and in overall coloration, with IHL.2344 using less saturated colors. While the dates of printing for these two prints, as printed in their left margins are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2344 and February 25, 1897 for IHL.2258. The artist seals are also different on the two prints.

title: View of Futamigaura, 6 (二見浦之景・六)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description:
The sixth print in a set of twelve color lithographs of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine. This print depicts pilgrims and visitors viewing the sunrise between the Wedded Rocks (meoto iwa), a natural torii, offshore of Futamigaura in Mie Prefecture.  Mt. Fuji is visible in the distance. The buildings on the right are Futami Okitama Shrine, dedicated to the deities Sarutahiko Ōkami and Ukanomitama. Pilgrims often visit this shrine and purify themselves before proceeding to Ise Shrine.<br>The inset in the upper right of the print, titled View of Hinjitsukan 賓日館及海水景, is a nighttime scene of the famous Hinjitsukan, built as a luxury inn which hosted Emperor Meiji's mother-in-law in March 1887, followed by other royals and the well-healed.
<br>This collection contains two copies of this print (IHL.2259 and IHL.2345), issued two weeks apart. The printer/publisher, Furushima Takejirō, has used his discretion in how he printed the insets on the two prints, changing both the coloration and the dappling on the ground. While the dates of printing for these two prints, as printed in their left margins are the same, February 1, 1897, their release dates are two weeks apart February 10, 1897 for IHL.2345 and February 25, 1897 for IHL.2259. Different artist seals, as printed in the lower left of the images, are also different on the two prints.

title: Illustration of Furuichi Dance, 7 (古市踊之図・七)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph, the seventh print in a set of twelve titled Famous Places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine, depicts female entertainers performing the folk dance Ise Ondo, also known as the Furuichi Dance, after the Edo-period town of Furuichi, adjoining Ise Shrine, famous for its red-light district and for its Ise Ondo dances held in the summer. The sole audience for this dance being performed at an inn near the shrine is a wealthy couple with daughter and attendant. The signboard above the dancers would normally contain the name of the inn where the dance is being performed, but in this print it contains Harutaka's signature.

title: Distant View of Yamada Town from Miyagawa Bridge, 8 (宮川橋より山田町を望む・八 Miyagawa bashi yori yamadamachi o nozomu)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph of the bustling Miyagawa Bridge connecting Yamada with Ise Shrine, is the eighth print in the twelve print series Famous Places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, which includes Ise City and Ise Shrine. Yamada was a bustling gateway to the shrines, filled with inns, teahouses and souvenir shops.

title: View of Toyomiyazaki Library, 9 (豊宮崎文庫之景・九)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph of the area around the former Toyomiyazaki Library, in the Outer Shrine, is the ninth print in a set of twelve prints of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine. The library closed in 1868 and burned in 1879 and by the time Harutaka designed this print, the walls and gate, seen on the left of the print, are most of what remained. As pictured by the artist, springtime brings with it the color of the cherry blossoms called "oyane zakura." The rectangular inset is titled 農業舘 (Agriculture Building) which may be a reference to the Jingu Agriculture Museum, established in 1891, Japan's oldest museum of industry and agriculture. With the theme of "How to make the best use of natural products", it exhibits materials related to the Jingu's imperial estate and valuable items related to agriculture, forestry, and fisheries of the Meiji period.

title: View of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, 10 (月夜見宮之景・十)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph of Tsukiyomi-no-miya, situated in Toyouke daijingū betsugu, the annex to Toyouke Daijingū Shrine (see IHL.2341) in Ise Jingū's Gekū (Outer Shrine), is the tenth print in a set of twelve prints of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine. Tsukiyomi-no-miya enshrines the god of the moon, the younger brother of Amaterasu, the sun goddess. The circular inset with scalloped edge, titled View of Asama dake in Snow 朝熊岳雪景 shows the vermillion-lacquered Asama dake Kongoshoji Temple located near the top of Mt. Asama, the highest peak in Ise-Shima National Park. This Buddhist Temple protects Ise Jingū as it faces kimon (the "unlucky" northeastern direction). Traditionally, pilgrims paid visits to this temple on their way to Ise Jingū.

title: View of Tsu Park, 11 ( 津公園之景・十 一)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph of Tsu Park, now known as Tsu Kairaku Park, situated near the train station in Tsu City (Tsu-shi), the current capital of Mie Prefecture, about 45 km north of Ise Jingū, is the eleventh print in a set of twelve prints of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise City and Ise Shrine. In the foreground of this print, an older woman calls out to a younger woman while pointing off to her left, perhaps saying they should spend a little more time enjoying themselves at the park on a beautiful spring day with cherry trees in bloom. Ise Bay is seen off in the distance and Tsu was a flourishing port-town on the Bay.<br>The print's inset in the upper right is in the shape of an eagle. A white banner flies with the characters 高山神社, Kōzan Shrine. Located in Tsu-shi, the shrine is devoted to Tōdō Takatora 藤堂高虎 (1556-1630) who was the daimyō of the Tsu area. He was a highly trusted commander under Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu, as well as an architect of numerous Japanese castles, including Tsu Castle. His family crest (mon) is used for the red and white title cartouche in the upper left of this print. Under Tōdō Takatora, Tsu became an important post station along the Ise-Kaidō, the main pilgrimage route to Ise Jinjū.

title: View of Akogi Heiji Monument, 12 (津公園之景 十二 [inset] View of Karasu Imperial Shinto Shrine (御香良州神社景)
creator: Hirose Harutaka 広瀬春孝 (1870-?)
description: This color lithograph of Akogi Heiji Monument in Tsu City (Tsu-shi), the current capital of Mie Prefecture, about 45 km north of Ise Jingū, is the twelfth and last print in a set of twelve prints of famous views/places in Ise, an old province in Japan that corresponds to most of modern Mie Prefecture, including Ise Jingū and Ise City. The legend of Akogi no Heiji, the young fisherman who was executed for capturing a rare fish in Akogi Bay, a preserve belonging to Ise Jingū, to cure his sick mother, has been told in chronicles, plays and popular lore. The inset, titled View of Karasu Imperial Shinto Shrine 御香良州神社景, features Karasu Shrine in Tsu City built by Emperor Kanmei (reigned 539-571) to enshrine the deity Wakahirume-no-Mikoto, sometimes described as the younger sister of the Sun Goddess, Amaterasu and the goddess of weaving. Pilgrims often visit this temple when visiting Ise Jingū.

title: Illustration of the Dutchman Engelbert Kaempfer’s Eastern Journey (和蘭人 エンゲルベルト ケンフエル東下リの東圖)
creator: Mizushima Nihofu (Nihou) 水島爾保布 (1884-1958)
description:
This print is the frontispiece and one of twenty-nine colored woodblock prints designed by Mizushima, who also wrote the text for the sketch-tour book (travel journal) "Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (supplement) Seto Inland Sea," issued in March 1920 by the publishing house Kanao Bun'endō. This print depicts the Dutchman Engelbert Kaempfer's (1651-1716) "eastern journey" to Edo along the Tōkaidō in 1691.
<br>"Nihou was capable of creating powerful compositions on the postcard sized pages of this book. Perhaps because cartooning trained him to make the most of small areas, some of Nihou's woodcuts and line illustrations create muscular, nearly monumental effects by modest means." -  Source: "Sketch-tour Books and Print of the Early Books Twentieth Century," Scott Johnson, appearing in Andon 37, June 1991.

title: Nissaka, Night Crying Stone (日坂 (夜泣石)

According to legend, "Long ago, a pregnant woman was attacked on Sayo-no-Nakayama Pass, where she was robbed and killed. A stone nearby began to cry loudly. Most versions of the story add that the child grew up to avenge his mother's murder." - Source: website of James Baquet "The Temple Guy." <br>You'll need to look closely at the above print to see the stone, but it's that small round object center right near the hut.<br>"Nihou was capable of creating powerful compositions on the postcard sized pages of this book. title: Double Bao W-543
creator: Kurosaki Akira 黒崎彰 (1937-2019)
description: Two yurts (bāo) in a driven snow. The first print in the artist's fourteen print series titled Nomads, the first seven prints being published in 2002; the remaining in 2004. "Seeing the wind-whipped snow on the grasslands of Bulgaria, which are at the western edge of nomadic territory, Kurosaki assembled his “Nomads Series” of 2002. It was his first use of white pigment rather than blank paper to denote the white of snow." - Hollis Goodall

title: Full Moon Akasaka Palace, No. 1 (赤坂離宮ヲ望ム・第一)

description: Yamashita, a Western-style (yoga) painter who spent over five years in Europe and helped introduce French Impressionism into Japan, designed this first print in the series "Twelve Views of the Moat Edge" created to celebrate the accession of the Showa Emperor, which took place from 1928 through the following year. description: The cover print to Takasawa Keiichi's album "Four Themes of Women"consisting of four prints plus this cover print. Takasawa, mainly known for his modern paintings in the bijin-ga tradition, studied with Fujita Tsugeharu (Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita, 1886-1968), whose influence can be seen on his work. Specializing in bijin-ga (images of beautiful women), Takasawa worked as a painter and an illustrator, and also created woodblock prints for the publishers Yuyudō and the Katō Print Institute. title: Forty-Seven Loyal Retainers Venting their Anger (義士四十七士宿憤ヲ晴ス)
creator: Tsunajima Kamekichi 綱島亀吉 (active 1866-1918)
description:
By 1914 when this chromolithograph was issued color lithography was the dominant color reproductive technology.
<br>In this scene from the Revenge of the Forty-Seven Loyal Retainers, set under a full moon, the avengers have discovered Lord Kira, whose actions led to the arrest and subsequent suicide of their master, Lord Asano, hiding in a storage shed (or outhouse, according to some accounts). They have dragged him out into the snowy courtyard where one of the ronin shines a lantern in his face. At right, Oishi Kuranosuke Yoshio, the leader of the ronin, sits on a folding stool, holding the dirk with which his master, Lord Asano, committed suicide. Oishi offers it to Kira to commit honorable seppuku, but Kira refuses (an act of cowardice) and the ronin behead him. 
<br>There a several versions of how Kira was killed and beheaded during the raid, but however he met his fate, the ronin would take his severed head to their master's grave at Sengaku-ji Temple and set his head before it - their master avenged.

description:
The tenth print appearing in Volume 1 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>In this print, Ōishi Yoshio, on the right, about to depart for Kyoto, hands his faithful servant Hachisuke a sketch he has drawn of himself and Hachisuke saying "Do you remember? This is the path we used to travel when I would take you along to the Yoshiwara Quarter as a young man in Edo. Perhaps this may serve as a memento." They then talked about the past and parted tearfully.

<br><br>GISHI TAIKAN 義士大観
<br>First published in a limited edition of 200 copies in March 1920 (Taishō 9) by Gishikai Shuppanbu 義士會出版部, the publishing house of the Chūō Gishikai 中央義士会 (Central Office of the Righteous Samurai Society), Gishi taikan 義士大観 [義士大觀] is the story, “according to historical facts,” of the 1701 to 1703 Akō Incident 赤穂事件, popularly known as Chūshingura 忠臣蔵 (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) and Shijūshichishi 四十七士 (The Forty-Seven Rōnin), told through eighty woodblock prints and accompanying text. The historical persons and incidents portrayed in the prints include both those involved in the Akō Incident itself and related events, both real and fictional.

title: The Loyal Retainers and Hosoi Kōtaku (義徒と細井広沢)
creator: Shimada Bokusen 島田墨仙 (1867-1943)
description:
The eleventh print appearing in Volume 4 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>On the evening of the day before the raid, the Righteous Samurai secretly gathered at Horibe Yasubei's 堀部安兵衛 home. Hosoi Kōtaku 細井広沢 (1658-1736), the Confucian scholar, calligrapher, and Horibe's friend who compiled his Written Records, was also there. During the evening they discussed their plans, which included setting fire to Lord Kira's mansion and disemboweling themselves, if their plan did not work. On the night of the raid, Kōtaku climbed up on his roof looking for a fire at Kira's mansion which was near his home. Seeing no flames he knew they succeeded and went back inside. Later that night Horibe pounds on his door calling out "We have taken our revenge. We are on our way to Sengakuji. I will never forget your kindness even after my death." Hearing this Kōtaku dashes out his door barefoot, without putting on his hakama [skirt-like pants]. Catching up with the avengers in the middle of Eitai Bridge, he bid each of them farewell. ​

title: Village Storehouse
creator: Saitō Kiyoshi 斎藤清 (1907-1997)
description:
A village storehouse (kura) with the character 松 (possibly "Matsu" a family or village name) on the plastered area above the entrance. Typically, grain would be stored on the lower level with household items up above.<br> 

This print is in an unusual almost square format for the artist and is printed with a thick, likely oil-based, ink on a heavy-weight paper. The few prints that Saitō created in this format usually have a sticker on the verso stating they were self-printed and self-carved. This print does not have that sticker, although it may have fallen off.

title: Bijin with white chrysanthemums (untitled)
creator: Unidentified
description:
A bijin and a display of white chrysanthemums in this frontispiece by an unidentified artist for a popular magazine of the time.
<br><br>THE GOLDEN AGE OF BIJIN KUCHI-E<br>
The period 1914 through 1921 has been called by Kendall Brown the "'golden age' of bijin kuchi-e.” During this golden age (and continuing into the 1930s), thousands of inserted pictures (kuchi-e), mostly printed using metal plate lithography and photo-offset printing, were commissioned from both well-known and little-known artists by publishers of mass-market popular culture magazines (taishū zasshi). The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.

<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.

<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

creator: Utagawa Hiroshige III 三代 歌川広重 (1842–1894)
description:
One of 118 prints in the series Dai Nippon Bussan Zue (Products of Greater Japan), issued in August 1877 to coincide with the opening of Japan’s first National Industrial Exposition (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) held in Tokyo’s Ueno Park. This prints illustrates the steps in producing bleached wax, often called Japan Wax, made from the fruit of the Japanese wax tree (hazenoki).<br>
Refined wax was a significant export to the West in the early Meiji period, but its value as an export was under pressure from the growing use of kerosene.

title: Distant Memory A (遠い記憶 A)
creator: Tajima Hiroyuki 田嶋宏行 (1911-1984)
description: While the lines on the green tablet-like object might look inscribed, they are flat with the 3-dimensional effect achieved through the use of various materials added to the carved woodblock, in this case possibly some type of string, and then printed using dense pigments. The titles "Memory" and "Recollection" figure prominently in Tajima's paintings from this period.<br>"In the 1960s and 70s he developed his typical densely pigmented abstract style, which, however, was based on the ideals of East Asian calligraphy, traditional Japanese painting structure, and a sense of space derived partly from his Zen Buddhist beliefs. His abstract prints typically have complex surfaces achieved by building up the block with various materials such as crumpled paper." - Source: Modern Japanese Prints: 1912-1989, Lawrence Smith, British Museum Press, 1994, p. 35.

description: Titled "Fantasye C" [sic], in the artist's hand, this print is another example of Tajima's densely pigmented abstract style. Volume 1, subtitled Kyōto, and volume 2, subtitled Yamato (Nara), were issued in 1911 and the third volume, subtitled Ōsaka, in 1912. title: The Ashura Notebook, Volume 4 (阿修羅帖, 第四巻 Ashurachō, dai yonkan)
creator: Itō Chūta 伊東忠太 (1867-1954)
description:
Volume 4 of five volumes in the satirical work Ashurachō (the work takes its title from the Buddhist demigods associated with war), illustrated by the architect and architectural historian Itō Chūta (1867-1954), with commentary by various prominent literary figures including tanka poet Toki Zenmaro 土岐善麿 (1885–1980), poet, translator and early feminist Yosano Akiko 与謝野晶子 (1878-1942), Taishō̄ modernist writer Akutagawa Ryūnosuke 芥川龍之介 (1892-1927) and novelist Kikuchi Kan 菊池寛 (1888-1948). Each volume contains 100 color woodcut prints (satirical manga) by  Itō and the prints reflect his own take on world events from the outbreak of WWI until its conclusion, Japanese domestic events and Japanese involvement in China. Itō originally drew his caricatures as postcards for his own pleasure between 1914 and 1919,  never intending to have them published, but when "Sugimura Kōtarō [a prominent journalist] saw Itō's work, he was immediately interested and advised that Itō publish these caricatures."[1] 

<br>Titled 國技館燬く (burning of the Kokugikan), caricature number 302 (see composite image on this page), depicts the burning of Tokyo's Ryōgoku Kokugikan (sumo arena) in a 1909 fire. A blue oni with flames leaping from its body is seen wreaking fire and mayhem on the Kokugikan. The untranslated text is by the poet Sasaki Nobutsuna 佐々木 信綱 (1872-1963).

<br>In caricature number 318 (see composite image on this page), Itō presents us with a scene from the week long January 1918 workers' strike ("Januarstreik") in Germany to force an end to WWI.[2] The strike, occurring at a time of shortages caused by the war and the success of the recent Bolshevik Revolution in Russia, began in Berlin and spread across Germany, but would quickly fail due to military repression and the disorganization of strike leaders. The sign behind the workers reads, 造兵廠 (armory), and many munitions workers joined the strike. The quote from American writer and politician Booth Tarkington (ブース・ターキントン ) reads, "Both the strikers and the police helped the Allies. The police helped by running away" and helmeted police are seen fleeing the strikers. The vertical characters on the right side read 獨逸同盟罷工 or German union workers strike.

creator: Morita Hisashi 森田久 (active c. 1920s)
description:
This bijin kuchi-e with its characteristic tri-fold, is the frontispiece for the October 1918 "special issue" of the popular women's magazine Fujin sekai (Women's World). This bijin kuchie serves as an illustration for the twelfth installment of the serialized novel Reishō by Tengai Kosugi 小杉天外 (1865-1912) which ran in the magazine prior to its publication in three volumes starting in 1919. (See IHL.2401.)
Morita Hisashi was a yōga-trained artist who worked as a reporter, illustrator and art director. He contributed illustrations to numerous popular magazines in the late Meiji and Taishō era, such as Kōdan Kurabo, Kōdan zasshi, Fujokai, Jogaku sekai, and a number of serialized novels. His illustrations were primarily of the bijin-ga genre. It is reported that his illustrations for a serialized novel appearing in the Yomiuri shinbun in 1921 were the first such illustrations to actually identify the illustrator by name.

<br>From an undated set of twelve prints depicting twelve Noh plays, one play for each month, published by Unsōdō Publishing. The vast majority of these illustrations depicted beautiful women (bijin) and they appeared as inserted frontispieces, illustrations to serialized novels, advertisements, promotional supplements, as well as cover illustrations.

<br>While employing new technology, the use of inserted pictures in both magazines and novels during this golden age was a continuation of the use of woodblock-printed multi-color illustrations in magazines and novels of the prior late Meiji period, c. 1890-1912, during which time the use of traditional woodblock printing technology for mass reproduction dramatically declined.

<br>Unfortunately most of the extant bijin kuchi-e have become separated from the original magazines they were inserted in, making it impossible to determine what they may have been illustrating or their titles. These frontispieces generally display a characteristic tri-fold as many of the prints were larger than the dimensions of the magazines they were inserted into.

title: Table of Contents - Album Box with Cover Print of Kannon - Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces
description:
Printed on both sides of a heavy cardboard sheet, the front side of the Table of Contents provides a list of the thirty-four temples (the thirty-three temples on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage and one affiliated [bangai] temple) visited by the trio of Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中澤弘光 (1874-1964) and his two friends, the haiku poet Ishikura Suiyō  石倉翠葉 (1875-1938) and the Western-style painter Akatsuka Chūichi 赤塚忠一 (1887-?). In addition to the temple's name and number on the pilgrimage route, the province the temple is locatedd in (using the old province names) and the temple's prefix, often the sacred mountain associated with the temple, are provided.<br>
The reverse side of the Table of Contents provides the names of four additional prints (including the bangai temple print of Nata-dera appearing on the front side) designed by Nakazawa. It also provides the names of the other contributors to the album - the Buddhist scholars Mochizuki Shinkō and Washio Junkyō, the poets Sasaki Nobutsuna and Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi and their respective contributions.

Sefuku-ji on Mt. Makinoo (Makinoo-san), the fourth temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, is the hardest of the thirty-three temples to access. A long steep trail leads to the temple and this is what Nakazawa depicts, with a small goddess along the way to ease the journey. title: Fujiidera - temple 5 (葛井寺 五)

Nakazawa shows us the shiunseki tōrō, a tall stone lantern originally made in the Kamakura period (about 800 years ago) located between Fujii-dera's main hall and gate. In Nakazawa's rendering the gate is the backdrop for the lantern rather than the more typical view of the lantern with the main hall in the background. The current lantern between the gate and the main hall is a replica made in Meiji period and the original  lantern, a Tangible Cultural Property of Osaka prefecture, is carefully preserved in the temple’s backyard. title: Okadera - temple 7 (岡寺 七)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
Oka-dera, the seventh temple on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, is also known as Ryugai-ji, "temple of the sealed dragon," based on the legend of the monk Gien discovering a fierce dragon who was terrorizing the land and subduing the beast with only his prayer beads and spiritual powers, Gien sealed the dragon in a small pond, with a large stone acting as a lid, in what is now the grounds of Oka-dera. The view of the pond and stone is what Nakazawa has chosen to share with us.<br> Along with his two traveling companions, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, Nakazawa undertook this 78 day 600 mile pilgrimage in December 1923, only three months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area.<br>

creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)

Nan'endō, located at the southwest edge of Nara Park, is the ninth temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. Nakazawa shows us couples strolling along Sarusawa Pond while the famous Nara Park deer tend to their business. In the background we see the octagonal Nan'endō Hall on the right and the pagoda, left-center, is likely the three-story Sanjū-no-tō. A distant view of Mimuroto-ji, the tenth temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, located in the hills of Uji City outside Kyoto. The three-story pagoda seen in the hills was built in 1704 and was moved to Mimuroto-ji in around 1910 from its former location the temple Kozo-ji in Harima (present day Hyogo prefecture).<br>Along with his two traveling companions, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, Nakazawa undertook this 78 day 600 mile pilgrimage in December 1923, only three months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area.<br>

creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)

Kami Daigō-ji, a complex of some of the oldest temple buildings in Japan, is the upper precinct of Daigō-ji and is the 11th temple on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. Nakazawa presents us with a view of a shrine building with a sign on its post reading 西國第十一番靈場納経所 (Saigoku sanjūsan reijo nōkyō-sho), telling us we're visiting the eleventh sacred place on the Saigoku pilgrimage and a donation of money or a sutra can be left there. title: Shinkiyomizudera - temple 25 (新清水寺 二十五)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
One of the many wonderful things about the designs created for this album by Nakazawa as he visited each temple with his friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, is his choice of scenes to represent each temple. In this print, titled Shin Kiyomizu-dera 新清水寺, the "shin" or "new" prefix differentiating from it's better known namesake in Kyoto, Nakazawa is focused on the path and small town beneath the temple. In the hills above the town Nakazawa shows us the top of the temple's pagoda. It is a charming portrayal of the mountainous area southwest Hyōgo Prefecture, often referred to as  Harima 播磨 or Banshū 播州, during the Taishō period.<br>Along with his two traveling companions, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, Nakazawa undertook this 78 day 600 mile pilgrimage in December 1923, only three months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area.<br>

creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)

Nakazawa chooses to show us a single pilgrim holding prayer beads with his traveling pack and staff lying next to him. title: Tanigumisan Kegonji - temple 33 (谷汲山華厳寺 三十三)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
Nakazawa presents us with a view of a small building on the temple grounds of Tanigumi-san Kegon-ji, the thirty-third and last temple along the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, which displays a circular sign, blue with a yellow frame, proclaiming "votive offering" 奉納. Pilgrim's have attached prayer slips and prayer boards to its walls. Perhaps this small building is related to the temple's Kannon, as described by Ian Reader, "Behind its main hall there is an enclosure housing a statue of the healing Buddha Yakushi. The statue is frequently swathed in clouds of incense lit by the many people who pray for his assistance in overcoming pains and sickness. To the side of the statue is a small kiosk where one can purchase strips of paper with Buddhist spells written on them: the purchaser then places the paper on Yakushi’s body and, while reciting a prayer, pours over it water from a ladle, thus symbolically washing the pain from the afflicted area."<br>Along with his two traveling companions, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, Nakazawa undertook this 78 day 600 mile pilgrimage in December 1923, only three months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area.<br>

title: On Lake Biwa - print 35 (琵琶湖上 三五)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description:
Nakazawa presents us with his view while sitting in the bow of a small sculled boat while being ferried across Lake Biwa on a stormy day. His traveling companion Akatsuka Chūichi sits huddled under a blanket as the oarsman leans into his sculling oar. Chikubu-shima, the location of Hōgon-ji, temple 30 on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, where they must have departed from, sits about 6km (3 3/4 miles) from shore, so a long wet ride is in front of them.<br>Along with his two traveling companions, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, Nakazawa undertook this 78 day 600 mile pilgrimage in December 1923, only three months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area.<br>

title: Mr. Nakazawa Hiromitsu Returns to the Inn in Kyoto from His Pilgrimage (巡禮より京の宿に帰れる中澤弘光氏)

description: The artist Nakazawa Hiromitsu relaxing on the veranda of his inn in Kyoto after completing the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage.<br>This print was designed by the Western-style  (yōga) artist, and close friend of Nakazawa's, Akatsuka Chūichi 赤塚忠一 (1887-?) who accompanied him, along with the poet Ishikura Suiyō, on the seventy-eight day pilgrimage during which they visited all thirty-three temples plus one bangai temple. title: Appendix 1, temples 1, 2 and 3 (附録 一)
creator: Unknown - the sketches of the honzon are not credited. Principle artist for portfolio is Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964). Haikai appearing on print by Ishikura Suiyō 石倉翠葉 (1875-1938).
description:
The first of eleven appendices in the Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces, each providing information on three of the thirty-three temples that make up the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage. Each appendix sheet provides a sketch of each temple's honzon 本尊 (enshrined principle image), its goeika 御詠歌 (a song/prayer recited by some pilgrims) and a haikai (comic linked verse) composed by the haiku poet Ishikura Suiyō 石倉翠葉 (1875-1938) who, along with the artist Akatsuka Chūichi 赤塚忠一 (1887-?), accompanied Nakazawa on his seventy-eight day pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples and surrounding sights beginning on December 11, 1923. The creator of the honzon sketches is unknown.<br>
The three temples on this sheet (including their locales, using the old province names, and sangō 山号) are: Kii no kuni Nachi-san Seiganto-ji 纪伊國 那智山 青岸渡寺 (temple 1, 一), Kii no kuni Kimii-san Kimii-dera 纪伊國 紀三井山 金剛宝寺 (temple 2, 二) [note: the appendix contains a misprint as it lists the temple's sangō as Fudaraku-san 普陀洛山 instead of Kimii-san 紀三井山. Kimii-san is correctly listed in the album's table of contents], Kii no kuni Fudaraku-san Kokawa-dera 纪伊國 補陀洛山 粉河寺 (temple 3, 三).

title: Sanjo Sanetomi (三條實美)
creator: Arai Shōri 新井勝利 (1895-1972)
description:
Sanjō, a central figure in the Sonnōjōi Movement ("revere the Emperor and expel the barbarians"), is shown fleeing to Chōshū along with six other noblemen (known as the "Seven nobles of decline," shichikyō-ochi) in 1863 in the aftermath of a coup d’etat at the imperial court which expelled members of the Sonnōjōi Movement and forced the emperor to stop his efforts to reassert authority over the shōgunate. Sanjō took shelter in the more sympathetic Chōshū domain in western Honshū.
<br><br> The eleven extant prints comprising the seemingly incomplete series Thirty Great Loyalists of Early Modern Times depict figures active in the mid/late Edo era and early Meiji era who displayed great loyalty to the Emperor and, thereby, the nation. Issued in 1942 when the war in the Pacific was raging, the patriotic theme of these prints was clear. Nine of the eleven extant prints portray a famous incident or anecdote in a Great Loyalist's life and two prints deal specifically with the 1860 assassination of the shōgunate's Chief Minister Ii Naosuke (1815-1860). Each print was issued in a folder which also contained a written commentary.

title: Minami-za kaomise (南座顔見せ)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichiro 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
Picturing the oldest kabuki theater in Japan, the Minami-za, founded in the early 1600s. The theater was rebuilt as a gabled building in the Momoyama style in 1929 and renovated in 1991. Tokuriki depicts the theater on a snowy December eve, ready for the kaomise season with its signboards bearing the names of the stars. This print is not dated, but the scene feels like one out of the 1930s.
<br>‘KAOMISE’ (‘face-showing’) originally referred to the month in which a theatre showed the actors who were newly contracted for the following year to the audience. The annual kaomise performances in Kyoto, the birthplace of kabuki, have continued their long tradition since the Edo period (1603-1868). Today it is an all-star performance and a big event for December in Kyoto. Decorating the theatre façade every December are signboards bearing the actors’ names, a sight that has come to be associated with the winter season in Kyoto. You can enjoy four fascinating masterpieces of Kabuki in both the matinee and evening shows. - Source: website of the Shochiku Company https://www.shochiku.co.jp/engeki/minamiza/kaomise/en/ [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Woman Carrying Kelp (昆布を運ぶ女 Konbu ohakobu onna)
creator: Kitaoka Fumio 北岡文雄 (1918-2007)
description: Kitaoka's respect for his subject is evident as this woman bears her heavy load of kombu. This scene is certainly set in Hokkaidō which produces almost all of Japan's crop. Dated 1967, this print was originally printed in 1959 and is a fine example of Kitaoka's wood engraving (end-grain engraving) and monochrome work which he largely abandoned in the 1960s in favor of more colorful prints using the more traditional woodblock technique of cutting along the wood grain. The paper, as in his earlier monochrome work, is mica impregnated and the black pigment he uses has a bright sheen.

title: A Brief Description of World Geography (Government Publication), Middle East, vol. 3 ([官版] 輿地誌略 巻三 亜細亜州 Yochi shiryaku, kanpan, kan 3, Ajia-shū)
creator: Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1827-1881) - copper plate prints attributed to the artist. Artist's name does not appear in this volume.
description:
Volume 3 of an eventual 13 volumes of the geography textbook Yochi shiryaku (1870-1880). Volume 3 covers the Middle East.

<br><br>Yochi shiryaku was the most widely used world geography textbook in the early Meiji era, compiled by former Edo Government officer, Uchida Masao. Uchida was sent to Europe from 1862 to 1866 by the Tokugawa government, to gather information to compile these lavishly illustrated textbooks. He returned to Japan with oil paintings, photographic albums, and hundreds of pictorial natural history images. Based upon the sources he collected on his travels, Uchida began to compile the Yochi Shiryaku in 1870, a thirteen-volume of encyclopedia of world geography. Its success was primarily due to the huge number of illustrations that Uchida called "shashin (photography)," the images copied from the Western photographic albums and traveling magazines by the artist Kawakami Tōgai 川上冬崖 (1827/1828-1881/1882) who turned them into copperplate illustrations. Yochi shiryaku was published in various editions over ten years and used in schools all over Japan, as well as being widely read as the book of "enlightenment." After Uchida's death, volumes 10 through 13 were compiled by the educator Nishimura Shigeki 西村 茂樹 (1828-1902), a colleague at the Ministry of Education, based on Uchida’s draft. 
<br> A premise of Yochi shiryaku was the existence of "a finely ordered hierarchy of peoples and states," with racial differences [the physical features and geographical dissemination of the "five human races" being described] being an "important factor underlying this hierarchical arrangement." - Source: "The Race and Racism Discourses in Modern Korea, 1890s—1910s," Vladimir Tikhonov, appearing in "Korean Studies, 2012, Vol. 36," University of Hawai'i Press, 2012, p. 41.

title: Tsūten-kyō Autumn Leaves (通天橋の紅葉)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description: One of 24 prints from a series of ōgi fan-shaped images of scenic places in the Kyoto area during the four seasons, with each season being represented by six prints. Each image is printed on a decorative background with floral motifs printed in silver mica. This print is part of the Kyoto in Autumn set and pictures Tsuten Bridge and Kaisandō in a driving rain. Kaisandō serves as the mausoleum of Tofukuji's first head priest.

title: Kōdaiji Temple, Hagi (高台寺の萩)
creator: Tokuriki Tomikichirō 徳力富吉郎 (1902-2000)
description:
One of 24 prints from a series of ōgi fan-shaped images of scenic places in the Kyoto area during the four seasons, with each season being represented by six prints. Each image is printed on a decorative background with floral motifs printed in silver mica. This print is part of the Kyoto in Autumn set and pictures Kōdaiji Temple in a driving rain.<br>Kōdaiji Temple, formally called Kōdaijusho-zenji, is located in the Higashiyama District on the lower slopes of Kyoto's eastern mountains. "The temple was established in 1606 by Kita-no-Mandokoro (1548-1624) in memory of her late husband Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1536-1598). Kita-no-Mandokoro was also known as Nene. She later became a priestess and assumed the name of Kodaiin Kogetsuni. In July 1624, Sanko Osho from Kenninji Temple was welcomed as the principal monk and the temple was then named Kodai-ji. Tokugawa Ieyasu (1542-1616) (the first Tokugawa shogun) financed the construction of the temple, resulting in its magnificent appearance.<br>
"Currently Kaisandō (Founder's Hall), Otama-ya (Sanctuary), Kasatei (Teahouse), Shiguretei (Teahouse), Omotetmon (Gate to Sanctuary) and Kangetsudai (Moon Viewing Pavilion) are designated as important cultural properties of Japan." - Source: Website of Kodai-ji Zen Temple https://www.kodaiji.com/e_index.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: Illustration of the Yamashiro Tea Company (山城制茶會社之圖)
creator: Unknown
description:
A rather large print promoting the Yamashiro Tea Company formed by Itō Kumao 伊東熊夫 (1849-1913), a driving force in modernizing Japan's tea industry, in 1885, during a boom in the export tea trade. This print depicts their tea plantation and curing and packing facilities in Uji, Kyoto Province, situated on the banks of the Lake Biwa Canal, completed in 1890, along with a stone monument erected in Manpukuji Temple in Uji in 1887 called “Koma-no-ashikage-en-ato-hi” (monument for horse hoof print tea gardens) dedicated to tea culture.<br>
The tea industry was subject to greatly fluctuating prices and it is likely the Yamashiro Tea Company failed by the mid-1890s, but its founder Itō Kumao would become the Vice President of the Japan Tea Association and continue his work to increase Japan's exports of tea to the West.

title: Black Cat (黒猫 Kuroneko)
creator: Takehisa Yumeji 竹久夢二 (1884-1934)
description:
This collection's print is a small size modern woodblock reproduction, by an unknown publisher, of an original 1921 watercolor painted by the artist as part of a group of ten watercolors commissioned by the Nagasaki collector, playwright and art historian Nagami Tokutarō.[1] 
<br>The first woodblock reproductions of the ten watercolors were created by Katō Junji in 1937-1938 in his Katō Print Institute ( 加藤版画研究所 Katō Hanga Kenkyūjō). Subsequently mutliple woodblock reproductions of these watercolors have been made in different sizes by various publishers. For another woodblock reproduction of a print from the original set of watercolors see IHL.1333.
<br><br>
[1] Takehisa Yumeji, Nozomi Naoi, et. al., Hotei Publishing, 2015 , p. 52 and Yumeji Modern: Designing the Everyday in Twentieth-Centry Japan, Nozomi Naoi, University of Washington Press, 2020, p. 175.

title: Illustration of Chinese Cabbage from Ukiyo-e World (白菜図  浮世絵界 第一巻 第五号 Ukiyo-e kai, dai ichi-kan, dai go-gō)
creator: Paul Jacoulet ポールジャクレー (1896-1960)
description: A frontispiece, a still-life of a Chinese cabbage, removed from the July 1936 issue of Ukiyo-e kai, a magazine published for the ukiyo-e aficionado. The French-born artist Paul Jacoulet (1896-1960), primarily known for his portraits, executed in woodblock, of South Sea Islanders and East Asian peoples, done in a hybrid of eastern and western styles, contributed this still-life to the magazine. It appears to be his one contribution, an unusual one at that, to the magazine over its sixty-seven issues published from March 1936 through June 1941. (See IHL.1805 for more information on this magazine.)

title: Illustration of the Fierce Important Battle of Seonghwan (成歡大激戰之圖)
creator: Yukawa Hiromitsu 湯川広光 (active c. 1894)
description:
A depiction of the first major land battle of the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) fought at the end of July 1894 at Seonghwan and Asan, Korea. The Japanese were victorious in both battles, suffering 34 killed and 54 wounded soldiers, while the Chinese army suffered 500 killed and wounded. Following this battle on August 1, 1894 Japan and China would issue formal declarations of war.<br>
This set of prints is unusal in its being  published in Ōsaka rather than in Tokyo where almost all Sino-Japanese War prints were published. Its publisher Ōbuchi Wataru of the publishing house Hatsubai Shinshindō was primarily a book publisher and this print was part of a twelve print gafu (picture book), a portfolio titled Sino-Japanese War Picture Book.

title: Illustration of Captain Matsuzaki’s Inspirational Battle (松崎大尉奮戰之圖)
creator: Yukawa Hiromitsu 湯川広光 (active c. 1894)
description:
Advancing under heavy fire, undaunted by personal danger, Captain Matsuzaki is portrayed charging ahead of his men. Leading his soldiers to the battle of Songhwan, Captain Matsuzaki was ambushed and shot through the leg.  Struck by another bullet in the head, he is reported to have shouted, “I’ve been hit!” and to have died bravely.<br>
This set of prints is unusal in its being  published in Ōsaka rather than in Tokyo where almost all Sino-Japanese War prints were published. creator: Unknown
description:
One of 38 photomechanical and woodblock illustrations in volume 2 of Kokushi daijiten (Encyclopedia of Japanese History). This print is the second of two providing a graphic overview of various garb worn by nobles and the samurai class during various periods of Japanese history. The illustrations, by an unknown artist, were based upon a display of clothed life-size dolls (ningyō) at the former Tokyo Imperial Museum (Tōkyō Kokuritsu Hakubutsukan), now the Tokyo National Museum.<br>
In this print, eight examples of clothing are shown, including ceremonial triumphal-style armor worn during the Kamakura period (1185-1333); formal kimono (naga-kamishimo) worn by daimyo during the Edo period (1600-1868); an Edo period bridal robe; a Kamakura period Buddhist warrior priest's garb, complete with cowl (katō 裹頭) to conceal his identity, and naginata 薙刀; a hunting outfit worn during the Muromachi (1333-1573) and Kamakura periods; and a woman and girl in Meiji period furisode.

title: Album Box cover with gold silk brocade - Scenes of China
creator: Unidentified
description: Portfolio covered with silk brocade housing the twelve prints in the series Scenes of China. (See IHL.2458.01 through IHL.2458.12.) The portfolio was published in 1936 by the Tokyo publisher Ōtsuka Minoru whose firm Ōtsuka Kōgeisha specialized in collotype reproduction. For these prints it appears that the collotype backgrounds have been overlaid with woodblock printing for the foreground to produce exquisite reproductions of designs by the Kyoto nihonga artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). This print portfolio produced towards the end of Seihō's career, reproduced his original ink on silk paintings created after his two trips to China in 1920 and 1921. Seihō's visits to China were seminal in evolving his style, as was his visit to Europe ten years earlier.

title: Reproduction of: New Year's Sunrise with Snow at Susaki (複製：洲崎雪之初日 Fukusei：Susaki yuki no hatsuhi)
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige 歌川広重 (1797-1858)
description:
This collection's print is a modern reproduction by Adachi Woodcut Prints (Adachi hanga), specializing in ukiyo-e reproductions, whose imprint appears on this print's verso. 
<br>In the early 1830's, Hiroshige, "started to discover himself as an artist, starting on the landscapes which became his forte, and changing his signature to Ichiyusai (sometimes Ichiryusai). His first landscape series was in 1829 or 1830, titled "Eight Famous Views of Omi", followed by a ten-print series "Famous Places of the Eastern Capital", which in addition to showing the influence of Hokusai, also marked the first revelations of Hiroshige's true genius." - Source: MIT website of J. Noel Chiappa http://mercury.lcs.mit.edu/~jnc/prints/hiroshige.html [accessed 8-17-23]

title: South China Scenery (南支風光 Nanshi fūkō)
creator: Takeuchi Seihō 竹内栖鳳 (1864-1942)
description:
One of six prints in the ninth and last envelope containing the prints comprising set two of Seihō's Masterpieces.
<br><br>SEIHŌ'S MASTERPIECES (1937-1942)
<br>Seihō's Masterpieces consists of sixty-six limited edition prints issued by Unsōdō Publishing over five years, beginning in April 1937 and ending in June 1942, produced from drawings made by the Kyoto artist Takeuchi Seihō (1864-1942). Using multiple printing techniques such as color woodblock and collotype, Unsōdō spared no effort in faithfully rendering into large-format prints Seihō’s watercolor and ink drawings. Jack Hillier in "The Art of the Japanese Book", 1987, called these works "one of the most magnificent printing achievements of the twentieth century." <br>Seiho's Masterpieces includes scenes from the artist's travels to South China in 1921-1922, renderings of animals (domestic and wild), still-lifes of fish and flora, depictions of cultural events such as festival floats and kabuki, and landscapes of the Japanese countryside, including two prints depicting Mt. Fuji.<br>While there are no historical records explaining how this project came about, it is reasonable to assume, given the artist’s declining health when the series was started in 1937 and his receipt of the Order of Culture in early 1937, that it was truly intended by his long-time publisher Unsōdō, in the words of Roger S. Keyes, as an “elegy and a testament” to one of the greatest painters and teachers of his time.

title: On Lake Biwa - print 35 (琵琶湖上 三五)
creator: Nakazawa Hiromitsu 中沢弘光 (1874-1964)
description: Nakazawa presents us with his view while sitting in the bow of a small sculled boat while being ferried across Lake Biwa on a stormy day. His traveling companion Akatsuka Chūichi sits huddled under a blanket as the oarsman leans into his sculling oar. Chikubu-shima, the location of Hōgon-ji, temple 30 on the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, where they must have departed from, sits about 6km (3 3/4 miles) from shore, so a long wet ride is in front of them.<br>In December 1923, only a few months after the Great Kantō Earthquake devastated the Tokyo area, Nakazawa along with his two friends, the poet Ishikura Suiyō and the artist Akatsuka Chūichi, began their pilgrimage to the thirty-three temples comprising the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage, taking seventy-eight days to complete the route.<br>This print is from the 1946 2nd edition of the album titled Saigoku sanjūsansho junrei gakan (Picture Album of the Thirty-Three Pilgrimage Places of the Western Provinces) published by Kanao Tanejirō featuring 37 woodblock prints made from Nakazawa's sketches, supplemented with poetry and information about the temples. See IHL.2413.43 for the first edition print issued in 1925.

title: Mirror of Portraits of All Sovereigns in the World (世上各国写画帝王鏡 Sejō kakkoku shaga teiō kagami)
creator: Yōshū Chikanobu 楊洲周延 (1838-1912)
description:
Seventeen world sovereigns (emperors, empresses, kings, queens and an American president) are portrayed along with Emperor Meiji and Empress Haruko (top of center panel), in this 1879 print, a time filled with visits from foreign sovereigns, as summarized in the below passage from Donald Keene's Emperor of Japan: Meiji and His World.

<br>"By this time [end of 1879] the [Emperor Meiji] was recognized as a 'cousin' by the royal houses of Europe, and he accordingly received regular and prolonged visits from foreign royalty.
<br>"Apart from visits by foreign royalty, the emperor was regularly informed of events in the lives of other monarchs. He responded correctly to his 'cousins,' sending messages of congratulations to Alfonso XII of Spain on his remarriage and to the czar of Russia on his narrow escape from assassins."[1]

<br>As with so many prints during the Meiji period that portrayed topical events, the important thing was not so much getting the facts right as conveying the nation's rise to power and, with this increasing power, the growing respect paid to its Imperial house. If we look closely at the artist's portrayals of royalty and rulers and the colored rectangular cartouches that list the personages being depicted, we notice a number of anomalies, the most interesting of which are the naming of the King of Portugal, King Dom Luis I at the time, as "King Frois" (フロイス国王), Frois being the name of the 16th-century Portuguese missionary Luis Frois, who arrived in Japan in 1563; depictions of the king and queen of "Madagarasu" (マダガラス), a country that has no known equivalent, but sounds strikingly like Madagascar; and the depictions of the king and queen of Switzerland (スイシル) which had become a republic in 1848 and had no recognized king and queen.

<br>As with other prints portraying contemporary or recent public figures, it is likely that the artist modeled some of his depictions after existing portraits. 

<br><br>[1]Emperor of Japan: Meiji and His World, 1852-1912, Donald Keene, Columbia University Press, 2002, p. 321.

description: One of an intended one hundred designs, of which twenty appear to have been completed, for an advertising campaign to help revive flagging demand for the traditional Takasago dyeing process. The designer of the prints, Itō Shinsui 伊東深水 (1898-1972), was the best-known bijin-ga designer of the time, working to create designs to be reproduced through traditional woodblock technique or through new technologies employing photo-offset technology, such as in the prints in this series. It appears that all the designs for the series were newly drawn by Shinsui. It is unknown who financed these prints (possibly a trade association) and while the name of the publisher, Kisendō 喜扇堂, located at the time in Suitengu-mae, Tokyo, appears on all the prints no information is readily available on this publisher.

title:
Garden of Flowering Plants a supplement to the newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun
(千草の庭, 讀賣新聞 附録  Yomiuri Shimbun furoku, Chigusa no niwa)
creator: Itō Shinsui 伊東深水 (1898-1972)
description:
Itō Shinsui, a painter and print designer, was one of the most prominent and best known designers of bijin-ga (pictures of beautiful women). <br>Yomiuri Shimbun was one of five new dailies created early in the Meiji period (1868–1912) to meet the need for a easy-to-read newspaper in the rapidly modernizing society of Japan. It is credited with being the first newspaper to introduce supplements (appendices), beginning in 1914, largely targeted at women, as a way to increase circulation.
<br>Supplements, not being subject to the news cycle would be printed in advance and with the advent of the changeover to rotary offset presses capable of faithful reproduction of artistic work during the early Taishō era, newspapers such as the Jiji shinpō 時事新報 and Yomiuri Shimbun 讀賣新聞 extended their supplemental offerings to the ever-popular bijin-ga genre as represented by this color lithograph.<br>This supplement is numbered 第二〇六七四號附録 (Supplement No. 20674) on the bottom margin.

title: Ukigumo (Floating Cloud), a supplement to the newspaper Jiji shinpō (Current Events) (時事新報 付録・浮雲)
creator: Kitazawa Rakuten 北澤楽天 (1876-1955)
description:
The designer of this chromolithograph print, Kitazawa Rakuten, was trained as a nihonga artist, but he was best known as a manga illustrator and one of the most important figures in modern Japanese manga. He joined the newspaper Jiji shinpō (Current Events) in 1899, drew the cartoons for Jiji manga 時事漫画, a supplement to Jiji shinpō from 1902, and founded the satirical magazine Tokyo Puck in 1905. This print, likely specifically designed for the newspaper Jiji shinpō, is a rare foray of the artist into the bijin-ga genre.
<br>Newspapers such as Jiji shinpō, founded 1882 by Fukuzawa Yukichi 福澤諭吉 (1835-1901), an author, educator and publisher, used supplements (appendices) as a way to increase circulation in the ongoing battle between newspapers for readership.
<br>Supplements could be printed in advance, scheduled for production outside of the regular news cycle. With the advent of the changeover to rotary offset presses capable of faithful reproduction of artistic work during the early Taishō era, newspapers such as the Jiji shinpō 時事新報 and Yomiuri Shimbun 讀賣新聞 extended their supplemental offerings to the ever-popular bijinga genre as represented by this color lithograph.

<br>The title of the print "blue eyebrows" is in reference to an eyebrow pencil used to draw a curved eyebrow in the crescent shape of a moth's antennae. The phrase found use in Japanese literature as early as the 11th century as a mark of female beauty.

title: Taira no Shigemori and Minamoto no Yoshihira fighting outside Shishinden Palace (重盛義平紫震殿外戦之図)
creator: Watanabe Nobukazu 渡辺延一 (1872-1944)
description: This triptych depicts the battle between the Minamoto and the Taira at the Taiken Gate outside the Shishinden Palace during the Hōgen Rebellion, a dispute over imperial succession, in Kyoto in 1156.  The triptych depicts Minamoto no Yoshihira on horseback, the half-brother of Minamoto no Yoritomo and Minamoto no Yoshitsune, attacking Taira no Shigemori, the eldest son of Taira no Kiyomori. During the battle, Minamoto no Yoshihira faced off against Taira no Shigemori's forces, who were leading a contingent of 500 cavalry to defeat Minamoto no Yoshiie and Fujiwara no Nobuyori. Despite being outnumbered, Minamoto no Yoshihira and his 17 warriors fought fiercely but were defeated.

title: Circus

description: The publisher Hasegawa Sonokichi has listed himself as the artist (画工 gako) on this print, the bottom half of an ōban-size print depicting two scenes from a performance of a Western circus. The print likely served as an advertisement for the Italian impresario Giuseppe Chiarini's Royal Italian Circus which performed in Japan (including a performance for Emperor Meiji) in the summer of 1886.  (See IHL.1246 for a related print.)  His troupe included acrobatic young women on horses and wild animals as depicted on this print.  Chiariini's circus was not the first to perform in Japan with Richard Risley ("Professor Risley") bringing his circus company in March 1864 and the Frenchman Louis Soullier bringing his circus to Japan in 1871.

Before the cement was set, Maki would texture it and after it dried he carved and chiseled the cement into the desired shape. creator: Sekino Jun’ichirō 関野準一郎 (1914-1988)
description:
A monochrome printing, likely the original printing, picturing the Great Wall of China in Badaling, in the Yanqing District about 50 miles northwest of Beijing's city center, the most visited area of the Great Wall. Sekino also created a multi-color version in 1977, likely using the same blocks, perhaps with some rework. Other than a 1979 visit to China, I have not been able to determine the years of any earlier trips he may have taken to this area, that would perhaps give insight into the date of this collection's print.<br> 

This collection's print has a label on the verso providing the print's title 長城八達嶺, artist's name 関野準一郎 and the name of the Nihon bijutsuka renmei 日本美術家連盟 (Japanese Artists Association) which Sekino was both an officer, in its early years, and member of. title: Dontarō 鈍太郎
creator: Tsukioka Gyokusei 月岡玉瀞 (1908-1994)
description:
One of thirty-four prints designed by Tsukioka Gyokusei (1908-1994) in the series Kyōgen Gojūban (Fifty Kyōgen Plays) started by her father Tsukioka Kōgyo (1869-1927). She created 34 prints and the table of contents for this series, using the artist’s name Kōbun 江文. Tsukioka Kōgyo designed sixteen prints for the series before his death.<br><br>
Play synopsis ("Japanese Noh and Kyogen plays: staging dichotomy," Zvika Serpera , appearing in Comparative Drama, Western Michigan University, Sept. 22, 2005.) - In the kyōgen Dontaro two women display disruptively comic selfish devotion to the same man, though the play ends in harmony. After three years in the capital, Dontaro returns home, but his ugly wife does not believe that it is really him and sends him away. His beautiful mistress reacts similarly, and he decides to become a monk. After both women, who had not previously accepted each other, understand what has happened, they search for him together, find him dressed as a monk, try to convince him to remain with them, and agree to anything he says. Dontaro uses this situation to force the two women in a comical way to accept each other; he then makes them bear him home in their joined arms as if carrying a baby, while they sing, announcing that this is the "personal jinrikisha" (teguruma) of Sir Dontaro. The play ends with a sense of agreement and intimacy among the three characters.

Following the senryū are the characters 雉子郎 or Kojirō, the pen name used by the novelist Yoshikawa Eiji 吉川 英治 (1892-1962) for the comic poetry he wrote, including the senryū appearing on this print. <br>All the titles assigned to prints in this series are more-or-less descriptive of the images, enhanced, on occasion, by isolated words translated from the senryū on the print. They are in no way translations of the senryū, which are extremely difficult to translate..

title: The Thief and the Cock (泥棒たちと雄鶏 Dorobū tachi to ondori)
creator: Hagiwara Hideo 萩原英雄 (1913-2007)
description:
Print number thirty in the series illustrating fifty of Aesop's Fables. The fables, written and compiled by the Athenian slave Aesop in the fifth century BCE, have been described as tales simple enough for children and profound enough for adults.<br>
This print illustrates the fable in which a cock stolen by thieves pleads for its life by saying how useful he is to man by waking him each morning.  Unfortunately for the cock, this gave the thieves an even better reason to kill it, teaching us that the safeguards of virtue are hateful to those with evil intentions.<br>Hagiwara, who had been familiar with Aesop's stories since he was a child, published the "Aesop Fables in Pictures" イソップ絵噺 series in 1976. The series, which took 20 years from conception to completion, was created using his intaglio techniques in woodblock carving, which allow for the expression of softer, freer lines that could not be achieved with conventional woodblock carving with chisels.

title: Pansies in a Vase (fan design sample)
creator: Unidentified
description:
Fan design samples such as this print were created as marketing tools for deluxe fan makers. While the fan design samples in this collection were likely created in the Taishō and early Shōwa eras (c. 1912-1940), fan design samples date back to the Meiji era. They showed the season's available designs, commissioned from some of the most eminent artists of the day. The designs range from Art Deco to traditional genre scenes. Once the season was over, the sample fans and books of fans were sold. Most of the samples in this collection do not carry a signature or seal and the artists will be forever unknown, but some famous names do appear on several of the prints, such as Fukuda Heihachirō 福田平八郎 (1892-1974), a nihonga painter who was awarded the Order of Culture, and Yokoyama Taikan 横山大観 (1868-1958), another famous nihonga artist and Order of Culture winner.<br><br>
The shape of these prints indicate they were designs for folding fans (sensu 扇子, or ōgi 扇 as they are also known.)  While often described as "woodblock prints", I believe most of these sample designs are hand painted or inked rather than printed, as on at least one sample a brush hair is embedded in the ink/paint and on several others the ink or paint has overlapped the paper edge and bled onto the back of the paper.<br><br>Some of the prints carry inventory numbers; some bear a cartouche with the word nambu (literally, "southern region" and possibly the name of a company) written in kanji 南部 or kana なんぶ, and some bear a fan-shaped cartouche with the kanji character 業 ("karma" or simply the character for "industry" or "business") inside it, possibly the trademark of another fan company.

description: Sekino's Goyu is devoid of people in his evening scene of the thirty-sixth station along the Tōkaidō (the "Eastern Sea Route") running from Tokyo to Kyoto. The print is the 35th, in chronological order, of 55 prints Sekino created for his modern version of the series Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō.<br>"In 1959 Sekino started a series of prints of the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Road.) He returned each year, sketching for a few more stations, until the entire series was complete in 1974. . . . In 1975, after the completion of the modern Tōkaidō series, the Ministry of Education Award was granted to Sekinō because of his outstanding achievement 'in using every possible technique in woodblock printing, Japanese traditional art, and the recreation of the old fifty-three stations on the Tōkaidō highway in a present-day light.'" - Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints - The Early Years, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1998, p.241-242 and Guide to Modern Japanese Woodblock Prints: 1900-1975, Helen Merritt, University of Hawaii Press, 1992, p. 259-260.

<br>This print was originally created for the dōjin (coterie magazine) Han geijutsu (Print Art), Volume 5 published in August 1932 in Tokyo by Shiro to Kurosha, the company of the artist Ryōji Chōmei (Kumata) (1899-1982). The theme for Volume 5 was mountains and sea (山と海).

title: Kiyomigaseki (清見が関)
creator: Kawakita Kahō 川北霞峰 (1875-1940)
description:
The seventh print appearing in Volume 2 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>The artist presents us with a view of the mountains and sea as witnessed by Yoshida Chūzaemon Kanesuke, the chief advisor to Ōishi Kuranosuke, as he passed Kiyomigaseki on his way to Edo. Ōishi has dispatched him to Edo to tell Horibe Yasubei and his radical faction that it is too early to take action against Kira because they have not made adequate preparation. Ōishi's message is, "If you know your enemy and know yourself, you will not be in danger in a hundred battles, but today, we do not yet know our enemy."<br>Approaching the pass above Kiyomigaseki on the night of the full moon, Chūzaemon was moved by the spectacular view to compose this poem: 天の原霞も靕れて清見潟, 月をゞめよ波の関守 (The heavens have parted, and the moon is seen in the clear sky.)

<br><br>GISHI TAIKAN 義士大観
<br>First published in a limited edition of 200 copies in March 1920 (Taishō 9) by Gishikai Shuppanbu 義士會出版部, the publishing house of the Chūō Gishikai 中央義士会 (Central Office of the Righteous Samurai Society), Gishi taikan 義士大観 [義士大觀] is the story, “according to historical facts,” of the 1701 to 1703 Akō Incident 赤穂事件, popularly known as Chūshingura 忠臣蔵 (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) and Shijūshichishi 四十七士 (The Forty-Seven Rōnin), told through eighty woodblock prints and accompanying text. The historical persons and incidents portrayed in the prints include both those involved in the Akō Incident itself and related events, both real and fictional.

title: Chiyoda Castle (千代田城)
creator: Kawai Gyokudō 川合玉堂 (1873-1957)
description:
The first print appearing in Volume 1 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>As written in the commentary accompanying the print, "The Chiyoda Castle shown in the illustration is the Edo Castle, which was originally the stronghold of the Edo Shogunate and the residence of the Tokugawa clan." The commentary goes on to provide, in its own words, "a very frank and accurate description of the castle in Chiyoda during the Genroku era [Oct 23, 1688 – Apr 15, 1704], a period of Japan’s power and prosperity." Today the Castle ruins are part of Tokyo Imperial Palace.<br>On April 21, 1701 the Castle's Great Pine Corridor (Matsunoroka Corridor) was the scene of the attack on the elderly Kira Yoshinaka, the shogun's master of ceremonies, by Asano Naganori, young lord of the Akō domain, during shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi's hosting of the annual ceremonies featuring "Tsunayoshi's welcoming emissaries bearing New Year's greetings from the emperor, Higashiyama, and retired emperor, Reigen, who resided in the imperial capital, Heian (modern Kyoto)." - source: The Forty-Seven Rōnin: The Vendetta in History, John A. Tucker, Cambridge University Press, 2018, p. 1.

title: The Imperial Envoy Leaves the Capital (天使の下向)
creator: Yamanaka Kodō 山中古洞 (1869-1945)
description:
The second print appearing in Volume 1 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br> As written in the commentary accompanying the print, "In February of the 14th year [1701] of the Genroku Era [1688-1704], the imperial envoys of Emperor Higashiyama, Lords Takano Yanagihara and Takano Yasuharu, and the imperial envoy of the [retired] Emperor Reigen, Lord Seikanji Hirosada, left Kyoto for Edo."<br>"It was a customary practice that each year the shogun would send an envoy to carry his New Year's greeting to the Kyoto court, and that imperial representatives would respond in turn by traveling to Edo. This year, the emissaries for Emperor Higashiyama (r. 1687-1709) and Retired Emperor Reigen (r. 1683-1687) arrived in Edo on the eleventh of the third month, presented their formal good wishes for the new year to the shogun in a ceremony on the twelfth, and were entertained with a noh performance on the thirteenth. In a final ceremony on the fourteenth, the shogun was scheduled to offer his thanks for the imperial greeting, an event known as the 'ceremony of response to the emperor'. Gifts were to be offered to the imperial envoys in thanks for their efforts by the shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi , by his consort, and by his mother, Keishōin. Asano Naganori was appointed to serve as host for the emperor's envoy, and Date Muneharu the daimyo of the domain of Yoshida (Iyo province), performed the same function for the representative of the retired emperor."[1]
<br>For Asano Naganori to attack a shogunal official, Lord Kira, in the Chiyoda Castle during the ceremonies showed, in John A. Tucker's words, a "complete disregard for the extraordinary circumstances of time and place [making] his deed intolerable and subject to immediate judgement and punishment."[2]

The fifth print appearing in Volume 4 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>The stealthy figure holding a spear in this print is Yoshida Chūzaemon 吉田忠左衛門, chief advisor to Ōishi Kuranosuke 大石内蔵助, who, on this snowy evening of December 14, 1703, is reconnoitering Kira's mansion in Honjo, an eastern suburb of Edo, just before the attack on Kira begins. The "elderly people" in the print's title references the sixty-four year old Yoshida Chūzaemon and his fellow righteous samurai, sixty-one year old, Onodera Jūnai 小野寺十内, a key senior leader of the group, both of whom were assigned to the rear gate detachment during the attack on the Kira mansion resulting in Kira's assassination.<br>
As summarized by historian John A. Tucker, "En route to Kira's residence, the rōnin were instructed to proceed at an ordinary pace, in small groups of two or three, heading toward the front or rear gates of Kira's mansion. They had been strategically divvied up, with half making entry through the front gate, led by Ōishi, and the other half through the rear, led by Ōishi's son Chikara and a senior rōnin, Yoshida Chūzaemon. Ōishi further divided each group into interior attack forces and peripheral guard forces, thus coordinating duties as systematically as possible for military efficiency. Sketches of the compound were reportedly provided to expedite the search."[1]
<br>Fukumoto's commentary accompanying this print provide details of the fighting these two men engaged in at Kira's rear gate.

<br><br>GISHI TAIKAN 義士大観
<br>First published in a limited edition of 200 copies in March 1920 (Taishō 9) by Gishikai Shuppanbu 義士會出版部, the publishing house of the Chūō Gishikai 中央義士会 (Central Office of the Righteous Samurai Society), Gishi taikan 義士大観 [義士大觀] is the story, “according to historical facts,” of the 1701 to 1703 Akō Incident 赤穂事件, popularly known as Chūshingura 忠臣蔵 (The Treasury of Loyal Retainers) and Shijūshichishi 四十七士 (The Forty-Seven Rōnin), told through eighty woodblock prints and accompanying text. The historical persons and incidents portrayed in the prints include both those involved in the Akō Incident itself and related events, both real and fictional.

<br><br><font size="-1">[1]  The Forty-Seven Rōnin: The Vendetta in History, John A. Tucker, Cambridge University Press, 2018, p. 85.</font>

description:
The eighth print appearing in Volume 2 of "Gishi taikan," edited by ultranationalist, historian and journalist Fukumoto Nichinan 福本日南 (1857-1921).
<br>Sixty year old Onodera Junai Hidetomo 小野寺十内秀和 (1643-1703), a retainer of Asano Naganori well-versed in the martial arts and a literary man known for his poetry, is shown walking along the Tokaidō to Edo in October 1702 where he will join Ōishi Yoshio for the attack on Kira's mansion. Previously he had left his home near Mount Hiei to rush to Akō Castle when it was still thought that it might remain in the hands of the Asano family and later he will join Ōishi in Kyoto as his chief of staff. In his commentary on the print, Fukumoto relates, "As he was travelling eastwards, the skies of the capital were now distant and he felt the loneliness of the journey. The mountains of O'Hiei, his hometown, are distant and shrouded in clouds." In a letter to his wife, Onodera has written, "Even if my dead body is shown, I think my duty will be fulfilled because my dead body will demonstrate Samurai loyalty to the entire country and it will strengthen their resolve." After her husband's ordered seppuku she will commit jigai, ritual suicide, as is prescribed for the wives of samurai.

title: The Blacksmith (鍛冶)
creator: Wada Sanzō 和田三造 (1883-1967)
description:
A first edition by the publisher Nishinomiya Shoin picturing a blacksmith and his assistant at work forging tools. A translation of the artist's commentary originally accompanying this first edition print reads, "Today, the manufacturing industry has reached the height of prosperity and even small shops have a lathe, air hammer, and welding machines. Even small blacksmiths are mobilized to make iron materials, working with formerly unknown complex techniques. However, it is very nostalgic to see that old-fashioned Japanese blacksmiths still exist. The slow expelling of the bellows and the symphony of hammers large and small that can be heard from a great distance and echo within the center of the village with a tranquil familiarity. From agricultural tools such as sickles and hoes to cartwheels, these simple products thoroughly incorporate a local sentiment and have a visible solid and modest beauty."[1]
<br><br>OCCUPATIONS OF SHŌWA JAPAN IN PICTURES
<br>Wada’s major contribution as a woodblock print artist came through his 72 print 3-part series Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures. The three part series was started during the Pacific War (1937-1945) in September 1938, was then interrupted by war shortages in 1943, and was restarted again after the war in November 1954. This series was a labor of love for Wada and he brought together woodblock print printers and carvers in Nishinomiya near Kobe to work on this project. Occupations of Shōwa Japan in Pictures has been praised for showing “the complexity of Shōwa society…. capture[ing] the pulse of Japanese life during the tumultuous decades of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s”[2] and condemned as providing a “visual message of subtle or blatant propaganda in support of government-sponsored ideas.”[3]
